Porphyrius and Ovid even maintain that they refrained from all fish, as well as the Syrians. But they had not probably carried their superstition so far, in the days of Moses. --- Garlic. These things are much more delicious and wholesome in hot countries. The Greeks fed much on cucumbers and garlic. (Aristophanes) --- The Turks still delight in them, eating the former raw with sour milk, (which would be very dangerous in our climate), and onions, which are as good as our pears. (Spon. Bellon. 3:18, etc.) The wounded Machaon feasts upon onions, etc. (Homer, Iliad ix.) The Egyptians afterwards scrupled to eat leeks and onions. (Calmet) --- Porrum et cepe nefas violare....O sanctas gentes! quibus haec nascuntur in hortis---Numina. (Juvenal, Sat. xv.) But in the earlier ages Moses represents them as accustomed to such food. (Haydock)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Numbers 11:5 is purely historical and cultural in nature. It discusses the Israelites' nostalgia for Egyptian foods (fish, garlic, onions, leeks, cucumbers) and provides comparative context about Egyptian, Greek, and Turkish dietary practices and religious food restrictions. The commentary makes no reference to any Old Testament type prefiguring a New Testament antitype, nor does it establish any connection between these foods and spiritual realities or future fulfillments. The content is entirely focused on ancient Near Eastern customs, historical documentation, and literary references (Herodotus, Homer, Juvenal, etc.). No typological relationship is present.

original_text: Answered him. The force of this reply must be very obvious. If a father had been so irritated by his daughter, as to shew his indignation in the strongest manner, (see Job 30:10.; Mark 14:65,) she would surely keep out of sight for a time: and can she complain, if I, who have been more injured in the person of my minister, exclude her from society seven days, after having covered her with the leprosy as with spittle. (Calmet) --- The excommunication, in the Christian Church, bears some resemblance with this exclusion. Mary did not undergo all the legal purifications, (Leviticus xxxiv.) as the miraculous cure dispensed her from them. (Menochius) --- Origen (hom. 6:7,) and other Fathers, explain the mystery of this historical event. Moses, taking to wife the Ethiopian, represents Christ calling the Gentiles, which excites the murmurs of the synagogue. Mary shews the deformity of the latter religion at the present day, without head or sacrifice. The encomiums bestowed upon the Jewish legislator, belong in a still stricter sense to Jesus Christ, the mildest of men, fully acquainted with all the secrets of God, and the most faithful in all his house. (St. Jerome, ep. ad Fab. mansion xiv.)

extractions.type_description: Moses' marriage to the Ethiopian woman, which provoked murmuring from the Israelite community (specifically Mary and Aaron)
extractions.antitype_description: Jesus Christ's inclusion of Gentiles in God's covenant, which provoked opposition from the Jewish religious establishment (the synagogue)
extractions.reasoning: Origen and the Fathers interpret Moses' action as prefiguring Christ's inclusion of non-Jewish peoples. The parallel structure is: Moses' controversial inclusion of a foreigner → Christ's inclusion of Gentiles; Jewish murmuring → synagogue opposition.

extractions.type_description: Miriam's punishment with leprosy and exclusion from the community for seven days as discipline for speaking against Moses

extractions.reasoning: The Haydock commentary explicitly states: 'The excommunication, in the Christian Church, bears some resemblance with this exclusion.' This indicates a typological connection between OT exclusionary discipline and NT ecclesiastical practice.

extractions.type_name: Miriam displaying the deformity of Judaism

extractions.antitype_description: The true religion represented by Christ and the Christian community, which possesses the head (Christ) and the sacrifice (Christ's crucifixion)
extractions.reasoning: This is allegorical interpretation by the Fathers rather than strict typology. Miriam is said to 'shew the deformity of the latter religion' in contrast to Christianity, but this is more polemical allegory than classical OT/NT typology, as Miriam is not presented as an intentional prefigurement but as an interpretive symbol.

notes: The commentary blends genuine typological interpretation (Origen on Moses/Christ, the excommunication parallel) with allegorical and polemical readings. The second and third extractions are less clearly typological and more interpretive overlay. The first extraction has clearest typological structure with explicit OT type/NT antitype correspondence.

original_text: Huri: Septuagint, "Souri." None of the tribe of Levi, the third son of Jacob, are sent; but two represent the different branches of the tribe of Joseph, ver. 9, 12. The tribe of Ephraim comes out of its natural order, and has been overlooked by Calmet. (Haydock)
notes: This Haydock commentary is purely descriptive and historical in nature. It discusses the tribal representation among the Israelite spies sent to scout Canaan (Numbers 13:6), noting that: (1) no one from the tribe of Levi was selected, (2) two representatives came from the tribe of Joseph's branches, and (3) the tribe of Ephraim appears out of its natural tribal order. The commentary is focused on historical-textual analysis and tribal genealogy, not on typological prefigurement of New Testament realities. No OT type pointing forward to an NT antitype is presented or implied in this passage.

original_text: Josue. His former name Osee, or Hoseah, means "one saved, or salvation;" but the addition of the i, taken from the name of the Lord, intimates, "he shall save, or the Saviour of God." Some think that Moses had given him this name after the defeat of the Amalecites; but the Book of Exodus, where the name is found, might have been written after he received this commission. (Calmet) --- The Septuagint have, "Ause, the son of Nave, Jesus," as he was a striking figure of our blessed Saviour, and their names are written with the same letters, Yehoshuah. This Moses foresaw, and also that he whould be the happy instrument, in the hand of God, of saving the Israelites, by introducing them to the land of promise, and establishing them in peace therein. (Menochius) --- The changing of his name imported likewise, that he should be the chief leader. (Theodoret, q. 25.) (Worthington)

extractions.type_description: The military leader of Israel who, under Moses' commission, would lead the Israelites into the Promised Land, establish them in peace, and serve as God's instrument of salvation for His people
extractions.antitype_description: The Saviour who saves and redeems God's people, establishing them in the ultimate promised inheritance of salvation and eternal peace
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly identifies Joshua as 'a striking figure of our blessed Saviour' and notes that their names are written with the same Hebrew letters (Yehoshuah/Yeshua). The parallelism is direct: just as Joshua saved Israel by introducing them into the earthly Promised Land and establishing peace, Jesus saves believers by introducing them to spiritual salvation and eternal rest. The name change itself—adding the 'i' (yod, representing God's name)—signifies divine authority in salvation, which prefigures Christ's role as God's instrument of redemption.

notes: This is one of the clearest Christological types in Scripture. The connection is strengthened by: (1) the explicit name identification by the Septuagint translators; (2) the etymological connection (both names mean 'salvation' or 'saviour'); (3) the functional parallel (both lead God's people to their promised rest); and (4) the theological interpretation by patristic sources (Menochius). The commentary indicates this typology was understood in the early Church tradition.

original_text: And came. The printed Hebrew has, "and he came:" but the Samaritan and all the versions, as well as some manuscripts, properly retain the plural, which the Massorets allow is right. (Kennicott, Diss. 1.) --- Enac, the founder of Hebron, and father of the giants of Chanaan, Josue 15:13. The Greek word anax, "king," was perhaps derived from him, as also the famous Inachides, who settled in Greece, after they were driven out by Josue. (Grotius) --- Tanis, where the tyrants of the Hebrews resided; a city, which the Egyptians represented as the most ancient in the world. Moses represses their vain boasting, by informing them that Hebron was of greater antiquity. It was afterwards assigned to the priests, and for a city of refuge, in the tribe of Juda, Josue 20:7.
notes: This Haydock commentary on Numbers 13:23 focuses on textual criticism (Hebrew vs. Samaritan manuscripts), historical and geographical information (Enac as founder of Hebron, Tanis as an Egyptian city), and chronological comparisons between ancient cities. While the commentary mentions Hebron's later assignment as a city of refuge and priestly city, it does not establish any explicit typological relationship between Old Testament persons, events, or institutions and New Testament fulfillments. The discussion is primarily historical-geographical rather than typological in nature.

original_text: Spoke ill, etc. These men, who, by their misrepresentations of the land of promise, discouraged the Israelites from attempting the conquest of it, were a figure of worldlings, who, by decrying or misrepresenting true devotion, discourage Christians from seeking in earnest and acquiring so great a good, and thereby securing to themselves a happy eternity. (Challoner) --- Devoureth, by being exposed to continual wars from the Arabs, Idumeans, and from its own inhabitants, the monsters of the race of Enac. With this God had threatened the Hebrews, if they proved rebellious, Leviticus 26:38. See Ezechiel 36:13. (Calmet)

extractions.type_name: The ten spies who spoke ill of the promised land
extractions.type_description: Men who misrepresented the land of Canaan and discouraged the Israelites from attempting its conquest through their negative report
extractions.antitype_description: People in the Christian era who misrepresent and discourage others from pursuing genuine devotion and seeking eternal salvation
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states these spies 'were a figure of worldlings, who, by decrying or misrepresenting true devotion, discourage Christians from seeking in earnest and acquiring so great a good.' This establishes a prefigurative relationship between OT negative exemplars and NT obstacles to Christian spiritual pursuit. The connection is ecclesial as it concerns the Church's ability to pursue its spiritual inheritance (paralleling Israel's pursuit of the promised land).

notes: The commentary presents this typology as a moral/spiritual parallel rather than a strict historical type. The emphasis is on the pattern of misrepresentation and discouragement recurring in both testaments. The secondary note about the land 'devouring' its inhabitants through warfare appears to reference threatened judgment (Leviticus 26:38) rather than typology, and is thus not extracted as a separate typological claim.

original_text: Sworn. God swore to give this land to the Hebrews, but not to this particular generation. His oath would be equally fulfilled by raising posterity to Moses, ver. 13. But, at his entreaty, he spared the descendants of this people, and gave the land to their children under Josue. (Haydock)
notes: This Haydock commentary discusses God's covenant promise to give the land of Canaan to the Hebrew people, focusing on the fulfillment of that oath through the next generation under Joshua rather than the wilderness generation that rebelled. While the passage involves covenant fulfillment (God's oath being kept), it does not establish a typological relationship between an Old Testament type and a New Testament antitype. The commentary addresses intra-testamental fulfillment (OT promise fulfilled within the OT narrative itself) rather than typology, which requires a prefigurative connection from the OT to the NT. Joshua's leadership of the conquest is presented as the literal fulfillment of God's promise, not as a type prefiguring a NT reality.

original_text: Spirit. The spirit of obedience and of courage. (Menochius) --- Followed me, as a guide, and hath fulfilled all my desires. (Vatable) --- This he was enabled to do by God's free grace. But his co-operation merited a reward. See St. Augustine, de Grat. et. Lib. vi.) (Worthington)
notes: This commentary on Numbers 14:24 (regarding Caleb) discusses his personal qualities (obedience, courage, faithfulness), his obedience to God, and theological concepts of grace and merit. While Caleb is an exemplary biblical figure, the Haydock commentary provided does not explicitly establish a typological relationship between Caleb (or his characteristics) and any New Testament person or reality. The commentary focuses on moral and theological lessons rather than on prefigurement of NT fulfillment. To identify typology, the commentary would need to explicitly connect Caleb's role or characteristics to a specific NT antitype (such as Christ, the Church, or another NT entity), which is absent here.

original_text: Eyes. These princes of Ruben were not desirous of the priesthood, as Core was; they repined, that Moses had got possession of the sovereign authority, and therefore they endeavour to represent him as an imposter, who had promised great things, but in reality had deprived the people of all the happiness which they formerly enjoyed in Egypt, and was now disposed to exercise his tyranny upon their very persons. (Haydock) --- "Do you wish that we should not see through your impostures?" Hebrew, "wilt thou put out the eyes of these men," who have informed us what sort of a country Chanaan is? Septuagint, "thou hast blinded these men," who are so stupid as to obey thee. (Calmet) --- Chaldean, "though thou pull out our eyes, we will not come."
notes: This commentary on Numbers 16:14 discusses the rebellion of Korah and the Reubenite princes against Moses' authority. The passage focuses on their accusations against Moses—that he is an imposter who has deprived them of Egyptian prosperity and now exercises tyranny. The commentary provides textual variants and interpretive nuances regarding their challenge to Moses' leadership ('putting out their eyes' = blinding them to truth, or their refusal to be deceived). While the rebellion itself has been understood typologically in some theological traditions (e.g., as prefiguring false teachers or rebellion against legitimate authority in the Church), this particular Haydock commentary does not explicitly establish or discuss any OT type-to-NT antitype relationship. It remains focused on the historical and lexical meaning of the verse rather than its typological significance.

original_text: Speak. The cause of the different families of the Levites now being fully decided, that none of the other tribes might pretend to the honour of the priesthood, God orders Moses to propose another miracle to them, of a less terrible nature than the preceding one. --- Man, or prince of the tribe. (Haydock) --- The name of Aaron was written upon his staff, which was taken from an almond tree; those of the princes of the other tribes appeared upon their respective rods, and represented their different families, ver. 3. (Calmet)
notes: This Haydock commentary describes a historical and miraculous event (Aaron's rod budding as a sign of his priestly authority) but does not explicitly connect it to any New Testament fulfillment or antitype. The commentary focuses on the immediate purpose of the miracle—to settle the dispute over priesthood among the tribes of Israel—rather than on typological prefigurement. While Aaron's priesthood could theoretically be discussed as a type of Christ's eternal priesthood in other contexts, this particular commentary does not make or suggest such a connection. It is purely historical-expository in nature.

original_text: Besides, etc. Hebrew and the other versions, "the rod of Aaron was in the midst of their rods." Whence some infer, that there were only 12 rods. But Origen, (hom. 9,) and most others, allow 13, as the tribe of Joseph was divided into those of Ephraim and Manasses; (Calmet) each of whom had a proper representative or prince. See (Numbers 2:18-20.; Numbers 10:22; Numbers 13:9-12.) The tribe of Levi is generally placed by itself. If there were only 12 rods, whether would the name of Elisama, or that of Gamaliel, designate the tribe of Joseph? Who was properly the prince of that udivided tribe? (Haydock)
notes: This Haydock commentary is primarily concerned with textual criticism and historical-tribal representation during the wilderness period. It discusses whether there were 12 or 13 rods presented before the Lord based on the division of the tribe of Joseph into Ephraim and Manasseh, and debates which tribal prince would represent an undivided Joseph. The commentary does not establish or discuss any typological relationship between the rod of Aaron (or the rods generally) and any New Testament fulfillment or antitype. While Aaron's rod elsewhere in scripture has been understood typologically (e.g., as prefiguring Christ's authority or priesthood), this particular commentary excerpt focuses entirely on historical-genealogical questions rather than typological interpretation.

original_text: The rod of Aaron for the house of Levi, was budded, etc. This rod of Aaron, which thus miraculously brought forth fruit, was a figure of the blessed Virgin conceiving and bringing forth her Son, without any prejudice to her virginity. (Challoner) --- Almonds. Buds, blossoms, leaves, and fruit just formed, (Isaias 18:5.) appeared upon the rod, which before was dry. Tostat believes, that it continued in the same state during the whole time that it was preserved in the ark. "The grace of the priesthood never fades." (St. Ambrose, ep. 63, or 58.) The almond tree is the first which blossoms, and therefore it is styled a watching rod, (Jeremias 1:11.) The Fathers observe in this of Aaron, a figure of Christ's passion and glorious resurrection; and Origen (hom. 9,) remarks, that from his cross proceed the sweet odours of virtue, and the fruits of converted nations. (Calmet) --- For Christ made peace through the blood of his cross, (Colossians 1:20.) The blessed Virgin, whom the blooming rod also represents, might as easily become a mother without losing her virginal integrity, as this dry rod might produce fruit, without receiving any moisture from the earth. (St. Augustine; St. Gregory of Nyssa; St. Bernard; etc.) (Worthington)

extractions.type_description: The dry rod of Aaron that miraculously budded, blossomed, and produced almonds, demonstrating the perpetual grace of the priesthood
extractions.antitype_description: Christ's cross, which through his passion and glorious resurrection, produces the sweet odors of virtue and the fruits of converted nations
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states: 'The Fathers observe in this of Aaron, a figure of Christ's passion and glorious resurrection' and notes that 'from his cross proceed the sweet odours of virtue, and the fruits of converted nations.' This directly connects the OT miraculous event to the NT redemptive work of Christ.

extractions.type_description: The dry rod that brought forth fruit without receiving moisture from the earth, demonstrating divine power over natural law
extractions.antitype_description: Mary who conceived and brought forth Christ while remaining a virgin, demonstrating divine power to preserve virginity while motherhood occurs
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states: 'This rod of Aaron, which thus miraculously brought forth fruit, was a figure of the blessed Virgin conceiving and bringing forth her Son, without any prejudice to her virginity.' Multiple Church Fathers (Augustine, Gregory of Nyssa, Bernard) are cited as making this connection, presenting the rod's fruitfulness without earthly moisture as prefiguring Mary's motherhood without loss of virginity.

notes: This commentary presents two distinct typological readings of Aaron's rod, both explicitly grounded in patristic tradition. The Christological typology emphasizes the rod's role as a sign of priestly grace leading to Christ's redemptive work. The Marian typology emphasizes the miraculous nature of the rod producing fruit naturally, paralleling the virgin birth. Both are presented as traditional interpretations rather than novel scholarly proposals.

original_text: Observance. Hebrew, "ceremony." Septuagint, "distinction, (diastole, St. Augustine, q. 33,) or ordinance." (Calmet) --- Victim. Hebrew, "the ordinance of the law." (Du Hamel) --- A red cow, etc. This red cow, offered in sacrifice for sin, and consumed with fire without the camp, with the ashes of which, mingled with water, the unclean were to be expiated and purified; was a figure of the passion of Christ, by whose precious blood, applied to our souls in the holy sacraments, we are cleansed from our sins. (Challoner) --- Age, three years old. Some translate, "entirely red." They suppose, that these regulations are in opposition to the customs of the Egyptians, who never sacrificed the cow, esteeming it sacred to Isis, or to the moon. Spencer (Rit. 2:15) adds, that the red colour was formerly in the highest estimation; and this victim represented the death of Christ, who expiated our defilements. The Egyptians immolated bulls of a red colour, in hatred of Typhon, and to appease that dangerous god, whom they depicted perfectly red. Plut.[Plutarch?] (Isis) observes, that they hate all animals of that colour; and the Copths precipitate a red ass down a precipice. The ancient kings of Egypt sacrificed red men on the tomb of Osiris or Dyphon; (Diod. Bib. 1,) and Manetho assures us, that they scattered their ashes in the wind. If this custom prevailed in the days of Moses, we need not wonder that he teaches the Hebrews to have so little dread of Typhon, as even to chose a red cow in preference, to purify themselves. --- Yoke. Such victims were generally chosen by the Romans, Greeks, and Egyptians, as more delicate and respectful. Intacta totidem cervice juvencus. (Georg. IV.; Bochart, anim. 2. 33.) St. Jerome (ep. 27,) says, that a red cow was sacrificed every year, as in reality one would be requisite for all the people, though the Rabbins pretend that only seven, or ten at most, were treated in this manner, from Moses till the destruction of the temple by Titus. (Drusius)

extractions.type_description: A red cow, three years old and never yoked, offered as a sacrifice for sin and consumed by fire outside the camp. Its ashes, mixed with water, were used to purify those who had become ceremonially unclean.
extractions.antitype_name: The Passion of Christ / Christ's Precious Blood
extractions.antitype_description: Christ's sacrificial death and the application of His precious blood to believers' souls through the holy sacraments, by which believers are cleansed from sin.
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states: 'This red cow, offered in sacrifice for sin, and consumed with fire without the camp...was a figure of the passion of Christ, by whose precious blood, applied to our souls in the holy sacraments, we are cleansed from our sins.' The red cow's sacrificial function (expiation of defilement) directly prefigures Christ's atoning work.

extractions.type_description: The ceremonial use of ashes mixed with water to expiate and purify the unclean from defilement.
extractions.antitype_name: Sacramental Grace / Baptism and the Eucharist
extractions.antitype_description: The application of Christ's redemptive work through the holy sacraments by which believers receive cleansing from sin.
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly connects the purification ritual to 'the holy sacraments' through which Christ's blood is applied to cleanse souls. The ashes and water parallels the sacramental means of applying Christ's redemption.

notes: The commentary provides strong typological interpretation grounded in patristic tradition (Challoner). The red color specifically is emphasized as representing Christ's atoning death. Contextual information about Egyptian religious customs is provided but does not alter the core typological claim. The commentary acknowledges rabbinical disagreement about frequency of sacrifice but does not undermine the typological connection.

original_text: Of all. Hebrew, "before his face." Septuagint, "they shall bring her out, slay and burn her before him," which must be referred to some other priests, who accompanied Eleazar on this occasion, ver. 8. (Calmet) --- Aaron did not perform this office, as the sacrifice was not solemn, but sorrowful, and designed for purification. (Menochius) --- The Rabbins say, however, that the high priest performed this ceremony ever after; and, since the building of the temple, they did it upon Mount Olivet. This is also remarked by St. Jerome, ep. 27. It was thus a more lively figure of Jesus Christ sweating blood on that same ground; as the smoke might represent his ascension, Acts 1:10., and Luke 22:44. (Calmet) --- He died out of Jerusalem, in full age, (ver. 2,) or 33 years old, being wounded in every part for our transgressions, (ver. 5,) setting us an example how to suffer, (ver. 6,) and by his blood communicating virtue to the sacraments, ver. 5. His body, derived from Adam, (or red earth, ver. 2,) was buried in a most clean place, (ver. 9,) and those who crucified him became more unclean; (ver. 8,) while even those who were employed in burying him, (ver. 9,) required to be cleansed by the grace of his passion, which must be communicated to them by baptism, in the name of the blessed Trinity, without which they cannot partake of any of the sacraments, (Numbers 12.) The old law could bring nothing to perfection. Those who lived under that dispensation, were forced to wait till the evening, (ver. 7,) when in the last ages the new law commenced, that by faith in Christ, they might obtain the remission of their sins. Thus we perceive the meaning of many things which to the Jews were veiled in shadows, Hebrews 10. (St. Augustine, q. 33.; Theodoret, q. 36.) (Worthington) --- The Fathers observe also, that the infirmity of our Saviour's flesh, and his liberty in giving and resuming his life, (John 10:18,) were denoted by the cow, which had never been yoked. (Calmet)

extractions.type_description: The ritual burning of a red heifer outside Jerusalem as a purification offering, with the cow never having been yoked, representing an unblemished sacrifice
extractions.antitype_description: Christ's suffering, blood, and death on Mount Olivet (the Mount of Olives) as the perfect sacrifice for purification from sin, with his ascension represented by the rising smoke
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly connects multiple elements: (1) the location (Mount Olivet where the heifer was burned prefigures where Christ sweated blood); (2) the sacrifice outside Jerusalem prefigures Christ dying outside Jerusalem; (3) the cow's unblemished nature and never being yoked prefigures Christ's sinless nature and freedom to give/resume his life; (4) the age of the cow (33 years) parallels Christ's age at crucifixion; (5) the wounding of the cow 'in every part' prefigures Christ 'wounded in every part for our transgressions.'

extractions.type_description: The ashes of the red heifer mixed with water used to cleanse those who touched death or the dead, requiring application for purification
extractions.antitype_description: Baptism in the name of the Trinity as the means of communicating Christ's grace and passion for the remission of sins, enabling participation in the sacraments
extractions.reasoning: The commentary states that those who buried Christ 'required to be cleansed by the grace of his passion, which must be communicated to them by baptism.' The purification water of the old law prefigures the sacramental grace of baptism in the new covenant, through which believers obtain remission of sins.

notes: The commentary, attributed primarily to Calmet with references to Augustine and other Church Fathers, employs rich typological interpretation characteristic of patristic hermeneutics. The connection between the literal location (Mount Olivet) and the type-antitype relationship adds historical concreteness to the typology. The commentary also notes that these meanings were 'veiled in shadows' to the Jews but are revealed in Christ through the new law.

original_text: Sin, Zin, or Tsin, nearer to Judea than the desert, where the Hebrews encamped before, Exodus 16:1. (Haydock) --- Moses informs us of very little from the time when the people murmured at Cades-barne, in the second year, till the beginning of the 40th year of their sojournment. --- In Cades. The Rabbins assert, they remained there the first time twenty-nine years, (chap. 14:45,) and the second, ten. (Genebrard, in the year of the world 2670.) But we do not believe they continued there above a year the first time. --- Mary. St. Gregory of Nyssa, and St. Ambrose, suppose she was always a virgin, in which respect she was a figure of our blessed Lady, as well as in her name. She was probably 130 years old, as she was very discreet at the time of the birth of Moses, and employed by Providence in preserving his life, as the blessed Virgin screened our Saviour from the fury of Herod. She had the superintendence over the Hebrew women; (Exodus 15:20.; Theodoret, in Mic. 6:4) and hence many apply to her and her brothers those words of Zacharias 11:8, I cut off three shepherds in one month. Mary died without being permitted to enter the promised land, on account of her murmuring, chap. 12. Thus the synagogue, though proud of her prerogatives, cannot enter the land of rest. (Calmet) --- There. Some place this Cades not far from the Red Sea, (ver. 20,) south of Idumea, while the other was to the north, and nearer Chanaan, being generally called Cades-barne. (Bonfrere and Cornelius a Lapide) (Chap. 20:16.) --- In this place Mary died, four months before Aaron. (Menochius)

extractions.type_description: Moses' sister who remained a virgin, was discreet and wise, preserved Moses' life in infancy, had superintendence over Hebrew women, and died without entering the promised land due to murmuring
extractions.antitype_description: Mother of Jesus who remained a virgin, and protected/screened the Saviour from Herod's fury
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that Miriam 'was a figure of our blessed Lady' (the Virgin Mary). The comparison is made on multiple grounds: perpetual virginity, divine providence in protecting a savior figure (Moses/Jesus) from danger in infancy, and maternal/protective roles.

extractions.type_name: Miriam's exclusion from the promised land
extractions.type_description: Miriam died without being permitted to enter the promised land due to her murmuring against Moses
extractions.antitype_description: Though proud of its prerogatives and heritage, it cannot enter the land of rest (eternal salvation/the Church)
extractions.reasoning: The commentary states 'Thus the synagogue, though proud of her prerogatives, cannot enter the land of rest.' This applies Miriam's exclusion typologically to represent the synagogue's spiritual exclusion, though this is a somewhat allegorical application rather than a direct OT-to-NT typology in the classical sense.

notes: The first typology (Miriam as type of Mary) is explicitly stated by the Fathers cited (St. Gregory of Nyssa and St. Ambrose). The second typology is more of a typological application/allegory drawn by Calmet. Both are presented in the patristic tradition represented in this Haydock commentary.

original_text: Rock. Your frequent murmurs will stop the course of God's bounty. If God had not condemned the conduct of his ministers on this occasion, we could hardly find any reason to blame them. But the Fathers observe, that they betrayed a want of resolution, and intended to throw the blame upon the incredulity of the people, in case they failed of success. Because they exasperated his spirit, and he distinguished with his lips, Psalm 105:33. See St. Chrysostom and St. Augustine on this psalm. They were not commanded to strike the rock at all; and when the water did not come at first, they struck again, (Calmet) being afraid lest they should now be taken for impostors. (Haydock) --- They speak as if the work was their own. --- Can we, etc. They exasperate the people, instead of promoting their conversion. In a word, they did not glorify God, (Calmet) by representing him as the sovereign holiness and mercy; and the God of unbounded power. (Haydock)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Numbers 20:10 focuses on the moral and theological failures of Moses and Aaron at Meribah - their lack of faith, their exasperation of the people, and their failure to glorify God properly. The commentary emphasizes their conduct as a cautionary example and their disobedience to God's command. While the passage itself (the striking of the rock) has been traditionally viewed as typological in Christian theology (the rock sometimes prefiguring Christ), this particular commentary does not explicitly draw out or discuss any Old Testament to New Testament typological relationships. The commentary is primarily exegetical and moralistic in nature, addressing why God condemned their behavior, rather than typological in its approach.

original_text: The rock. This rock was a figure of Christ, and the water that issued out from the rock, of his precious blood, the source of all our good; (Challoner) while the striking twice with the rod, denoted the cross, composed of two pieces of wood. (St. Augustine, q. 35.) (Worthington)

extractions.type_description: The rock struck by Moses in the wilderness (Numbers 20:11) from which water flowed to sustain the Israelites
extractions.antitype_description: Jesus Christ, whose blood was shed for the redemption and sustenance of humanity
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly identifies the rock as 'a figure of Christ,' establishing a direct OT type to NT antitype relationship. This is a well-established typological interpretation in Christian tradition.

extractions.type_description: The water that issued from the struck rock, which provided life-sustaining drink to the Israelites in the wilderness
extractions.antitype_description: Christ's precious blood shed on the cross, described as 'the source of all our good'
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states the water 'was a figure of...his precious blood, the source of all our good,' establishing a clear typological correspondence between the life-giving water and Christ's redemptive blood.

extractions.type_description: Moses striking the rock twice with his rod, representing two pieces of wood
extractions.antitype_description: The cross upon which Christ was crucified, composed of two pieces of wood intersecting
extractions.reasoning: St. Augustine's interpretation links the striking action and the rod's composition (denoting two pieces of wood) to the cross as an architectural symbol. This is more symbolical than some typologies, but represents a recognized patristic interpretation of the event as prefiguring Christ's crucifixion.

notes: This commentary reflects classical patristic typological interpretation, particularly from St. Augustine and Catholic exegetical tradition (Challoner, Worthington). All three typological relationships are explicitly stated in the source material and center on the single event of Numbers 20:11 as a multi-faceted type of Christ and his redemptive work.

original_text: Vesture, or pontifical attire. Eleazar had been anointed already, so that perhaps he stood in need of no other ceremony to be acknowledged high priest. He was dispensed with on this occasion to attend his dying father. The spirit of God gives great encomiums to Aaron, Malachias 2:4-7., and Ecclesiasticus 45:7, 27. He, at the same time, prefigured Christ, the gospel, and the old law. He spoke plainly, and was allowed to enter the holy of holies; while Moses was excluded, spoke with difficulty, and had a veil on his face. See St. Jerome, ep. ad Fab. man. 33. But on the other hand, he represented the law with all its defects. He falls into several great faults, and dies despoiled of his glorious vestments, to shew the abrogation of his priesthood. The pagans have, perhaps, introduced some parts of his history into that of Mercury, the god of thieves and of travellers, the messenger of the other gods, whom they adorn with a wand, etc., in imitation of the rod of Aaron, who was the interpreter of Moses, and the head of that people, which wandered for 40 years, after plundering Egypt. (Calmet)

extractions.type_description: Aaron serving as high priest with his pontifical attire, speaking plainly, entering the holy of holies, and serving as interpreter/messenger of Moses to the people
extractions.antitype_description: Christ as the ultimate High Priest who speaks plainly and has direct access to the holy presence of God
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states 'He, at the same time, prefigured Christ' and develops the parallel: Aaron spoke plainly and entered the holy of holies (unlike Moses who was excluded, spoke with difficulty, and wore a veil), prefiguring Christ's direct access and clear communication

extractions.type_name: Aaron and his priestly vestments being removed
extractions.type_description: Aaron dying despoiled of his glorious vestments, representing the abrogation of his priesthood and the law with its defects
extractions.antitype_name: The Abrogation of the Old Law/Priesthood
extractions.antitype_description: The Old Testament law and priestly system being superseded by the New Covenant and Christ's eternal priesthood
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that Aaron's death and despoilment of vestments prefigure 'the abrogation of his priesthood' and represent 'the law with all its defects,' indicating a typological fulfillment where the old system gives way to the new

notes: The commentary presents Aaron with a dual typological function: positively prefiguring Christ's priesthood in his access and speech, and negatively representing the defects and eventual abrogation of the Old Law. The commentary also mentions non-typological material (the pagan Mercury legend), which has been excluded from the typological analysis.

original_text: Dead, in the 123d year of his age. (Menochius) --- Neither Moses, Aaron, nor Mary, representing the Law, the priests, and the prophets of the Old Testament, could introduce the people into the promised land. This honour was reserved for Josue, the illustrious figure of Jesus Christ, and of his Church. (Calmet)

extractions.type_description: The leader who succeeded Moses and actually led the Israelites into the promised land, as Moses and Aaron could not enter due to their sin
extractions.antitype_description: Jesus Christ, who fulfills what the Old Testament leaders could not accomplish and leads God's people into the ultimate inheritance
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that Joshua is 'the illustrious figure of Jesus Christ' and notes that neither Moses, Aaron, nor Mary could introduce the people into the promised land, emphasizing that this honor was reserved for Joshua/Jesus. This is a classic typological connection where the OT figure prefigures the NT fulfillment.

extractions.type_name: Moses, Aaron, and the Prophets of the Old Testament
extractions.type_description: Representatives of the Law, the priesthood, and prophecy in the Old Testament who were unable to bring Israel into the promised land
extractions.antitype_description: Jesus Christ and the New Testament Church, which together accomplish what the Old Testament institutions could not
extractions.reasoning: The commentary contrasts the limitations of the Old Testament representatives (Law, priests, prophets) with Joshua's role, implying that Christ succeeds where the Old Testament order failed. This suggests a typological relationship showing the superiority and fulfillment of Christ over the Old Testament system.

notes: The commentary uses the principle of typological interpretation to explain why Joshua, not Moses or Aaron, led Israel into Canaan. This reflects a theologically significant typology: just as Joshua (whose name in Hebrew is the same root as 'Jesus') brought Israel into the promised land, Jesus brings God's people into ultimate salvation and the Church into its inheritance.

original_text: Fiery serpents. They are so called, because they that were bitten by them were burnt with a violent heat. (Challoner) --- Hence they are called seraphim, by which name an order of angels is known. The Egyptians adored a serpent which they called serapis, at Rome; and they represented their god serapis, with a serpent entwining a monstrous figure, composed of a lion, a dog, and a wolf. (Macrob. Saturn 1:20.) The seraph was a winged serpent, Isaias 14:29. 30:6. Such often infested Egypt, in spring, coming from Arabia, unless they were intercepted by the ibis. Their wings resembled those of bats. (Herodotus, 2:76.; Mela, etc.) God probably sent some of this description into the camp of the Israelites. (Calmet) --- Some call them proester, (Pliny, [Natural History?] 24:13,) from their burning; others the hydra, or, when out of water, the chershydra, the venom of which is most dangerous. The Septuagint style them simply, "the destroying, or deadly serpents." See Bochart, T. 2:B. 3:13.; Deuteronomy 8:15.; Wisdom 16:5, 10.) (Haydock)
notes: This Haydock commentary focuses on identifying what the 'fiery serpents' (seraphim) were from a natural history and etymological perspective. While the commentary mentions that seraphim is the name of an order of angels and references Egyptian religious symbolism (the god Serapis depicted with serpents), it does not establish a typological relationship between the OT serpents of Numbers 21:6 and any NT antitype or fulfillment. The commentary is primarily descriptive and comparative (Egyptian worship practices, various natural species identifications) rather than typological. No explicit connection to Christ, the Church, Mary, sacraments, covenant fulfillment, or eschatological realities is made in this passage. Note: While Numbers 21:8-9 (the bronze serpent) is famously typological of Christ's crucifixion (John 3:14-15), that typological connection is not addressed in this particular verse 6 commentary.

original_text: Brazen. Hebrew, "fiery." But in the following verse, it is said to have been "of brass." We might translate, "make a seraph, and fix it upon a standard," (Calmet) in which form it would resemble one suspended on a cross. It was placed at the entrance of the tabernacle. (St. Justin Martyr, First Apology) Ezechias afterwards destroyed it, because it was treated with superstitious honours, 4 Kings 18:4. Thus the best things are often abused. (Haydock) --- God commands this image to be erected, while he forbids all images of idols. (Worthington) --- By comparing the different passages of Scripture, we may discern the true import of them. Pictures may often prove very useful and instructive. They serve the ignorant instead of books. But then the ignorant must be carefully instructed not to treat them with improper respect, as St. Gregory admonishes. And is not the same caution requisite for those who read even the word of God, lest they wrest it to their own destruction, as both the unlearned and the unstable frequently do, 2 Peter 3:16. If every thing must be rejected which is liable to abuse, what part of the creation will be spared? The Bible, the sacraments, all creatures must be laid aside. For we read, (Romans 8:20, 22,) the creature was made subject to vanity --- every creature groaneth. (Haydock) --- It is probable that Moses represented on the standard, such a serpent, as had been the instrument of death. This was not intended for a charm or talisman, as Marsham would impiously pretend. (Chron. 10. p. 148.) Such inventions proceed from the devil; and the Marsi were famous for curing the bites of serpents, by giving certain plates of brass. (Arnob. ii.) See Psalm 58:5. But this image was set up by God's express command; and the Book of Wisdom (xvi. 5, 7) assures us, that the effect was entirely to be attributed to him, the figure of a brazen serpent being rather calculated to increase than to remove the danger. (Kimchi; Muis) Hence Jonathan well observes, that only those were healed who raised their hearts to God. (Calmet)

extractions.type_name: The Brazen Serpent on a Standard
extractions.type_description: The serpent made of brass and fixed upon a standard by God's command in the wilderness, which healed those bitten by fiery serpents who looked upon it in faith
extractions.antitype_description: Jesus Christ suspended on the cross, whose lifting up brings healing and salvation to those who believe in Him
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states the brazen serpent 'in which form it would resemble one suspended on a cross.' The passage indicates a direct prefigurement of Christ's crucifixion. Furthermore, the commentary notes that healing came through faith in God rather than the image itself, paralleling how salvation comes through faith in Christ rather than the symbol. The structure of the type (serpent lifted up, bringing healing through faith) directly prefigures the antitype (Christ lifted up on the cross, bringing salvation through faith).

notes: While the commentary does not explicitly cite John 3:14-15 (where Jesus Himself applies this typology: 'just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up'), the Haydock commentary's reference to the serpent resembling 'one suspended on a cross' makes the typological connection clear and well-established in Christian exegetical tradition. The emphasis on faith as the mechanism of healing in both type and antitype further strengthens this connection.

original_text: A brazen serpent. This was a figure of Christ crucified, and of the efficacy of a lively faith in him, against the bites of the hellish serpent, John 3:14. (Challoner) (St. Ambrose; Apol. 1:3.) As the old serpent infected the whole human race, Jesus Christ gives life to those that look at him with entire confidence. (Theodoret, q. 38.) The brazen serpent was destitute of poison, though it resembled a most noxious animal; so Jesus Christ assumed our nature, yet without sin. (Calmet)

extractions.type_description: The serpent fashioned from bronze that Moses lifted up in the wilderness (NUM 21:8-9) as a remedy for those bitten by the fiery serpents, which people looked upon to be healed
extractions.antitype_description: Jesus Christ on the cross, whose redemptive work and the efficacy of faith in him provide spiritual healing and salvation from sin (the 'hellish serpent')
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly cites John 3:14 where Jesus himself identifies this typological relationship: 'as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up.' The type directly prefigures the antitype through the parallel act of 'lifting up' and the mechanism of faith/trust leading to salvation/healing.

extractions.type_description: The brazen serpent that resembled a noxious animal but was destitute of poison, representing the assumption of a dangerous form while remaining harmless
extractions.antitype_name: Christ Assuming Human Nature Without Sin
extractions.antitype_description: Jesus Christ who assumed human nature (appearing as a man, potentially subject to temptation like humans) yet remained entirely without sin, thus harmless despite the appearance
extractions.reasoning: Calmet explicitly draws this parallel: the brazen serpent's paradoxical nature (resembling poison yet without poison) prefigures Christ's paradoxical nature (assuming human nature yet remaining sinless). This demonstrates Christ's victory over the nature that contains sin.

notes: The commentary attributes this typology to authoritative sources including John 3:14 (direct scriptural validation), St. Ambrose, Theodoret, and Calmet. The connection between the 'old serpent' (Satan/the source of sin) and the brazen serpent remedy establishes a typological antithesis that reinforces the Christological significance. All extractions are explicitly stated in the commentary rather than inferred.

original_text: Rhinoceros. Hebrew ream, which is sometimes rendered unicorn. Bochart thinks it means the oryx, or the strong Arabian goat. The animal, of which the Scripture so often speaks, was remarkable for its strength, (Calmet) and could not easily be tamed, Job 39:9. (Haydock) --- The Septuagint generally translate monoceros, which is a fish, with a horn proceeding from its upper jaw. This is often shewn in cabinets for the horn of the unicorn. There are various animals which have only one horn. Pliny and Aristotle instance the oryx, etc. Various authors of credit specify likewise the rhinoceros, which has "a horn upon its nose," and is found in Ethiopia. The emperor of that country sent one to the court of Persia, which Chardin saw and describes. It is as large as an elephant, and the people have learnt the method of taming both these huge beasts. (Calmet) --- It seems the art was unknown in the days of Job, if this be the animal of which he speaks. (Haydock) --- Moses (Deuteronomy 33:17,) seems to attribute two horns to the ream; and Pausanius allows a greater and a less one to the rhinoceros; the latter is very strong and erect. It is of a brownish colour. (Calmet) --- Whatever may be the precise meaning of ream, it certainly denotes an animal of superior strength, and very formidable. Balaam represents God, or the people of Israel, in this light. God had given repeated instances of his dominion over all nature, in delivering the Hebrews out of Egypt. They were also capable of striking the Moabites with terror, on account of their known prowess, and surprising numbers, ver. 24. (Haydock)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Numbers 23:22 focuses on zoological identification and symbolism rather than typology. The passage discusses what animal 'ream' (Hebrew term) refers to—likely the rhinoceros or oryx—and emphasizes its strength as a natural symbol. The commentary explains that Balaam uses the ream's strength as a metaphor for God's power and Israel's formidable nature, demonstrated through their deliverance from Egypt and military prowess. This is symbolic/rhetorical language within the Old Testament context, not a prefiguration of New Testament fulfillment. There is no indication that this OT image or animal prefigures a NT antitype, person, event, or sacrament.

original_text: Him. The great personage whom I have in view, whose coming is deferred yet for many ages. (Haydock) --- The whole prediction refers to the Messias, whom Balaam beheld by the eyes of his posterity, the wise men, (Calmet) or in the prophetic vision. (Menochius) --- Some modern Rabbins pretend that he speaks of David, who was indeed a figure of Christ, (Calmet) and defeated the Moabites, 2 Kings 5:8. But the prophecy was perfectly fulfilled only in our Saviour's person, who is called the bright and morning star, (Apocalypse 22:16,) to whom all nations were given for an inheritance, Psalm ii., and Acts 1:8. (Worthington) --- Hebrew also, "I see this thy ruin, but," etc. Septuagint, "I will shew to him, yet not now; I will make him happy, (Calmet); but (makarizo, I bless) it, or he does not approach." God executed what he ever promised in favour of all Israel, when he sent them his beloved Son. --- A Star. Christ, the light of the world, the splendour of his Father's glory, whose birth was made known in the East, by a star, or meteor of unusual brightness. (Haydock) --- This material star is not the primary object of the prediction, since it did not rise out of Jacob, but it pointed out the orient from on high, and then disappeared. The ancient Jews understood this passage of the Messias. (Onkelos, etc.) Hence the impostor, Ben. Cusiba, took advantage of this general opinion, to draw the people after him, as the person designated; when he assumed the title of Bar-chocheba, "the son of the star," in the second age [century] of the church. --- Of Seth. Though David, as the figure of the Messias, conquered the Moabites, he cannot be said to have subdued all nations, the descendants of Seth, by Noe, nor all the just of whom Seth was the father, in opposition to the children of Cain. But Christ will subject all the just to his empire, and will judge all mankind. Some, nevertheless, take the children of Seth to be the Moabites, who had been already mentioned; and Junius translates the Hebrew with allusion to the shameful origin of that people. The Samaritan may also signify, if we substitute d for r in korkor, as Jeremias also reads (chap. 48:45,) kodkod. "He shall penetrate the ends of Moab, and shall overturn the walls of the children of elevation, or of pride." There were many hills in the country of the Moabites, and the people were noted for haughtiness, Jeremias 48:28, 29, 45. (Calmet) --- Some also assert, that Seth was the name of a king, (Grotius) and of a town of Moab. (Rabbi Nathan) --- But of this there is no proof. (Haydock)

extractions.type_description: The historical king of Israel who defeated the Moabites and other enemies, serving as a prefiguring figure of the ultimate victor
extractions.antitype_description: The ultimate fulfillment of the messianic promise, called 'the bright and morning star' who conquered spiritual enemies and was given all nations as an inheritance
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states 'David...was indeed a figure of Christ' and notes that while David defeated the Moabites historically, 'the prophecy was perfectly fulfilled only in our Saviour's person.' This is a direct type-antitype relationship where the OT figure prefigures the NT fulfillment.

extractions.type_description: The astronomical sign that arose at Jacob's line, symbolizing Christ as 'the light of the world, the splendour of his Father's glory'
extractions.antitype_name: Jesus Christ as 'the bright and morning star'
extractions.antitype_description: Christ fulfills the messianic promise, identified with the morning star that brings light and whose birth was announced by a star in the East
extractions.reasoning: The commentary identifies the star prophecy as ultimately referring to Christ, who is explicitly called 'the bright and morning star' in Apocalypse 22:16. The material star of Bethlehem pointed to and prefigured Christ as the true spiritual 'star' and light of the world.

notes: The commentary also mentions Seth as potentially prefiguring the righteous/just, but this interpretation is presented more ambiguously and without clear NT antitype identification, so it was not extracted as a distinct typological relationship. The primary typological focus is on David as a type of the Messiah and the star as symbolizing Christ's coming.

original_text: City of this world. Jesus will destroy their evil habits, (Origen, hom. 18,) and will select some whose lives had been hitherto scandalous, to be his intimate friends. (Haydock) --- He will save those who abandoned paganism, which had fixed its seat at the great city of Rome, (Calmet) and he will raise up Constantine (Menochius; Tirinus) to rule over Jacob, his people. At his second coming, he will exterminate all who shall have refused to acknowledge his sovereignty, and who have remained out of the city of his Church. (Haydock) --- Those who have fled out of the cities for safety, shall be sought out by David, and destroyed. He slew all the male children of Edom, 3 Kings 15:15. (Calmet) --- In this prophecy, some particulars relate to him, as that he shall subject Moab and Idumea by the valour of his troops, while other things can belong only to Christ, the star, who shall destroy the remains of the city. (Menochius) --- By changing one letter, Calmet would translate, "Princes shall spring from Jacob: but Seir shall perish from his cities." A long train of princes in Jacob prefigured the Messias, while the Idumeans have been unknown for many ages. (Calmet)

extractions.type_name: David's conquest and rule over Edom/Moab
extractions.type_description: The historical David subduing enemies (Edom, Moab, Seir) and establishing his kingdom over Jacob's people, as recorded in the Old Testament
extractions.antitype_description: Jesus Christ who will destroy evil, subject all peoples, and at his second coming exterminate those who refuse to acknowledge his sovereignty and remain outside his Church
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that while some particulars of this prophecy relate to the historical David, 'other things can belong only to Christ, the star, who shall destroy the remains of the city.' This directly presents David's kingship and conquests as prefiguring Christ's messianic rule and eschatological judgment. The commentary also notes that 'A long train of princes in Jacob prefigured the Messias.'

extractions.type_description: The Old Testament people of Israel/Jacob over whom David ruled and whom God established as his covenant people
extractions.antitype_description: Christ's Church, described as 'the city of his Church,' comprising those who acknowledge Christ's sovereignty and have abandoned paganism
extractions.reasoning: The commentary contrasts those 'out of the city of his Church' with those within it, presenting the Church as the fulfillment of God's people. The historical Jacob's people and city prefigure the eschatological Church community.

notes: The commentary attributes these typological interpretations to multiple patristic and medieval sources (Origen, Calmet, Menochius, Tirinus, Haydock). The interpretation acknowledges that NUM 24:19 contains both literal historical fulfillment regarding David and typological fulfillment regarding Christ, which is characteristic of messianic prophecies in the Pentateuch.

original_text: Sinai, if we except the Levites. (Menochius) See (Numbers 14:23.) --- Origen (hom. 21.) makes a very good remark on this subject. This circumcised, but rebellious people, conducted by Moses into the desert, clearly points out the Hebrews, who come to the frontiers of the promised land, but are not suffered to cross the Jordan. The uncircumcised are introduced into the land flowing with milk and honey, not by Moses, but by Josue, the figure of our Saviour, who opens heaven to true believers. "The first people is rejected, which had received circumcision, and the second is introduced, which is gathered from the Gentiles; and it is this people which obtains its father's inheritance....If Moses give any inheritance, it is not within the Jordan....it is a land fit for cattle....he does not distribute it by lot....nor can he know the merits of each. This is done by Jesus only, to whom his Father has given all judgment." (Haydock)

extractions.type_description: The leader who conducts the uncircumcised generation across the Jordan into the promised land of milk and honey, distributing the inheritance by lot and judging the merits of each person
extractions.antitype_description: The true leader who opens heaven to believers, distributes the Father's inheritance, and possesses all judgment from the Father
extractions.reasoning: Origen explicitly identifies Joshua as 'the figure of our Saviour.' The parallel is drawn through Joshua's role as one who succeeds where Moses failed, leading people into their inheritance and making judgments about distribution—functions explicitly attributed to Christ in the commentary.

extractions.type_description: The circumcised but rebellious people conducted by Moses into the desert who are not permitted to cross the Jordan and enter the promised land
extractions.antitype_name: The Rejected Jewish People (First Covenant Community)
extractions.antitype_description: The Hebrew people who received circumcision but are rejected and not allowed to enter heaven, superseded by a people gathered from the Gentiles
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states: 'The first people is rejected, which had received circumcision, and the second is introduced, which is gathered from the Gentiles.' This typological interpretation presents the wilderness rejection as prefiguring the later rejection of the Jewish people under the old covenant in favor of the Church gathered from Gentiles.

notes: This commentary represents Origen's allegorical-typological interpretation of Numbers 26:64, presenting a supersessionist reading common in patristic theology. The typology involves both a Christological type (Joshua prefiguring Christ) and an Ecclesial type (the wilderness generation prefiguring covenant replacement). Modern biblical scholarship may question the historical basis and theological implications of this interpretation.

original_text: Month. This is not reckoned among the festivals, Leviticus xxiii. The Rabbins look upon it as a day of devotion, particularly for women. (Buxtorf. Syn. xvii.) Spencer (Rit. 3:1,) maintains, that the Hebrews began their month when the moon first appeared, and that they imitated the pagans in keeping that day holy. But his proofs on both heads are very unsatisfactory. The Hebrews followed the solar year for many ages after Moses, though they might have adopted the lunar towards the close of the republic; and the pagans themselves ridiculed those as vile imitators of the Jews, who kept the new moons as a festival. (Hor.[Horace,?] Sat. 1:9.) Sabbata Vin tu Curtis Judaeis oppedere. --- The Greeks, Romans, Egyptians, Arabs, and Turks, have given in to various superstitious practices in honour of the moon. See Macrob. Sat. 1:15, etc. (Calmet) --- The devil is commonly the ape of God, and teaches his votaries to adopt the ceremonies of the true religion, either to elude them more easily, or to bring those practices into discredit. Thus Middleton has endeavoured to shew the conformity of Pagan and Papal Rome, as if the ceremonies of the Catholic religion were to be rejected, because some of them have been in use among the heathens. By the same argument, he may ridicule the revelation of God himself, on this subject, and represent vestments, holy water, etc., as superstitious. He may pull down altars, condemn all forms of prayer, abolish all worship, both of soul and body. For such things have all been prostituted to idols! But those who are not totally infatuated by prejudice, will deplore the abuse of these things, and will not refrain from adoring the true God according to his will, with all the faculties both of their soul and body, on account of the devil and his false prophets having extorted similar acts of worship from their followers. It is no wonder that Protestants should ridicule our holy ceremonies, since they scruple not to assign so base an origin to those which God expressly prescribed. (Haydock) --- The sacrifices which were ordered to be offered up on the first day of the month, were probably designed to renew the memory of the world's creation, or rather of the divine Providence, which regulates the seasons. Nothing was sold on this day, Amos 8:5. But people went to hear the prophets, (4 Kings 4:23,) and feasted among themselves, 1 Kings 20:18. It is thought that many rested also from servile work, though this is no where commanded. (Calmet) --- Tirinus agrees with Tostat and Sanctius, in supposing that servile work was prohibited, for which he refers to 1 Kings 20:19. He also asserts, that the Jews observed the lunar system, and that their months consisted of 29 and 30 days alternately, as 29 days and a half elapse from one moon to another. The sound of trumpets probably announced this solemnity, chap. 10:10., and Leviticus xxiii. (Haydock)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Numbers 28:11 (the new moon offering) does not describe any typological relationships between Old Testament types and New Testament antitypes. The commentary focuses on: (1) historical and cultural context regarding lunar calendar practices among Jews and pagan nations, (2) debates about whether the Hebrews used solar or lunar calendars, (3) theological reflection on how the devil imitates God's ceremonies, and (4) the practical significance of the new moon observance (renewal of God's providence, cessation of commerce, attendance at prophetic teaching). While the passage discusses OT sacrificial practices and their meaning, it does not connect them to NT fulfillment or prefigurement. The commentary is primarily historical, comparative, and devotional rather than typological.

original_text: Vows. The general regulations did not hinder any private ones from being fulfilled. (Calmet) --- Sacrifice. Mincha, or offering of flour, etc. (Haydock)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Numbers 29:39 addresses regulatory and definitional matters rather than typological prefigurement. The passage discusses how private vows and offerings (mincha/flour offerings) were permitted alongside the general sacrificial regulations prescribed in Numbers 29. The commentary is primarily concerned with clarifying the scope of Jewish sacrificial law—that general ritual requirements did not preclude individual devotional practices. This is exegetical clarification of Old Testament law, not a discussion of how Old Testament types prefigure New Testament antitypes. No OT/NT typological relationship is articulated or implied in the commentary.

original_text: Jordan. They are a figure of those who would possess heaven without labour. But none is crowned, except he strive lawfully, 2 Timothy 2:5. (Worthington)
notes: This commentary presents a moral allegory rather than a typological relationship. The Reubenites and Gadites' desire to possess land east of the Jordan without crossing it is used as a symbolic illustration of a moral principle (attempting to gain heavenly reward without spiritual effort). However, this is not typology because: (1) there is no explicit Old Testament type prefiguring a New Testament antitype, (2) the connection is moralistic/ethical rather than redemptive-historical, and (3) the relationship flows from the OT narrative to a general NT principle (2 Timothy 2:5) rather than establishing how an OT person/event/institution prefigures a specific NT fulfillment. The commentary uses the narrative symbolically to reinforce a spiritual lesson about the necessity of 'striving lawfully' for heavenly reward, which is exhortation based on typological thinking rather than typology itself.

original_text: Defile not. To inspire a greater horror for murder, the earth was represented as defiled by blood, and only to be purified by the death of the criminal. Without shedding of blood, there is no remission, Hebrews 9:22. (Haydock) --- On the same principle, our churches, etc., are deemed profane, when murder, or some great indecencies, have been committed in them, so that they require a fresh consecration. (Calmet)

extractions.type_name: Blood sacrifice for purification of defilement (Numbers 35:33)
extractions.type_description: The OT principle that murder defiles the earth and requires the death of the criminal to purify it; blood shed for atonement
extractions.antitype_name: Christ's blood shed for remission of sins (Hebrews 9:22)
extractions.antitype_description: The shedding of Christ's blood as the ultimate sacrifice that provides remission (forgiveness) of sins; 'without shedding of blood, there is no remission'
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly connects the OT principle of blood purification in Numbers 35:33 to the NT fulfillment in Hebrews 9:22, establishing that Christ's sacrificial blood is the antitype to which OT blood sacrifices for atonement point. The Haydock commentary directly cites Hebrews 9:22 to establish this typological relationship.

notes: The Haydock commentary also mentions a secondary application regarding church profanation requiring consecration, but this is presented as a principle of analogy (how the same logic applies to sacred spaces) rather than as an explicit typological relationship. The primary typology is clearly Christological, focusing on sacrificial blood as the means of atonement and purification.

original_text: Carefully. Hebrew, "Be therefore particularly attentive, as much as you love your own soul." (Vatable) By keeping my commandments, you can alone obtain salvation, ver. 9. (Menochius) --- Similitude of any living creature, such as were the objects of adoration among the pagans. Some represented their gods under the forms of men, women, beasts, birds, or reptiles; while others adored the sun, moon, and stars. (Haydock) --- This last was indeed the most ancient species of idolatry, Job 21:26. Baal, Astarte, Moloc, Chamos, etc., were different names by which they denoted the heavenly bodies. But the Egyptians carried their superstition to the greatest excess. There was hardly any sort of animal which did not obtain sovereign worship among them. (Calmet) --- Their great gods, Isis and Osiris, were sometimes depicted like a man and woman; at other times, like beasts, and frequently they appeared with parts of both. The head of Isis was generally adorned or disfigured with the horns of a bull; (Haydock) and that animal, either alive or in a picture, as well as dogs and cats, were adored throughout the country, while some places had their peculiar idols. The lion, the wolf, and the fish called latus, gave their names to the cities Leontopolis, etc., which had a particular veneration for them. Moses takes care to inform the Hebrews, that the true God is like none of these things; and that they cannot pretend to represent him under any such forms, without doing him an injury. (Calmet) --- If Catholics endeavour to put the people in mind of the blessed Trinity, by representing a venerable old man, Jesus Christ in his human nature, and a dove, under which forms the Scripture has introduced the three divine persons, they do not pretend that their divine and most spiritual nature can be thus expressed. "If," says the Council of Trent, Session 25, "the historical accounts of Scripture be sometimes set forth in paintings, for the benefit of the illiterate, let the people be informed that the Divinity is not thus represented, with a design to insinuate that it may be seen with the eyes of the body." So neither can the figure of a triangle, with the ineffable name of God in Hebrew, etc., explain this adorable mystery. But such things may recall to our remembrance, the innumerable benefits which we have received from the three divine persons, after we have been once informed what we have to believe respecting them. This is the laudable motive which has induced the Church to encourage the keeping of such pictures, as well as those of the saints, with due respect. "Not as if we believed that any divinity or virtue resided in them for which they were to be worshipped, or that we should ask any thing of them, or place our confidence in images, as the Gentiles formerly did, who hoped in their idols, (Psalm cxxxiv.,) but because the honour given to them is referred to the originals, which they represent," etc. (Council of Trent, Session 25.) (Haydock)
notes: This commentary on Deuteronomy 4:15 focuses on prohibiting idolatry and false representations of God. While it discusses how pagan nations represented their gods through various forms (animals, celestial bodies, etc.) and contrasts this with the true God's nature, it does not establish a typological relationship between an Old Testament type and a New Testament antitype. The commentary is primarily concerned with: (1) explaining the historical context of ancient idolatry practices, (2) establishing that God cannot be represented through created things, and (3) defending Catholic practice regarding religious images and artwork. The extended discussion about the Council of Trent's position on religious imagery addresses sacramental theology and ecclesial practice, but does not connect an OT prefigurement to its NT fulfillment. The passage is didactic and polemical in nature rather than typological.

original_text: Fire. God often appeared in the midst of fire. All the land shall be devoured by the fire of his jealousy, Sophonias 1:18., and 3:8. (Calmet) --- By these expressions, we are exhorted not to do any thing which would excite the indignation of our true lover, nor ever be unfaithful to him. (Haydock) --- The pagans thought that fire was the fittest symbol of the divinity. (Porphyr. de Abstin.)
notes: This commentary discusses God's appearance in fire as a symbol of divine presence and attributes (divinity, jealousy, indignation), but does not establish a typological relationship between an Old Testament type and a New Testament antitype. The references to Sophonias (Zephaniah) 1:18 and 3:8 discuss eschatological judgment using fire as imagery, but this is not presented as a type-antitype fulfillment. The commentary focuses on: (1) symbolic meaning of fire in theophanies, (2) moral exhortation regarding faithfulness to God, and (3) pagan philosophical perspectives on fire as a symbol of divinity. These are matters of symbolism, theological reflection, and ethical application rather than typological prefigurement.

original_text: There. Hebrew, "thence" from the place of captivity, or returning from the love of idols to the services of the true God. --- Soul. Hebrew, "with all thy soul. (Ver. 30) In thy tribulation after," etc. (Calmet) --- God often sends chastisements as the most effectual means of salvation, to make his children enter into themselves. In this state, the soul is more at liberty to consider the folly of adhering to any thing in opposition to the sovereign Lord. Then she is forced to confess that her idols cannot afford her any protection. How, in effect, could any one fall into such an abyss of corruption and stupidity, as to imagine those things to be gods which have not even the dignity and advantages which they themselves possess? Their soul must first have been strangely blinded, and their heart corrupt. Even the more enlightened pagans acknowledged the folly of pretending to represent the Divinity under sensible forms. "God, says Empedocles, has no human members....He is a pure and ineffable spirit, who governs the world by his profound wisdom." Numa would not allow any picture of Him, conformably to the doctrine of Pythagoras; and, for the first 170 years of Rome, no representation of God was set up in the temples. (Plutarch) --- The ancient Phoenicians seemed to have acted on the same principle, as the temple of Hercules, at the Straits, had no image. It is well known that the Persians rejected both the statues and temples erected in honour of the gods; and the Germans esteemed it beneath the majesty of the heavenly Beings, to represent them under any human form. (Tacitus, Hist. v.) (Calmet) --- Yet these sages gave way to the folly of the people, and, against their better knowledge, adored the stupid and senseless idols. (Haydock)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Deuteronomy 4:29 focuses on moral and spiritual instruction regarding repentance, the dangers of idolatry, and God's use of chastisement for salvation. While it discusses the soul's return to God and rejection of false gods, these are presented as moral lessons and theological principles rather than typological prefigurations of New Testament realities. The commentary includes historical examples from pagan philosophers and cultures to illustrate points about idolatry and the nature of God, but these are comparative illustrations, not typological connections. No explicit OT type → NT antitype relationships are articulated in the text.

(Calmet) Among us, who believe that the law was first given by the will of God, nothing is pious but the exact observance of it. For who can introduce any change, or invent any thing better?" Augustine's distinction between 'grace' (fulness of charity) and 'truth' (completion of prophecies) reinforces the typological completion of OT law in the NT gospel.

original_text: If....a prophet, or even an angel from heaven, as St. Paul (Galatians 1:8,) says on a similar occasion, (Calmet) should work a miracle, and afterwards adduce it in proof of a false religion, believe him not. The Jews and Christians had already received such convincing proofs from God, of the truth of what they had been taught, that they had reason to conclude either that the miracle was false, or that the person who would persuade them to embrace a different religion had fallen, after God had honoured him with miraculous powers: or, in fine, that if he were an impostor at the time when he exercised that power, like the magicians of Egypt, or Balaam, the miracle was either not wrought in confirmation of what he preached, or at least it was eclipsed by some greater miracle in favour of the truth. Whether God will ever suffer a real miracle which may seem to countenance error, or not, this appears to be unquestionable, that he will never deny himself, or, in a contest of miracles, permit falsehood to gain the victory. If the magicians performed wonderful works, they were forced at last to confess their inferiority, and yield to Moses, Exodus 8:18, 19. Miracles are generally a proof of the truth of any doctrine; but when the doctrine is already established, as in this case of the unity of God, (ver. 2,) it may be adduced with propriety as a criterion of miracles. Truth can never be in contradiction to truth. The light of reason suffices to evince that there is but one God. The same truth had been repeatedly confirmed by miracles, particularly during the last forty years, during which God had manifested his power over all nature, in the sight of all the Hebrews, and had trampled on the idols of the Gentiles. If therefore any person should attempt, by his dreams or predictions, to invalidate this most fundamental and undeniable article, his testimony could not be received. (Haydock) --- The Jews, in vain, allege this passage against the religion of Jesus Christ. He did not subvert, but fulfilled the law; so far was he from endeavouring to persuade them to abandon the true God. (Calmet) --- If he had not come to act in this manner, the law would have contained in itself the seeds of dissolution, by falsely holding forth the expectation of a future Messias, who would bring all things to perfection, chap. 18:15., Genesis 3:15., and 49:10, etc. Hence when he really appeared, the Jews desired him to prove his mission by a miracle, as he did repeatedly, Matthew 12:38., John 8:40., and 10:25. --- A dream, of a mysterious kind, like those of Joseph and of the prophets. (Haydock)
