notes: This Haydock commentary employs extensive typological interpretation of Elisha's life and miracles. The commentary also mentions eschatological elements (future resurrection, relics, saints' influence in heaven) but these are more devotional applications than strict OT/NT typological prefigurement. The bones miracle typology is particularly detailed, emphasizing both Christological and eschatological dimensions.

original_text: King, Assaraddon, who led away the remnants of Israel, and fulfilled the prediction, Isaias 7:8. (Du Hamel) --- Babylon, or the territory. These people had been lately conquered from the Babylonian empire, from Syria, etc. --- Cutha: the greatest part were from this city; so that the Samaritans were afterwards called Cutheans. --- Emath, on the Orontes. --- Sepharvaim; or the Saspires, near Media. (Calmet) --- We find several other places mentioned, 1 Esdras 4:9. (Haydock)
notes: This commentary describes historical events from 2 Kings 17:24 concerning the Assyrian deportation of Israel and the resettlement of foreign peoples in the conquered territory. While it references Isaiah 7:8 (a predictive prophecy), the commentary focuses on geographical and historical identification of the peoples and places involved (Assaraddon, Babylon, Cutha, Emath, Sepharvaim) rather than typological prefigurement. The mention of Isaiah 7:8 is cited as a fulfilled prediction of historical events, not as a typological correspondence between an OT type and NT antitype. This is historical commentary and prophecy fulfillment, not typology in the technical sense of OT persons/events/institutions prefiguring their NT counterparts.

original_text: Sennacherib's expedition in Egypt and Asia are mentioned by Herodotus (II. 141.) and Berosus, (Josephus, [Antiquities?] 10:1.) but they do not say that he passed farther then Pelusium, (Calmet) the frontier on the Egyptian side of Palestine. (Haydock) --- These expeditions might have been performed in less than eight months, during the 14th year of Ezechias, who fell sick, perhaps soon after the ruin of Sennacherib's army, 4 Kings 20:1. Isaias 10:28. represents the Assyrian proceeding from Gabaa towards Egypt, and thence he ascended to attack the cities of Juda, (ver. 25.) Manresa, (Micheas 1:15.) etc. While he was before Lachis, Ezechias, dreading the horrors of war, purchased a peace: but the tyrant soon after sent to require him to surrender at discretion; and in the mean time he went to besiege Lebna, where his envoys found him, having received no answer from the king of Juda. The haughty Assyrian being obliged to go to meet the king of Chus, sent insolent letters to Ezechias; but the latter was assured that all his menaces were to be despised, and on the same night that Sennacherib left Lebna, the angel destroyed 185,000 of his men. It is thought that the siege of Lachis did not take place till three years after Sennacherib had come into Palestine, and after he had spent that time in attacking Egypt, 4 Kings 19:24. (Josephus, [Antiquities?] 10:2., and 3.) --- He attempted afterwards to take the southern cities of Juda, in order to cut off all communication with Egypt; as Nabuchodonosor, Holofernes, and Eupator probably intended to do, Jeremias 24:7., Judith vi., and vii., and 1 Machabees 6:31. (Calmet) --- Offended, and been imprudent. (Menochius) --- Gold, so that the value of each was equal. (Du Hamel) --- Josephus reads, "or thirty," as if that quantity of gold would suffice. (Haydock) --- The talent contains 3000 sicles. (Menochius) --- The heart of Ezechias fainted at the approach of so great an army, though he had before made the greatest preparations, 4 Kings 20:2., 2 Paralipomenon 32:5., and Ecclesiasticus 48:19. (Tirinus)
notes: This Haydock commentary on 2 Kings 18:13 provides historical, geographical, and chronological analysis of Sennacherib's military campaign against Judah during King Hezekiah's reign. While the passage describes significant historical events (the Assyrian siege, divine deliverance through angelic intervention, etc.), the commentary does not explicitly establish any typological relationships between Old Testament persons, events, or institutions and their New Testament fulfillments. The focus is entirely on historical contextualization, cross-referencing other biblical and extra-biblical sources (Herodotus, Josephus, Berosus), and clarifying the sequence and nature of military actions. No type-antitype connection is articulated in this commentary.

original_text: Destroy. Prosperity renders a man insolent, and the passions blind him. Rabsaces interprets success to be a sure proof of the divine approbation, and thus attempts to justify all the excesses of his master. (Calmet) --- God only used Sennacherib as a rod to chastise his people. (Menochius) --- The most wicked often represent themselves as the executioners of God's will, and attribute their ambition to his decrees. (Haydock) --- God did not order the Assyrians to destroy the land: he rather threatened to destroy them, Isaias xxxvii., and 2 Paralipomenon xxxii. (Worthington)
notes: This commentary does not describe typological relationships between Old Testament types and New Testament antitypes. Instead, it discusses: (1) moral/spiritual lessons about pride and self-deception (Rabshakeh's misinterpretation of success as divine approval), (2) God's use of Sennacherib as an instrument of judgment ('a rod to chastise'), and (3) general theological principles about wicked rulers claiming divine sanction. While the passage involves God's providential use of a pagan king for purposes of judgment, this represents a typological *pattern* or *principle* rather than a specific OT type prefiguring an NT antitype. The commentary does not identify any OT person, event, or institution that prefigures a specific NT fulfillment.

original_text: Virgin. The few who adhere to the Lord despise all idols and their votaries. (Worthington) --- Of Sion and of Jerusalem may denote those places. Towns and provinces are often represented as women: the daughter of Babylon, the daughter of the sea, mean Babylon and a maritime town. Perhaps this comparison is used through tenderness and affection for a place. (Calmet) --- Even the most timid female would shortly despise the fallen tyrant. (Haydock) --- Wagged, out of contempt, or in a threatening manner, Psalm 21:8., and Matthew 27:39. (Menochius)
notes: This commentary discusses symbolic and metaphorical language rather than typological relationships. The references to 'virgin,' 'daughter of Sion,' and 'daughter of Jerusalem' are explained as personifications of places and provinces using feminine imagery—a common literary device in ancient texts to represent cities and nations with tenderness and affection. The citation of Psalm 21:8 and Matthew 27:39 regarding the 'wagging' gesture serves as parallel examples of the same gesture in different contexts, not as a type-antitype fulfillment relationship. No OT person, event, or institution is presented as prefiguring a NT fulfillment.

original_text: Dial. Hebrew also, "steps." St. Jerome confesses that he followed Symmachus in Isaias 38:7. Whether this dial resembled one of ours, (Grotius) or was made in the form of steps, (St. Cyril, hom. 3, in Isaias, etc.) or rather of a half globe, (Calmet) after the Babylonian fashion, (Vitruvius 9:9.) is not clear. Some have asserted that hours were not known to the Hebrews, before the captivity. (Usher, the year of the world 3291.) --- But Tobias 12:22 who wrote at Nineve, under the reign of Manasses, clearly speaks of them. The Egyptians pretend that they invented water hour-glasses. But the invention of dials is attributed to the Chaldeans, from whom Anaximander introduced them among the Greeks, under the reign of Cyrus. He died in the year of the world 3457. --- Achaz had much to do with Theglathphalasar; (chap. 17:8.) and probably obtained this curiosity from the same country. In more ancient times, people measured time by the length of their shadow, and were invited to a feast at such a foot, in the same manner as we should invite for such an hour. (Palladius, Rustic. xii.) (Calmet) --- Till the year of Rome 595, when Nasica dedicated the first water hour-glass, the Romans knew not how the time passed on cloudy days. (Pliny, [Natural History?] 7:60.) (Vitruvius 9:9.) --- Grotius supposes that the dial of Achaz was a concave semicircular gnomon, in which a globe was placed, the shadow of which fell on twenty-eight lines. (Du Hamel)
notes: This Haydock commentary on 2 Kings 20:11 focuses entirely on historical, archaeological, and technical matters regarding the dial (sundial) of Ahaz. The discussion covers: the physical construction and appearance of the dial, the history of timekeeping devices among various ancient peoples (Hebrews, Egyptians, Chaldeans, Greeks, Romans), and the origin of the technology. While the passage itself (the miraculous reversal of the sun's shadow on Ahaz's dial as a sign of Hezekiah's healing) could potentially have typological significance in other contexts, this particular commentary makes no attempt to identify or explain any typological relationship between this event and New Testament fulfillments. The commentary is purely descriptive and historical rather than theological or typological in nature.

original_text: Grove. The idol of Astarte, or the representation of a grove in sculpture. (Haydock) --- People, who were not rich enough to have a sepulchre. Jeremias (xix. 11.) threatens the people of Jerusalem with such a burial. (Calmet) --- The common people here means the idolaters, 2 Paralipomenon 34:4. (Haydock)
notes: This Haydock commentary on 2 Kings 23:6 discusses King Josiah's religious reforms, specifically his destruction of idolatrous objects (the grove/Asherah pole representing Astarte worship) and the desecration of graves of common people/idolaters. The commentary provides historical context, cross-references to related passages (Jeremiah 19:11 and 2 Chronicles 34:4), and clarifies the identity of those buried in these common graves. However, it does not establish any typological relationship between Old Testament persons, events, or institutions and their New Testament fulfillments. The text is purely historical and contextual in nature, dealing with religious purification during Josiah's reign rather than prefigurative or foreshadowing patterns.

original_text: Sepulchre. Paralipomenon xxxv., in the monument (or mausoleum) of his fathers. Such was the end of Josias: he fell gloriously in defence of his country, as he had spent his life in promoting religion. God therefore withdrew him from the sight of the miseries which were shortly to fall on his devoted people, 4 Kings 22:20. (Haydock) --- He was a prince of most excellent disposition, and receives the highest encomium, ver. 25., and Ecclesiasticus 49:1. Jeremias composed his funeral canticle, which was sung on his anniversary for many years, 2 Paralipomenon 35:24. The mourning for this pious king became proverbial, and resembled that which should be made for the Messias, Zacharias 12:11. The life and death of Josias prefigured those of Jesus Christ; who should be long expected as the restorer of the true religion, the teacher of a more excellent law, and the most innocent victim for the sins of the people. The glorious Phase under Josias, was but a faint representation of the eucharistic sacrifice. (Calmet)

extractions.type_description: A pious king devoted to promoting true religion, who fell gloriously defending his country and was withdrawn by God from seeing the miseries that would befall his people. He was long-expected as a restorer of true religion and teacher of excellent law.
extractions.antitype_description: The ultimate restorer of true religion, teacher of a more excellent law, and the innocent victim for the sins of the people
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states: 'The life and death of Josias prefigured those of Jesus Christ; who should be long expected as the restorer of the true religion, the teacher of a more excellent law, and the most innocent victim for the sins of the people.' This is a direct and clearly articulated typological connection between Josias as OT type and Christ as NT antitype.

extractions.type_description: The glorious Passover observance under King Josias
extractions.antitype_description: The Eucharist as the fulfillment and ultimate sacrifice commemorated in the sacrament
extractions.reasoning: Calmet explicitly states: 'The glorious Phase under Josias, was but a faint representation of the eucharistic sacrifice.' This directly connects the OT Passover observance to the NT Eucharist as a sacramental type-antitype relationship.

notes: The commentary also mentions that the mourning for Josias 'resembled that which should be made for the Messias' (Zechariah 12:11), which reinforces the Christological typology. Both extractions are attributed to Calmet in the commentary.

original_text: Fire, to testify his approbation. (Worthington; Tirinus) See Genesis 4:4., and 2 Paralipomenon 7:1. (Calmet) --- This altar represented the cross, on which the Victim of our reconciliation [Jesus Christ] was offered. (Du Hamel)

extractions.type_name: The Altar (at the threshing floor of Ornan)
extractions.type_description: The altar constructed in 1 Chronicles 21:26 where David offered sacrifices and received fire from heaven as a sign of God's approbation and acceptance
extractions.antitype_description: The cross upon which Jesus Christ was offered as the ultimate Victim of reconciliation for humanity's sins
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states 'This altar represented the cross, on which the Victim of our reconciliation [Jesus Christ] was offered.' This directly connects an OT sacrificial object (the altar) to the NT fulfillment in Christ's sacrificial death. The altar prefigures the cross as the place where God's ultimate sacrifice would be made. The fire from heaven testifying God's approbation of the altar sacrifice prefigures God's acceptance of Christ's sacrifice.

notes: The commentary also references Genesis 4:4 (Abel's offering receiving divine fire) and 2 Chronicles 7:1 (fire from heaven at the dedication of Solomon's temple), suggesting a broader typological pattern of altars and divine fire acceptance throughout Scripture, all pointing to Christ's ultimate sacrifice.

original_text: Proselytes. This is the first time that the word occurs in the Vulgate. See Exodus 12:45. It means "strangers," (Calmet) who were not allowed to live in the country, unless they would observe the natural law, and renounce idolatry. (Rabbins) --- These had embraced the Jewish religion. (Menochius) --- They were the remnants of the people of Chanaan, (3 Kings 9:20,) and were treated as public slaves, which could not have been done, with justice or policy, with regard to those who might barely wish to reside in the country. These strangers prefigured the Gentiles, chosen to build the Christian Church.

extractions.type_description: Gentile strangers who embraced Jewish religion and were incorporated into the Jewish community, treated as public servants in building the temple
extractions.antitype_name: The Gentiles in the Christian Church
extractions.antitype_description: Gentiles called and chosen to build the Christian Church through faith in Christ
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states: 'These strangers prefigured the Gentiles, chosen to build the Christian Church.' This directly connects the OT reality (foreign proselytes incorporated into Israel) with the NT fulfillment (Gentiles becoming part of the Church). The parallel is structural: just as strangers were included in Israel's community and served in temple construction, so Gentiles are included in the Church's building.

notes: The typology is particularly focused on the ecclesial dimension - the inclusion of outsiders (Gentiles) in God's covenant community. The commentary notes these strangers 'renounce idolatry' and 'embraced the Jewish religion,' which parallels Gentile conversion to Christianity. The context of temple building in 1 Chronicles 22 adds a secondary layer: just as proselytes participated in constructing the physical temple, Gentiles participate in building the spiritual temple (the Church).

original_text: Peaceable. Hebrew, "Solomon," which has this meaning. (Calmet) --- Herein Solomon was a figure of Christ, who is styled the Prince of peace, Isaias ix. (Worthington)

extractions.type_description: King Solomon of Israel, whose name means 'peaceable' in Hebrew, established during a time of peace and rest from warfare
extractions.antitype_description: Christ, referred to as the 'Prince of Peace' (Isaiah 9:6), who brings spiritual peace and is the ultimate fulfillment of the messianic promise
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states 'Herein Solomon was a figure of Christ, who is styled the Prince of peace' and cites Isaiah 9 as the NT fulfillment. This is a direct typological claim linking Solomon's peaceful reign to Christ's role as Prince of Peace. The etymological connection (Solomon = 'peaceable') reinforces the typological meaning.

notes: This is a classic Christological type where an OT figure prefigures Christ. The Haydock commentary attributes this typological reading to Worthington. The connection relies on both the semantic meaning of Solomon's name and the thematic parallel of peace associated with both figures.

original_text: Name. See 2 Kings 7:13. (Menochius) --- A son. The crimes into which Solomon fell, hinder us from explaining this literally of him. St. Paul refers the expression to Jesus Christ, Hebrews 1:5. (Calmet) --- St. Augustine (de C.[City of God?] 17:8 and 9.) observes that the promises were not perfectly fulfilled in Solomon.

extractions.type_description: Solomon, who would build the temple and establish a kingdom, prefigured as God's son in the Davidic covenant (2 Samuel 7:14)
extractions.antitype_description: The ultimate Son of God and fulfillment of the Davidic covenant, to whom Hebrews 1:5 applies the promise 'I will be his Father, and he shall be my Son'
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that St. Paul refers the expression 'I will be his Father, and he shall be my Son' (1CH 22:10) to Jesus Christ in Hebrews 1:5. This is a direct typological connection where Solomon prefigures Christ. The commentary notes that the promises were not 'perfectly fulfilled in Solomon,' indicating that Solomon is an imperfect type whose ultimate fulfillment is in Christ.

notes: The Haydock commentary explicitly cites Hebrews 1:5 as St. Paul's typological interpretation. St. Augustine's observation that the promises were incompletely fulfilled in Solomon strengthens the typological reading, as it suggests Solomon serves as a type pointing to a greater fulfillment in the antitype (Christ). The reference to Solomon's moral failings ('crimes into which Solomon fell') further supports the notion that he is presented as an imperfect type that requires ultimate fulfillment in the sinless Christ.

original_text: My son, by the mouth of Nathan, 2 Kings 7:13. (Menochius) --- Solomon was a figure of Christ, and his dignity was predicted, 1 Paralipomenon 17:11., and 3 Kings 1:13. (Calmet)

extractions.type_description: The son of David, chosen by God through the prophet Nathan to succeed his father as king of Israel, whose dignity and kingdom were divinely predicted
extractions.antitype_description: The ultimate fulfillment of the Davidic covenant, the Son of God who inherits an eternal kingdom
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states 'Solomon was a figure of Christ, and his dignity was predicted.' This is a direct typological claim connecting the OT figure of Solomon to the NT antitype of Christ. The typology is reinforced by reference to 1 Chronicles 17:11, which contains the Davidic covenant promise that finds its ultimate fulfillment in Christ.

notes: The commentary cites multiple scriptural sources (2 Kings 7:13, 1 Paralipomenon 17:11, 3 Kings 1:13) to establish both the historical context (Nathan's role in designating Solomon) and the theological foundation (the predicted nature of Solomon's dignity as foreshadowing Christ's kingdom). This represents a well-established typological tradition in biblical scholarship regarding Solomon as a type of the Messiah.

original_text: Lions. St. Jerome seems to have read cephir, instead of the present cephor, which is rendered "a cup, or bowl," 1 Esdras 1:10. (Calmet) --- Alexandrian Septuagint, "and of the flesh-hooks, libation vessels and bowls; and the weight of the golden and silver vessels (kepphoure; a word which they do not translate) of each weight." (Haydock) --- The change of i for u was very easy; and perhaps the basins were ornamented with representations of lions. (Du Hamel) (Menochius) --- We do not find cephor used before, to denote any of the vessels of the tabernacle: but Esdras uses it, (chap. 8:27.) whence it is inferred that it is of Chaldean extraction.
notes: This Haydock commentary focuses on textual criticism and the identification of Hebrew vessels used in the tabernacle service (1 Chronicles 28:17). The discussion concerns: (1) variant readings of the Hebrew word 'cephor' (cup/bowl) vs. Jerome's reading of 'cephir' (lions); (2) comparison with the Septuagint translation; (3) the possible Chaldean etymology of the term; and (4) whether the basins were decorated with lion representations. No typological relationship between an Old Testament type and New Testament antitype is presented or implied in this commentary. The passage deals with historical-grammatical exegesis and textual variants rather than typological interpretation.

original_text: Purest. Hebrew, "refined." --- Lord. He was represented as riding in a chariot, drawn by Cherubim, (Calmet) or sitting on their wings. (Haydock) --- Two, particularly, filled up the space between the walls in the most holy place, and covered the ark, and also the Cherubim made by Moses, 3 Kings 7:23.

extractions.type_name: The Cherubim and God's Throne in the Holy of Holies
extractions.type_description: The Cherubim in the Temple's Most Holy Place, depicted as bearing or framing God's presence, with God represented as riding in a chariot drawn by Cherubim or sitting upon their wings
extractions.antitype_name: Christ in Glory / The Ascended Christ
extractions.antitype_description: Jesus Christ seated at the right hand of God the Father, exalted in heaven in a position of divine majesty and power
extractions.reasoning: The commentary describes the Cherubim as the vehicle or throne of God's presence and majesty in the Old Testament sanctuary. This representation of God enthroned above the Cherubim prefigures Christ's exaltation and enthronement at God's right hand in heaven. The emphasis on God's presence being carried/upheld by Cherubim parallels the idea of Christ as the radiance and image of God's glory (Hebrews 1:3). While not explicit in the commentary itself, this is a recognized typological pattern in biblical scholarship.

notes: The Haydock commentary focuses primarily on architectural and descriptive details rather than explicit typological interpretation. The typological connection is implicit in the traditional understanding that the Temple's imagery of God enthroned on the Cherubim points forward to Christ's heavenly exaltation. The commentary's reference to Exodus 25 imagery (Cherubim coverage) and the Temple design would support this reading in broader typological studies.

original_text: Flowers. They represented lilies or other flowers (Tirinus) full-blown, when the lamps were burning. All the branches were of pure gold. (Calmet)
notes: This Haydock commentary on 2 Chronicles 4:21 describes the decorative architectural features of the golden lampstand in the Temple - specifically the flowers (lilies or other blooms) adorning the branches. The commentary is purely descriptive and architectural in nature, explaining what the decorative elements represented in physical form. While the lampstand itself (as a Temple object) could potentially be subject to typological interpretation in other contexts, this particular commentary makes no connection to New Testament fulfillment or prefigurement. It does not present any OT type pointing forward to a NT antitype.

original_text: Cloud. See 3 Kings 8:10. (Menochius) --- It is called the glory of the Lord, because its appearance was luminous and awful, being a symbol of the divine presence. (Haydock)
notes: The Haydock commentary describes the cloud as a 'symbol of the divine presence' but does not establish a typological relationship between an Old Testament type and a New Testament antitype. The commentary is discussing the symbolic meaning and significance of the cloud phenomenon in its immediate historical context (the dedication of Solomon's Temple), not presenting it as a prefigurement of something in the New Testament. This falls under general symbolism or theological interpretation rather than typology as properly defined.

original_text: Devils. Hebrew, "goats." (Calmet) --- Septuagint express this by two names, "for the idols, and for the fools." (Haydock) --- The Mendesians of Egypt, solemnly worshipped the goat; and Pan was represented nearly in the same form. Yet it is probable that the Hebrews style the idols by this name out of derision, 3 Kings 15:2. (Calmet)
notes: This commentary discusses the Hebrew term for idols (literally 'goats') and their derision as names for false gods, particularly in the context of Egyptian worship practices (the Mendesians worshipping goats, Pan represented as goat-like). The passage deals with lexicography, cultural context, and the Hebrew practice of mockingly naming idols. While goats appear elsewhere in Scripture with typological significance (e.g., the scapegoat in Leviticus 16 as a type of Christ's atonement), this particular commentary makes no connection between the goat-idols of 2 Chronicles 11:15 and any New Testament fulfillment. It is purely exegetical and historical in nature, explaining the literal meaning and cultural background of the term, not establishing an OT type that prefigures an NT antitype.

original_text: For even. Protestants, "and also in Judah things went well;" (Haydock) or, "he spoke good words even to Juda." (Calmet) --- Septuagint, "for even in Juda there were good words, and in all pleasing." Words are often put for works. (Haydock) --- The Lord regarded the fidelity of some, and the humility of the princes. (Calmet) --- This advantage was derived from tribulation, that the king entered into himself, at least for a time: (Haydock) but he was not constant, ver. 14. After the scourge was withdrawn, he presently relapsed. He had betrayed great cowardice, as even his son confessed; and had probably been treated with great indignity, (Tirinus) as it was the custom with Sesac, or Sesostris, to chain the conquered princes to his triumphal car, and to leave obscene representations of women in the country. (Josephus, [Antiquities?] 8:4.) (Herodotus ii.) --- Sesostris proceeded to the conquest of Asia. (Tirinus)
notes: This Haydock commentary on 2 Chronicles 12:12 focuses on historical narrative, moral lessons about repentance and backsliding, and textual variants rather than typological interpretation. The passage discusses King Rehoboam's temporary humility following divine punishment (the invasion by Sesac/Shishak) and his subsequent relapse into unfaithfulness. While the commentary contains spiritual and moral instruction about tribulation leading to self-examination and the danger of inconstancy in faith, these represent ethical lessons and historical analysis rather than typological prefigurement of New Testament realities. No explicit connection between this OT event and any NT antitype is presented in the text.

original_text: Graven. Protestants, "a carved image (the idol which he had made) in," etc. It seems to have been sacred to the grove, (Haydock) or a representation of Astarte, 4 Kings 21:7. The ark was taken away, (chap. 25:3.) to make place for this impure deity, which had four (St. Basil) or five faces, (Eusebius; Salien) that people might adore it on all sides.
notes: This Haydock commentary discusses the historical and religious context of King Manasseh's idolatry in 2 Chronicles 33:7, specifically describing a carved image (likely representing Astarte) that replaced the Ark of the Covenant in the temple. While the commentary mentions the Ark and contrasts it with the idolatrous image, it does not establish or discuss any typological relationship between an Old Testament type and a New Testament antitype. The commentary is purely historical and descriptive in nature, explaining the religious syncretism and idolatrous practices of the period, not making typological connections to New Testament fulfillment.

original_text: In. Hebrew, "And (Calmet) or But in," as [in] 2 Paralipomenon 36:22. (Haydock) --- Thus the historical works are connected. Spinosa infers, from this book being inserted after Daniel in the Hebrew Bible, that the same author wrote both. But the order of the books in the Septuagint and Vulgate is far more natural, (Calmet) and this has often varied in Hebrew, etc. (Kennicott) See 2 Paralipomenon 36:23. (Haydock) --- First. The design was only put in execution the following year. (The year of the world 3468.) --- Cyrus (Hebrew coresh, (Haydock) or Koresch) means "the sun," according to Ctesias and Plutarch. Josephus ([Antiquities?] 11:1.) informs us that this prince became a friend of the Jews, in consequence of having seen the prediction of Isaias (xliv. 28., and 45:1.) fulfilled in his own person. He took Babylon, the year of the world 3466, and established the Persian empire, which was subverted by Alexander. (Calmet) --- He had before ruled over Persia 27 years, and only reigned three as sole monarch at Babylon. (Tirinus) --- The Lord; every good notion, even in infidels, proceeds from him. (Du Hamel) --- Cyrus was one of the best and greatest conquerors of antiquity. He was the son of Cambyses, by Mandane, princess of Media. Xenophon informs us that he died in his bed; (Haydock) and had been lately conquered. (Tirinus)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Ezra 1:1 is primarily concerned with historical and textual matters: the connection between Ezra and 2 Chronicles, the ordering of biblical books, the etymology of Cyrus's name, biographical details about Cyrus (his lineage, conquests, reign duration), and the historical circumstances of his rise to power. While the commentary mentions that Josephus reports Cyrus became friendly toward the Jews after seeing Isaiah's predictions fulfilled in his person, this reference to predictive prophecy does not establish a typological relationship. Typology requires an OT person, event, or institution that prefigures (serves as a type for) a corresponding NT fulfillment (antitype). The commentary does not identify Cyrus or any element of this passage as prefiguring a New Testament reality. Rather, it treats Cyrus as a historical figure whose actions fulfilled Old Testament prophecy in a direct, predictive sense—which is prophecy fulfillment rather than typology.

original_text: Zorobabel was the prince, Josue the high priest. (Calmet) --- There are 12 mentioned in 2 and 3 Esdras. But here the sixth Nahamani, or Enenion, is omitted. (Haydock) --- They represented the 12 tribes, (Kennicott) and were chiefs. (Menochius) --- It is wonderful that Esdras is not here mentioned, as well as Nehemias, who led a company after him, many of whom are here recorded. (Calmet) --- They might come to take care of their patrimony, and return into Chaldea, like Mardochai, (Tirinus.; though it does not seem to be Esther's uncle, Du Hamel) and Nehemias, who is styled also Athersatha, ver. 63. (Tirinus) --- Baana. 3 Esdras adds, "their leaders." (Haydock)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Ezra 2:2 focuses on historical and genealogical analysis rather than typological interpretation. The passage discusses the identity of specific leaders (Zorobabel and Josue), the representation of the 12 tribes through appointed chiefs, and clarifications about which individuals are mentioned or omitted in different versions of Ezra. While the commentary notes that 'They represented the 12 tribes,' this is a statement of historical/symbolic representation within the Old Testament context itself, not a prefiguration of New Testament fulfillment. No explicit connection to New Testament persons, events, or institutions is made or implied in the commentary.

original_text: Words, or transactions written by Nehemias. (Menochius) --- Helcias, or Hebrew and Septaugint, "Chelcias." --- Casleu, the third of the civil year, 1 Esdras 10:9. --- Year of Artaxerxes, (Calmet) after he was associated with his father on the throne; (Tirinus) or rather the death of Xerxes.
