(Haydock) --- St. Chrysostom represents this place as visited by pilgrims, instructive and more brilliant than any throne. (Hom. 5. ad Pop. Ant.) -- Septuagint add, "upon the dung, without the city: and after a long time had elapsed, his wife also said to him, How long wilt thou wait, saying: Lo, I will still tarry a little while, expecting the hope of my salvation? For behold thy memory is perished from the land, thy sons and daughters, the pains and labours of my womb, whom I brought forth in labour and sorrow, to no purpose. But thou sittest in the open air, the night long, amid the corruption of worms, while I wander like a slave, seeking for one place and house after another, in expectation of the sun setting, that my labours may cease, and the sorrows which now surround and hold me fast. But speak thou some word to (or against) the Lord, and die." (Haydock) --- This addition has been omitted in the Complutensian edition, to make it like the Vulgate, (Calmet) though it is found in all the Greek copies (Nobilius) and fathers, and also in several Latin Bibles. It seems, however, to be only a gloss of some transcriber. The devil had not destroyed this wife, as she would prove one of his most powerful auxiliaries. (Calmet)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Job 2:8 focuses on the literal details of Job's suffering (scraping himself with a potsherd while sitting on ashes/dunghill) and includes textual criticism comparing the Hebrew, Vulgate, and Septuagint versions. While St. Chrysostom's observation that the dunghill became 'more brilliant than any throne' carries symbolic or spiritual weight, the commentary does not explicitly establish a typological relationship between Job's suffering and a New Testament antitype. The commentary treats Job's affliction as a historical narrative detail and occasion for moral/spiritual reflection rather than as a prefigurement of Christ or another NT reality. No OT type/NT antitype pairing is articulated.

original_text: Seven days, etc. They sat with him for a good part of the day, and of the night, during seven days: and spoke nothing all that time that could give him any uneasiness. (Challoner) (Menochius) (Olympiad.) --- They mourned for him as if he had been dead. Their mutual grief was too great for utterance. But the text seems to intimate that they remained with Job, all this time. (Scultet.) (Calmet) --- Their design in coming was really to afford him consolation; but being under a mistake, respecting the conduct of Providence towards mankind, (Calmet) they erred involuntarily, (Tirinus) and by attempting to prove their assertions, as if none but criminals could be so grievously afflicted, they eventually insulted the holy man, Tobias 2:15. --- They argued on the principle, "that under a just God no one is miserable, unless he have deserved it;" not reflecting that God sometimes puts his best servants to the trial, that their merit and glory may increase. Notwithstanding their piety and learning, they became therefore the devil's most powerful agents unawares: (Calmet) and though they were not properly heretics, as they acquiesced when better informed, they were a figure of them, by drawing from many undeniable truths false inferences, and by a parade of learning, and of new things. (St. Gregory, Mor. 3:24., and 5:18.) --- They also judged rashly of Job's secret behaviour. (Worthington)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Job 2:13 does not present typological relationships between Old Testament types and New Testament antitypes. While the commentary mentions that Job's friends 'were a figure of them [heretics],' this represents a typological analogy within the Old Testament itself (Job's friends as figures of later heretics) rather than an OT type prefiguring an NT antitype. The reference to Tobias 2:15 is comparative but not typological. The discussion focuses on moral theology, the problem of suffering, and the nature of false reasoning about divine providence—themes relevant to biblical commentary but not to typology as traditionally defined in the OT-to-NT prophetic fulfillment sense.

original_text: Themanite. People of this city, about twelve miles from Petra, in Arabia, were renowned for wisdom, Jeremias 49:7., and Baruch 3:22. Pythagoras therefore visited this country. (St. Cyril, contra Jul. x.) --- Eliphaz attempts to prove that no innocent person is chastised. He does not speak of small faults, to which any person may be exposed, and which God may severely punish. But he will have Job to be a great offender, at least in secret, and represents himself in too advantageous a light; though he was really a good man, and meant well. (Calmet) --- But this did not exempt him from sin, (chap. 42.) no more than Eliu, Job 32. Bonum ex integra causa; malum ex quolibet defectu; as theologians agree. (Haydock)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Job 4:1 contains no typological relationships. The passage discusses the historical identity of Eliphaz the Temanite, his geographical origins, and the theological argument he presents to Job regarding suffering and sin. The commentary includes references to Jeremiah 49:7 and Baruch 3:22 (historical/geographical context), mentions of Pythagoras (historical reference), and theological principles about sin and divine punishment. While the commentary touches on Old Testament figures (Job, Elihu) and theological concepts, it does not establish any prefigurative connection between Old Testament persons, events, or institutions and their New Testament fulfillments. The content is primarily exegetical and moral-theological rather than typological.

original_text: Sea. Ungovernable and malicious. Some of the ancients looked upon the sea as a huge animal, whose breathing caused the tides. (Strabo i.; Solin xxxii.) --- They represented its fury as proverbial. "Fire, the sea, and woman are three evils;" and they call the most savage people sons of Neptune. (Agel. 15:21.) --- Am I so violent as to require such barriers? Am I capacious, or strong enough to bear such treatment? (Calmet)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Job 7:12 discusses the symbolic and metaphorical meanings of 'the sea' in ancient literature and philosophy, but does not establish any typological relationship between an Old Testament type and a New Testament antitype. The commentary focuses on: (1) ancient pagan interpretations of the sea as a living creature, (2) the sea as a symbol of ungovernable fury in classical literature, and (3) Job's rhetorical question about whether he deserves such harsh treatment. While 'the sea' functions symbolically in the text, this commentary does not connect it to any Old Testament prefigurement of New Testament fulfillment. This is general symbolism and literary analysis rather than biblical typology.

original_text: How long. He seems tired with hearing, (Haydock) and accuses Job of want of moderation, representing him as a hypocrite, (Calmet) and an obstinate defender of his own opinion, against the better judgment of Eliphaz; (Menochius) though he was in reality only a constant asserter of truth. (Worthington)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Job 8:2 discusses Bildad's impatient response to Job's lengthy defense, characterizing Job's words as excessive and representing him as a hypocrite or obstinate defender of his own opinion. The passage is concerned with the immediate historical context of the dialogue between Job and his friends—their interpersonal dynamics and moral assessments of each other's character. No typological relationship between an Old Testament type and New Testament antitype is present. This is exegetical and moral commentary on the book of Job itself, not a typological prefigurement of New Testament fulfillment.

original_text: Pillars. These are represented as fixed in the waters, Proverbs 8:29., and Psalm 27:16., etc.
notes: This Haydock commentary discusses the cosmological imagery of earth's pillars being set in waters (referencing Job 9:6, Proverbs 8:29, and Psalm 27:16). While it contains symbolic and metaphorical language about creation's stability, it does not present a typological relationship between an Old Testament type and a New Testament antitype. The commentary is descriptive of OT cosmological symbolism rather than establishing a prefiguration of NT fulfillment. No OT person, event, or institution is connected to a NT fulfillment in this passage.

original_text: Dim. Hebrew and Septuagint, "covered with the shadow of death," (Haydock) greatly impaired. Some have almost lost their sight by weeping; and death seemed ready to close Job's eyes. (Calmet)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Job 16:17 discusses Job's physical and emotional suffering—specifically the dimming of his eyes due to weeping and his proximity to death. The commentary is primarily concerned with explaining the literal meaning of the Hebrew and Septuagint texts and describing Job's deteriorated condition. While Job is occasionally understood typologically in Christian tradition (as a type of the suffering righteous or prefiguring Christ's passion), this particular commentary makes no explicit connection between Job's suffering and any New Testament fulfillment or antitype. The commentary remains at the level of historical-literal exegesis rather than typological interpretation.

original_text: Example. Protestants, "a tabret." (Haydock) --- The people sing over my misfortune, Lamentations 3:14. I am represented as a victim of God's just indignation. (Calmet) --- Septuagint, "a laughter," or laughing-stock. (Haydock)

extractions.type_name: Job as a victim of God's indignation
extractions.type_description: Job suffering as a representation of one who bears God's just judgment, becoming a laughing-stock and spectacle to others
extractions.antitype_name: Christ as the suffering servant and victim
extractions.antitype_description: Jesus Christ bearing God's indignation for humanity's sins, becoming a spectacle and object of mockery (as referenced in Lamentations 3:14 pattern and fulfilled in the Passion narratives)
extractions.reasoning: The Haydock commentary explicitly states Job 'is represented as a victim of God's just indignation,' which parallels the scapegoat/suffering servant typology. The reference to Lamentations 3:14 (a messianic lamentation psalm) and the emphasis on Job becoming a laughing-stock suggests a prefigurement of Christ's suffering and humiliation on behalf of others. Job's vicarious suffering represents the pattern of Christ as the ultimate victim who bears divine judgment.

notes: This typology is implicit rather than explicit in the commentary. The connection relies on the interplay between Job's status as 'a victim of God's just indignation' and the messianic framework established by the Lamentations reference. Haydock does not directly state 'Job prefigures Christ,' but the language of vicarious suffering and divine judgment suggests a typological reading consistent with patristic and medieval exegesis.

original_text: Understand ye. Teach this man to comprehend what we say. He deigns not to address Job in person: but repeats most of his former remarks respecting the wicked, as if they were unquestionably applicable to Job, Job 8. (Calmet) --- Hebrew, "mark ye." Septuagint, "do thou attend." (Haydock) --- Baldad speaks to many who might be of Job's opinion, as he was a figure of the Church, defending the common cause; while his friends, like heretics, speak both true and false things. (St. Gregory 14:1.) (Worthington)

extractions.type_description: Job as a figure in the Old Testament narrative, representing the righteous sufferer defending truth against false accusers
extractions.antitype_description: The New Testament Church, which defends the common cause of faith and truth against heretical errors
extractions.reasoning: St. Gregory (cited via Worthington) explicitly states that 'he [Job] was a figure of the Church, defending the common cause; while his friends, like heretics, speak both true and false things.' This establishes Job as a type prefiguring the Church's role in defending orthodoxy against false doctrine.

notes: The typological connection here is somewhat secondary to the immediate historical interpretation of Job 18:2, but St. Gregory's patristic commentary does establish Job as an ecclesial type. The antitype is the Church in its role as defender of truth against heretical teachings. The friends of Job are presented as a contrasting type of heretics who mix truth with falsehood, which helps clarify the ecclesial typology by opposition.

original_text: Redeemer may be understood of the Deity, without confining it to the second Person; (Isaias 41:14., and 49:7.; Piscator) though it may have a more peculiar reference to Christ: (Junius; Haydock) in whom he believed, as the Redeemer of all mankind. (Calmet) --- Earth. Yea, ere long I shall be restored to health, (St. Chrysostom; Grotius) as an earnest and figure of the resurrection. Nothing is more common, in Scripture, than for the same prophecy to have a double accomplishment; one soon after it is made public, and another more sublime and remote. Job seemed to have no expectation of surviving his present misery, (ver. 7., and Job 7:7., and 24:15.) unless God now revealed it to him, as a figure of his future resurrection, founded on the hope of our Saviour's, which he expresses in much clearer terms. Hebrew, "I know that my Redeemer is living, and that he will raise himself one day upon the earth," (Calmet) like a conqueror, (Haydock) or wrestler, having overthrown his antagonist: (Amama) or, "he will stand the last upon the earth, or dust," (Piscator) ascending his throne, to judge all. (Deodat.) --- Yet Luther translates, "and one day he will raise me up from the earth;" which is not conformable to the Hebrew. Others explain, "he....will place (26) this, my skin, after they (worms) shall have ruined it." (Pagnin; Montanus) --- But Amama suspects that the latter is not in earnest. Pineda defends the Vulgate and observes that yakum (Haydock) may signify, "will raise" himself, or "me;" the latter being at least a consequence of the former, if St. Jerome did not read it me in his copy. So St. Paul argues; If Christ be risen, we also shall rise again. Septuagint, "For I know that he is eternal, who will set me free," (Haydock) by death, (Calmet; or redemption; ekluein) "upon the earth."

extractions.type_name: Job's restoration to health from his suffering and misery
extractions.type_description: Job's expected recovery from his present afflictions, presented as a sign and earnest (pledge) of future restoration
extractions.antitype_name: The resurrection of Christ and believers through Him
extractions.antitype_description: Christ's resurrection from death and the consequent resurrection of all believers, which Job's anticipated healing prefigures
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that Job's restoration to health serves as 'an earnest and figure of the resurrection.' The text identifies Job's expected healing as a type that prefigures the ultimate antitype of resurrection through Christ, citing the principle that 'Nothing is more common, in Scripture, than for the same prophecy to have a double accomplishment; one soon after it is made public, and another more sublime and remote.' The connection is reinforced by St. Paul's argument: 'If Christ be risen, we also shall rise again.'

notes: The commentary emphasizes that Job 19:25 operates on multiple levels: an immediate level (Job's recovery from illness) and an ultimate prophetic level (Christ's resurrection and the believer's resurrection). The typology is explicitly acknowledged as a 'figure' or prefigurement. The redeemer is identified as Christ specifically, though the commentary notes it may reference the Deity more broadly. This is a clear case of eschatological typology where an OT event (anticipated personal restoration) prefigures NT fulfillment (bodily resurrection through Christ).

original_text: Myself. Hebrew, "for myself," and for my comfort; not like the reprobate, who shall see their judge to their eternal confusion. Job insists so much on this point, that he shews he is not speaking merely of the divine favour being restored to him, in the re-establishment of his health and affairs, but that he raises his mind to something more solid and desirable, of which the former was only a faint representation. (Calmet) --- "No one since Christ has spoken so plainly of the resurrection, as this man did before the coming of the Messias." (St. Jerome, ad Pam.) --- This. Hebrew, "though my reins be consumed within me;" (Protestants; Haydock) or, "my reins (desires and tender affections) are completed in my bosom." (Calmet)

extractions.type_name: Job's expectation of bodily resurrection and seeing God
extractions.type_description: Job's faith and confident assertion (Job 19:25-27) that he will be resurrected from death and will see God with his own eyes, despite his present suffering and bodily deterioration
extractions.antitype_name: Christ's resurrection and the resurrection of believers
extractions.antitype_description: The New Testament fulfillment of bodily resurrection through Christ's resurrection and the promise of believers seeing God face-to-face in the resurrection
extractions.reasoning: The Haydock commentary explicitly cites St. Jerome's statement: 'No one since Christ has spoken so plainly of the resurrection, as this man did before the coming of the Messias.' This directly identifies Job's testimony to resurrection as a prefigurement of Christ's resurrection and the doctrine of resurrection fulfilled in the New Testament. The commentary also notes that Job 'raises his mind to something more solid and desirable, of which the former [restoration of health and affairs] was only a faint representation,' indicating that the temporary restoration typifies the ultimate resurrection reality.

notes: The commentary frames Job's statement as a type rather than mere allegory or moral lesson, explicitly connecting it to messianic fulfillment. The typological relationship is eschatological in nature, involving both bodily resurrection and the beatific vision (seeing God). The commentary distinguishes between surface-level comfort (restoration of earthly circumstances) and the deeper typological meaning (eternal resurrection).

original_text: Hearken to. Literally, "look steadfastly on me." (Haydock) --- Compare my present with my former condition, and do not pretend to fathom God's judgments; which fill me also with astonishment, when I consider why the virtuous are distressed, and the wicked prosper, ver. 7. --- Mouth be silent. Harpocrates, the god of silence, was represented in this posture; and Virgil says, Intentique ora tenebant. (Aeneid ii.) --- Septuagint, "upon the cheek," like men in deep consideration. (Calmet)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Job 21:5 contains no typological relationships. The passage discusses Job's exhortation to his friends to listen to him and consider his perplexing circumstances—why the virtuous suffer while the wicked prosper. The commentary provides linguistic and literary parallels (references to Harpocrates, Virgil's Aeneid, and the Septuagint) but these are illustrative comparisons from classical sources, not typological connections between Old Testament prefigurations and New Testament fulfillments. The focus is on Job's rhetorical plea and the theological mystery of divine justice, not on types and antitypes.

original_text: Acceptable to the gravel of Cocytus. The Hebrew word, which St. Jerome has here rendered by the name Cocytus, (which the poets represent as a river in hell) signifies a valley or a torrent: and in this place, is taken for the low region of death, and hell: which willingly, as it were, receives the wicked at their death: who are ushered in by innumerable others that have gone before them; and are followed by multitudes above number. (Challoner) --- Isaias (xiv. 9.) and Ezechiel (xxxii. 21.) describe the splendid reception in hell of the kings of Babylon and of Egypt, nearly in the same manner as Job does that of any sinner who has lived in prosperity, Job 38:17. He gives life to the whole creation, in the true spirit of poetry. (Calmet) --- The rich man is represented as tenderly embraced by his mother earth; (chap. 1:21.; Haydock) the very stones and turf press lightly upon him; as the ancients prayed, Sit tibi terra levis. Hebrew, "the stones or clods of the torrent (Calmet) shall be sweet to him, and he," etc. (Haydock) --- St. Jerome has chosen to mention a particular river, instead of the general term nel, "a torrent or vale," to intimate that Job is speaking of the state after death. --- Cocytus is a branch of the Styx, a river of Arcadia, of a noxious quality, which the poets have place in hell. (Pineda) --- Septuagint, "The pebbles of the torrent became sweet to him, and in his train every man shall come, and unnumbered men before him." Alexandrian manuscript has "men of number;" the two first letters of anarithmetoi being omitted. (Haydock) --- The Church reads in her office for St. Stephen, Lapides torrentis illi dulces fuerunt: ipsum sequuntur omnes animae justae. Many explain this passage of Job as a menace. The wicked have carried their insolence so far as to (Calmet) give orders to (Haydock) be buried with the utmost pomp: but in the other world, they shall be thrown ignominiously among the other dead. (St. Gregory, etc.) (Calmet) --- They were little moved with the thought of death, as it was common to all. But what will they think of eternal misery? (Haydock)

extractions.type_name: Job's description of the wicked receiving earth/stones sweetly in death
extractions.type_description: Job 21:33 describes how the wicked are received into the grave/underworld (Cocytus/torrent/valley of death) where earth and stones become sweet to them, and they are followed by multitudes of the dead
extractions.antitype_name: St. Stephen and the righteous in the Church's understanding
extractions.antitype_description: The Church applies this passage to St. Stephen in her liturgical office, reinterpreting it: 'Lapides torrentis illi dulces fuerunt: ipsum sequuntur omnes animae justae' (The pebbles of the torrent became sweet to him; all the souls of the just follow him). The stones that were instruments of his martyrdom become sweet/precious, and he is followed by the righteous rather than the wicked
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that the Church reads Job 21:33 in the office for St. Stephen, reapplying the OT passage to describe the reversal of the wicked's fate into a description of the righteous martyr's reception in the afterlife. This represents a typological inversion where the OT type (wicked received in death) is fulfilled in an NT antitype (righteous received by God after martyrdom), thus foreshadowing the eschatological reversal of fortunes between the wicked and the just.

notes: This is a subtle typological relationship involving typological inversion or contrast. The Church's liturgical application to St. Stephen transforms the threatening prophecy about the wicked into a triumphant affirmation about the righteous, suggesting Job's words prefigure the ultimate eschatological distinction between the fate of sinners and saints. The commentary mentions Gregory of Nyssa and other Church Fathers interpret this as a menace/threat, suggesting eschatological judgment is the interpretive lens.

original_text: Heaven. The mountains are so styled by Pindar; and the poets represent them supporting the heavens. Totum ferre potest humeris minitantibus orbem. (Petronius) --- Yet others understand that power which keeps all things together, (Calmet) or the angels, to whose rule the ancients attributed the celestial bodies. (St. Gregory; Ven. Bede, etc.)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Job 26:11 discusses various interpretations of 'heaven' and what 'supports' the heavens—including mountains, divine power, or angels. However, these are exegetical and cosmological interpretations rather than typological relationships. The commentary does not establish an Old Testament type that prefigures a New Testament antitype. It engages in poetic symbolism (mountains representing heaven per Pindar and Petronius) and theological speculation about divine or angelic agency, but not typology as formally defined in biblical scholarship. No OT/NT prefigurement relationship is described.

original_text: Enemy, or opponent. Hebrew, "my enemy shall be," etc. (Haydock) --- In effect, those who maintained the contrary to what Job taught, favoured the cause of impiety, as they represented God never punishing his servants, etc., (Calmet) which is contrary to experience; (Haydock) though it was not so evident at that time. (Houbigant) --- Job is so far from thinking riches a proof of sanctity, that he rather would wish his enemy to have them, (Menochius) as they are too frequently an incentive to sin. (Haydock)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Job 27:7 discusses Job's statement about his enemies and contains theological and moral teachings about wealth, sin, and divine punishment. However, it contains no typological relationships connecting Old Testament persons, events, or institutions to New Testament fulfillments. The commentary focuses on: (1) the literal meaning of Job's words, (2) moral lessons about riches being an incentive to sin, and (3) theological arguments about divine justice and punishment of servants. These are general biblical wisdom and doctrine, not typological prefigurements. No OT type/NT antitype connections are described or implied.

original_text: He (God) hath, etc. (Haydock) --- Darkness, before which these inventions could not be made; (Menochius) or, man has been able to measure the hours of day and night by the shadow of the sun, and by other means. He always strives to perfect his works, and examines with care the mines which lay concealed in the most profound obscurity. (Calmet) --- Precious stones and metals lie the deepest. (Menochius) --- From the consideration of these beautiful works, men ought to raise their minds to the Creator, and wisely rest in him alone. (Worthington)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Job 28:3 discusses God's knowledge of hidden things in the earth (precious stones and metals in deep mines) and encourages readers to recognize God's creative works and turn their minds to the Creator. While the passage contains spiritual and moral lessons about seeking God through contemplation of His works, it does not establish a typological relationship between an Old Testament type and a New Testament antitype. The commentary is exegetical and hortatory in nature rather than typological. No OT person, event, or institution is presented as prefiguring a NT fulfillment.

original_text: Face. This most people explain literally; while some, (Calmet) as Job was herein a figure of Christ, (Menochius; Matthew xxvi.; Worthington) think that the expression denotes the utmost contempt; (St. Gregory, etc.) or that the people spit upon the ground (Calmet) for fear of contracting any infection; (Haydock) and because lepers were held in the utmost abhorrence. (Calmet)

extractions.type_description: Job experiencing spitting, rejection, and utmost contempt from people, particularly in connection with leprosy and infection avoidance
extractions.antitype_description: Christ subjected to spitting, contempt, and rejection during his passion (Matthew 26), fulfilling the pattern of suffering and disgrace
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states 'Job was herein a figure of Christ' and directly references Matthew 26 (Christ's passion accounts), where spitting upon Christ is recorded. The parallel between Job's experience of contempt and spitting and Christ's similar treatment during the passion establishes a clear typological relationship.

notes: The commentary attributes this typological interpretation to multiple sources (Menochius, Worthington, St. Gregory). The connection is made more specific by the reference to leprosy symbolism—as lepers were held in utmost abhorrence in the OT period, Job's treatment as one despised and avoided prefigures Christ being treated as accursed and rejected. This is an explicit typological claim rather than implied.

original_text: Brother of dragons, etc. Imitating these creatures in their lamentable noise. (Challoner) -- I was like those beasts which retire in order to lament. (Worthington) --- The dragons hiss dreadfully, when crushed by the elephant; (St. Jerome) and the young ostriches, being abandoned, make great lamentations. (Menochius) (Delrio, t. 2:adag. 18.) --- This comparison occurs, Micheas 1:8. Natural history does not, however, represent these animals as very plaintive. The former term may denote sea monsters, or crocodiles; thannim: (Septuagint, syrens) and "the daughters of the yahana," signify "swans," (Isaias 13:21.) though commonly rendered ostriches, as they are by the Septuagint, etc. (Calmet) --- Protestants have, "owls." But we may adhere to the Vulgate. (Haydock)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Job 30:29 focuses on lexical analysis and natural history interpretation rather than typology. The passage discusses Job's comparison of himself to various animals (dragons, ostriches, owls) that make mournful sounds, reflecting his own lamentation and suffering. The commentary provides alternative translations of Hebrew terms (thannim, yahana), discusses which creatures are meant, and references parallel usage in Micah 1:8, but does not establish any typological connection between these Old Testament animals or events and New Testament realities or fulfillments. The commentary is primarily concerned with accurate translation and understanding of the literal meaning of the text rather than prefigurative theological significance.

original_text: Angel, by secret inspirations, (St. Thomas Aquinas; Tirinus, etc.) or a man sent by God, to announce the truths of salvation. (Mariana) --- Man's, or "to man." (Calmet) --- Hebrew, "a messenger with him, an interpreter, one....to declare to man his uprightness." Protestants, (Haydock) "If there be any merit in him, the angel comforter, chosen from a thousand accusers, is ready to declare to the son of man his rectitude." Septuagint, "If there be a thousand destroying angels, not one of them shall hurt him; if the consider in his heart to be converted unto the Lord. Though he (the angel) lay before man his reproof, and shew his folly, He (God) will take hold of him, that he may not die. He will renew his flesh as the plaster of a wall, and fill his bones with marrow: (25) he will make his flesh soft, like that of an infant, and will place him in manhood among men." (Haydock) --- But this is different from the Hebrew. (Calmet) --- The intercession of angels is very powerful. They are represented as suggesting motives, which prevail on God to shew mercy, ver. 24. (Haydock)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Job 33:23 discusses the intercession of angels and their role in declaring God's mercy and uprightness to humanity. While the passage mentions an 'angel' or 'messenger' as an intermediary between God and man, the commentary does not establish a typological relationship where this OT figure or event prefigures a specific NT antitype. The discussion focuses on angelology, the mechanics of divine mercy, and the intercessory power of angels—themes that are theological and moral in nature rather than typological. There is no explicit connection drawn between this angelic mediation and Christ or any other NT fulfillment that would constitute typology proper.

original_text: Then. Septuagint, "After Eliu had ceased to speak." (Haydock) --- Lord. That is, an angel speaking in the name of the Lord. (Challoner) --- The name Jehova (Haydock) here occurs, though it never does in the speeches; whence many have inferred that the Lord spoke in person; which argument, however, is not conclusive; and that this work was written after the apparition in the burning bush. (Calmet) --- The Hebrew edition would at least be given after that event. --- Whirlwind, designed to strike the senses, (Haydock) and to represent the distressed condition of Job. (Pineda) --- This awful appearance imposed silence upon all. (Haydock) --- Some think that a time was allowed for reflection and repentance, before God passed sentence; but the Septuagint, etc., seem to suppose that the cause was decided as soon as Eliu had ended his discourse. (Calmet) --- God discusses the controversy, and gives sentence in favour of Job. (Worthington)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Job 38:1 does not contain typological analysis. The passage discusses the literary and historical aspects of God's appearance to Job (whether spoken through an angel or in person, the significance of the divine name Jehova, the symbolic meaning of the whirlwind, and the judicial outcome favoring Job). While the commentary includes interpretive observations about divine communication and God's judgment, these are exegetical and theological interpretations rather than typological connections between Old Testament and New Testament realities. There is no explicit or implicit suggestion that Job's experience or God's theophanic appearance prefigures or is fulfilled in New Testament events, persons, or institutions.

original_text: Shut. Hebrew also, (Haydock) "facilitated the birth of the sea," as a midwife. (Grotius) (Calmet) --- Forth. Septuagint, "raged." (Haydock) --- God represents the waters ready to overwhelm all when first produced out of nothing, if he had not shut them up in the abyss, like a child in a cradle, or a wild beast in its den, ver. 10. (Calmet)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Job 38:8 discusses God's creative power and control over the waters at creation, using metaphorical language (midwife, cradle, den) to describe how God confined the chaotic waters. However, the commentary does not establish any connection between an Old Testament type and a New Testament antitype. It remains focused on the literal historical event of creation and God's sovereignty, employing symbolism and allegory for theological emphasis rather than typological prefigurement. No OT/NT fulfillment relationship is described.

original_text: Seal. Men, formed to the image of God, shall die; and others shall be place in their stead, (Menochius) with as much ease as an impression is made upon clay. (Haydock) --- Garment. The body seems to be the clothing of the soul, and will be changed, Psalm 101:27. (Menochius) --- Chaldean, "their form will be changed to clay, and they shall resemble a tattered garment." Hebrew, "their seal shall change like clay," etc. All their glory shall perish. (Calmet) --- Septuagint, "hast thou taken earth or clay, and formed a living creature, and endued it with speech on the earth?" Is man the workd of thy hands? (Haydock)
notes: This commentary on Job 38:14 discusses the mortality of human beings and the transience of earthly glory through metaphors of clay, seals, and garments. While there is symbolic language (the body as 'clothing of the soul,' human mortality compared to clay impressions), these are general theological symbolism and moral lessons about human fragility rather than typological relationships. The commentary does reference Psalm 101:27, but this is used for thematic comparison about change and impermanence, not as a typological prefigurement of New Testament fulfillment. No clear OT type → NT antitype connection is established.

original_text: Darkness. The poetical style of this book represents these things as real beings, in the same manner (Calmet) as the house, (ver. 20) or palace of the sun, etc., are described by the ancients. (Haydock)
notes: The Haydock commentary on Job 38:19 is discussing poetic and literary devices, not typological relationships. The commentary notes that the Book of Job employs personification and poetical style to represent natural phenomena (darkness, the sun's house/palace) as real beings, following a convention used by ancient poets. This is a comment on rhetorical style and literary convention, not on how Old Testament types prefigure New Testament antitypes. There is no OT-to-NT prefigurement being described here.

original_text: Leviathan: the whale, or some sea monster. (Challoner) --- Protestants' marginal note, "or a whirlpool." (Haydock) --- But some animal is designated; and Bochart understands the crocodile, which agrees very well with the context. The Thalmudists also say that the calbish is a small fish, which gets into the throat of the leviathan. They mean probably the ichneumon, which kills the crocodile by that means. Leviathan, "the winding serpent," (Calmet) often denotes the dragon or crocodile, (Psalm 103:26., and Isaias 27:1.) which frequents the Nile. (Haydock) --- It can live as well by land as under water, (Watson, p. 293) and hence may be translated, (Haydock) "the coupled dragon." (Parkhurst) --- Moses mentions the choled, (Leviticus 11:29.) which the Septuagint and most others translate, "the land crocodile:" but what could induce the Protestants "to render it tortoise, we are at a loss to determine." Crocodiles lay about sixty eggs, like those of geese, in the sand, the warmth of which soon hatches them. Their bodies are covered with scales, which are scarcely penetrable, except under the belly; and they are between twenty and thirty feet in length, running very fast, straight forward, though their feet be short, and they cannot turn easily. They have several rows of sharp teeth, which enter one within another, and their throat is very wide. (Button.) --- The same word may however denote whales, (Parkhurst) which are the greatest fishes with which man is acquainted. (Haydock) --- They may also be styled coupled dragons, because many smaller fishes accompany them, and they are well protected by scales, etc. (Menochius) --- This huge fish, perhaps the whale, representing the devil, is subject to God. (Worthington) --- Cord. The crocodile may be taken, but with the utmost hazard; though the Tentyrites attacked it without fear, Job 3:8. Herodotus (II. 70.) says it may be caught with a hook, baited with hog's flesh, while the fisher has a pig grunting, at which the crocodile comes open-mouthed. Having swallowed the hook, it is drawn to land, and its small eyes being filled with dirt it is easily slain. But the method was not yet invented, or was deemed too rash in Job's days.

extractions.type_description: A huge, powerful sea creature in Job 40:20, described as being subject to God despite its fearsome nature and apparent invulnerability
extractions.antitype_description: The spiritual enemy who, despite appearing powerful and dangerous, is ultimately subject to God's authority
extractions.reasoning: Worthington's note explicitly states: 'This huge fish, perhaps the whale, representing the devil, is subject to God.' This indicates a typological prefigurement wherein the OT creature (Leviathan) represents and prefigures the NT reality of Satan's subjection to divine authority. The emphasis on Leviathan being subdued despite its formidable appearance parallels Christ's ultimate victory over Satan.

notes: The typological reference is attributed to Worthington and appears toward the end of the commentary. This is a relatively modest typological claim compared to more elaborate OT/NT typologies. The connection rests on the symbolic representation of the devil's ultimate subjection to God, which can be understood as prefiguring Christ's triumph over Satan. The category is classified as Christological rather than Eschatological because the focus is on Christ's implicit authority over Satan, though an Eschatological reading (anticipating Satan's final defeat) would also be defensible.

original_text: Hammer. Septuagint sphura, means also, "the bottom of a rock." This would not overwhelm the whale; as some are represented like floating islands. Protestants, "darts." (Haydock) --- Chaldean, "axe." Others have, "the ballista;" an instrument to throw stones. (Calmet)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Job 41:20 discusses textual variants and translation options for weapons or implements (hammer, darts, axe, ballista) that might be used against Leviathan. The commentary is purely exegetical and lexicographical in nature, addressing how different ancient versions render a single Hebrew word. There is no discussion of how this Old Testament passage or its imagery prefigures any New Testament person, event, or institution. The commentary remains focused on historical-linguistic analysis rather than typological interpretation.

original_text: Brethren. Who had before shamefully abandoned him, Job 6:13. (Calmet) --- Bemoaned. Literally, "shaked their heads at him," (Haydock) out of pity, (Menochius) or astonishment, (Tirinus; Calmet) at his fallen state, and at the present change for the better. They helped to restore him to affluence, in conformity with the will of God, who caused their presents of multiply. The kindred and friends of Job were undoubtedly numerous. (Haydock) --- Ewe. Kesita, "lamb," as most of the ancients agree, (Spanheim) or a piece of money, (Bochart) marked with the figure of a lamb. (Grotius) See Genesis 33:19. (Calmet) --- Ear-ring. Hebrew Nezem, an ornament (Haydock) "for the nose," still very common in the East. Symmachus adds, "it was unadorned," (Calmet) or plain. Septuagint, "a piece of gold worth four drachms, and not coined," asemon. (Haydock) --- Oleaster supposes that the nose was perforated, like the ear. But the ornament would thus be very inconvenient, and we may rather conclude that it hung down from the forehead upon the nose. (St. Jerome, in Ezechiel xvi.) (Pineda)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Job 42:11 focuses on textual analysis and historical-cultural details rather than typological interpretation. The discussion centers on: (1) the meaning of 'brethren' who abandoned Job earlier, (2) the significance of their return and gifts as restoration, (3) philological analysis of Hebrew terms (kesita, nezem) and their meanings as currency or ornaments, and (4) scholarly debate about ancient Eastern customs regarding jewelry. While the passage describes Job's restoration and vindication, the commentary does not explicitly or implicitly connect this narrative to any New Testament fulfillment or person. No OT/NT typological relationship is drawn.

original_text: Years, in all, as Judith is said to have dwelt in the house of her husband 105 years; though it is agreed that she only lived that space of time. (Haydock) --- Authors are much divided about the length of Job's life. Some suppose that he was afflicted with the leprosy at the age of 70, for several months, (Tirinus) or for a whole year, (Calmet) or for seven, (Salien) and that he lived twice as long after his re-establishment, in all 210. (Calmet) (Tirinus) Septuagint, "Job lived after his chastisement 170," (Grabe substitutes 140 years. Then he marks with an obel as redundant) "but all the years which he lived were 248;" and adds from Theodition, "And Job saw his sons and their children, even the fourth generation." (Haydock) --- The old Vulgate had also 248 years; while some Greek copies read 740. But Grotius thinks the life of Job was not extended beyond 200. Petau and Spanheim say 189, (Calmet) and Pindea 210, or rather 280, years. Yet the life of man, in the days of Moses, his contemporary, was not often longer than 120; so that if we allow Job 140, he would be an old man, and might see the fourth generation, ver. 10. (Haydock) --- The Greeks celebrate his festival on the 6th, the Latins on the 10th of May. (Pineda) --- Days. Here a long addition is found in the Greek, Arabic, and old Vulgate; and Theodotion has also inserted it in his version, as it seems to contain a true and ancient tradition, (see Eusebius, praep. 9:25.) though the Fathers have properly distinguished it from the inspired text. It stands thus in the Alexandrian Septuagint with an obel prefixed: "But it is written, that he shall be raised again, with those whom the Lord will restore to life." He, this man, as it is translated from the Syriac book, lived in the land of Ausites, (Hus.) on the borders of Idumea, and of Arabia, and was before called Jobab. But marrying an Arabian woman, he begot a son by name Ennon. But his father was Zareth, a descendant of the sons of Esau, and his mother was Bossora; (Arabic, a native of Bosra) so that he was the 5th (Arabic, the 6th) from Abraham. Now these were the kings who reigned in Edom; over which country he also ruled. First, Balac, son of Semphor; (others have Beor) and the name of his city was Dennaba. After Balak, Jobab, who is called Job. After him, Assom, a leader from the country of Theman. After this man, Adad, son of Barad, who slew Madian in the plain of Moab; and the name of his city was Gethaim. But the friends who came to him were, Eliphaz, [son of Sophan] of the sons of Esau, king of the Themanites; Baldad, [son of Amnon, of Chobar] of the Auchite tyrant; (Grabe substitutes the tyrant of the Saucheans, as they call our Suhites) Sophar, king of the Mineans." What is marked with crotchets, (Haydock) has been probably taken from Theodotion. See the Greek Catena. What follows occurs in the Alexandrian manuscript. (Calmet) --- "[Theman, son of Eliphaz, he, as the Syriac book is rendered, lived in the land of Ausites, on the borders of the Euphrates. His former name was Jobab, but Zareth was his father, from the sun rising."] or eastern country. (Haydock) --- Job might very well be the 5th or 6th from Abraham, if he were a contemporary with Moses, as Levi and Amram would live at the same time with Rahuel and Zare; (See 1 Paralipomenon 1:35, 44.) so that this tradition agrees with history. But what is said of the Syriac version is not so certain. (Calmet) --- Some think the Syriac or Arabic was the original text, as the Greek seems to indicate, outos ermeneuetai ek tes Suriakes Biblou, en men ge katoikon, etc. The passage at the end, where this is repeated, may be an interpolation, as the latter part seems rather to belong to Job. For how could Theman have both Eliphaz and Zareth for his father? Grabe therefore, marks it as such. It would be too long for us to transcribe (Haydock) the praises which the Fathers have given to Job, and the resemblance which they have discovered between him and Jesus Christ. See Hebrews 4:15 and 13:12.; Tertullian, patient.; St. Chrysostom, hom. xxxiv. in Matt. St. Ambrose, in Psalm 37:21., observes, that his behaviour on the dunghill was the greatest condemnation of satan, who fell by pride, though so highly favoured. (Calmet) --- Besides the literal sense of this book, which displays the trials and victories of Job, we may consider him as a lively figure of Christ; who was perfectly innocent, and yet a man of sorrows: we may raise our minds to the contemplation of the greater glory which will attend the bodies of the just, after the resurrection; and, above all, we may discover lessons of morality, enforcing the observance of every virtue, and particularly of patience and resignation. (St. Gregory, etc.) (Worthington) --- The books of Machabees, which are the only remaining pieces of sacred history, might have been here inserted, as they are in Calmet's edition, that so all the historical part might come together. But it is more common to place those books after the prophets. They only relate a few of the transactions which took place during the 400 or 500 years preceding the Christian era. The rest must be borrowed from Josephus, or from profane authors. It would, however, be proper to read those books, and to have an idea of that period, before we attempt to explain the prophecies. (Haydock)

original_text: Discipline. Chaldean, "doctrine." St. Jerome, "adore purely." Protestants, "kiss the Son, lest he be angry," etc. (Haydock) --- Houbigant, "adore the son, lest he be angry, and you perish. For he comes forward, and shortly his wrath will be enkindled." This version seems to be judicious: that of the Vulgate is less energetic, but comes to the same end, as those who adore the Messias, must follow his doctrine. (Berthier) --- Lord and just is not in [the] Hebrew. (Haydock) --- The way or projects of sinners will perish; (Psalm 1:6.) they will be hurried before the tribunal, as soon as they are dead; (St. Hilary) and when they least expect it, 1 Thessalonians 5:2. (Calmet) --- Some fall from salvation, and God will bring them to judgment at the end of this short life. (Worthington) --- Hebrew, "Kiss purely." Kissing is often used in Scripture to express submission, love, and adoration. (St. Jerome, contra Ruf. i.) (Genesis 41:40.) (Calmet) --- We testify our respect for God, by kissing the Bible, etc. (Haydock) --- But it cannot be shewn that bar means "a son," in Hebrew. (Calmet) --- Amama blames the Vulgate for withdrawing a text in favour of Christ's divinity. We must, however, submit to the law and faith of Christ with confidence and love, if we desire to escape his indignation and enter heaven, Acts 4:12. Mr. Nightingale (Portrait of Cath. 1812. p. 117 and 332) may represent this doctrine as uncharitable and groundless, though he allows it has been maintained by most (p. 473) who have professed to be the true disciples of Christ, whether Catholics or Protestants. The principle is good, though some apply it wrong. If he and Lord Milton, (speech. 1812. to whom we must express our manifest obligations) had contented themselves with saying that they believed our doctrine was "unscriptural," etc., (p. 18) we should not have much wondered; as they could not consistently have said less, and remained out of the Catholic Church. But for any man who has read the Bible, to persuade himself that it is not necessary to profess the one only true religion, wherever it may be, after Christ has so plainly declared, He that believeth not is already judged, and shall be condemned; (John 3:18., and Mark 16:16.) and after the apostle has delivered over to satan those who only asserted that the resurrection was past, (2 Timothy 2:17.) this fills us with astonishment. Not a single text can be produced in favour of the contrary system leading to indifference about religion; which, if true, would shew the preaching of the prophets and apostles as nugatory, and their blood shed in vain. All the "Scriptures" proclaim the necessity of faith and good works. We may observe, that the doctrine of the blessed Trinity seems to be no less objectionable to Mr. N. than the rest of our faith, p. 117, etc. Yet (Haydock) we must not refuse him the praise of liberality. (Catholic Review, etc., Jan. 1813.) (Haydock)

extractions.type_description: The anointed king figure in Psalm 2 who demands submission, adoration, and obedience, characterized by righteous judgment and wrath against those who refuse to submit
extractions.antitype_description: The incarnate Son of God who demands faith and submission (Acts 4:12), whose judgment determines salvation or condemnation (John 3:18, Mark 16:16), and whose wrath falls upon those who reject Him
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly identifies the 'Son' (bar) in Psalm 2:12 as prefiguring the Messiah/Christ. The editorial notes state 'those who adore the Messias, must follow his doctrine' and reference Acts 4:12 regarding Christ's exclusive role in salvation. The typological connection is reinforced by the parallel structures: the OT king demands submission and pronounces judgment on the disobedient, which the commentary connects directly to Christ's role as judge and savior in the NT.

notes: While the commentary is lengthy and addresses various theological controversies, the core typological relationship is the connection between the royal/messianic figure of Psalm 2 and Jesus Christ. The commentary's extensive polemical sections do not contain additional typological material but rather defend the necessity of Christian faith and submission to Christ's doctrine.

original_text: By. Hebrew and St. Augustine, "From the time of their corn and wine" (Calmet) gathering. I rejoiced "more" than those who live in the greatest affluence, which is nothing but vanity. No mention is made of oil, but the original term, "liquor," includes it. (Berthier) --- St. Jerome found it not in the Hexapla. But it now occurs in the Arabic, Syriac, etc. (Calmet) --- David envies not the present prosperity of the rebels. (Haydock) --- He comforts his followers with the assurance of God's favour, which he had again testified by sending provisions. (Bullenger) --- He may also here express the disappointment of the rebels, who promised themselves great riches, of which Providence would soon deprive them, by restoring the king, whom he had chosen, and hitherto so wonderfully protected. (Haydock) --- God gave temporal advantages to the just in the old law, as a figure of heavenly rewards. (Worthington)

This represents a typological relationship where the lesser, temporal good points to the greater, spiritual good.

notes: The typological connection here is somewhat implicit and transitional in nature—it suggests that the material blessings of the Old Law era serve as types or foreshadowings of the superior spiritual rewards of the New Covenant. This is a relatively modest typological claim, focusing on the principle of reward rather than a specific person or event. The confidence is marked as 'medium' because while the commentary explicitly uses typological language ('as a figure of'), it is a brief interpretive note rather than an elaborate typological exposition.

original_text: The presses. In Hebrew Gittith, supposed to be a musical instrument: (Challoner) or, "the musicians from Geth," who were famous, and might follow David, 2 Kings 1:20., and 15:18. The Septuagint must have read a v for 1:(Calmet) Gothuth. Yet St. Jerome and Pagnin agree with them; (Haydock) and that sense seems as plausible as any other. The psalm relates to Christ alone; (Matthew 21:16., 1 Corinthians 15:26., and Hebrews 2:6.) who is represented treading the wine-press, Isaias 63:3., and Apocalypse 19:13. (Berthier) --- The Jews confess that it speaks of the Messias. (Ferrand.) --- We may explain it also of the natural prerogatives of man, (Calmet) though (Haydock) this weakens the force of the prophecy. (Berthier) --- St. Augustine applies the expressions to the good and bad in the Church. (Worthington) --- It might be sung during the feast of tabernacles, after the vintage. (Menochius)

original_text: Death, by mortal sin, (Worthington) or through excessive sorrow, Jeremias 51:39. Shew me thy favour, (Calmet) and I shall be secure. Sleep is represented as nearly related to death. (Homer, Iliad xiv.) Tum consanguineus lethi sopor. (Virgil, Aeneid vi.) (Haydock)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Psalm 12:4 discusses sleep as a metaphor or symbol for death, drawing on classical literary parallels (Homer, Virgil) and biblical cross-references (Jeremiah 51:39). However, this represents general symbolism and allegory rather than typology proper. Typology requires a specific OT person, event, or institution that prefigures a NT fulfillment. The commentary does not establish any Old Testament type that points to a New Testament antitype. original_text: David. The word psalm being appropriated to some, while others are styled hymns, etc., does not hinder the latter from being also psalms or spiritual songs, to be set to music: so the insertion of David, "the beloved's name," in some of these divine canticles, is no proof that the rest were not written by him. (Worthington) --- The author describes the perfection of priests, etc., contrasts the sanctity of those who shall inhabit Jerusalem with that of the wicked mentioned in the last psalm. Some copies have To the end in the title, while others omit it, with the Hebrew, St. Chrysostom, etc. --- Hill. The Jews comforted themselves with the hopes of seeing Jerusalem rebuilt, Psalm 131:1. The prophets describe those who should return from captivity, as holy people, (Isaias 26:3., and Sophonias 3:13.; Calmet) a figure of the Church. (Haydock) --- Heaven is also styled a tabernacle and mountain, (Apocalypse 15:5., and Hebrews 12:22.; Berthier) and is here chiefly (Haydock) meant. See ver. 5. (Worthington)

original_text: Appear. St. Jerome, "I shall be filled, when I shall awake in thy likeness," (Haydock) at the resurrection: (Philippians 3:21., and 1 Corinthians 13:12.) or "when thy likeness, the Messias, shall rise again:" or (as the same expression is used by the Septuagint, as [in] Numbers 12:8.) David begs for actual inspiration, "thou wilt comfort my with the prophetic spirit." (Calmet) --- Perhaps he might also desire to see the tabernacle again, or even now prepare to erect a temple unto the Lord; (2 Kings 7:2.; Haydock) or he begs for the gifts of grace and glory, which will restore the image of God, effaced by sin, 1 John 3:2. (Berthier) --- Then the just being approved, will taste that joy which alone can satiate the heart of man, when he shall behold God. (Worthington)

original_text: This title is almost wholly taken from the book of Kings, except Unto the end for; instead of which we read, And David spoke, etc., (2 Kings 22.) (Haydock) which are the words of the inspired writer; so that Ferrand is very rash in rejecting both these titles. David wrote this psalm after he had subdued the Moabites, etc. (Calmet) --- He was inspired to write it (Worthington) twice, with some variations, (Berthier) 74 in number, (Aberbanel) or many more, if we believe Kennicott, who lays them to the charge of transcribers, perhaps, (Haydock) with greater reason. (Calmet) --- We cannot doubt but this psalm regards David. But there are some passages which refer to Jesus Christ and his Church more directly; and in general, David must here be considered as only (Berthier) the figure of the Messias, and of the just in his Church. (Worthington) --- James Paine has endeavoured to prove, with great ingenuity, that the whole must be explained of Jesus Christ, and that the name of Saul stands for "the grave;" as the points which are of modern date, only need to be changed. Thus the sufferings of our Saviour, and the punishment of the Jews in the last siege of Jerusalem are described; and thus it is clear that St. Paul (Romans 15:9.) has cited this psalm in it proper sense. (Berthier) --- See ver. 10, 41. --- Sts. Jerome and Augustine explain it of the victories of David, of the Messias, and of his Church. (Calmet) --- Saul may be particularly mentioned, because he was the most powerful. (Worthington)

The commentary also references James Paine's argument that the whole psalm explains the sufferings of Christ, and cites St. Paul's application of this psalm to Christ (Romans 15:9).

extractions.type_description: David's victories, trials, and relationship with God as depicted in Psalm 17
extractions.antitype_name: The Church and the just in the Church

notes: The commentary presents David as a dual type—prefiguring both Christ individually and the Church collectively. There is scholarly debate about the interpretive approach: some (like James Paine) argue for a purely Christological reading, while the traditional patristic view (Jerome, Augustine) sees both Christological and ecclesial applications. The commentary acknowledges variations in how the text should be interpreted while maintaining the typological framework.

original_text: I will love thee, as a mother does her son. He that loves has fulfilled the law. This word is omitted [in] 2 Kings. 22:2. (Calmet) --- Strength. Ibid. --- Rock. (Worthington) --- Others attribute the variations to David, or to the mistake of transcribers. (Haydock)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Psalm 17:2 focuses on textual criticism, manuscript variations, and translation differences between Hebrew, Greek (Septuagint), and other versions (2 Kings 22:2). The reference to love fulfilling the law is a moral/theological statement rather than a typological prefigurement. No Old Testament type is described as prefiguring a New Testament antitype in this passage.

(Eusebius, praep. evan. 13:13.) --- The Fathers explain the former verse of Christ's incarnation, or of his second coming; and this of his ascension. extractions.type_description: God appearing on a chariot with winds/clouds to come to David's assistance, modeled on Ezekiel's vision of God's chariot-throne
extractions.antitype_description: Christ's ascension into heaven, interpreted by the Church Fathers as the fulfillment of the divine chariot imagery
extractions.reasoning: The Fathers (St. Athanasius, etc.) explicitly connect the theophanic chariot imagery in this Psalm verse to Christ's ascension. The type is the OT manifestation of God's glory and power through the chariot; the antitype is Christ's ascension as the ultimate fulfillment of divine exaltation and movement between realms.

extractions.type_description: God mounting his chariot to come speedily to David's assistance
extractions.antitype_description: The Fathers also apply this verse to either Christ's incarnation or his second coming, representing God's decisive intervention in history
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that 'The Fathers explain the former verse of Christ's incarnation, or of his second coming.' The rapid divine assistance prefigures Christ's intervention in human history either at his first or final advent.

notes: The commentary presents multiple patristic interpretations of this theophanic imagery. The connection to Christ's ascension appears most clearly established, while the incarnation/second coming applications are broader Christological readings. All three interpretations view the OT chariot theophany as prefiguring different aspects of Christ's work and glory.

original_text: Pavilion. Job 22:14., and 26:9. The Jews had this idea of God's throne, of which we behold only the less brilliant side, as the Egyptians did that of the cloud, Exodus 14:19. The poets represent Jupiter surrounded with clouds and darkness. (Hesiod, op. 125 and 255.; Homer, Iliad O.) --- Air. The parallel passage, (2 Kings) seems more accurate. Dropping waters out of the clouds of the heavens. Hebrew, "waters bound up in darksome clouds." (Calmet) --- God is incomprehensible in himself, and his counsels are inscrutable. (Worthington)
notes: This Haydock commentary discusses God's incomprehensibility and inscrutability through the imagery of divine darkness, clouds, and pavilions. While it references comparative religious imagery (Egyptian clouds, Homeric Jupiter), it does not establish a typological relationship between an Old Testament type and a New Testament antitype. The commentary focuses on the symbolic meaning of God's hiddenness and the limits of human understanding rather than on how an OT prefigurement anticipates or finds fulfillment in the NT. The references to Job and Exodus are illustrative of a theological theme rather than typological connections.

original_text: Sent his angel, etc. --- Waters, which often represent multitudes, (Apocalypse 17:15.; Calmet) and afflictions. (Worthington) --- David seemed in danger of perishing. (Calmet)
notes: This Haydock commentary discusses symbolic interpretation rather than typology proper. While it notes that 'waters' represent 'multitudes' and 'afflictions' (citing Apocalypse 17:15 as a symbolic parallel), this is general symbolism or allegory rather than a typological relationship. Typology requires an OT person, event, or institution that prefigures a specific NT fulfillment. Here, the commentary is explaining David's metaphorical distress in Psalm 17:17 through symbolic language ('waters'), not establishing how an OT type prefigures a NT antitype. The reference to Apocalypse is used to support the symbolic meaning of 'waters' in Scripture generally, not to establish a typological connection between an OT and NT reality.

original_text: Him, by his grace. (Worthington) --- Iniquity, and be careful not to relapse. Others explain it in the past time. I have not shed the blood of my enemy when I could have done it, 1 Kings 24:6, 14. (Calmet) --- Fui immaculatus. (St. Jerome) (Haydock) It seems most probable that David composed this before his fall, as Aberbanel, one of the most learned of the Jews, asserts. If he be only a figure of Jesus Christ, we may easily conceive how the latter might speak thus of his innocence, and declare his abhorrence of all sin, though he was made a sin-offering, having undertaken to expiate the iniquities of mankind. extractions.type_description: King David in his innocence and moral integrity, maintaining purity and refusing to shed the blood of his enemies despite having opportunity (as evidenced in 1 Samuel 24:6, 14)
extractions.antitype_description: Christ as the sinless one who declared his abhorrence of all sin and maintained perfect innocence, even while being made a sin-offering to expiate the iniquities of mankind
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states 'If he be only a figure of Jesus Christ,' directly identifying David as a prefiguring type of Christ. Berthier's explanation clarifies how Christ, as the antitype, can speak of his own innocence while simultaneously serving as a sin-offering for humanity, paralleling David's maintenance of personal innocence while serving as a type.

notes: The commentary indicates this typology is conditional on David having composed Psalm 17 before his moral fall, suggesting the typological validity depends on understanding David's innocence at the time of composition. The typology operates on the level of moral/spiritual innocence and the paradox of maintaining personal purity while engaging in redemptive sacrifice.

extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that David's experience of rejection by his own people 'prefigured' (the technical term for typology) Christ's rejection by the chosen people. The parallel structure is: just as David was rejected by Israel despite his military/political achievements, so Christ was rejected by the Jews despite his messianic credentials, while outsiders (Gentiles/nations) accepted him. However, the typology is somewhat implicit rather than explicitly developed—the commentary notes the connection but doesn't elaborate extensively on how David functions as a type of Christ in this specific scenario.

notes: The commentary attributes this typological interpretation primarily to Worthington. The typology operates at the level of parallel experiences rather than David being a complete or primary type of Christ—it is a specific situation (rejection by one's own people) that prefigures a similar situation in Christ's ministry. The commentary also notes that the verse may have had primary application to David's own circumstances while simultaneously pointing forward to messianic fulfillment.

original_text: Firmament. Hebrew, "expansion," or region of the stars, far above our atmosphere. (Berthier) --- These two sentences express the same idea, unless the former may denote what we behold, and the firmament be explained of the higher heavens, (Haydock) where we imagine the throne of God to be placed. (Worthington) --- St. Paul reproaches the philosophers of paganism for not understanding the language of the creation, Romans 1:20., and Job 12:7. (Haydock) --- The Church, which is so often styled the kingdom of heaven, makes God known, not only as a Creator, but also as a Redeemer. The figure is here most beautifully preserved. extractions.type_description: The celestial bodies in their orderly progression (day and night cycle) that silently declare God's majesty and works
extractions.antitype_description: The Church as the kingdom of heaven, with apostolic men (represented by stars) who continuously perform their duties day and night, in prosperity and persecution, making God known as Creator and Redeemer
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states 'Heaven denotes the Church, as the stars represent apostolic men' and draws a direct prefigurative connection between the OT imagery of the heavens declaring God's glory and the NT reality of the Church's role in making God known. The parallel is further developed through the analogy of continuous witness (day/night cycle) to apostolic succession and unbroken doctrine.

extractions.type_description: The natural light that illuminates and gives life to creation
extractions.antitype_description: Christ as 'the true sun of justice, enlightening every man that cometh into the world' (John 1:9)

notes: The commentary applies Patristic interpretive methods, particularly drawing from the Fathers' typological reading of Psalm 18. The ecclesial typology emphasizes the permanence and succession of the Church's doctrine, while the Christological typology aligns with traditional patristic exegesis of Christ as the light of the world. Both types are rooted in the Psalm's celebration of God's glory revealed through creation.

original_text: Sound. So, St. Paul reads this text, though the Hebrew have, "line." Yet there is no reason why we should suppose that the Septuagint read differently, or that the Jews have corrupted their copies, as they could derive no advantage from so doing (Berthier) here, unless it were to discredit the apostle; as infidels assert the truth of the Old Testament, to vilify the new. Kum (Haydock) may signify a "line," (Berthier) or "writing." (Abenezra) --- The greatest exactitude has been observed in forming the world, as if all had been measured by an architect. But the sense of the Vulgate is preferable, and is adopted by Symmachus, St. Jerome, and the Syriac. (Calmet) --- Protestants, "their line." Marginal note, "their rule or direction." Kolam, "their voice," occurs in the preceding verse. The l might easily be lost, (Haydock) or omitted by a poetical licence. (Genebrard.) (Menochius) --- Their, refers to the heavens representing the apostles, as St. Paul explains this text, to prove that all were inexcusable who would not believe the gospel. (Berthier)

This represents the heavens as a type of the apostolic office/mission in proclaiming the gospel universally.

notes: This typological connection is explicitly attributed to St. Paul's interpretation (Romans 10:18), cited by Berthier. The typology is somewhat allegorical in nature—the heavens don't directly prefigure apostles as persons, but rather their function in universal proclamation. The connection exists primarily in the application of Psalm 18 to demonstrate that the gospel's proclamation is as universal and inescapable as the testimony of creation itself.

original_text: Sun. Here God seems to reside, (Ferrand) and the magnificence of his works shines forth, insomuch that almost all nations have offered divine honours to the sun, and even the Manichees adored it, imagining that it was the very body of Jesus Christ. (St. Augustine, contra Faust. 14:12., and 20:6.) --- Hebrew, "For the sun he has place a tent in them," the heavens, (St. Jerome; Haydock) or the ends of the world. The Jews supposed that the heavens rested, like a tent, upon the earth. (Calmet, Diss.) --- The Hebrew preposition l, may have (Haydock) different meanings, ad solem posuit, etc. "He placed a tent in them, at or for the sun." (Amama) --- The Vulgate may admit the fig. hypallage, (M. Geneb.) as good authors say dare classibus austros, and thus it may signify "he placed the sun in his tent." (Haydock) --- This vast body stands in need of no vehicle, or tent, but itself. (Diodorus) --- It was placed in the firmament at first, (Genesis 1:16.) and still performs its revolutions exactly. (Haydock) --- Giant. Moderns would render "a strong man;" and Bythner remarks that the bulk of a giant would render him less fit for running, as if the stoutest wrestlers were not often the most active. (Berthier) --- The sun is represented as a hero at some of the ancient games. St. Augustine and St. Jerome explain all this of Jesus Christ, who diffuses the light and warmth of his grace throughout the world. (Calmet) --- He always resides with the Church, and is never divorced from her. (Worthington)

extractions.type_description: The sun placed in the firmament (Genesis 1:16), described as a strong man/giant running its course across the heavens, providing light and warmth to all the world
extractions.antitype_description: Christ who diffuses the light and warmth of his grace throughout the world, always resides with the Church, and is never divorced from her
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states: 'St. Augustine and St. Jerome explain all this of Jesus Christ, who diffuses the light and warmth of his grace throughout the world.' The sun's universal illumination and constancy are presented as prefiguring Christ's role as the source of grace and his perpetual presence with the Church. This is a direct patristic typological interpretation.

notes: The commentary also mentions the erroneous Manichean interpretation that the sun was the body of Christ, which is rejected. The typological reading here is that the sun's properties (light, warmth, constancy, universal reach) and its placement in the heavens prefigure Christ's spiritual properties and his relationship to the Church. Augustine and Jerome are cited as primary sources for this Christological typology.

original_text: Sacrifices. Hebrew mincha, a sacrifice of flour, or unbloody; a figure of the Mass. (Worthington) --- Minchothec, "thy presents" (Mont.; Haydock) of fruits, etc. --- Fat. notes: The commentary also references the acceptance of sacrifices through miraculous fire (Abel, Elias) as evidence of God's favor, but this functions as supporting illustration rather than a distinct typological relationship. The emphasis on the 'fat' and acceptable offerings relates to the principle that God values the offerer's heart and faith (Hebrews 11:4), which is theological principle rather than typology per se.

original_text: Princes; or, "lift up your chief or highest gates:" portas principes. Hebrew, "gates, lift up your heads." (Haydock) --- This apostrophe to the gates is very striking, commanding them to allow more room for the crowd to pass in the train of the conqueror, who was usually seated on a lofty chariot. (Calmet) --- The prophet contemplating the ascension of Christ, inviteth the angels to receive him; and by the figure, prosopopeia, speaketh also to the gates by which he is to enter. (Worthington) --- Homer (Iliad 8.) represents the Hours as door-keepers of heaven removing a thick cloud, which obstructs the entrance. (Haydock) --- These gates are supposed to open, by being lifted upwards. The Greeks style them cataracts, Genesis 7:11. (Tournemine)

The typology operates through imagery rather than historical narrative—the psalmist's poetic vision of exalted gates prefigures the eschatological reality of Christ passing through the gates of heaven. The 'eternal gates' are distinguished from earthly temple or Jerusalem gates, reinforcing the heavenly/eschatological dimension of the antitype.

original_text: Innocent. Hebrew, "in innocence," avoiding every thing which may defile and render me unfit to approach thy holy altar. Many things (Calmet) of themselves innocent, (Haydock) excluded the priests of the old law from officiating, and if they had partaken of any idolatrous sacrifices, they lost their dignity for ever, Ezechiel 44:12. How much greater ought to be the sanctity of Christian priests! The Jews carefully abstained from eating what the law forbade, Daniel 1:8., and Tobias 1:12. David would not sit down to a feast with the proud, Psalm 100:5. It was customary to wash before meat (Matthew 15:2., and Mark 7:3.) and prayer. Aristeas informs us that the Septuagint washed their hands every morning, before they began to translate the Bible, to shew what purity of soul was requisite. Pilate used the like ceremony, when he would have no hand in the condemnation of our Saviour; (Matthew 27:24.; Calmet) and thus people declared their innocence, Deuteronomy 21:6. (Menochius) --- People entering the house of God, and priests at the altar, adopt the same symbols of interior purity, and ought to be penetrated with the like sentiments. (Haydock) --- David opposes the society of the good to that of the wicked, knowing that the former is a great inducement to virtue, and he declares that he will wash or converse with such. (Berthier) --- These words are recited by the priest, to put him in mind of the purity required, Leviticus 16:4. (Worthington)

original_text: Shall reduce them to pieces, etc. In Hebrew, shall make them to skip like a calf. The psalmist here describes the effects of thunder, (which he calls the voice of the Lord) which sometimes breaks down the tallest and strongest trees; and makes their broken branches skip, etc. All this is to be understood mystically, of the powerful voice of God's word in his Church; which has broke the pride of the great ones of this world, and brought many of them meekly and joyfully to submit their necks to the sweet yoke of Christ. (Challoner) --- Calf, or "branch," as the Greek word also implies. But Hebrew seems more naturally to signify "a calf; Libanus and Sirion, (or Sarion.; Deuteronomy 3:9.) as the son of the unicorn." These two mountains are represented jolting together. (Calmet) --- The violence of an earthquake has sometimes produced such effects. (Pliny, [Natural History?] 2:83.) See Psalm 113:4., Judges 5:5., and Habacuc 3:10. (Calmet) --- And as. The construction et dilectus, seems rather to make this another nominative, "the Lord shall, etc., and the beloved, (Haydock) the Messias, like the son of the unicorn," shall perform the like wonders. It seems probable that the Septuagint have read Jeshurun for Shirion, (Berthier) or vissron, instead of ussriun; as i would only be a little transposed. (Haydock) --- Jeshurun is a title of Israel, (Deuteronomy 32:15., and 33:5, 26.) who was a figure of the Messias, the beloved of God. (Berthier) --- "And he will scatter them as a calf would do; Libanus and Sarion, are in motion, like the son of the rhinoceros." (St. Jerome) (Haydock) The most powerful submit to Christ, who works these wonders. (Worthington)
