This is reinforced by the cross-reference to Isaiah 53:4 (a clear messianic prophecy) and the statement that the psalmist introduces the Messias 'uttering his own sentiments, respecting his passion and resurrection.'

notes: The commentary indicates some interpretative debate about the psalm's historical occasion (Hezekiah's sickness, David's sickness before Absalom's revolt), but unanimously affirms its typological application to Christ. The connection is explicitly Christological rather than merely allegorical, as the commentary insists it would be 'rash not to acknowledge' Christ as the principal subject.

original_text: Bread. This characterizes the traitor, who had recieved the holy Communion, and had been intrusted with the purse by our Saviour, yet betrayed him with the sign of peace. (Calmet) --- To violate the laws of hospitality was greatly resented by the very pagans. (Plutarch, Symp. 7:4.) --- Supplanted me, or kicked like a wild colt, as Plato complained that Aristotle had done, when he set up another school. (Haydock) Emas apelaktise. (Laertius, Elian 4:9.) --- David might allude to Absalom, though the Holy Ghost speaks of Judas. (Calmet) --- Our Saviour himself says, (Worthington) that the Scriptures may be fulfilled, he that eateth bread with me, shall lift up his heel against me: Qui manducat mecum panem levabit contra me calcaneum suum: eperen ep eme ten pternan autou, "has lifted up," etc., as the Hebrew expresses it here. Judas had attempted to betray Christ already, and would do it more effectually hereafter; so that both the present and future might agree with him. We also find the psalm translated qui edebat panes meos, etc. But the difference is very small. (Haydock) --- To lift up the heel, is the posture of one who attempts to supplant his adversary. (Menochius)

extractions.type_name: David's betrayal by one who ate bread with him
extractions.type_description: Psalm 40:10 describes a companion who ate bread with David yet lifted up his heel against him—a violation of the sacred laws of hospitality and fellowship
extractions.antitype_description: Judas, who received the Eucharist (holy Communion) with Jesus, was entrusted with the purse by Christ, yet betrayed him with a sign of peace
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that Jesus himself applies this psalm to Judas's betrayal, citing John 13:18: 'he that eateth bread with me, shall lift up his heel against me.' This is a direct fulfillment citation where the OT type (David's betrayal) prefigures the NT antitype (Judas's betrayal of Christ). The shared elements—eating bread together, violation of trust, and hostile action—establish the typological connection.

notes: The commentary notes that 'David might allude to Absalom, though the Holy Ghost speaks of Judas,' indicating that while the psalm may have had an immediate historical reference, its ultimate typological fulfillment is in Judas's betrayal of Jesus. The commentary emphasizes the sacrilege of violating hospitality laws, which intensifies the typological parallel between the two betrayals.

original_text: For them that shall be changed, i.e., For souls happily changed, by being converted to God; (Challoner) or it may allude to the variety of speakers here introduced. (Berthier) --- Protestants leave shoshannim, which some translate, "on the lilies," (Aquila; St. Jerome) or "instrument of six strings." (Calmet) --- The beloved, viz., our Lord Jesus Christ. (Challoner) --- Hebrew, "of loves;" or of the young women, friends of the bride, (yedidoth) who sung the Epithalamium, as we see in the 18th Idyl of Theocritus. The Jews formerly explained this psalm of the Messias, as well as all the Fathers after the apostles, Hebrew, 1:8. Many passages cannot refer to Solomon's marriage with the daughter of Pharao, though some might be referred to that event, as a figure of Christ's union with his Church. (Calmet) --- The whole had better be understood of Christ, (Berthier) being intended for the instruction of all converts from paganism and schism. (Worthington)

extractions.type_name: Solomon's marriage with the daughter of Pharaoh
extractions.type_description: An Old Testament historical event in which Solomon took a foreign bride, celebrated with an epithalamium (wedding song)
extractions.antitype_description: The New Testament reality of Christ as the bridegroom joined to the Church as His bride
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that while some passages in this psalm 'might be referred to that event, as a figure of Christ's union with his Church.' This represents a typological prefigurement where the historical marriage event prefigures the spiritual reality of Christ's relationship with the Church. However, the commentary also notes that 'many passages cannot refer to Solomon's marriage,' indicating the typology is partial rather than complete throughout the psalm.

extractions.type_description: An Old Testament psalm that the Jews and Church Fathers interpreted as referring to the Messiah and His beloved Church
extractions.antitype_description: The New Testament reality of Christ as the Messiah and His relationship with the Church as His beloved bride
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states: 'The Jews formerly explained this psalm of the Messias, as well as all the Fathers after the apostles' and 'The whole had better be understood of Christ.' This indicates that Psalm 44 was understood typologically as prefiguring Christ and His union with the Church, making it a Christological type.

notes: The commentary presents Psalm 44 as a composite typology with multiple levels: (1) the historical referent to Solomon's marriage, (2) the typological prefigurement of Christ's union with the Church, and (3) instructional meaning for 'converts from paganism and schism.' The typology is primarily Christological, focusing on Christ as the bridegroom. The commentary acknowledges that some portions might refer to Solomon's historical marriage while the whole psalm is better understood messianically.

original_text: Beautiful. The corporal beauty of Christ may be problematical. (Haydock) --- But justice is the truest beauty. (St. Augustine) --- All admired his eloquence, (Luke 4:22., and John 7:46.) and innumerable converts were made, by the preaching of his word. (St. Jerome) --- The young women here address the spouse. --- Therefore, I say, (Rabbins) or "because" God hath chosen thee freely. Solomon was styled the beloved, (2 Kings 12:25.) and was highly favoured, Wisdom 8:20., and 3 Kings 4:29., etc. But this was only a figure of Jesus Christ, (Calmet) whose hypostatical union was an effect of gratuitous predestination, (St. Augustine, praed. xv.) though his other graces were merited. (St. Chrysostom) (Sa) (Calmet) --- He was most excellent in all sorts of gifts. (Worthington)

extractions.type_description: The beloved king of Israel, styled 'the beloved,' highly favored by God, and excellent in all gifts of wisdom and eloquence (2 Kings 12:25; 1 Kings 4:29; Wisdom 8:20)
extractions.antitype_description: The ultimate beloved, chosen freely by God through hypostatical union and gratuitous predestination, whose eloquence converted multitudes and who possesses all gifts in supreme excellence (Luke 4:22; John 7:46)
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states 'this was only a figure of Jesus Christ' (Calmet), establishing a direct typological connection. Solomon's status as beloved, divine favor, and excellence in gifts prefigure Christ's chosen status, divine predestination, and supreme excellence in all gifts.

notes: The commentary attributes this typological interpretation to Calmet. The connection is made explicit through the phrase 'But this was only a figure of Jesus Christ.' The passage discusses how Solomon's attributes (being styled 'beloved,' highly favored, excellent in gifts) serve as types of corresponding aspects of Christ's nature and status.

original_text: Fall. This seems to be placed too soon, in order to shew the rapidity of the conquest. (Calmet) --- "Thy arrows are sharp, shot into the hearts," etc. (Haydock) --- Some explain in corde, (as the Hebrew, Septuagint, etc., read) of the voluntary submission of those who had formerly been enemies of the Messias. (St. Chrysostom, etc.) --- "Thy sharp arrows, the people subject to thee, shall fall into," etc. --- Men are sometimes represented as arrows, Isaias 49:2. (Berthier)

extractions.type_name: Sharp arrows shot into the hearts of enemies
extractions.type_description: From Psalm 44:6, arrows representing God's instruments of conquest, with the alternative interpretation that they represent the voluntary submission of former enemies through penetration to the heart
extractions.antitype_description: The Messiah's sharp arrows represent His effective word and message that penetrates hearts, causing voluntary submission of those who were formerly enemies
extractions.reasoning: St. Chrysostom and other commentators explicitly interpret the arrows as prefiguring the Messiah's efficacy in winning hearts and converting enemies. The commentary also references Isaiah 49:2 ('Men are sometimes represented as arrows'), which is a messianic passage where the Servant of the Lord (Christ) is like a sharp arrow in God's quiver, further supporting the Christological typology.

notes: The typology is somewhat implicit in this commentary but gains clarity through the patristic interpretation (St. Chrysostom) and the cross-reference to Isaiah 49:2, a recognized messianic text. The 'voluntary submission' language suggests the antitype involves the spiritual conquest through Christ's word rather than merely military conquest.

original_text: Seen. All the promises have been fulfilled. How could any one have thought that we should have been permitted to dedicate this temple under the patronage of the king of Persia? (1 Esdras 6:8.) Who would not have feared, lest the Christian religion should perish, under such violent persecutions? Converts admire its beauty and strength. (Calmet) --- The completion of the prophecies is a wonderful confirmation and comfort of Christians, (Worthington) whose faith is founded indeed for ever. (Haydock) --- The gates of hell shall not prevail. [Matthew 16:18.] (Menochius)

extractions.type_description: The physical temple rebuilt under Persian patronage after the exile, representing God's faithfulness in restoring His house and people despite persecution and adversity
extractions.antitype_description: The spiritual temple and body of Christ that persists through persecution and whose foundation in faith cannot be shaken, as referenced in Matthew 16:18 ('the gates of hell shall not prevail')
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly connects the completion and dedication of the physical temple (Psalm 47 context) to the permanence and strength of the Christian Church. The phrase 'gates of hell shall not prevail' from Matthew 16:18 is cited as the fulfillment of the temple's indestructibility, directly linking the OT temple type to the NT Church antitype. The commentary emphasizes how the temple's survival despite threats prefigures the Church's triumph over persecution.

notes: The commentary emphasizes typology through the fulfillment of promises ('All the promises have been fulfilled') and uses the stability and completion of the physical temple as a prefigurement of the Church's eternal foundation and strength. The connection to Matthew 16:18 provides explicit NT grounding for this typological interpretation.

original_text: Only, or principally, who art the only God, (1 Timothy 1:17.; Worthington) the judge and witness of my crime. (Haydock) --- David was a king, and acknowledged no judge among men. (St. Ambrose, c. x.) --- Soli Deo reus est. (Cassiodorus) --- Urias, whom he had injured, was no more. (St. Augustine) --- The action had been done in secret: (2 Kings 12:12.) but many began to suspect, and to blaspheme. (Haydock) --- Judged. St. Paul reads thus, (Romans 3:4.) though the Hebrew be, "when thou judgest." St. Jerome has also judicaberis, so that we might infer, that the Hebrew is now incorrect, or that beshophtec means in judicare te. (Berthier) --- Houbigant changes the order of the verses, "cleanse me from my sins, that thou mayst be blameless when thou comest into judgment: For I know," etc. (Haydock) --- Susanna was preserved from sinning by the thought of God's presence, Daniel 13:25. --- If David fell, he confessed his fault. (Berthier) --- God is faithful to his promises, and desires the conversion of sinners, though some would represent him as cruel, and unconcerned about his creatures. The psalmist prevents this unjust inference, (Haydock) and proves, that God is both just and merciful. (Worthington) --- He acknowledges his ingratitude, as the captives confess, that their sins have brought on them this chastisement, though they had not injured the Babylonians. (Theodoret) (Flaminius) (Calmet) --- God had often promised pardon to those who truly repent. An appeal is made to his truth and mercy.
notes: This Haydock commentary on Psalm 50:6 focuses on David's confession of sin and God's role as judge and witness. While it references typological figures (Susanna in Daniel 13:25 as an example of one preserved from sin by God's presence, and general references to captives and repentance), these are used as illustrative parallels or moral examples rather than as explicit typological relationships where an OT type prefigures an NT antitype. The commentary emphasizes David's personal accountability, God's justice and mercy, and the theology of repentance—all moral and theological themes rather than typological connections. No clear OT person, event, or institution is presented as prefiguring a specific NT fulfillment in Christ, the Church, or eschatological realities.

original_text: Lions. Poetry gives life to all things. It represents mercy and truth as God's messengers; and Saul as a young lion. He might have entered the cave with his men, and destroyed David: but Providence caused him to enter alone, so that David had an opportunity to cut off the hem of his garment, and to shew his clemency. --- Sword. Thus were the Jews armed, to demand Christ's death. (Eusebius) (Calmet) --- The persecutors use artificial weapons, and excite one another to fury, 1 Kings 22:16. (Worthington)

extractions.type_name: David's persecution by Saul and the Jews' demand for Christ's death
extractions.type_description: The historical persecution of David by King Saul, where David showed clemency toward his persecutor (cutting off Saul's garment hem in the cave), prefigures the persecution of Christ
extractions.antitype_name: Christ's passion and the Jews' demand for His death
extractions.antitype_description: Jesus Christ's suffering and crucifixion, including the role of Jewish leaders in demanding His death, which fulfills the typological pattern of innocent suffering and persecution
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly connects the historical narrative of David's persecution to Christ's passion by stating 'Thus were the Jews armed, to demand Christ's death' (attributed to Eusebius and Calmet). This creates a typological parallel where David's suffering at the hands of persecutors prefigures Christ's suffering. However, the connection is somewhat compressed and the commentary doesn't develop the full typological correspondence in detail.

notes: The commentary conflates two related elements: (1) David's persecution by Saul as a type of Christ's persecution, and (2) the specific mention of 'Jews' and 'sword' as instruments used to demand Christ's death. The typological relationship suggested is that David's innocent suffering and persecution in the Old Testament narrative anticipates Christ's Passion in the New Testament. The reference to David's clemency toward Saul may also suggest a contrast-type, where David's mercy differs from the mercilessness shown toward Christ.

original_text: King. They wish long life to the king, expecting that the predictions of the prophets insured to them temporal dominion. But when they saw Zorobabel possess no such splendour, they were naturally taught to extend their thoughts to the Messias, of whom the Chaldeans and ancient Jews, as well as the Fathers, explain this passage. (Calmet) --- Chaldean, "the days of the future world thou wilt add to the days of the king, the Messias. His years shall be like the generations of this world, and the generations of the world to come." Eternity is clearly meant. If David speaks of himself, and of his successors on the throne for many ages, he must be considered as a figure of Christ, who is also designated. (Berthier) --- The Church will continue to the end, and be triumphant throughout eternity. (Worthington)

extractions.type_name: King David and his successors on the throne
extractions.type_description: David as a historical king of Israel whose reign and dynasty were promised continuance and splendor, representing earthly kingship and longevity
extractions.antitype_description: Christ as the ultimate King whose reign is eternal and extends throughout all ages, both of the present world and the world to come
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that David and his successors serve as 'a figure of Christ' when understood typologically. The historical promises to David's line are reinterpreted as prefiguring Christ's eternal kingship. The Chaldean interpretation quoted directly connects the king's years to 'the Messias' and eternity.

extractions.type_description: The earthly Davidic kingdom with its temporal dominion and succession of kings
extractions.antitype_description: The Church as Christ's spiritual kingdom that continues to the end of time and remains triumphant throughout eternity
extractions.reasoning: The commentary concludes that 'The Church will continue to the end, and be triumphant throughout eternity,' drawing a typological parallel between the continuation of David's kingdom and the eternal continuation and triumph of the Church.

notes: This commentary demonstrates a shift from literal/historical interpretation (early expectations of Zorobabel's temporal dominion) to typological interpretation (David as type of Christ, the Davidic kingdom as type of the Church). The typology becomes clearer in the context of unfulfilled literal expectations, which prompted extension of thought to messianic fulfillment.

original_text: Fence. This may refer to the persecutors, who resembled a leaning wall. (Berthier) (Isaias 30:13.) (Calmet) --- Protestants, "ye shall be slain all of you, as a bowing wall shall ye be," etc. He threatens them with speedy destruction, (Haydock) or represents to them the baseness of attacking a man ready to fall. (Calmet) --- He informs them, that their attempts will be in vain, though they be very numerous, and he himself apparently so weak. (Worthington)
notes: This commentary on Psalm 61:4 discusses the metaphorical language of a 'leaning wall' or 'bowing wall' as a representation of the psalmist's persecutors and their weakness. The reference to Isaiah 30:13 provides a parallel Old Testament passage with similar imagery, but this is intertextual parallelism rather than typology. The commentary focuses on the literal/historical meaning of the threat against persecutors and the assurance of God's protection, not on any prefigurement of New Testament realities. No OT type is presented as prefiguring an NT antitype.

original_text: Price. Septuagint, St. Hilary, etc., "my honour." They wish to dethrone me, and to represent me as unfit to govern. --- I ran. Septuagint edramon, "they ran" likewise, as Hebrew implies, and as the Greek Fathers generally explain it. David thought proper to flee, that he might be at a distance from traitors, 2 Kings 15:14. His enemies sought his destruction. (Calmet) --- They wished to deprive him of the reward of his labours; but he ran more earnestly. --- Blessed. Flattery is very dangerous. (Worthington)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Psalm 61:5 discusses David's historical persecution and flight from enemies (referencing 2 Kings 15:14), along with textual variants and moral lessons about flattery. While David is a significant OT figure who does prefigure Christ in various typological contexts elsewhere in Scripture, this particular commentary does not explicitly describe or argue for a typological relationship between David's flight/persecution and any New Testament fulfillment or antitype. The commentary focuses on historical narrative, textual interpretation, and practical moral application rather than typological connection. No OT-to-NT prefigurative relationship is articulated.

original_text: The king. David, (Berthier, etc.) or Zorobabel, for whom the Jews had the highest regard, though he was not an independent monarch, nor wore a crown, Aggeus 2:24., and Zacharias 3:8. It was customary to swear by the life of the king, 1 Kings 1:26., and 20:3. The Fathers understand Jesus Christ to be meant, and this is the true and primary sense; as Zorobabel was only a figure of Him, and never really possessed the throne, that the Jews might not think that the prophecies were fulfilled in his person. --- By him. The king, (Du Pin; Calmet) or God. (Menochius) (Bossuet) (Tirinus) --- Those who follow the true religion, (Deuteronomy 6:13., and Isaias 45:23.; Calmet) and act accordingly (Haydock) shall be kings for ever, Apocalypse. (Berthier) (1 Peter 2:9.) (Haydock) --- As David came to the throne, on the death of his rival, so was Christ's name exalted, after the Romans had destroyed the Jews. (Worthington)

extractions.type_description: The post-exilic Jewish leader who, though highly regarded, was not an independent monarch nor wore a crown, and never truly possessed the throne
extractions.antitype_description: The true King whose name was exalted after the destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans, fulfilling the messianic prophecies
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that 'The Fathers understand Jesus Christ to be meant, and this is the true and primary sense; as Zorobabel was only a figure of Him, and never really possessed the throne, that the Jews might not think that the prophecies were fulfilled in his person.' This directly identifies Zorobabel as a prefiguring type of Christ.

extractions.type_name: David coming to the throne after his rival's death
extractions.type_description: David's exaltation and establishment as king following the death/removal of his rival Saul
extractions.antitype_name: Christ's exaltation after Roman destruction of Jerusalem
extractions.antitype_description: Christ's name and kingdom were exalted after the Romans destroyed the Jewish political system, fulfilling messianic expectation
extractions.reasoning: The commentary notes: 'As David came to the throne, on the death of his rival, so was Christ's name exalted, after the Romans had destroyed the Jews.' This draws a typological parallel between David's rise to power and Christ's ultimate exaltation.

notes: The commentary emphasizes that Zorobabel served as a type specifically to prevent the Jews from mistakenly believing messianic prophecies were fulfilled in his person rather than in Christ. This represents a deliberate divine arrangement where the incomplete fulfillment in Zorobabel pointed to the true and complete fulfillment in Jesus Christ.

original_text: River. Hebrew, "the division," or all the seas and fountains (Berthier) of consequence, (Menochius) particularly the Jordan, which overflows, like the Euphrates, about Pentecost, Josue 3:15., and Jeremias 12:5. (Calmet) --- Its, the earth's, after a plentiful rain. (Haydock) --- God has wrought many wonders by water, and hath fed his people, (Exodus 7:14., and 16:3., etc.) to prefigure the graces conferred in baptism, the holy Eucharist, etc. (Worthington)

extractions.type_name: God's wonders wrought by water (Exodus miracles)
extractions.type_description: The Old Testament miracles and provisions God performed through water, including the plagues of Egypt and the provision of water in the wilderness (references to Exodus 7:14 and 16:3)
extractions.antitype_description: The New Testament sacrament of Baptism, through which God confers grace upon believers
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that God's OT water miracles were given 'to prefigure the graces conferred in baptism.' This is a direct typological statement connecting OT water events to the NT sacrament.

extractions.type_name: God's provision of food and water in the wilderness
extractions.type_description: The Old Testament sustenance provided by God to His people in the desert (manna, water, etc.), referenced in Exodus 16:3
extractions.antitype_description: The New Testament sacrament of the Eucharist, through which God provides spiritual nourishment and grace to believers
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly connects God's feeding of His people in the OT 'to prefigure the graces conferred in...the holy Eucharist.' This establishes a clear typological prefigurement of the Eucharist.

notes: Both typological relationships are explicitly stated by the commentator (Worthington), making them high-confidence extractions. The commentary groups these as examples of how 'God has wrought many wonders by water' to prefigure sacramental grace.

original_text: The king of powers. That is, the mighty King, the Lord of Hosts, is of the beloved, of the beloved; that is, is on the side of Christ, his most beloved Son; and his beautiful house, viz., the Church, in which God dwells for ever, shall by her spiritual conquests, divide the spoils of many nations. The Hebrew (as it now stands pointed) is thus rendered: The kings of armies have fled, they had fled, and she that dwells at home (or, the beauty of the house) shall divide the spoils. (Challoner) --- Yet Symmachus comes nearer the Septuagint and St. Jerome has in the same sense, (Berthier) "the kings of armies shall form leagues," etc. The great King, is the Lord (ver. 12.) of hosts, who shall enable many to publish his wonders. They are represented as women, to denote the particular Churches of Christ, which have risen on the ruins of idolatry, though they may also refer to the victories of the Israelites, under Debora, when mighty kings came to invade the country, Judges iv., and 5:19, 24. (Haydock) --- The glory of that victory was given to her, and to Jahel, who slew Sisara. (Calmet) --- Soon after the preaching of the gospel, the most potent monarchs (Calmet) submitted to its authority, and thus a glorious prey was rescued from the power of the devil. (Worthington) --- Women sometimes promoted this great work. (Menochius)

extractions.type_name: The victory of Debora and the defeat of Sisara (Judges 4-5)
extractions.type_description: An Old Testament account where the prophetess Debora led Israel to victory over mighty kings and their armies, with Jael playing a crucial role in slaying the enemy commander Sisara. The glory of this military victory was attributed to women.
extractions.antitype_name: The triumph of the Church and the preaching of the Gospel
extractions.antitype_description: The New Testament fulfillment where the Church (represented as women/particular churches) achieves spiritual victory over worldly powers through the preaching of the Gospel. Potent earthly monarchs submit to the authority of Christ and the Church, rescuing souls from the devil's power.
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that the Debora account 'may also refer to the victories of the Israelites, under Debora' and directly parallels this to how 'Soon after the preaching of the gospel, the most potent monarchs submitted to its authority.' The commentary clearly presents the OT military victory as prefiguring the NT spiritual conquests of the Church. The parallel structure (women leading to victory in both cases) reinforces the typological connection.

extractions.type_name: The Church dwelling in and beautifying the house (the temple/dwelling place)
extractions.type_description: The Old Testament concept of God's dwelling place (the Temple) and the Church as God's beautiful house that endures and grows.
extractions.antitype_name: The Church as the dwelling place of God and the bride of Christ
extractions.antitype_description: The New Testament Church understood as God's eternal dwelling place, His beloved, which grows through spiritual conquests and rises on the ruins of idolatry, dividing the spoils of spiritual victory among the nations.
extractions.reasoning: The commentary references 'his beautiful house, viz., the Church' and notes that 'God dwells for ever' in it. While less explicitly typological than the Debora reference, there is a connection between the Old Testament temple/house and the New Testament Church as God's dwelling place, though the commentary treats this more as direct application than strict typology.

notes: The primary typological relationship is explicit: Debora's military victory with women as protagonists prefigures the Church's spiritual victories in the Gospel age. The second extraction is more interpretive, as the commentary conflates OT and NT concepts of God's dwelling place rather than strictly presenting one as the type of the other. The commentary also mentions that these references 'may also refer to' the Israelite victories, indicating some interpretive flexibility in how the passage is understood.

original_text: Let their table, etc. What here follows in the style of an imprecation, is a prophecy of the wretched state to which the Jews should be reduced, in punishment of their wilful obstinacy; (Challoner) or it may be a sentence pronounced on them by Jesus Christ. They are driven from their own country, and the sacred books (Calmet) being misunderstood, (Menochius) prove their ruin. Our Saviour and St. Paul confirm this prediction. The latter adheres to the Septuagint (Romans 11:9.) though some would translate lishlomim, "for peace"-offerings, instead of recompenses, as it also means. (Berthier) --- "Let their sacrifices become a scandal to them;" (Chaldean) or rather, May their table, the symbol of friendship, be a snare for them, that they may be destroyed, or betrayed by their dearest friends. (Calmet) --- The overthrow of the Jews, when they were assembled to eat the paschal lamb, is here foretold. (Worthington)
notes: This commentary does not describe a typological relationship in the technical sense. Rather, it presents Psalm 68:23 as a prophecy of judgment against the Jews for their rejection of Christ and misunderstanding of Scripture. While the commentary mentions that 'Our Saviour and St. Paul confirm this prediction' (Romans 11:9), this is cited as confirmation of a prophecy, not as a typological fulfillment. The reference to the 'paschal lamb' and the 'table' (possibly the sacrificial table) are mentioned symbolically as 'a symbol of friendship' and 'a snare,' but these are not presented as OT types prefiguring NT antitypes. The commentary is primarily eschatological in nature—describing the punishment and overthrow of the Jewish people—rather than typological. Typology requires that an OT person, event, or institution prefigure a corresponding NT fulfillment; this text instead presents a predictive prophecy confirmed by NT figures.

original_text: Justice. These blessings shall be so common; (Psalm 35:6., and Joel 3:18.) or, let princes pursue the paths of justice and peace, Micheas 6:1. Solomon was to enjoy a perpetual peace, (1 Paralipomenon 22:9.) as he was a figure of Jesus Christ, who has procured a more solid one for us, Ephesians 2:14., John 14:27., and Isaias 52:7. (Calmet) --- Hebrew has "by righteousness," as this is the source of true peace, Romans 14:17. These virtues are publicly enforced in the Church, as from a mountain, Isaias 2:2. (Berthier) --- Christ, the rock, (Haydock) and his ministers, the hills, preach reconciliation. (Worthington)

extractions.type_description: The Old Testament king who enjoyed perpetual peace and ruled with righteousness and justice, as recorded in 1 Chronicles 22:9
extractions.antitype_description: The New Testament fulfillment who procured a more solid and eternal peace for believers, as referenced in Ephesians 2:14 and John 14:27
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states 'Solomon was to enjoy a perpetual peace...as he was a figure of Jesus Christ.' This is a direct typological statement connecting the OT king to the NT Messiah, with Solomon's reign of justice and peace prefiguring Christ's redemptive work and the peace He brings.

extractions.type_description: Symbolic OT figures representing natural elevation from which truth and righteousness flow, as referenced in Isaiah 2:2
extractions.antitype_name: Christ (the rock) and his ministers preaching reconciliation
extractions.antitype_description: The NT fulfillment wherein Christ and Church ministers proclaim the gospel of reconciliation and peace
extractions.reasoning: The commentary identifies Christ as 'the rock' and his ministers as 'the hills,' connecting OT imagery of mountains as sources of divine teaching (Isaiah 2:2) to the NT proclamation of Christ's reconciliation message. While more symbolic than narrative typology, it represents how OT geographical/structural metaphors prefigure NT spiritual realities.

notes: The first extraction represents explicit typology as stated in the source. The second extraction involves symbolic typology interpreting OT imagery as prefiguring NT ministry roles. Both connections emphasize themes of justice, righteousness, and peace flowing from their respective types to antitypes.

original_text: Before. Or, in the presence of the moon, as the Hebrew indicates, (Berthier) though St. Jerome translates, ultra, "beyond, or after." (Haydock) --- Yea, Christ existed before all the creation, (Psalm 109:3.; Calmet) and these comparisons do not insinuate that he will ever cease to be. (Theodoret) --- The kingdom of David and Solomon is described in the same poetic language, (Psalm 88:28., and 37.; Calmet) as it will remain for ever in the hands of the Messias. (Haydock) --- Hebrew makes a sudden address to the king, "they shall fear thee with the sun," which Houbigant dislikes. Some letters may have been changed, though the sense is not bad. (Berthier) --- "They shall fear thee at the rising of the sun, and shall pray to they by the light of the moon," Chaldean, both day and night. (Calmet) --- Solomon, as a figure of Christ, was good for some time; but no king, except our Saviour, will reign for ever. (Worthington) --- The mind of the prophet is now raised to behold him. (Menochius)

extractions.type_description: Solomon's earthly kingdom, described in poetic language as enduring and characterized by fear/reverence from subjects and perpetual reign
extractions.antitype_description: Christ's eternal kingdom that will remain forever in His hands, surpassing Solomon's temporal kingdom
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states: 'Solomon, as a figure of Christ, was good for some time; but no king, except our Saviour, will reign for ever.' This directly establishes Solomon as a type prefiguring Christ's eternal kingship. The commentary also notes that 'the kingdom of David and Solomon is described in the same poetic language...as it will remain for ever in the hands of the Messias.'

extractions.type_description: David's earthly reign, described in poetic language suggesting permanence and universal reverence
extractions.antitype_description: The Messiah's permanent reign over all creation, surpassing David's temporal rule
extractions.reasoning: The commentary indicates that David's kingdom, like Solomon's, is presented as a type that finds its ultimate fulfillment in the Messiah's eternal kingdom. The poetic language describing both kingdoms suggests a typological progression from shadow to reality.

notes: The commentary emphasizes that while both David and Solomon were 'good for some time,' only Christ achieves perpetual, eternal reign. The typological relationship is explicitly acknowledged by the Worthington source cited. The commentary also notes that Christ 'existed before all the creation,' distinguishing Him from the merely temporal kings who prefigured Him.

original_text: Justice. Hebrew, "the just," who appear most under a good king, being animated by his example. (Haydock) --- Away. Chaldean, "till those who adore the moon be exterminated." This idolatry pervaded almost all the east. Solomon's reign was very peaceable, 3 Kings 4:25. But this was only a feeble representation of the peace which Christ should bring. At his birth, the whole world was at peace. Angels proclaimed it to all the earth, Luke 2:14., and Isaias 2:4. (Calmet) --- It is certain, that the internal peace of Solomon's reign did not continue to the end, (Haydock) much less till the moon should be taken away. (Berthier)

extractions.type_description: The internal peace and justice that characterized Solomon's kingdom, where the just flourished under a good king's example, and idolatry was absent
extractions.antitype_name: Christ's Advent and the Peace He Brings
extractions.antitype_description: The peace proclaimed at Christ's birth (Luke 2:14) and the ultimate peace described in Isaiah 2:4, representing the eschatological peace that Christ initiates
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that Solomon's peaceful reign 'was only a feeble representation of the peace which Christ should bring.' This directly connects the OT type (Solomon's reign) to the NT antitype (Christ's peace). However, the commentators note this is an imperfect type, as Solomon's internal peace did not endure to the end, whereas Christ's peace is ultimate and eschatological.

notes: The typology here is somewhat qualified by the commentary itself—it acknowledges Solomon's reign as only a 'feeble representation' rather than a complete type. The connection is to eschatological peace (the peace Christ brings, associated with the end times and fulfillment of Isaiah's prophecy) rather than to Christ's person directly. The commentary also notes the incompleteness of the type, since Solomon's peace was temporary and limited, whereas Christ's peace is eternal.

original_text: Drink. The just themselves shall suffer something. But their part will be comparatively the clear wine, while sinners shall have the dregs. Many suppose that God holds in his had two cups, which he mixes according to each one's deserts. So the Septuagint, Syriac, St. Augustine, etc., seem to intimate. Jupiter is thus represented with two barrels of goods and evils near his throne. (Homer, Iliad xxiv.) --- But most interpreters suppose that only one chalice is here specified, filled with red wine, the sediment being reserved for sinners, though it was usually thrown away at feasts. Wine was mixed with water in those hot countries. (Calmet) --- Yet here the mixture is of a different nature. (Haydock) --- Fire, (Psalm 10:7.; Menochius) gall, brimestone, etc., compose the bitter chalice of the damned, who will never arrive at the term of their inexpressible misery. In this life, sinners are frequently punished: but their sufferings do not end here. They shall experience a variety of torments in heat and cold, Job xxiv. (Worthington) (Apocalypse 14:10., Isaias 51:17., and Ezechiel 23:34.)

extractions.type_description: The Old Testament image of God holding a cup or chalice containing wine mixed with bitter substances (fire, gall, brimstone), with the sediment/dregs reserved for sinners as punishment, while the just receive the clear wine
extractions.antitype_name: The Cup of God's Wrath in the Last Judgment
extractions.antitype_description: The New Testament fulfillment in Revelation 14:10, Isaiah 51:17, and Ezekiel 23:34, where sinners drink from the cup of God's wrath in the final judgment, experiencing eternal torments and inexpressible misery
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly connects the OT image of the cup/chalice containing judgment to its NT fulfillment in Revelation 14:10, Isaiah 51:17, and Ezekiel 23:34. The type (OT cup of divine judgment) prefigures the antitype (NT final judgment when sinners experience eternal punishment). The progression from temporal suffering in this life to eschatological suffering in eternity demonstrates clear typological fulfillment.

notes: The commentary also references the general symbolism of Jupiter's two barrels from Homer's Iliad as a parallel concept, but this is not typology since it lacks an OT-to-NT connection. The distinction between the just receiving 'clear wine' and sinners receiving 'dregs' establishes the moral differentiation that the type communicates.

original_text: Just. Zorobabel, (Theodoret) the figure of the Messias. The Jews were shortly after set at liberty by Cyrus, who was the scourge of their oppressors. (Calmet) --- The virtuous, who use well their free-will, are thus rewarded. (Worthington)

extractions.type_description: The Jewish leader who led the restoration of Jerusalem and the Temple after the Babylonian exile, representing the deliverance and vindication of God's people
extractions.antitype_description: Jesus Christ as the ultimate deliverer and restorer who brings spiritual liberation and vindication to God's people
extractions.reasoning: Theodoret explicitly identifies Zerubbabel as 'the figure of the Messias.' Zerubbabel's role in restoring the Jewish people after exile prefigures Christ's role as the ultimate liberator and restorer. The context of divine vindication and freedom from oppression connects the type to the antitype.

notes: The commentary is somewhat brief and the typological connection relies on Theodoret's patristic interpretation. While the explicit statement 'figure of the Messias' makes the typological claim clear, Zerubbabel as a Christological type is not as universally emphasized in biblical typology as some other OT figures. The confidence is rated 'medium' due to the reliance on a single patristic source rather than broader scholarly consensus. The additional note about Cyrus as a 'scourge of oppressors' and the moral lesson about virtue are not typological in nature.

original_text: Heard. Some editions of the Septuagint read, "thou hast darted judgment." (St. Augustine) --- Still. All were filled with astonishment, and Sennacherib was glad to escape in the most private manner. (Calmet) --- Persecutors will all be terrified when the signs of judgment begin to appear in heaven, which are here represented as past, on account of their certainty. (Worthington) --- The divine power will be again displayed. (Menochius)

extractions.type_description: The OT historical event where God displayed divine power to terrify persecutors and deliver His people from the Assyrian king Sennacherib, causing all to be filled with astonishment
extractions.antitype_name: The final judgment and divine intervention at the end times
extractions.antitype_description: The future display of divine power when signs of judgment appear in heaven, terrifying all persecutors and vindicating God's people at the eschaton
extractions.reasoning: Worthington's commentary explicitly states that the OT historical event of God's judgment against Sennacherib prefigures future judgment: 'Persecutors will all be terrified when the signs of judgment begin to appear in heaven, which are here represented as past, on account of their certainty.' The past deliverance is treated as a type of the future eschatological judgment, with the certainty of the OT event guaranteeing the certainty of the future antitype.

notes: The typological connection here is eschatological in nature, using a past historical deliverance as assurance of a future divine judgment. Menochius adds that 'the divine power will be again displayed,' reinforcing the typological pattern of repetition and fulfillment. This is a typology of historical pattern rather than a personal or institutional type.

original_text: Ever. Hebrew adds, "is his word ineffectual?" which the Vatican Septuagint neglects, (Berthier) though gamar omer be thus rendered in other editions. "Has he completely fulfilled his word," which may be the true sense, consumabitur verbum. (St. Jerome) (Haydock) --- "Will he execute this threat from generation?" etc. (Calmet) --- God will never abandon his Church, (Worthington) though he may chastise his people. (Haydock)

extractions.type_name: God's Chastisement of His People (OT pattern)
extractions.type_description: The Old Testament pattern of God chastising His people while maintaining His covenant promises and never abandoning His chosen community
extractions.antitype_description: The New Testament Church, which experiences divine discipline and testing but remains under God's eternal protection and covenant faithfulness
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states 'God will never abandon his Church, though he may chastise his people.' This indicates a typological relationship where the OT pattern of God's faithfulness to Israel despite chastisement prefigures God's unwavering commitment to the Church in the NT. The principle of covenantal fidelity transcends both testaments.

notes: The typology here is somewhat implicit rather than explicitly stated as a direct prefigurement. The commentary applies the OT principle of God's faithfulness-amid-judgment to the Church ecclesially. This reflects the broader typological principle that OT Israel's covenant relationship with God finds its fulfillment and expansion in the NT Church. The confidence is medium because the commentary focuses more on doctrinal application than explicit typological terminology.

original_text: Propositions. Deep and mysterious sayings. By this it appears, that the historical facts of ancient times, commemorated in this psalm, were deep and mysterious; as being figures of great truths appertaining to the time of the New Testament. (Challoner) --- St. Matthew (xiii. 35.) has, things hidden from the foundation of the world. Hebrew minni kedem, "from of old." St. Jerome, "ancient riddles." (Haydock) --- Mashal and chidoth, "parables and enigmas." frequently denote things very plain, but spoken in a sententious poetic style, Numbers 23:7. (Calmet) --- The facts, etc., of the Old Testament, prefigured the mysteries of the New. (Worthington)

extractions.type_name: Historical facts and events of ancient times (OT)
extractions.type_description: The commemorated historical facts of ancient times recorded in the Old Testament, described as 'deep and mysterious sayings' or 'parables and enigmas'
extractions.antitype_description: The spiritual truths and mysteries of the New Testament era, including the 'things hidden from the foundation of the world' referenced in Matthew 13:35
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that 'The facts, etc., of the Old Testament, prefigured the mysteries of the New' and that historical facts were 'figures of great truths appertaining to the time of the New Testament.' This is a direct statement of typological prefigurement across testaments.

notes: The commentary emphasizes that Psalm 77's historical references function as types—understood through the Hebrew terms 'mashal' (parables) and 'chidoth' (enigmas)—which veiled deeper spiritual truths about New Testament fulfillment. The reference to Matthew 13:35 ('things hidden from the foundation of the world') reinforces this typological hermeneutic. The specific content of which OT events prefigure which NT mysteries is not detailed in this commentary, only the principle that such prefigurement occurs.

original_text: As of unicorns. That is, firm and strong, like the horn of the unicorn. This is one of the chief of the propositions of this psalm, fore-shewing the firm establishment of the one, true, and everlasting sanctuary of God, in his Church. (Challoner) (Menochius) --- It was preserved before Christ, and will remain till the end of time. (Worthington) --- The temple was not built by David: but the spot was consecrated for it, (2 Kings xxiv.) and the ark was placed on Sion; which was the land which he had founded for ever for this purpose. Hebrew ramim, means "unicorns, (Chaldean; St. Jerome) heights, (Montanus) palaces," (Pagnin) etc. Santificium and sanctuarium, have the same import. (Haydock) --- In the land. Hebrew, "as the land." Septuagint have read b for c, as well; (Berthier) and it is observable that Montanus translates the latter, though the former occur in the Hebrew text below, edition 1632: so easily may these letters be confounded! (Haydock) --- The temple was to have the same stability as the earth, and was but one, like the horn of the unicorn, which is most solid and beautiful. (Calmet) --- Yet this could not be understood of the material temple, which was the most magnificent structure in the world. It was fulfilled in the Church of Jesus Christ, who is also the true David, ver. 72. (Haydock) --- The crowning of David, who was his figure, was a great blessing to Israel. (Worthington)

extractions.type_description: The physical sanctuary built in Jerusalem with the ark placed on Zion, characterized by stability and singular uniqueness (like the unicorn's horn), established by David's consecration of the spot
extractions.antitype_description: The spiritual, everlasting sanctuary of God that fulfills the material temple's purpose, remaining stable and unified from Christ's time until the end of time
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states: 'It was fulfilled in the Church of Jesus Christ' and notes that the material temple's stability and singularity prefigures the Church's permanent establishment. The commentators acknowledge that the typology could not apply to the material structure itself, but rather points to its spiritual fulfillment.

extractions.type_description: The crowned king of Israel whose establishment brought blessing to Israel and whose designation of the sanctuary site prefigured a greater reality
extractions.antitype_description: The true David who is the ultimate king and foundation of the Church, fulfilling the Davidic covenant and sanctuary imagery
extractions.reasoning: The commentary states 'Jesus Christ, who is also the true David, ver. 72' and notes that 'The crowning of David, who was his figure, was a great blessing to Israel.' This identifies David as a prefigurement of Christ's kingship and blessing.

notes: The commentary emphasizes that while the psalm speaks of the temple's physical establishment, its true fulfillment is spiritual and eschatological—the Church enduring 'till the end of time.' The unicorn horn imagery represents both the uniqueness and unshakeable stability of the sanctuary's ultimate antitype. Multiple commentators (Challoner, Menochius, Worthington, Haydock) converge on this interpretation.

original_text: The man of thy right hand. Christ, (Challoner) where he sits, (Calmet) being as man in the highest place of heaven, Matthew 26:64., and 12:32. (Haydock) --- Who else could redeem Israel? (Calmet) --- Zorobabel was only a figure of Him. (Haydock) --- Christ's birth was miraculous, (Menochius) and he was appointed by the right hand of God to do great things; and, as man, is moved to take compassion on the distresses of his people. (Berthier)

extractions.type_description: The governor of Judah who led the Jewish people in rebuilding the Temple after the Babylonian exile, representing a restored and renewed Israel
extractions.antitype_description: The ultimate redeemer of Israel who sits at the right hand of God in heaven, appointed to accomplish great things and show compassion on his people
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states 'Zorobabel was only a figure of Him' (Christ), directly identifying Zorobabel as a typological prefigurement of Christ. The connection is further reinforced by the rhetorical question 'Who else could redeem Israel?' implying that while Zorobabel foreshadowed redemption, only Christ accomplished true redemption.

notes: The broader context of Psalm 79:18 speaks of 'the man of thy right hand,' which the commentators apply Christologically to Christ's exaltation. Zorobabel serves as an OT type whose historical restoration work prefigured Christ's ultimate redemptive work. This represents a common patristic and medieval hermeneutical approach of identifying lesser historical figures as types of the greater Christ-antitype.

original_text: Joseph. Who represents all the family of Israel, as he took care of it. (Calmet) (Psalm 79:2.) (Worthington) --- Not. The Israelites heard the voice of God at Sinai, (St. Jerome, etc.; Calmet) and for the last time, where forced to hear the insults of the Egyptians at their heels; (Haydock) whose language was barbarous to them, (Psalm 113:1.; Menochius) and not well understood by all, as they had very little society together. Joseph spoke to his brethren by an interpreter. (Haydock) --- Some explain this of Joseph himself, when he first came into Egypt, (Chaldean. Bossuet) or of the Israelites, at their arrival there. (Vatable) --- But this agrees not with the Vulgate or Hebrew, (Haydock) the latter of which is very confused and incorrect, though it be adopted (Calmet) by St. Jerome: "I heard a tongue which I knew not, I withdrew," etc., (Haydock) or, making a small alteration, "God hast established this festival in Joseph, when He appeared in the land of Egypt to rescue his people: then said the Lord, I made him hear a language which he knew not, that I was the protector of my people, I will remove," etc. (Calmet) --- The authors of the Pin. disc. take this liberty, which would make the sense pretty clear. But the Hebrew means, "I heard," etc. Some not being able to understand this, have substituted, "He heard," with the German version. (Berthier) --- The ancient Greek interpreters seem to have read the same, as no variation is noticed. (Calmet) --- If, however, we must explain the Hebrew of St. Jerome, we must suppose that, "I knew not, means I condemned, as it often does; and God certainly reprobated the harsh language of the Egyptian task-masters, and came to deliver his people from oppression, Exodus 2:25., and 3:8., and 5:14. (Haydock)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Psalm 80:6 discusses the historical narrative of Joseph and the Israelites in Egypt, focusing on linguistic and cultural barriers ('a tongue which I knew not'). While Joseph is mentioned as representing 'all the family of Israel,' this is presented as a historical representation or prefigurement within the Old Testament itself, not as a type prefiguring a New Testament antitype. The commentary explores various interpretative approaches to the Hebrew text and the Egyptian oppression narrative, but does not establish an explicit connection between an OT type and NT fulfillment. The reference to God's deliverance is treated as historical redemptive action rather than as typological prefigurement of Christ or the Church.

original_text: And. Or "though." This increases their ingratitude. --- Filled. Hebrew, "I will fill thee;" which reading few admit. St. Jerome agrees with us. (Berthier) --- Protestants, (16) "the haters of the Lord should have submitted (marginal note, lied) to him; but their time should have endured for ever. (17) He should have fed them, (v rather signifies "him;" Haydock) also with the finest of wheat, and with honey out of the rock, should I have satisfied thee." This sudden change seems rather abrupt, though God may have spoken either in the first or third person, from ver. 6. (Haydock) --- Rock. He fed them in the desert with manna, and the water seemed most delicious, as they were thirsty; unless he speaks of real honey. (Menochius) --- The promised land was very fruitful; but all this prefigured the favours which God bestows upon his servants, in the blessed Eucharist, 1 Corinthians 10:4. (Calmet) --- How many, like Judas, partake of them, and prove faithless! (St. Augustine)

extractions.type_name: God's feeding in the desert with manna and water from the rock
extractions.type_description: The miraculous provision God gave to Israel in the wilderness - manna as food and water flowing from the rock during their desert wanderings (Exodus 16-17)
extractions.antitype_description: The sacrament of Christ's body and blood, through which God nourishes His servants spiritually in the New Testament era
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states: 'all this prefigured the favours which God bestows upon his servants, in the blessed Eucharist' and cites 1 Corinthians 10:4 as support. This is a direct typological claim that the wilderness provision (type) prefigures the Eucharist (antitype). The commentary also notes the parallel of unfaithfulness - just as some Israelites proved faithless despite God's provision, so too do some communicants (like Judas) partake of the Eucharist and prove faithless.

notes: The commentary invokes St. Augustine's observation about Judas to reinforce the typological parallel between Israel's ingratitude in the wilderness and unfaithfulness among those who receive the Eucharist. This strengthens the typological connection by showing parallel human responses in both testaments.

original_text: Core. See Psalm viii., xli., and lxxx. (Haydock) --- The Corites were musicians, as well as porters in the temple, 1 Paralipomenon xxvi. They here represent the faithful upon earth, (St. Augustine; Worthington) who sigh after the heavenly Sion. David was animated with these sentiments, more than with the desire of revisiting Jerusalem, during the revolt of his son. (Berthier) --- This psalm might have been written by him under the persecution of Saul, (Grotius) or it may refer to the captives. (Theodoret) (Calmet) --- Yet, at those times, the tabernacle was not subsisting on Sion, as it seem to have been when this beautiful piece was composed. (Berthier) --- The Jews are said to recite it every night, in hopes of seeing Jerusalem rebuilt, and it might very well be used by all Israelites, when they went to celebrate the three great festivals. (Calmet)

extractions.type_name: Heavenly Zion (the tabernacle and temple on Mount Zion)
extractions.type_description: The physical location of God's dwelling place in the Old Testament - the temple/tabernacle on Mount Zion in Jerusalem, which the faithful longed to reach and where they celebrated religious festivals
extractions.antitype_description: The eschatological city of God in the New Testament - the ultimate dwelling place of God with His people, the final destination toward which the faithful aspire
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that the Corites 'represent the faithful upon earth, who sigh after the heavenly Sion.' This directly connects the earthly Zion (OT type) to a heavenly Zion (NT antitype). The faithful's longing for the rebuilt Jerusalem in Psalm 83 prefigures the Christian hope for the eschatological heavenly Jerusalem described in Revelation 21, where God dwells with His people forever.

notes: The commentary emphasizes that the faithful 'sigh after the heavenly Sion,' indicating they are looking beyond the physical, earthly temple to a transcendent, ultimate fulfillment. St. Augustine and other fathers understood the psalm's references to Zion/Jerusalem as pointing to the heavenly rather than merely earthly restoration, making this an eschatological typology. The Jews' nightly recitation hoping for Jerusalem's rebuilding also prefigures Christian longing for the eschaton.

original_text: Thousands elsewhere, (Calmet) among sinners. He is so much affected, as to leave the sentence imperfect, ver. 4. But the meaning is clear. Temporal must yield to eternal happiness. Eternity is all as one point: it has no division of time, which has a thousand parts. (Haydock) --- Heaven is represented as a palace, (Berthier) in which the blessed enjoy perpetual felicity. (Haydock) --- With respect to future rewards, one day in the Church is better than thousands out of it. (Worthington), ver. 4. --- Abject. Protestants, "door-keeper." Marginal note, "on the threshold." (Haydock) --- This was the office of the Corites, (Calmet) and they prefer it before the finest occupations among sinners. Hebrew, "the tents of wickedness." (Haydock) --- The poorest condition in the Catholic Church, is better than the highest dignities which the wicked can bestow. (Worthington) --- Indeed poverty, and attention to God's service, is the most secure road to heaven, and gives even present content to those who are actuated by the divine spirit. (Haydock)

extractions.type_name: The office of the Corites (doorkeepers in the Temple)
extractions.type_description: The humble service of doorkeepers in the Old Testament Temple, representing the lowest positions in God's earthly sanctuary
extractions.antitype_description: The poorest condition and humblest service within the Catholic Church, which is superior to all worldly dignities and prefigures eternal heavenly reward
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly compares the OT Temple office of doorkeepers (the Corites) to service within the Church, establishing that the humble position in God's earthly sanctuary prefigures/typifies the blessed state in the Church. The commentary states 'The poorest condition in the Catholic Church, is better than the highest dignities which the wicked can bestow,' drawing a parallel between OT Temple service and NT Church membership as types of heavenly reality.

extractions.type_name: The Temple/Palace of God in the OT
extractions.type_description: The Old Testament sanctuary where God's presence dwelt and where His people served
extractions.antitype_description: The eternal heavenly palace where the blessed enjoy perpetual felicity and God's presence eternally
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states 'Heaven is represented as a palace, in which the blessed enjoy perpetual felicity.' This represents an OT/NT typological connection where the earthly Temple sanctuary (God's earthly palace) prefigures heaven as God's eternal palace, with eschatological fulfillment in the New Testament reality of eternal communion with God.

notes: The commentary emphasizes that temporal earthly service (particularly in the OT Temple) prefigures and is surpassed by eternal heavenly reward. The typology is somewhat implicit but clearly intended by the commentators, particularly Worthington and Haydock, who draw explicit comparisons between OT sanctuary service and NT Church reality leading to eschatological fulfillment.

original_text: Blessed. Hebrew, "taken into favour," or "hast rendered fruitful." (Judea) (Calmet) --- God had bestowed many benefits upon his people, rescuing them from the Egyptian bondage, and not punishing them as much as they deserved. (Worthington) --- Others explain it of the captivity at Babylon, or under the devil. (Menochius) --- David speaks of the former event by the prophetic spirit, and the latter misfortune was always deplorable, and to be terminated only by the Messias. (Berthier) --- The redemption of man was prefigured by the liberation of the Jews. (Du Hamel)

extractions.type_name: Liberation of the Jews from Egyptian Bondage
extractions.type_description: God's rescue of the Israelites from Egyptian slavery, a foundational redemptive event in Old Testament history
extractions.antitype_name: The Redemption of Man/Mankind through Christ
extractions.antitype_description: The salvation and liberation of humanity accomplished through the Messiah (Jesus Christ), prefigured by the historical exodus
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states: 'The redemption of man was prefigured by the liberation of the Jews' (Du Hamel). This directly identifies the Exodus as a type of Christ's redemptive work, making it a clear typological relationship where the OT deliverance event prefigures the NT salvation through the Messiah.

notes: The commentary also mentions the Babylonian captivity as potentially relevant to the passage, and notes that the 'latter misfortune was always deplorable, and to be terminated only by the Messias.' However, this reference is less explicitly developed as a typological relationship compared to the Egyptian exodus connection. The explicit typological claim comes from Du Hamel's interpretation at the end of the cited text.

original_text: Good. Mark me for thy slave, (Calmet) which will be the highest honour. (Haydock) --- Give me such a sign as the angel did when he was going to destroy the first-born of Egypt. (St. Athanasius) --- By some prodigy convince our oppressors that there is a God. (Calmet) (Berthier) --- The resurrection, prefigured by Jonas, was the great proof of Christ and his Church; and this serves either for the conversion or for the condemnation of mankind. See St. Augustine. (Worthington) Quod precor eveniet, sunt certa oracula vatum, Nam Deus optanti prospera signa dedit. (Ovid, 2 de Ponto 1.) --- Comforted. St. Cyprian was in sorrow while suffering, but was comforted when crowned. "All the martyrs, with Christ, pray for us." (St. Augustine) (Du Hamel)

extractions.type_description: The Old Testament prophet Jonah, whose resurrection from the belly of the whale after three days prefigured a greater resurrection
extractions.antitype_description: Christ's resurrection, which is presented as the fulfillment and ultimate proof of divine power, serving for the conversion or condemnation of mankind
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states 'The resurrection, prefigured by Jonas, was the great proof of Christ and his Church.' This is a clear OT type (Jonah's deliverance/resurrection) prefiguring an NT antitype (Christ's resurrection). The citation of St. Augustine reinforces this as a recognized typological relationship.

notes: The commentary also references the angel destroying the firstborn of Egypt as a potential 'sign,' but this is presented as an example of a miraculous sign the psalmist is requesting, not as an explicit typological prefigurement of a New Testament reality. Therefore, it was not included as a typological extraction. The reference to martyrs being 'comforted' and crowned is presented as a moral/spiritual principle rather than a typological relationship.

original_text: Mountains. So far the Jews extend the title, supposing that the subject of this canticle was concerning Sion, Moria, etc. Others think that, thereof, refers to a part of the psalm which has been lost, (Calmet) or to the temple or city which occupied the prophet's thoughts; or it is sufficiently explained by the word Sion, which follows, as the relative sometimes comes first. (Du Hamel) See Proverbs 14:3. --- This psalm might be composed (Berthier) by some of the Corites, during, or after the captivity, when Jerusalem received strangers within her walls, as a figure of the Christian Church; (Isaias 2:2., and Zacharias 8:20.; Calmet) or David (Berthier) might write it when he had removed the ark to Sion, which was to be the seat of the true religion. (Ferrand) --- Mountains. The apostles and prophets; (Ephesians 2:20.; Challoner) on which the Church is founded. (Haydock) --- The city was styled holy, from the temple built on Moria. Several other mountains were included within its walls. (Calmet)

extractions.type_name: Jerusalem receiving strangers within her walls
extractions.type_description: Jerusalem during or after the captivity as a city that welcomed foreigners and strangers into its walls
extractions.antitype_description: The Church as a community that embraces all peoples and nations, transcending ethnic and national boundaries
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that Jerusalem 'received strangers within her walls, as a figure of the Christian Church.' This represents a typological prefiguring of the Church's inclusive, universal character.
