extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states: 'The few who were converted under Ezechias were a figure of those who should embrace the faith of Christ.' This directly connects an OT historical event (the remnant saved under Hezekiah) to its NT fulfillment (the converted Jews in the Christian era), establishing a clear typological relationship where the preservation of a faithful remnant prefigures the gathering of believers in Christ.

notes: The commentary cites Romans 9:27 as the apostle Paul's interpretation of this passage, indicating this typology has explicit New Testament authorization. The commentary also notes that Jerome emphasized Paul's interpretation as definitive: 'As the apostle has explained this passage, every other interpretation must cease.' This strengthens the typological reading as apostolically confirmed.

original_text: Root. Juda shall not be exterminated, like the Assyrians. (Calmet) --- Christ shall spring from the blessed Virgin [Mary], (Worthington) for the salvation of mankind. The Jews agree, that this prediction regards the Messias; though some, with Grotius, would explain it literally of Ezechias. They do not reflect that he was now ten years old, and that the prophet speaks of an event which should still take place after he had been a long while upon the throne. If we were to look for any figure of the Messias, to whom this might be applicable, it would be Zorobabel, Zacharias 3:8. But how disproportionate would be the promises to the execution? Some passages may indeed relate to the return of the captives, (ver. 11.) as the people must have a more immediate object, to insure the accomplishment of the more elevated predictions concerning the Messias: but these also refer ultimately to the propagation of the gospel, which the prophet had also in view. (Calmet)

extractions.type_description: The promise that a righteous descendant will spring from the line of David (Jesse), who will not be exterminated despite the destruction of surrounding nations
extractions.antitype_description: Christ who springs from the Virgin Mary as the ultimate fulfillment of the Davidic promise, bringing salvation to mankind
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that 'Christ shall spring from the blessed Virgin [Mary]' as the fulfillment of this prediction, and notes that 'The Jews agree, that this prediction regards the Messias.' This is a direct type-antitype relationship where the OT prophecy of a righteous heir from David's line prefigures Jesus Christ.

extractions.type_description: The governor of the Jews after the Babylonian captivity, a descendant of David who led the restoration
extractions.antitype_description: The ultimate restorer and messianic figure who fulfills the promises made to David's line
extractions.reasoning: The commentary suggests that 'If we were to look for any figure of the Messias, to whom this might be applicable, it would be Zorobabel' (referencing Zech 3:8). However, this is presented as an incomplete or inferior type, with the commentary noting the disproportion between the promises and Zorobabel's execution, indicating that the ultimate antitype is Christ.

notes: The commentary emphasizes that while some passages may relate to the return of captives under Zorobabel, these serve as intermediate figures pointing ultimately to Christ. The primary typological relationship is between the promised Davidic heir (OT type) and Jesus Christ as Messiah (NT antitype). The commentary also indicates that these predictions ultimately concern 'the propagation of the gospel.'

original_text: O Lucifer. O day-star. All this, according to the letter, is spoken of the king of Babylon. It may also be applied, in a spiritual sense, to Lucifer, the prince of devils, who was created a bright angel, but fell by pride and rebellion against God. (Challoner) (Luke 10:18.) (Calmet) --- He fell by pride, as Nabuchodonosor did. (Worthington) --- Homer (Iliad xix.) represents the demon of discord hurled down by Jupiter to the miserable region of mortals.
notes: The Haydock commentary presents multiple interpretative approaches to Isaiah 14:12, but none constitute typology as classically defined. The commentary discusses: (1) the literal historical sense referring to the king of Babylon, (2) a spiritual/allegorical application to Satan/Lucifer based on theological interpretation rather than OT-to-NT prefigurement, and (3) a parallel with Nebuchadnezzar's pride as a moral lesson. While Luke 10:18 is cited regarding Satan's fall, this represents typological interpretation applied to a spiritual reality rather than the OT figure prefiguring an NT fulfillment. The king of Babylon is not presented as a type that finds its antitype in the New Testament; rather, Satan is understood through a spiritual lens as the deeper meaning of the passage. This is allegorical interpretation and typological application of Scripture rather than true typology in the technical sense of OT types prefiguring NT antitypes.

original_text: Just. This regards Christ, (St. Jerome) prefigured by (Haydock) Ezechias. (Calmet)

extractions.type_description: The righteous Judean king of the Old Testament who represents just rule and faithfulness to God
extractions.antitype_description: The ultimate just judge and ruler who embodies perfect righteousness and justice
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that Christ is prefigured by Ezechias in relation to the concept of 'Just' mentioned in Isaiah 16:5. This is a direct type-antitype relationship where the righteous king prefigures the coming Messiah as the embodiment of justice and righteous judgment. St. Jerome and Calmet are cited as authoritative sources for this connection.

notes: The commentary attributes this typological interpretation to St. Jerome (Patristic authority) and Calmet (modern scholar). The context suggests Isaiah 16:5 is speaking of a throne established in mercy and justice, which the commentators read as prefiguring Christ's messianic reign. The connection is relatively explicit in the source material.

original_text: Sackcloth. The prophets lived in poverty, Zacharias 13:4. Their persons were prophetic. It is not agreed whether Isaias went quite naked, or only without his upper garment. The former supposition would represent better the condition of slaves, (ver. 4.) and is adopted by St. Jerome, etc. (Calmet) --- People are said to be naked when they are almost so, 2 Kings vi., and John xxi. (Haydock) --- Yet "nothing is more honest than to obey God." (St. Jerome) (Worthington)
notes: This Haydock commentary discusses Isaiah's symbolic action of removing his garments and walking naked/nearly naked as a prophetic sign. While the commentary notes that this 'would represent better the condition of slaves' and references Isaiah 20:4, it does not establish a typological relationship where an OT person, event, or institution prefigures a NT fulfillment. The commentary focuses on: (1) the poverty and austere lifestyle of OT prophets, (2) the symbolic meaning of the action (representing slave condition), and (3) references to similar uses of 'nakedness' language in other biblical passages (2 Kings 6, John 21). These are instances of biblical symbolism and comparative usage rather than OT types prefiguring NT antitypes. The moral lesson about obedience to God, while present, does not constitute typology in the technical sense.

original_text: Commit. Septuagint, "be the emporium for all." Great injustice prevailed formerly among merchants, so that it is represented as a dishonest calling. (Haydock)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Isaiah 23:17 discusses the moral character of merchants and commercial activity in Tyre, noting that merchants were often viewed as dishonest. The commentary provides textual notes on the Septuagint rendering ('be the emporium for all') and reflects on the ethical reputation of merchants in ancient times. However, it does not establish or describe any typological relationship between an Old Testament type and a New Testament antitype. The passage is concerned with historical commentary on commercial practices and moral reputation rather than prefigurative theology.

original_text: Mountain of Sion, a figure of the Church, and of heaven. The Jews shall feast: yea, some of all nations shall partake of the blessed Eucharist, and obtain heaven. The expressions are too grand for a corruptible feast. (Calmet) --- Wine. Literally, "of vintage," (Haydock) on which occasion great rejoicings were made. (Hesiod, Hercul. 297.) --- Protestants, "of wines on the lees." (Haydock) --- In the East, the wines were very thick, Psalm 75:9. (Calmet) --- On the rejection of the Jews, the Gentiles were converted. (Worthington)

extractions.type_name: Mountain of Sion / Feast on the Mountain
extractions.type_description: Isaiah's prophetic vision of a great feast prepared on Mount Zion, featuring rich foods and aged wines, where peoples from all nations gather
extractions.antitype_description: The blessed Eucharist as the fulfillment of the messianic feast, participated in by Jews and Gentiles alike, prefiguring the heavenly banquet and the Church's ultimate communion
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly identifies the OT feast as a 'figure' (type) of the Church and heaven, and directly connects the 'expressions too grand for a corruptible feast' to the sacramental reality of the Eucharist. The mountain of Sion represents the Church, and the feast prefigures the blessed Eucharist that unites Jews and Gentiles in the New Testament.

extractions.type_name: The Feast on Mount Zion with wines
extractions.type_description: The vintage feast in Isaiah's prophecy representing the eschatological banquet of God's people
extractions.antitype_description: The final consummation in heaven where God's people (both Jews and Gentiles) participate in eternal communion and blessing
extractions.reasoning: The commentary notes that 'expressions are too grand for a corruptible feast,' indicating the language transcends earthly celebration and points to eschatological fulfillment. The inclusion of 'all nations' and the rejection of Jews leading to Gentile conversion positions this as an end-times reality.

notes: The commentary conflates the Eucharistic and eschatological aspects of the antitype, suggesting both sacramental present fulfillment and future heavenly consummation. The typology is fairly explicit in Calmet's interpretation. The reference to 'On the rejection of the Jews, the Gentiles were converted' adds historical-theological context about the antitype's realization in the NT era.

original_text: Ever. Hebrew, "he shall swallow up death in victory," 1 Corinthians 15:54. Christ, by dying, conquered death, and rescued us from its power, if we do not voluntarily subject ourselves to it again. This was faintly represented by the liberation of the captives.

extractions.type_description: The OT event of God liberating captives from bondage, faintly representing deliverance from a power that enslaves
extractions.antitype_name: Christ's conquest of death and liberation from death's power
extractions.antitype_description: Christ's death and resurrection by which He conquered death and rescued humanity from its dominion, as referenced in 1 Corinthians 15:54
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that the liberation of captives 'was faintly represented' Christ's victory over death. This establishes a typological prefigurement relationship where the OT deliverance from captivity serves as a type of Christ's eschatological and soteriological triumph over death itself. The use of 'faintly represented' indicates a deliberate typological parallel, though acknowledging its limited correspondence.

notes: The commentary presents a somewhat attenuated typology—the captive liberation is described as a 'faint' representation, suggesting the type is incomplete or shadowy compared to the antitype. The primary antitype is Christological (Christ's victory over death), though it has eschatological dimensions given its connection to resurrection and final triumph over death.

original_text: Rejoice. Our Saviour alludes to this text, (Luke 7:22.) which, under the figure of the deliverance from captivity, points out the vocation of the Gentiles, Isaias 35:5., and 42:7, 19.

extractions.type_description: The liberation of Israel from Babylonian captivity, as described under the figure in Isaiah 29:19
extractions.antitype_description: The calling of the Gentiles to salvation through Christ, as alluded to by Jesus in Luke 7:22 and further developed in Isaiah 35:5 and 42:7, 19
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that the OT figure of deliverance from captivity 'points out' (prefigures) the NT reality of the Gentiles' vocation to salvation. Jesus himself alluded to this text, confirming the typological connection. The pattern shows an OT liberation event prefiguring the NT spiritual liberation and inclusion of Gentiles in God's people.

notes: The commentary cites multiple Isaiah passages (35:5, 42:7, 19) as additional typological witnesses to this same pattern. The typology operates at a redemptive-historical level, where physical deliverance from exile becomes a type of spiritual deliverance through the gospel. Jesus's allusion in Luke 7:22 serves as the hermeneutical key confirming this typological interpretation.

original_text: Sevenfold. Exceedingly great, equal to the light of 49 days. (Calmet) --- The fame of Ezechias spread widely. His kingdom was a figure of that of Christ, when this was more perfectly realized, the preaching of the gospel having dispelled the darkness of error. (Calmet) --- He alludes to the day of judgment. (St. Jerome) (Menochius)

extractions.type_description: The earthly kingdom of King Hezekiah (Ezechias) in Isaiah's time, characterized by his fame spreading widely and spiritual restoration
extractions.antitype_description: Christ's kingdom realized through the preaching of the gospel, which dispels the darkness of error and brings spiritual light
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states 'His kingdom was a figure of that of Christ, when this was more perfectly realized, the preaching of the gospel having dispelled the darkness of error.' This directly connects Hezekiah's kingdom (OT type) to Christ's kingdom (NT antitype), with the gospel serving as the fulfillment of the spiritual restoration prefigured in Hezekiah's reign.

extractions.type_name: The Light imagery in Hezekiah's restoration (sevenfold light)
extractions.type_description: The symbolic 'sevenfold light' or great illumination associated with Hezekiah's kingdom and the removal of darkness
extractions.antitype_name: The Gospel's illumination and eschatological judgment
extractions.antitype_description: The gospel as spiritual light dispelling error, and ultimately the day of judgment when all is revealed
extractions.reasoning: The commentary references both the gospel's present illumination ('darkness of error' dispelled) and St. Jerome's interpretation of the day of judgment. The sevenfold light prefigures both the spiritual enlightenment of the gospel age and the final judgment's revelation.

notes: The commentary presents a layered typological interpretation: primarily Hezekiah's kingdom as a type of Christ's kingdom, with secondary eschatological dimensions related to judgment. Calmet emphasizes the Christological typology while Jerome emphasizes the eschatological dimension. Both interpretations maintain the OT/NT typological framework.

original_text: King. Ezechias or Josias, as figures of Jesus Christ, who is meant. (Calmet) --- They and their counsellors only foreshewed the advantages derived from Christ and his apostles in a more abundant manner. (St. Jerome) --- Judgment and justice. These words have a higher meaning than what is assigned to them by philosophers. In God, the former implies the preparation of the means for man's redemption, as the latter does the execution; and in man, judgment denotes the selection of what is right, and justice implies the putting it willingly in practice. Thus Christ will fulfill all that he has graciously purposed, with the two other divine persons; and the princes, his pastors, shall discern what is good for their own and people's eternal welfare. (Worthington)

extractions.type_description: Two righteous Old Testament kings who ruled with judgment and justice, serving as figures or prefigurements of an ideal ruler
extractions.antitype_description: The ultimate King who fulfills all judgment and justice with perfection, executing redemption and righteousness in abundance through His reign
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states 'Ezechias or Josias, as figures of Jesus Christ, who is meant.' This directly identifies the historical kings as types that prefigure Christ. The commentary further explains that these kings 'foreshewed the advantages derived from Christ and his apostles in a more abundant manner,' establishing a clear OT type to NT antitype relationship where the earthly kings foreshadow Christ's perfect and abundant fulfillment.

extractions.type_name: Princes and counsellors of the Old Testament kings
extractions.type_description: Advisors and leaders who served alongside righteous kings in Israel, implementing judgment and justice
extractions.antitype_name: The apostles and pastors of Christ
extractions.antitype_description: Christ's apostles and spiritual leaders who serve under Christ and discern what is good for eternal welfare
extractions.reasoning: The commentary states that 'They and their counsellors only foreshewed the advantages derived from Christ and his apostles' and references 'the princes, his pastors' in the context of the Church's leadership. This suggests a typological prefigurement of ecclesiastical leadership, though the connection is less explicit than the Christological type.

notes: The commentary emphasizes that the typological fulfillment in Christ and His Church is 'more abundant' than the OT prefigurement, suggesting intensification or completion rather than mere correspondence. Worthington's exposition provides theological depth by distinguishing between divine judgment (preparing redemption) and divine justice (executing it), showing how these concepts find their ultimate antitype in Christ's redemptive work.

original_text: Spoilest. This is particularly directed to Sennacherib. (Challoner) --- He was a figure of persecutors of the Church, to which many passages here allude. (Calmet) --- Remota justitia quid sunt regna nisi magna latrocinia? (St. Augustine, City of God 4:4.) --- Sennacherib plundered Samaria and Juda, and despising God, was himself contemned. (Worthington)

extractions.type_description: The Assyrian king who spoiled/plundered Samaria and Judah, despised God, and was himself contemned (brought to nothing)
extractions.antitype_description: Those who persecute the Christian Church in the New Testament era and beyond
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states 'He was a figure of persecutors of the Church.' This establishes Sennacherib as an OT type prefiguring NT persecutors. The pattern of persecution followed by divine judgment reflects the broader typological principle that God's judgment on enemies of His people in the OT prefigures judgment on enemies of the Church in the NT era.

notes: The commentary attributes this typological reading to Calmet. The connection is somewhat general (persecutors of the Church rather than a specific NT antitype) and relational rather than personal typology. The moral principle underlying the type—that those who spoil God's people will themselves be despised/judged—projects forward to the Church's persecutors.

original_text: Free. Our Saviour healed both soul and body, (Calmet) shewing by his works (John x.; Worthington) that he had fulfilled this prediction, Luke 7:22., and Matthew 11:5. --- Waters. Baptism has sanctified the most wicked.

extractions.type_description: Old Testament prediction of physical and spiritual healing - the blind seeing, the lame walking, the deaf hearing, and waters flowing in the desert
extractions.antitype_description: The New Testament fulfillment where Jesus heals both body and soul, demonstrating his messianic identity through works that match Isaiah's prediction (Luke 7:22, Matthew 11:5, John 10)
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that Christ 'healed both soul and body, shewing by his works that he had fulfilled this prediction' with direct biblical cross-references to Matthew 11:5 and Luke 7:22, which are Jesus's own claims to fulfill messianic prophecy.

extractions.type_description: The symbolic waters mentioned in Isaiah's eschatological vision of restoration and healing
extractions.antitype_description: The sacrament of Baptism, which has sanctified even the most wicked, representing spiritual cleansing and renewal
extractions.reasoning: The commentary states 'Waters. Baptism has sanctified the most wicked,' indicating a typological connection between the waters of Isaiah's prophecy and the sacramental waters of Baptism. However, the connection is stated more as theological application than explicit type-antitype correlation.

notes: The first extraction represents a clear Christological typology explicitly affirmed by the commentary with scriptural cross-references. The second extraction regarding baptism is present but less formally developed—it appears as a typological application rather than a strongly argued type-antitype relationship. Both are legitimate typological interpretations found in the Haydock commentary.

original_text: For me. He represents his disease, as an inexorable creditor.
notes: The Haydock commentary at ISA-38-14 uses metaphorical/figurative language (describing disease as 'an inexorable creditor') but does not establish a typological relationship between an Old Testament type and a New Testament antitype. This is a rhetorical device or allegory used to illustrate Hezekiah's distress, not a type-antitype connection spanning the testaments.

original_text: Image. Catholics never pretend to represent the Deity, when they depict the Father as a venerable old man, etc. They do not adore pictures, as our adversaries would insinuate. If we were disposed to cavil, we might bring the same charge against them. For a few weeks ago, "a beautiful altar-piece, painted and presented by the lady of major general Cheney, was put in Hornsea church, representing Christ blessing the bread and wine." But Protestants can confine such things to their proper use, and Catholic must adore them. (Haydock) --- "Such things the Jew, Apella, may believe: not I." (Horace)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Isaiah 40:18 does not contain typological analysis. The passage addresses the theological question of representing the Deity through images and defends Catholic practice regarding religious art and iconography. The commentary engages in a polemical discussion about whether Catholics properly use religious images without adoring them, citing a specific altarpiece example featuring Christ and the Eucharist. While the altarpiece does depict Christ (which could theoretically involve Christological themes), the commentary makes no attempt to connect any Old Testament type to this New Testament antitype. Instead, it focuses on doctrinal defense and practice regarding religious imagery. The reference to Horace's maxim at the end is purely a classical rhetorical flourish, not a typological connection.

original_text: Dead. Though you were in the grave, I could protect you. Captivity is often represented under this idea. (Calmet) --- You who are despised, fear not, since Christ will protect and reward you. (Worthington)

extractions.type_name: The Despised and Dead (Israel in Captivity)
extractions.type_description: Israel represented as dead or in the grave during captivity - a state of helplessness, degradation, and divine abandonment that appears hopeless
extractions.antitype_name: Christ Protected and Rewarded by God
extractions.antitype_description: Christ, though despised and rejected, is protected and ultimately rewarded by God; the faithful who follow Christ share in this pattern of vindication despite present suffering
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states 'You who are despised, fear not, since Christ will protect and reward you,' establishing a connection between Israel's condition of despair (represented as death/captivity) and Christ's role as protector and rewarder. The despised and afflicted status of Israel prefigures Christ's own despised condition, with the promise of divine vindication foreshadowing Christ's exaltation.

notes: The typology here is somewhat implicit rather than explicit. The commentary mentions that the despised remnant should find courage in Christ's protection and reward, suggesting a typological correspondence between Israel's suffering and humiliation under captivity and Christ's suffering before his vindication. However, Worthington's comment is more hortatory (encouraging believers through Christ) than strictly typological in the classical sense. The connection to 'dead' (captivity) as a prefigurement is present but underdeveloped in this excerpt.

original_text: My servant. Christ, who, according to his humanity, is the servant of God, (Challoner) and Redeemer of others; none else being able to satisfy for themselves. (Worthington) (Philippians 2:7.) (Calmet) --- This passage clearly refers to the Messias, (Chaldean; Kimchi) who was prefigured by Cyrus, ver. 6. (Calmet) (Hugo.) --- It is quoted by St. Matthew 12:18. who has some variations both from the Hebrew and the Septuagint, (Calmet) particularly the first part of ver. 4., which the Septuagint renders, "He shall shine, and shall not be broken."

extractions.type_description: The Persian king mentioned in Isaiah 42:6, who served as God's instrument for deliverance and restoration
extractions.antitype_description: Jesus Christ, who according to his humanity is the servant of God and Redeemer of others, as referenced in Philippians 2:7
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that the Messiah 'was prefigured by Cyrus' (ver. 6). The primary focus of Isaiah 42:1 is the direct description of the Messiah as God's servant, with Cyrus serving as a secondary prefigurement of this redemptive role.

notes: The commentary's primary claim is that Isaiah 42:1 directly refers to the Messiah/Christ. The typological relationship with Cyrus is mentioned as secondary ('who was prefigured by Cyrus, ver. 6'). The commentary also notes that Matthew 12:18 quotes this passage, confirming its messianic interpretation in the New Testament.

original_text: House. The Jews out of captivity, prefigured the redemption of mankind. These miracles proved that Jesus was the Messias, Luke 7:22.

extractions.type_description: The deliverance of the Jewish people from captivity, as prefigured in Isaiah 42:7
extractions.antitype_name: The Redemption of Mankind through Jesus Christ
extractions.antitype_description: The spiritual redemption and liberation of all humanity accomplished through Christ's messianic work

original_text: Stock. I will give fresh life to my people, as to the figure of Christ's Church.

extractions.type_name: God's restoration of His people with fresh life (Isaiah 44:3)
extractions.type_description: The Old Testament promise that God will pour out His Spirit upon Israel's descendants, giving them fresh spiritual life and vitality as a people
extractions.antitype_description: The New Testament Church as the spiritual fulfillment and continuation of God's people, receiving new life through Christ and the Holy Spirit
extractions.reasoning: The Haydock commentary explicitly states that God's giving 'fresh life to my people' in Isaiah functions as 'the figure of Christ's Church.' This establishes the OT promise of restored Israel as a type prefiguring the Church as the spiritual antitype. However, the commentary is quite brief and does not elaborate extensively on the typological mechanics.

The 'fresh life' language connects to themes of spiritual renewal and the indwelling of the Holy Spirit characteristic of the Church.

original_text: Cyrus. This was spoken 110 years before his birth, which shews the prescience and power of God, so as not to injure free-will. The parents of Cyrus could not give him this name to fulfill the prediction, as they knew nothing of it. Amon was apprised that a person called Josias would overturn idolatry; but he had no reason to suppose that it would be his son, 1 Kings 13:2. --- My shepherd. Chaldean, "that he shall reign." This was shewn by the Jews to Cyrus, on which account, (Calmet) he gave them leave to return, etc. (Josephus, [Jewish Antiquities?] 11:1.) --- The title of shepherd is given to Agamemnon by Homer, and it denotes a good prince, such as historians represent Cyrus to have been. He observed that kings and shepherds had the like duties to perform; (Xenophon viii.) and after his death he was bewailed as a "father." (Herodotus 3:89.) --- At first he did not bear the name of Cyrus, (Herodotus 1:113.) which in the Persian language means "the sun." (Ctesias.) (Plut.[Plutarch?])
notes: This Haydock commentary on Isaiah 44:28 discusses Cyrus as a historical figure and God's prophetic foreknowledge of him, but does not establish a typological relationship between an Old Testament type and a New Testament antitype. The commentary focuses on: (1) the historical accuracy of the prophecy (spoken 110 years before Cyrus's birth), (2) the meaning of the title 'shepherd' as applied to Cyrus as a good ruler, and (3) etymological and historical details about Cyrus from classical sources (Homer, Xenophon, Herodotus, Plutarch). While Cyrus is sometimes viewed typologically in Christian tradition as prefiguring Christ (particularly as an 'anointed one' who delivers God's people), this particular commentary does not develop or reference such a typological connection. It remains at the level of historical and linguistic analysis rather than typological interpretation.

original_text: Saviour. We confess that thou hast delivered the Jews; or rather, we acknowledge that thou, O Christ, art true God under the veils of thy human nature, and Saviour of all. Cyrus was only a feeble representation of thee.

extractions.type_description: The Persian king who delivered the Jews from Babylonian captivity, presented as a feeble representation or prefigurement
extractions.antitype_description: The true God and Saviour of all, who delivers humanity through His human nature and divine nature
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that Cyrus was 'only a feeble representation' of Christ, establishing a direct typological relationship where the historical deliverance accomplished by Cyrus prefigures the ultimate salvation accomplished by Christ. Both are deliverers, but Christ is the ultimate antitype who fulfills what Cyrus merely foreshadowed.

notes: The commentary interprets Isaiah 45:15 christologically, reading the acknowledgment of a savior/deliverer as ultimately pointing to Christ rather than only to Cyrus. This reflects a common patristic and medieval exegetical approach to reading messianic fulfillment into Old Testament passages about deliverance.

original_text: Knew. Therefore I did not speak of the liberation from Egypt, but from Babylon, which is represented as just taking place. (Calmet)
notes: The Haydock commentary discusses a contrast between two historical events within the Old Testament itself: the liberation from Egypt versus the liberation from Babylon. This is a comparison of two OT historical events, not a typological relationship connecting an OT type to an NT antitype. The commentary is clarifying that Isaiah 48:7 refers to the Babylonian exile and return rather than the Egyptian exodus. This is historical exegesis and contextual analysis, not typology as defined by the OT-to-NT prefigurement relationship.

original_text: Things, as I have done respecting Cyrus? (St. Cyril, etc.) who was a figure of Christ, ver. 15.

extractions.type_description: Cyrus, the Persian king mentioned in Isaiah 48, who was used by God to accomplish His purposes and restore Israel
extractions.antitype_description: Jesus Christ, who fulfills the role of God's agent and instrument for accomplishing divine purposes and restoring God's people
extractions.reasoning: The Haydock commentary explicitly states that Cyrus 'was a figure of Christ' (referencing ver. 15). This is a direct statement of typological prefigurement, where the OT historical figure of Cyrus prefigures the NT antitype of Christ. Both function as instruments through whom God accomplishes His redemptive purposes.

notes: The commentary references 'ver. 15' which likely provides additional context for this typological relationship. The attribution to 'St. Cyril, etc.' indicates this interpretation has patristic support. While Cyrus as a type of Christ may seem unusual to modern readers (given his non-Israelite status), medieval and patristic scholarship frequently identified figures who served God's purposes as typological prefigurements of Christ.

original_text: Just. Christ, prefigured by Cyrus, whose empire was very mild, Isaias 44:28.

extractions.type_description: The Persian king whose empire was characterized by mildness and justice, mentioned in Isaiah 44:28 as God's instrument for restoring Jerusalem
extractions.antitype_description: Jesus Christ, who embodies ultimate justice and righteousness
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that Christ is 'prefigured by Cyrus,' establishing a typological relationship. Cyrus's mild rule and role as God's agent of restoration prefigure Christ's just and merciful reign. This is a clear typological statement where the OT figure (David/Davidic kingship) prefigures the NT antitype (Christ as the ultimate king of David's line).

notes: The commentary distinguishes between a possible historical reference (Zorobabel) and the ultimate typological fulfillment (Christ). This reflects the patristic and scholastic principle that Old Testament prophecies may have immediate historical applications but find their complete and definitive fulfillment in Christ. The cross-references to Ezekiel and Hosea strengthen the typological connection across multiple prophetic books.

original_text: And it. Jerusalem, as figure of the Church. (Menochius) --- Fear, worship, and desist from persecuting God in his saints, (Haydock) whom he so highly favours.

extractions.type_description: The historical city of Jerusalem in the Old Testament, particularly as restored and rebuilt in Jeremiah's prophecy of restoration
extractions.antitype_description: The New Testament Church, the spiritual community of believers who worship God and receive His favor
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states 'Jerusalem, as figure of the Church.' This directly identifies Jerusalem as a type (figure) that prefigures the Church as its antitype. The commentary further explains the functional parallel: just as Jerusalem's restoration causes people to fear and worship God, so the Church (the spiritual Jerusalem) causes worship and reverence for God among those who recognize His favor toward the saints.

notes: This is a straightforward ecclesial typology. The commentary attributes this interpretation to Menochius. The typological connection draws on the common patristic theme of Jerusalem as a type of the Church, particularly emphasizing the restoration/rebuilding motif and the resultant glorification of God's name among nations.

original_text: Joakim, when Nabuchodonosor besieged him again in his 7th year. The Rechabites then pitched their tents in Jerusalem, ver. 11. (Calmet) --- Here we behold a figure of religious orders in the Church, as well as in the Nazarites and disciples of the prophets, Numbers vi., and 4 Kings 1:They observed certain rules for acquiring greater perfection, and refrained from many things which were otherwise lawful. Thus various religious orders, both of men and of women, have flourished in the Church, and though they have different names and regulations, yet they are not sects, as heretics would pretend, but all follow the same faith, use the same sacraments, and are a great ornament to the Catholic Church by their profession of the three essential vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience, in imitation of the apostles, Matthew 19:12. --- Joakim. This happened before the preceding prophecies. (Worthington)

extractions.type_name: The Rechabites and their observance of rules
extractions.type_description: The Rechabites who observed strict rules and refrained from lawful things to achieve greater perfection, dwelling in tents in Jerusalem during Jeremiah's time
extractions.antitype_name: Religious orders in the Church (monasticism and consecrated life)
extractions.antitype_description: Christian religious orders of men and women who profess vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience, following rules for acquiring greater perfection in imitation of the apostles
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states 'Here we behold a figure of religious orders in the Church' and draws a direct parallel between the Rechabites' discipline and practices and the structure and purpose of Christian monastic and religious communities. The OT observance prefigures the NT institutional expression of dedicated religious life in the Church.

extractions.type_description: OT figures who took vows of separation and observed special rules for consecration, as mentioned in Numbers vi
extractions.antitype_name: Disciples and religious practitioners in the Church
extractions.antitype_description: Those in the New Testament Church who follow special disciplines and vows for spiritual perfection
extractions.reasoning: The commentary references the Nazarites as a parallel figure to the Rechabites, suggesting they prefigure similar ecclesial structures, but the connection is mentioned briefly and not developed in detail within this passage.

notes: This commentary employs typology somewhat loosely by identifying the Rechabites as 'a figure' (figura) of religious orders rather than as a strict type in the classical typological sense. The connection is more institutional/analogical than predictive. The commentary also clarifies that religious orders are not sects but legitimate expressions of Church life, using typological reasoning to establish their legitimacy through OT precedent.

original_text: They. Literally, "their supplication may fall prostrate before," etc. (Haydock) --- It is personified. So Homer represents (Calmet) "supplications," as daughters of Jupiter, lame, and with eyes averted, (Iliad ix.) to shew how we ought to pray. Jeremias finds means to instruct the people: the word of God is not bound, 2 Timothy 2:9. (Calmet) --- As many refused to hear his discourses, God ordered him to write what might be a perpetual warning and reproach, or testimony against them. (Worthington)
notes: This commentary does not describe typological relationships between Old Testament types and New Testament antitypes. Instead, it contains: (1) Literary analysis (personification of supplications, Homeric parallels), (2) A general theological principle about God's word not being bound (2 Timothy 2:9 reference), and (3) Moral instruction about how God uses written testimony as warning and reproach. While the passage does reference a New Testament verse (2 Timothy 2:9), it is cited as a thematic parallel or principle rather than as a fulfillment of Jeremiah's writing. The commentary focuses on hermeneutical and moral lessons rather than on an Old Testament type prefiguring a New Testament antitype.

original_text: Worship. Hebrew, "to represent." The cakes had a crescent on them. (Calmet) See Hesychius in selenai. --- Husbands. The women are most zealous. But all partook of this idolatry, Jeremias 7:18. (Calmet)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Jeremiah 44:19 discusses the idolatrous worship of the Queen of Heaven through crescent-shaped cakes. The passage focuses on historical and archaeological details (the crescent symbol on cakes, the participation of women and men in idolatry) and references parallel passages in Jeremiah 7:18. No typological relationship between an Old Testament type and New Testament antitype is presented or implied in this commentary. The text is descriptive of pagan religious practice rather than prophetic or prefigurative in nature.

original_text: Enemies. Herodotus (II. 161, 169.) informs us that Apries reigned fortunately twenty-five years, when he lost many of his men fighting against the Cyreneans, and was dethroned by Amasis, and strangled by his subjects. Usher (the year of the world 3433) suspects that Amasis was assisted and confirmed by Nabuchodonosor, and he might thus fulfill the prophecies, Jeremias 43:11., etc., and Ezechiel xxix., etc. Josephus (Antiquities 10:11.) and Berosus (contra Apion i.) assert, that Nabuchodonosor defeated and slew the king of Egypt, though Herodotus is silent on this subject, his account being communicated by the Egyptian priests, and full of fables. (Calmet)
notes: This Haydock commentary discusses the historical fulfillment of Jeremiah's prophecy regarding the judgment of Egypt under Pharaoh Apries by Nebuchadnezzar. The commentary presents historical and archaeological evidence (Herodotus, Josephus, Berosus, Usher) about the downfall of the Egyptian pharaoh. While the passage involves Old Testament prophecy being historically fulfilled, this represents predictive prophecy fulfillment in historical events (OT prophecy → OT/historical fulfillment), not typological prefigurement where an OT person, event, or institution points forward to a New Testament antitype. The commentary contains no reference to or connection with any New Testament persons, events, or spiritual realities that would constitute a typological relationship.

original_text: Mountain. So Babylon is styled in derision. See Jeremias 21:13., and Isaias 1:10., and 20:6., and 22:1. The city stood on a plain. Some think that its palace and walls are designated. --- Burnt; unfruitful. This happened long after Cyrus, though it then ceased to be the capital, and became only a shadow of its former greatness.
notes: This Haydock commentary on Jeremiah 51:25 discusses the metaphorical designation of Babylon as a 'mountain' and provides historical context about the city's destruction and decline after Cyrus. The commentary employs symbolic language (mountain = city, burnt = unfruitful) but does not establish any typological relationship between an Old Testament type and a New Testament antitype. The references to other Old Testament passages (Jer 21:13, Isa 1:10, 20:6, 22:1) are used to support the symbolism of calling cities 'mountains,' not to indicate typological prefigurement. This is historical and literary analysis of prophetic judgment, not typology in the strict sense of OT/NT prefigurement.

original_text: Broad wall. The pagan historians agree not in the dimensions, but allow it was excessively broad and lofty. (Calmet) --- Six chariots might go abreast. It was 360 stadia long, (Ctesias); or 480 (Herodotus 1:178.) that is above 23 leagues, allowing 2,500 paces for each. This author says the breadth was fifty cubits of the king, three inches larger than the common one, or about twenty-one inches. Pliny ([Natural History?] 6:26.) improperly applies this to Roman feet, and says the walls were two hundred feet high; while Herodotus assigns so many cubits. (Calmet) --- There were three different walls. (Curt. v.) --- Cyrus demolished the outer one. (Berosus) --- What remained, (Calmet) with the hundred brazen gates, Darius treated in like manner. (Herodotus 1:179., and 3:159.) --- Thus was the prediction fulfilled, and the works of so many captive nations brought to nothing. It is asserted that 200,000 (Calmet) daily finished a stadium, (Curt. v.) or 125 paces. (Calmet)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Jeremiah 51:58 focuses entirely on the historical, archaeological, and architectural details of Babylon's walls. It discusses the dimensions of the walls, their construction by multiple nations, and their destruction by Cyrus and Darius. While the passage deals with the fulfillment of Jeremiah's prophecy about Babylon's destruction, the commentary does not establish any typological relationship between Old Testament persons, events, or institutions and their New Testament fulfillments. The commentary is historical and architectural in nature rather than typological.

original_text: Watches. Jerusalem is here represented in the midst of danger and misery. (Calmet)
notes: The Haydock commentary on LAM 2:19 provides only a literal, historical description of Jerusalem's circumstances during the siege and destruction. It identifies Jerusalem as being 'in the midst of danger and misery' but makes no reference to any prefigurative relationship between this Old Testament event and New Testament fulfillment. The commentary is descriptive of the immediate historical context rather than typological in nature. No type-antitype relationship is articulated or implied.

original_text: Man. Jeremias had a share in the common misery, (Worthington) and bewails his own condition, as a figure of Christ, Psalm 87:16., and Isaias 53:3. (Calmet) --- His disciples must expect to suffer. (Haydock)

extractions.type_description: The prophet Jeremiah experiencing and bewailing personal misery and affliction as part of the common suffering of his people
extractions.antitype_description: Jesus Christ's suffering, affliction, and expressions of grief, as prefigured in Psalm 87:16 and Isaiah 53:3
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that Jeremiah 'bewails his own condition, as a figure of Christ' and cites Psalm 87:16 and Isaiah 53:3 as supporting scriptural connections. This is a direct statement of typological prefigurement where the OT prophet's suffering prefigures Christ's suffering.

notes: The commentary also includes a secondary application (not strictly typology) that disciples should expect to suffer following Christ's example. The primary typological connection is between Jeremiah's lamentation and Christ's passion as described in the prophetic passages cited.

original_text: Another. Greek, "an everlasting covenant," (Haydock) by Christ, (Maldonat) prefigured by that which Nehemias renewed, 2 Esdras 9:38. (Calmet) --- The law of Moses was in force till Christ came. His law continues unto the end. (Worthington)

extractions.type_description: The everlasting covenant that Nehemiah renewed (2 Esdras 9:38), representing the restoration and reaffirmation of God's covenant with Israel under the Law of Moses
extractions.antitype_description: The everlasting covenant established by Christ, which supersedes and fulfills the Mosaic covenant and continues until the end of time
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that the covenant renewed by Nehemiah is 'prefigured by' (i.e., serves as a type for) Christ's everlasting covenant. The text directly establishes an OT/NT prefigurative relationship. Worthington's note reinforces this by contrasting the temporal nature of the Mosaic Law with the perpetual nature of Christ's law, indicating a typological progression from type to antitype.

notes: The commentary presents a clear typological framework where the historical covenant renewal under Nehemiah anticipates and prefigures the ultimate, eternal covenant established through Christ. The contrast drawn between the limited duration of the Mosaic Law and the perpetual nature of Christ's Law underscores the typological fulfillment pattern.

original_text: Ever. True wisdom may be found in the law. It constitutes the happiness of Israel, Deuteronomy 4:7. Christ perfected and fulfilled it, Matthew 5:7. --- Life. Moses promised temporal blessings; (chap. 3:14., and Deuteronomy 30:15.) yet the faithful would be rewarded eternally. (Calmet) --- Wisdom is the law of God, Baruch 3:12. (Worthington)

extractions.type_description: The Mosaic law as given in Deuteronomy, which constitutes the happiness of Israel and promises temporal and eternal blessings to the faithful
extractions.antitype_name: Christ and His Fulfillment of the Law
extractions.antitype_description: Christ perfected and fulfilled the law, as referenced in Matthew 5:7, representing the culmination and completion of the Mosaic legal system
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states 'Christ perfected and fulfilled it' in direct reference to the law, establishing a clear typological relationship where the Old Testament Mosaic law prefigures Christ's role as the perfect fulfillment and completion of that law.

notes: The commentary also discusses wisdom as the law of God and the promise of life (both temporal and eternal), but these are presented more as thematic connections than explicit typological relationships. The primary typology is the Law → Christ fulfillment relationship, which is clearly articulated through the Matthew 5:7 reference.

original_text: Garment. Hebrew, "cloak," (Sanctius) such as were worn by people under no disgrace, Baruch 4:20. Thamar had one very costly, 2 Kings 13:18. (Calmet) --- Justice, or mercy. God is bound to fulfill his gracious promises. (Worthington)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Baruch 5:2 discusses the literal meaning of 'garment' (cloak) and provides historical context about similar garments mentioned elsewhere in scripture (2 Kings 13:18). The reference to 'Justice, or mercy' is theological commentary on God's character and fulfillment of promises, representing general symbolism and moral instruction rather than typological prefigurement. No Old Testament type is presented as prefiguring a New Testament antitype. The commentary is primarily philological and historical in nature, not typological.

original_text: Them, on account of the many votaries, ver. 16. Arnobius (6) ridicules such gods. (Calmet) --- Protestants adopt similar arguments against the real presence as if we believed that Christ was hurt when the sacramental species were broken or devoured by vermin. A little more boldness will prompt them to reject the divinity of Christ, who was pleased to give up his body to those who treated him shamefully. Almost every argument which is levelled against Christ's real presence in the blessed Eucharist, may be turned against the incarnation; and hence so many now become Socinians, being unwilling to submit their understanding to the mysteries of religion. To apply these texts to holy pictures, would be nugatory. See Isaias xl 18. (Haydock) --- The absurdities here specified, shew how foolish are those who serve idols or take any images to be gods. (Worthington) --- Calvin represents the pagans as adoring God under the images, as if they used them in the same light as Catholics do; which is contrary to this epistle, etc. (Tirinus)
notes: This Haydock commentary discusses idolatry and the absurdity of idol worship in the Book of Baruch, but it does not establish typological relationships between Old Testament persons, events, or institutions and New Testament fulfillments. The commentary primarily engages in doctrinal debate regarding the Real Presence in the Eucharist, defends Catholic sacramental theology against Protestant critiques, and warns against idolatry and the worship of images as gods. While the commentary makes an analogy between arguments against the Real Presence and arguments against the Incarnation, this is a theological comparison rather than a typological connection. The reference to Isaiah 40:18 is cited as a proof text against image worship, not as an example of typology. No OT type prefiguring an NT antitype is explicitly or implicitly identified in this passage.

original_text: Chaldeans. The priests themselves despise the idols most, (Calmet) and expose them to contempt, by pretending that they work miracles. (Haydock) --- "Those who first set up representations of the gods, deprived cities of reverential awe, and increased the error," said Varro; "prudently supposing that gods might easily be contemned, when like stupid images." In simulacrorum stoliditate. (St. Augustine, City of God 4:26.)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Baruch 6:40 discusses the contempt shown toward idols by Chaldean priests and pagan philosophers. The commentary cites Varro and St. Augustine to illustrate how idol worship was despised even by those who promoted it, exposing the foolishness of idolatry through false miracles and deceptive representations. However, the text contains no typological relationship connecting an Old Testament type to a New Testament antitype. The passage is primarily historical and philosophical criticism of idolatry rather than typological interpretation. While the broader book of Baruch contains anti-idolatry themes, this specific commentary excerpt does not articulate or reference any OT/NT typological correspondence.

original_text: Women. Aristophanes calls harlots, "corded bodies." (Eccles. Act. i.) The women of Babylon "prostituted themselves once, in honour of Venus, (Haydock. Mylitta. Calmet) sitting with crowns on their heads in the temple, till some stranger selected them, and took them from their partition, made with cords," (Haydock) to some more secret place, where they broke their bands. (Herodotus 1:199.) (Calmet) --- That some deluded women, led by various desires, should think thus to honour that impure deity, by an action which some modern casuists have not scrupled to rank among simple venial sins, cannot excite our astonishment so much, when we reflect on the tenets of the ancient Gnostics, and of Antinomians at the present day, whom J. Wesley, the late founder of the Methodists, applauded and followed even in the meridian of the gospel light! See Deuteronomy 16:22., and 23:17. Yet these men read and perhaps distributed the Bible! --- Stones. Literally, "bones;" (Haydock) or the refuse of what had been crushed, (pitura. Atheneus 2:14.) to excite impure love. (Menochius) (Tirinus) --- Theocritus (Phar.) represents a witch doing the like; and Sanchez tells us, that some were taken in the fact in Spain. (Calmet) --- Fumigation, used by the Babylonians after marriage, (Herodotus 1:198.) may be insinuated. (Grotius)
notes: This Haydock commentary discusses the historical and cultural practices of Babylonian women engaging in temple prostitution rituals. While the passage references Deuteronomy 16:22 and 23:17 (Old Testament law regarding idolatry and prostitution), the commentary does not establish these as types prefiguring New Testament antitypes. Instead, it provides: (1) historical-cultural context about Babylonian religious customs, (2) comparative references to ancient Greek and Roman sources, (3) moral critique of idolatrous practices and false theology, and (4) warnings about antinomianism in modern times. The references to Deuteronomy function as parallel prohibitions rather than typological prefigurements. The commentary is exegetical and moralistic rather than typological in nature.

original_text: Living creatures. Cherubims, (as appears from Ecclesiasticus 49:10.) represented to the prophet under these mysterious shapes, as supporting the throne of God, and as it were drawing his chariot. All this chapter appeared so obscure and full of mysteries to the ancient Hebrews, that, as we learn from St. Jerome, (ep. ad Paulin.) they suffered none to read it before they were thirty years old. (Challoner) --- The pagans had many such compound figures as are here represented. (Parkhurst, p. 411.) (Haydock) --- Sanchoniathon (apud Eusebius, praep. 2.) seems to have borrowed his description from this place. --- In them. They stood upright, and had some parts of the human figure. (Calmet) --- Indeed, it seems to have been predominant. (Haydock)
notes: This commentary describes the cherubims as mysterious symbolic figures supporting God's throne and drawing His chariot, but it does not establish a typological relationship between an Old Testament type and a New Testament antitype. The passage discusses the nature and composition of the cherubims (their human-like features, compound forms), historical context (their restriction from readers under 30 years old), and possible pagan parallels, but makes no connection to New Testament fulfillment or antitype. The commentary is primarily concerned with symbolic representation and historical-cultural context rather than typological prefigurement.

original_text: Wings. Their arms were covered with feathers, and the hand appeared at the extremity; or they had four arms under the wings, Ezechiel 10:8. They all came from the shoulders, so as to correspond with the four faced animal, ver. 6. (Calmet) --- Others believe that each face had four wings, so that the animal would have sixteen. (Maldonat) --- In Isaias 9:2., the cherub has six wings. The form was variable, as there was nothing in nature similar. They were perhaps designed to represent the eternity and dominion of God over the whole creation, ver. 28. (Haydock)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Ezekiel 1:8 discusses the symbolic and representational features of the cherubim's wings and form, but does not establish any typological relationship between an Old Testament type and a New Testament antitype. The commentary explains that the variable form of the cherubim was designed to represent God's 'eternity and dominion over the whole creation' - this is symbolic theology and divine representation, not typology. Typology requires an explicit connection showing how an OT person, event, or institution prefigures a specific NT fulfillment, which is not present in this text. The discussion remains at the level of general biblical symbolism and theological interpretation rather than OT-to-NT typological fulfillment.

original_text: Pan, or plate, on which bread was usually baked. This was to represent the walls of the city. (Calmet)
notes: This commentary describes a symbolic or prophetic representation within Ezekiel's sign-act (the prophet using a pan to represent Jerusalem's walls during a siege), but it does not establish a typological relationship between an Old Testament type and a New Testament antitype. The pan representing the city walls is part of Ezekiel's symbolic prophecy about Jerusalem's destruction, not a prefigurement of New Testament fulfillment. Typology requires an OT person, event, or institution that foreshadows its NT counterpart; this commentary discusses only the symbolic meaning of objects within a single prophetic act.

original_text: Three, etc. St. Jerome says some "Vulgate," (Haydock) Latin, (Calmet) or rather incorrect Greek (Haydock) copies read 100, others 150. See Origen, etc. (Calmet) --- The Alexandrian copy has the former, (Haydock) the Roman edition the latter number; and is followed by Theodoret and Maldonat. (Calmet) --- But the more accurate Septuagint agree with the Hebrew, etc. The captivity of Israel must be dated from Phacee, (4 Kings 15:29.) to the end of the reign of Darius Memnon, who espoused Esther, and granted liberty "to all the Jews;" or rather from Manathem, (4 Kings 15:19.) to the 28th of the same king Assuerus. Thus God's "grace, we think, and we may so speak without arrogance, has enabled us to explain this difficulty, which no other has done." (St. Jerome) --- Many confound the duration of the iniquity of Israel with that of Juda, forming 430 years; and they explain it of the time during which the nation had prevaricated. But this seems unnatural. We may rather conclude, that the prophet speaks of a separate judgment, and dates from the destruction of Samaria and of Jerusalem. The former city was taken the year of the world 3283. If we add 390 years, we shall find the year 3673 the very year when Alexander [the Great] overcame Darius, and soon after granted the Jews full liberty to return, or live according to their own laws. This he granted to those in Babylon, and to the Israelites (Calmet) in Media. Josephus, Antiquities xi. ultra et contra Apion 1:--- Philadelphus afterwards liberated many in Egypt, (Josephus, Antiquities 12:2.) as Osee 11:11. had foretold. The chastisement of Juda must be dated from the destruction of Jerusalem under Sedecias, till Darius, the Mede, favoured the Jews about forty years afterwards. (Calmet) --- St. Jerome only allows forty years to have elapsed from the first of Jechonias till the first of Cyrus. The want of an exact chronology gives rise to many such difficulties. (Haydock) --- It is very hard to explain how the ten tribes were 390 and the two tribes 40 years in captivity, as it is certain that the latter were seventy year banished from their own country. (Worthington) --- Perhaps during the last thirty their condition was greatly ameliorated, after the decree of Cyrus, though the liberation was only perfect under Hystaspes and Esther. (Haydock) --- The iniquity of Israel, from Solomon to Salmanasar, lasted 390 years; and that of Juda, under the reign of Manasses, was most abominable for the space of forty years; (Tournemine) or it continued so long from the 18th of Josias till the 4th, after the city was destroyed, and the land became a desert. (Usher, the year of the world 3380 to 3420.) --- But how shall the reign of the virtuous Josias be included in this period? (Haydock) --- The action of the prophet lying 430 days, denoted the length of the siege of Jerusalem, during which extreme scarcity should be felt, and also the captivity of the people. Some have thought that he could not remain 390 days on one side, and that all passed in spirit. But what impression would that make upon the people? He was chained down, (Calmet) to represent their miserable condition. (Haydock) --- Praedo saw a fool who lay tied in one posture for above fifteen years. (Calmet) --- The remaining so long in one posture must have been painful to the prophet. (Tirinus)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Ezekiel 4:5 focuses primarily on historical-chronological interpretation rather than typology. The passage discusses: (1) textual variants in different manuscript traditions; (2) historical dating of the Israelite and Judean captivities; (3) the symbolic meaning of the prophet's action (lying on his side for 390 and 40 days to represent the siege duration and captivity). While the prophet's physical posture carries symbolic significance (representing the 'miserable condition' of the people), this is symbolic action or sign-act rather than typology proper. The commentary does not establish an OT type that prefigures a NT antitype. The only NT reference (Osee 11:11, referring to liberation) is cited as prophetic fulfillment rather than typological correspondence. The discussion remains within the OT historical-chronological framework without connecting to NT fulfillment patterns.

original_text: That. Hebrew, "the scissors of clippers." The same term is used for clipping sheep as for cutting hair. Shaving was not probably then in use. --- Beard, as in mourning or for ignominy, 2 Kings 10:4., and Jeremias 47:5. --- Balance, to shew that God does nothing unjustly. (Calmet) --- The hair. Literally, "them." (Haydock) --- This was to be done before he lay down. Hew was to burn, cut, and divide the hair as the siege represented on the tile advanced, to denote that some should perish in the city by famine, others by the sword, while a few should be scattered among the nations: yet of these a small number should be gathered round Godolias, and perish with him, or in Egypt, etc., and the rest be thence led captive to Babylon.
notes: This Haydock commentary on Ezekiel 5:1 describes a symbolic prophetic action rather than a typological relationship. Ezekiel is instructed to shave his hair and divide it into portions to symbolize the various fates of Jerusalem's inhabitants during the Babylonian siege (famine, sword, scattering, captivity). While the passage contains rich symbolism and prophetic sign-action, the commentary does not establish a connection between this OT event and any NT fulfillment or antitype. The commentary focuses on historical interpretation and the meaning of the symbolic gesture within its immediate context, not on how this prefigures a New Testament reality. Therefore, this falls outside the category of typology as traditionally defined in biblical scholarship.

original_text: Adonis, the favourite of Venus, slain by a wild boar, as feigned by the heathen poets, and which being here represented by an idol, is lamented by the female worshippers of that goddess. In Hebrew the name is Tammuz, (Challoner) which means "concealed," as Adonis signifies "my lord." This idol, which the Egyptians called Osiris, was placed in a coffin, and bewailed till it was pretended he was come to life, when rejoicings took place. Obscene pictures were carried about; and the more honest pagans were ashamed of these practices, which began in Egypt, and became almost general. Moses alludes to them, Leviticus 19:27., and Deuteronomy 14:1. (Calmet) --- David and Solomon say that the image was made of brass, with eyes of lead, which seemed to weep, melting when it was hot. (Worthington) --- But this is destitute of proof.
notes: This commentary discusses the pagan idol Tammuz (Adonis/Osiris) and its cultic practices in Ezekiel's time. While the passage condemns idolatry and references Mosaic laws against certain practices (Leviticus 19:27, Deuteronomy 14:1), the Haydock commentary does not establish any typological relationship between this pagan practice and New Testament fulfillment. The commentary is primarily historical and exegetical in nature, explaining the identity of the idol and the nature of its worship among heathen peoples. It does not present Tammuz worship as prefiguring any Christian reality, sacrament, or aspect of Christ's work. The allusions to Mosaic law are prohibitive (forbidding such practices) rather than typological in character.

original_text: Upper, leading to the court of the priests. These were six angels, representing the army coming from Babylon. The seventh was an angel of peace. (Calmet) --- God never abandons his whole Church. (Worthington)
notes: This commentary describes symbolic representation rather than typology. The six angels 'representing the army coming from Babylon' are symbolic of a historical military event (the Babylonian invasion), not a prefiguration of New Testament fulfillment. The seventh angel representing 'peace' is also symbolic but lacks an OT-to-NT typological connection. Worthington's note about God never abandoning his Church is a theological principle or assurance, not a typological relationship. Typology requires an explicit OT prefiguration of NT fulfillment; this passage employs symbolism and allegory to explain the vision's meaning within its historical context.

original_text: Mark Thau. Thau, or Tau, is the last letter in the Hebrew alphabet, and signifies a sign or a mark: which is the reason why some translators render this place set a mark, or mark a mark, without specifying what this mark was. But St. Jerome, and other interpreters, conclude it was the form of the letter thau, which, in the ancient Hebrew character, was the form of a cross. (Challoner) --- Of this many inscriptions still extant bear witness. (Montfaucon.) --- Some Rabbins allow that the last letter was used but in honour of "the law," Thorah. The cross is supposed to be the hieroglyphic of a future life, (Hist. Rufini. 2:29.) and found frequently in the pictures or (Haydock) in the tables of Isis. But it rather represents a key. Soldiers who were acquitted received the letter T, and those who were sentenced to die had Th, (Calmet) alluding to Thanatos, "death." (Haydock) --- We may, however, suppose that if God designated any letter, it would be some letter of the Hebrew alphabet, and accordingly the last had formerly the figure of a cross: "X" though this text may signify "a sign" in general. The virtuous would be discriminated from the guilty, as if they were marked. (Calmet) --- The door-posts of the Hebrews were stained with blood, in Egypt, to shew that all should be redeemed by that of Christ; and here those who shall be saved, received the mark of his cross. This sign has always been held in veneration among Christians, (Worthington) and used in conferring baptism, consecrating the blessed Eucharist, etc. (St. Chrysostom, hom. lv. in Matthew, and lxxxiv. in John) (St. Augustine, tr. cxviii. in John, and ser. ci. de temp., etc.) --- It appeared to Constantine with this inscription, "In this conquer;" (Eusebius, vit. 1:22.) and again over Jerusalem; (St. Cyril, ep. ad Constantium.) and will be borne before Christ, at his last coming, (Matthew xxiv.) to the joy of those who have performed their baptismal promises, and to the confusion (Worthington) of the enemies of the cross of Christ. (Haydock)

extractions.type_name: The Mark of Tau (Cross) on the Righteous in Ezekiel's Vision
extractions.type_description: In Ezekiel 9:4, God commands the angel to mark the foreheads of the righteous with the letter Tau (in ancient Hebrew character form, a cross) to distinguish them from those to be destroyed. This mark signifies divine protection and salvation of the faithful.
extractions.antitype_name: The Cross of Christ and Christian Baptism
extractions.antitype_description: The cross of Christ as the means of redemption and salvation, and the sign of the cross applied in Christian baptism and sacramental practice. Those who bear the mark of Christ through baptism are marked for salvation and distinguished as belonging to Christ.
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly draws a direct OT-to-NT connection: the mark of Tau prefigures the mark of Christ's cross. The text states: 'here those who shall be saved, received the mark of his cross' and emphasizes that this sign 'has always been held in veneration among Christians, and used in conferring baptism, consecrating the blessed Eucharist, etc.' The parallel to the blood-marked doorposts in Egypt (prefiguring redemption by Christ's blood) reinforces this typological reading.

extractions.type_name: Discrimination of the Righteous from the Guilty by Divine Mark
extractions.type_description: The marking of the virtuous with Tau distinguishes them from those destined for judgment and death, separating the saved from the condemned.
extractions.antitype_name: The Final Judgment and Eschatological Marking
extractions.antitype_description: The cross borne before Christ at his second coming (Matthew 24) as a sign distinguishing the saved (those who kept their baptismal promises) from the enemies of Christ at the final judgment.
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states: 'will be borne before Christ, at his last coming...to the joy of those who have performed their baptismal promises, and to the confusion of the enemies of the cross of Christ.' This directly connects Ezekiel's marking of the righteous to end-times judgment and Christ's return.

notes: The commentary presents a rich typological interpretation connecting the ancient mark of Tau to Christian sacramental practice and eschatology. Both typological relationships center on the cross as a sign of divine election and protection. The connection to the Passover blood on doorposts (EXK-12) strengthens the Christological dimension, as Christ is understood as the antitype of the Passover lamb.

original_text: Mount Olivet, whence he might behold the conflagration of the city, before his ascent into heaven. (Menochius) --- He leaves his habitation by degrees, to shew how Jerusalem would be treated, and the Jews suffer after the ascension of our Saviour. Theodoret well observes, that the person on the throne represented Him, the upper part of the body being different from the lower, (chap. 1:26.) to denote the two natures. (Calmet)

extractions.type_name: The divine throne figure departing from Jerusalem in Ezekiel's vision
extractions.type_description: The person seated on the throne in Ezekiel 11, whose upper and lower body parts differ, gradually departing from the temple and city before ascending
extractions.antitype_name: Jesus Christ's ascension from Mount Olivet
extractions.antitype_description: Christ ascending into heaven from the Mount of Olives after his resurrection, following his departure from Jerusalem
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly connects the throne figure's two natures (denoted by differing upper and lower body parts) to Christ's two natures (divine and human), and interprets the figure's gradual departure as prefiguring Christ's ascension from Mount Olivet. This represents a Christological type where the OT figure prefigures the person and actions of Christ.

extractions.type_name: Jerusalem's abandonment and the people's suffering following the glory's departure
extractions.type_description: The OT event of the divine glory leaving Jerusalem, presaging the city's destruction and the Jewish people's subsequent affliction
extractions.antitype_name: The consequences following Christ's ascension: judgment upon Jerusalem and Jewish suffering
extractions.antitype_description: The destruction of Jerusalem in 70 AD and the subsequent dispersion and suffering of the Jewish people after Jesus's ascension
extractions.reasoning: The commentary notes that Ezekiel's vision shows 'how Jerusalem would be treated, and the Jews suffer after the ascension of our Saviour.' This interprets the OT departure of divine presence as typologically prefiguring the NT consequences (Jerusalem's fall and Jewish dispersion) that followed Christ's ascension.

notes: The typological interpretation here relies on Patristic exegesis (Theodoret and Calmet) that reads the Ezekiel theophany as prophetically prefiguring Christian eschatological events. The connection between the throne figure's two natures and Christ's incarnation is explicitly stated in the commentary.

original_text: Born, as it were in Egypt. He represents the Jews as a female from her infancy, till she be advanced in years.

extractions.type_name: Jerusalem/Judah as a female figure from infancy
extractions.type_description: The personification of Jerusalem/the Jewish people as a woman from birth, representing the nation's origin and development through history
extractions.antitype_description: The Church as the Bride of Christ, developed from infancy through spiritual maturation, fulfilling the prophetic pattern of a feminine community under divine care
extractions.reasoning: The commentary presents Jerusalem as a female figure whose development from infancy prefigures the Church's growth and formation. This follows the typological pattern of OT Jerusalem prefiguring the NT Church as the Bride of Christ. However, the connection is implicit rather than explicit in this particular commentary, which focuses primarily on describing the metaphor rather than explicitly stating a NT fulfillment.

notes: This typology is subtle in the given commentary. The Haydock commentary is primarily descriptive of Ezekiel's metaphor rather than explicitly connecting it to NT fulfillment. However, the broader context of Ezekiel 16 (God's covenant with Jerusalem portrayed as marriage) has classical typological application to the Church as Christ's Bride, making this extraction medium confidence rather than high.

original_text: My gold, for the temple, or thy most precious ornaments, which were sacrificed to gratify thy lubricity, (Calmet) or to form the golden calf, etc., Exodus xxxii. (Haydock) --- Obscene representations were also used in the worship of Osiris. (Herodotus 2:48.)
notes: This Haydock commentary discusses Ezekiel 16:17 in the context of Israel's idolatry and misuse of sacred objects (gold meant for the temple being used for obscene representations and idols like the golden calf). While the passage contains typological elements elsewhere in Scripture (e.g., the golden calf as a type of false worship), this specific commentary focuses on: (1) historical/exegetical analysis of Jerusalem's apostasy, (2) comparative religious symbolism (Osiris worship), and (3) cross-references to parallel OT events (Exodus 32). None of these constitute explicit OT-to-NT typological relationships. The commentary is primarily concerned with understanding the literal meaning and historical context of Ezekiel's prophetic condemnation, not with identifying how OT types prefigure NT antitypes.

original_text: Covenant. After punishing thee I will fulfill my promises, as we see was done (Calmet) after the captivity, and (Haydock) in the Christian Church. (Calmet) --- All shall be converted, not by the Jewish but by the evangelical covenant. (Worthington)

extractions.type_description: The covenant made with Israel under Moses, represented by the Old Testament legal system and Jewish observance
extractions.antitype_name: The Evangelical Covenant (New Covenant in Christ)
extractions.antitype_description: The covenant established through Christ in the New Testament, through which salvation and conversion come to all people through the Gospel
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly contrasts the Jewish covenant with the evangelical covenant as the means by which 'All shall be converted.' This represents a classic typological fulfillment where the Old Testament covenant type finds its antitype in the New Testament's new covenant in Christ, superseding and perfecting the previous covenant arrangement.

notes: The commentary also references the post-captivity restoration as a historical prefigurement of the Christian Church's reality, though this is presented more as a historical pattern than a formal typological relationship. The primary typological content focuses on covenant fulfillment - how God's covenantal promises made to Israel (the type) are fulfilled in the Christian Church through the Gospel (the antitype).

original_text: Will. God sincerely wishes that the sinner should be converted. If he refuse grace, it is only in punishment of former transgressions. (St. Augustine, ep. 217.) --- He wills antecedently their salvation, (1 Timothy 2:4.) though he has a consequent will to punish them, as they speak in the schools, because they themselves will not be saved. (Sanctius) (Calmet) --- God's absolute will is always fulfilled, not that which is conditional. (St. John Damascene, Fide 2:29.; St. Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae p. 1. q. 19. a. 6.) --- He does enough by offering his graces and the death of Christ, to shew that his will is sincere; though by a consequent will his justice punishes the impenitent. Thus a virtuous judge would have all to observe the laws and live: but finding some transgress, so as to become pernicious, he punishes them with death. (Worthington)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Ezekiel 18:23 focuses on theological doctrine regarding God's will for human salvation and repentance, specifically the distinction between God's antecedent will (that all be saved) and His consequent will (to punish the impenitent). The passage discusses divine justice, grace, and moral accountability through doctrinal analysis and philosophical distinctions (drawing on Augustine, Aquinas, John Damascene, and scholastic theology). While the commentary uses an analogy of a virtuous judge to illustrate God's justice, this is a moral/philosophical illustration rather than a typological prefigurement of Old Testament reality pointing to New Testament fulfillment.
