No OT person, event, or institution is presented as prefiguring a NT antitype.

original_text: Walk, etc. It is not an allowance, much less a commandment to serve idols; but a figure of speech, by which God would have them to understand, that if they would walk after their idols, they must not pretend to serve him at the same time: for that he would by no means suffer such a mixture of worship. (Challoner) (St. Jerome) --- Continue, if you dare, to serve idols. I will still bring you back. (Calmet) --- Septuagint, "take away each your devices; and then if you hear me, (Grabe's copy adds, not) and defile not my," etc. (Haydock) --- God would rather have idolaters leave him wholly, than halt between two, (3 Kings xviii.) neither hot nor cold; (Apocalypse iii.) for such dishonour God's name the most, Romans 2:24. (Worthington)
notes: This commentary discusses God's disapproval of syncretistic worship (mixing idolatry with service to God) in Ezekiel 20:39. While the passage references New Testament texts (3 Kings xviii, Apocalypse iii, Romans 2:24) for comparative moral and theological principles, these are cited as parallel examples of the same spiritual principle rather than as typological fulfillments. The commentary uses these NT references to illustrate the timeless principle that God rejects divided allegiance and 'lukewarmness' in worship, but does not present the OT passage as a type prefiguring a NT antitype. This is exegetical and thematic comparison rather than typology proper.

original_text: Resemblance. The king of Tyre, by his dignity and his natural perfections, bore in himself a certain resemblance to God, by reason of which he might be called the seal of resemblance, etc. But what is here said to him is commonly understood of Lucifer, the king over all the children of pride. (Challoner) --- A seal is perfect when it represents things exactly. The prophet speaks ironically, to repress the king's vanity.

extractions.type_description: An earthly ruler who bore resemblance to God through his dignity and natural perfections, described as 'the seal of resemblance'
extractions.antitype_description: The king over all the children of pride, understood as the spiritual reality behind the earthly king's pride and rebellion
extractions.reasoning: The commentary indicates that the historical King of Tyre prefigures or represents Lucifer/Satan as the ultimate rebel against God. This is a typological correspondence where the earthly king's pride and claim to divine resemblance foreshadow Satan's prideful rebellion. While not strictly OT-to-NT in the traditional sense, this represents a type of spiritual reality that extends into eschatological understanding of cosmic rebellion.

notes: This is a complex case. The commentary presents the King of Tyre as a type, but the antitype (Lucifer/Satan) is not explicitly a New Testament figure, though Satan appears throughout the NT. The Haydock commentary itself acknowledges this is 'commonly understood' as referring to Lucifer, suggesting an interpretive tradition rather than explicit textual typology. The typological relationship here operates more in the realm of spiritual symbolism and foreshadowing of cosmic conflict rather than direct OT-to-NT historical typology.

original_text: Stretched out. That is, thy wings extended. This alludes to the figure of the cherubims in the sanctuary, which with stretched out wings covered the ark, (Challoner) on the holy mountain. (St. Jerome, etc.) --- Fire. That is, bright and precious stones, which sparkle like fire. (Challoner) --- With these the king's robes glittered, or he walked upon them, Esther 1:6. (Calmet) --- Calcacabatur onyx. (Lucan x.)
notes: This commentary does not establish a typological relationship between an Old Testament type and a New Testament antitype. Rather, it explains the figurative language in Ezekiel 28:14 by drawing comparisons to: (1) the cherubims in the sanctuary with stretched wings covering the ark (descriptive/illustrative parallel), and (2) precious stones and bright materials used in royal garments (explanatory comparison). These are exegetical aids to understanding the metaphorical description of the king of Tyre's beauty and adornment, not typological connections that prefigure New Testament fulfillment. The reference to the sanctuary cherubim is historical/descriptive context rather than a statement that the cherubim 'type' or prefigure something in the New Testament.

original_text: Eleventh. Hebrew, "twelfth." Septuagint, "first of the twelfth month of the twelfth year." There are other variations in the versions. St. Jerome reads the first in Hebrew, as Theodoret does, who says that it and the Syriac have the twelfth year: which is true, if we neglect the points. (Calmet) --- The prophets do not observe the order of times. What is here delivered, was sooner fulfilled; or Tyre and Sodom lay nearer than Egypt. (Worthington) --- The three next chapters regard that country.
notes: This Haydock commentary on Ezekiel 29:1 is purely textual and chronological in nature. It discusses textual variants among different biblical versions (Hebrew, Septuagint, Syriac) regarding the dating of the prophecy ('eleventh' vs. 'twelfth' month/year), and notes that the prophets do not necessarily present events in chronological order. The commentary mentions Egypt, Tyre, and Sodom as subjects of prophecy but does not establish any typological relationships between Old Testament types and New Testament antitypes. It is a philological and historical analysis, not a typological one.

original_text: Dragon. Hebrew tannin, (Haydock) whence thunnus may be derived, means any water monster, and seems here put for the crocodile, (Calmet) which Pharao signifies. (Grotius) --- It was the symbol of Egypt, (Calmet) and adored by the people, Jeremias 15:2. --- Rivers; the different branches of the Nile, and the canals. --- Myself. I owe my power to no other. (Calmet) --- "Apries is said to think that no god could deprive him of the kingdom, so well he seemed to have established it." (Herodotus 2:169.) --- So the ancient Pharao said; I know not the Lord, Exodus 5:2. He boasts of having conducted the waters of the Nile through the land, ver. 9. (Menochius) --- This river was honoured as the greatest of the gods. (Heliod. 9.) --- Terra suis contenta bonis non indiga mercis Aut Jovis; in solo tanta est fiducia Nilo. (Lucan viii.)
notes: This commentary discusses symbolic and historical meaning rather than typological prefigurement. The 'dragon' (crocodile) is presented as a symbol of Egypt and Pharaoh's power, and the passage illustrates Pharaoh's pride and false confidence in his own authority (paralleling Exodus 5:2). However, no explicit connection is made between this OT figure/event and a corresponding NT antitype or fulfillment. The commentary emphasizes the historical context (Apries' reign, Egyptian religious beliefs about the Nile) and the theological lesson about human pride versus God's sovereignty, but does not establish a typological relationship whereby the dragon or Pharaoh prefigures a New Testament person, event, or institution.

original_text: Not. Some copies of Septuagint omit the negation. Others render the Hebrew, "Have they not slept?" etc. These nations were deprived of military honours, dying like cowards; and therefore their swords were not placed with them in the grave. (Calmet) --- It was customary to inter such things as the deceased had liked the most. (Serv. in Virgil's Aeneid X. Arma quibus laetatus habe tua, etc. Simon (1 Machabees 13:29.) placed arms and representations of ships on the pillars at Modin, in honour of his kindred. If Elam, etc., had not received such distinction, why should the Egyptian repine? Were they any better? (Calmet) --- The country and king of the Elamites, Assyrians, and other infidels, shall be destroyed. (Worthington)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Ezekiel 32:27 discusses the historical practice of interring weapons and military honors with the deceased in ancient Near Eastern cultures. It explains that certain nations (Elam, Assyria, Egypt) were denied such honors because they died as cowards rather than warriors. The commentary references comparative examples from pagan sources (Virgil's Aeneid) and Jewish history (1 Maccabees 13:29) to illustrate burial customs. The passage serves as a moral and historical commentary on divine judgment against these nations, but contains no explicit connection between an Old Testament type and New Testament antitype. It is didactic and illustrative in nature rather than typological.

original_text: Heights. Septuagint, "deserts." The mountains are often styled eternal, as being the best symbols of durability, Deuteronomy 33:15.
notes: This Haydock commentary discusses symbolic language rather than typology. It explains that 'heights' (mountains) are described as 'eternal' in Scripture because they serve as symbols of durability and permanence. The reference to Deuteronomy 33:15 supports this as a general symbolic/poetic convention in biblical language, not a typological prefigurement of New Testament realities. No OT type-to-NT antitype relationship is established in this commentary.

original_text: Israel. Some apply what follows to the captives returning; others, perceiving that the expressions were not then literally verified, have recourse to the reign of 1000 years. Others again explain the whole of Christ's Church. But some expressions refer to it, and others to the captives; which, though mixed together, induce no confusion, as what belongs to the Jews was a figure of what regarded Christ; and the predictions of the Messias might be applied to the Jews in an hyperbolical sense. (St. Augustine, Doct. 3:34.) (St. Jerome) (Menochius) (Tirinus) (Calmet)

extractions.type_name: The Jewish captives returning from exile
extractions.type_description: The restoration of Israel/the Jews returning from Babylonian captivity, described in Ezekiel 36
extractions.antitype_description: The spiritual Church of Christ in the New Testament era
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that 'what belongs to the Jews was a figure of what regarded Christ' and that expressions in this passage refer both to the literal return of Jewish captives and to Christ's Church. The Jewish restoration serves as a type prefiguring the spiritual restoration and establishment of the Church.

extractions.type_name: The Jewish restoration and renewal of the land
extractions.type_description: The literal and physical restoration of Israel and its land during the post-exilic period
extractions.antitype_description: The spiritual and eschatological fulfillment through Christ, potentially including the millennial reign
extractions.reasoning: The commentary notes that some scholars apply the passage to 'the reign of 1000 years,' indicating that the Jewish restoration prefigures end-times fulfillment. The predictions about Israel are interpreted 'in an hyperbolical sense' as applying to the Messias, suggesting typological correspondence between the Jewish restoration and eschatological/Messianic realities.

notes: This commentary demonstrates the hermeneutical principle that OT historical events can simultaneously refer to their immediate historical context (Jewish return from captivity) while prefiguring NT spiritual realities (the Church and Messianic fulfillment). The commentators (Augustine, Jerome, Menochius, Tirinus, Calmet) acknowledge the mixed nature of the prophecy—some expressions are literal/historical while others are typological/spiritual—without creating confusion because the OT reality serves as a figure of the NT reality.

original_text: Water. R. David and the Chaldean explain this of the remission of sin; and all Christians understand it of baptism in water, remitting all offences, Ephesians 5:26., and Titus 3:5. (Worthington) --- He alludes to the purification of the Jews, which prefigured baptism and penance, in which the blood of Christ is applied to our souls. This of course was only fulfilled in his church.

extractions.type_description: The ceremonial purification practices of the Old Testament Jews, involving water and blood for cleansing from sin and uncleanness
extractions.antitype_description: The sacraments of baptism (remission of sins through water) and penance in the Christian Church, through which the blood of Christ is applied to souls
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states 'the purification of the Jews...prefigured baptism and penance' and connects this to the application of Christ's blood to souls. This is a clear OT type (Jewish purification practices) pointing to NT antitypes (Christian sacraments). The reference to Ephesians 5:26 and Titus 3:5 confirms this as intentional typological interpretation by early Christian theology.

notes: The commentary presents water purification as the primary type. While 'blood of Christ' is mentioned in connection with the antitype, the typological focus is on the purificatory practice itself rather than on Christ as a separate type. The commentary notes this fulfillment occurred specifically 'in his church,' indicating an Ecclesial dimension as well, though the primary category is Sacramental. The Haydock reference to 'R. David and the Chaldean' indicates this typological reading has medieval and earlier Jewish exegetical roots.

original_text: Month; April 30, the year of the world 3430. (Usher) (Calmet) --- In explaining this last most obscure vision: 1:The Jews say it was verified after the captivity. But thus the temple would be four miles round, and the city thirty-six, which never was the case. 2:Hence more modern Jews assert it will be fulfilled by the Messias. 3:Rejecting these errors, Lyranus, etc., suppose that the promise was conditional, and that the sins of the Jews prevented the city and temple from being so large; and that the mystical temple of the Church is also insinuated, into which both Jews and Gentiles shall enter. 4:Though this opinion be probable, it seems better to follow St. Jerome, St. Gregory, etc., who cannot apply all to the Old Testament, nor think that such a huge temple and city were indeed promised, but explain some parts of the captives at their return, as a figure of those redeemed by Christ, and brought into his Church, which is adorned with all graces. Yet the greatest part must be understood of the Church triumphant. (Worthington) --- St. Jerome confesses his ignorance of this subject; and those who have come after him, though they imitate not his modesty, add little to dissipate the mist with which this vision is surrounded. Some have adhered too close to Josephus, while Villalpand has here discovered all the magnificence of Greek and Roman architecture, and has represented the temple six times as large as it really was. It seems that the prophet has described the same temple of Solomon which he had seen, that the dimensions might be preserved, and the hopes of the people kept up; (Calmet) and that they might comprehend what a loss they actually sustained on account of their sins, (Haydock) and might strive to come up to this pattern (Du Hamel) as "near as they should be able," the wealth of the people being much less than Solomon's. (Grotius) --- These arguments do not, however, shew that the buildings were to resemble each other. They vary in many particulars; and the prophet would specify what was to be really executed. He says nothing of the ornamental part, and little of the height, which are the most expensive. (Houbigant) (Preface) --- If some things appear to be too grand for the temple of Solomon, and of Zorobabel, we must reflect that the prophet passes from the figure to the Church of Christ, which is not unusual. (Menochius) --- Alcasar and Bossuet explain it wholly of the Church, so that the letter requires few notes. (Du Hamel)

extractions.type_description: The prophet Ezekiel's detailed vision of a future temple with specific dimensions and architectural features, presented as a figure or pattern to the exiled Jewish people
extractions.antitype_description: The mystical Church composed of both Jews and Gentiles, adorned with all graces, into which the redeemed are brought by Christ; also understood as the Church triumphant
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that St. Jerome and St. Gregory interpret 'some parts' of Ezekiel's temple vision 'as a figure of those redeemed by Christ, and brought into his Church.' The temple is presented as a type that prefigures the Church as its fulfillment. Multiple commentators cited (Lyranus, Menochius, Alcasar, Bossuet) affirm this typological interpretation, with one noting 'the prophet passes from the figure to the Church of Christ, which is not unusual.'

notes: The commentary presents this typology as the most defensible interpretation among several competing views (literal fulfillment after captivity, messianic fulfillment, conditional promise). The confidence is 'high' because multiple authoritative medieval and patristic sources (Jerome, Gregory, Lyranus, Menochius) explicitly frame this as a typological relationship. However, the commentary acknowledges significant interpretive difficulty and notes that some details may refer to the post-exilic temple while others refer typologically to the Church.

original_text: Face. This astonishment and attention (ver. 5.) intimate the mysteries of the Church, prefigured by the Jewish rites. (Worthington)

extractions.type_name: Jewish Rites (Temple worship and ritual practices)
extractions.type_description: The ceremonial practices, rituals, and institutional worship of the Jewish temple system as described in Ezekiel's vision
extractions.antitype_description: The New Testament Church and its spiritual mysteries, which fulfill and replace the Old Testament temple worship
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that 'the mysteries of the Church' are 'prefigured by the Jewish rites,' establishing a direct typological relationship where OT Jewish ceremonial practices anticipate and foreshadow NT ecclesial reality. The mention of astonishment and attention (verses 4-5) in response to these rites suggests their prophetic significance pointing forward to the Church.

notes: This is a broad typological relationship rather than a specific type-antitype pair. The commentary suggests that the entire system of Jewish temple rites functions typologically to prefigure the Church's mysteries. The context (Ezekiel's vision of the temple) reinforces this as a vision with prophetic significance for the Church.

original_text: Israel. People from all parts might serve the Levites. This tribe was not to engage in labourious or sordid employments, being attached to the service of the Lord, and bound to instruct others. But this was more perfectly fulfilled in the Christian Church, where the clergy enjoy great immunities, and are forbidden to exercise any trade or employment which may take them off from their more important spiritual concerns, or render their ministry contemptible. See Exodus 19:6.

extractions.type_name: The Levitical Tribe and their service restrictions
extractions.type_description: In OT Israel, the tribe of Levi was set apart for divine service, exempted from laborious or sordid employments, and dedicated to serving the Lord and instructing others
extractions.antitype_description: In the Christian Church, clergy are granted immunities and forbidden to engage in trades or worldly employments that would distract from spiritual ministry or diminish the respect due to their office
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states 'this was more perfectly fulfilled in the Christian Church,' establishing a clear typological relationship where the OT Levitical arrangement prefigures NT ecclesiastical structure and clerical discipline. The parallel is structural and institutional rather than merely illustrative.

notes: The commentary provides an explicit typological progression from OT to NT: what was foreshadowed in the Levitical system (separation from secular work, dedication to sacred service) finds its fuller realization in Christian clergy. The reference to Exodus 19:6 ('a kingdom of priests') suggests the commentary may be drawing on broader priestly typology, though the immediate focus is on the Levitical tribe's exemptions.

original_text: The fourth kingdom, etc. Some understand this of the successors of Alexander, the kings of Syria and Egypt: others, of the Roman empire and its civil wars. (Challoner) --- The former supposition seems best, though the latter is almost universally received, and will be explained hereafter. (Calmet) --- The Roman empire did not immediately rise out of Alexander's, and had no relation to the Jews, etc. (Grotius, L'Empereus.) --- But it surely swallowed up all that he had left to his generals, and proved the greatest scourge to the Jewish nation; which has been ever since scattered, while the kingdom of Christ gains ground, and will flourish till that of Rome shall be no more. Antichrist will then appear to cast a cloud over, but not destroy it for three years and a half. It is the opinion of many Fathers, etc. that the Roman empire will subsist till that event take place; (see 2 Thessalonians 2:3, 7.) and thus it may be said, that the fourth empire shall not be given to another people. For antichrist will not strive to exalt a particular nation, but to rule over all. Yet his dominion will be short, and will end in the general dissolution of nature; so that the Roman empire may be deemed to last for a long time, or even for ever. (ver. 44.) Those who adopt the former system, allow (Haydock) that the stone designates both the Roman empire and that of Christ; so that some parts of the prediction may refer to one and some to the other. The origin and progress of the Roman empire, might be a figure of the spiritual power of the Church. It is certain that the successors of Alexander owed their dominion to their valour, and established it by the slaughter of many great generals. The kings who followed Seleucus and Ptolemy were remarkable for a mixture of good and bad qualities. Their efforts to preserve their power by intermarriages, proved abortive. The prophet seems also to have had them in view, Daniel 7:7., and 8:22. (Calmet)

extractions.type_description: The stone cut without hands that breaks the iron, bronze, clay, silver, and gold of the four kingdoms in Daniel 2:34-35, 44-45
extractions.antitype_name: The Kingdom of Christ / The Church
extractions.antitype_description: The spiritual kingdom of Christ that will grow and flourish, ultimately replacing all earthly kingdoms and lasting eternally
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states: 'the stone designates both the Roman empire and that of Christ' and describes how 'the kingdom of Christ gains ground, and will flourish till that of Rome shall be no more.' The stone represents Christ's eternal kingdom that will supersede all temporal powers.

extractions.type_description: The fourth kingdom in Nebuchadnezzar's dream, portrayed as strong and destructive, breaking and crushing all other kingdoms
extractions.antitype_name: The Spiritual Power of the Church
extractions.antitype_description: The Church's spiritual dominion and authority that mirrors the Roman empire's temporal expansion and power
extractions.reasoning: The commentary states: 'The origin and progress of the Roman empire, might be a figure of the spiritual power of the Church.' This suggests the rise and expansion of Rome typifies the Church's growth in spiritual power, though the commentary presents this as one interpretive option among others.

notes: This commentary presents multiple interpretive frameworks (Alexandrine successors vs. Roman empire) and acknowledges scholarly disagreement. The typological connection to Christ's kingdom is more firmly established in the text than the ecclesial type. The commentary also discusses eschatological fulfillment involving Antichrist, which reinforces the eschatological category for the primary extraction.

original_text: Of gods, above all those of the country for explaining hidden things: yet he did not acknowledge him to be the only true God. (Calmet) --- He afterwards erected an idol to represent his own greatness. (Worthington)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Daniel 2:47 discusses Nebuchadnezzar's acknowledgment of Daniel's God as superior to other gods, and notes his later idolatry. While the passage involves religious themes and moral lessons about incomplete faith and pride, the commentary does not establish or describe any typological relationship between an Old Testament person, event, or institution and a New Testament fulfillment. The commentary is primarily historical and moral in nature, addressing Nebuchadnezzar's limited spiritual conversion and subsequent apostasy, rather than presenting typological connections.

original_text: Statue. It was not the figure of a man, (Calmet) the dimensions 90 feet high and 9 broad (Worthington) being disproportionate; though a man might be represented on the pillar. Some take it for Nabolpolassar, (Calmet) or for the king himself. (St. Jerome) (Worthington) --- But he never complains of the injury shewn to his own person, and therefore it probably was meant for Bel, the chief god, Daniel 4:5., and 14:1. This nation adored statues, Baruch 6:3. The Persians worshipped only the elements. (Calmet) --- Ochus first set up the statue of the goddess Tanais or Anais. (Clem. Protr.) --- Dura. Septuagint, "enclosed." (St. Jerome) --- This happened towards the end of the king's reign, (ver. 98, etc.) of course the three young men might be about fifty years old. (Calmet)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Daniel 3:1 focuses on identifying what the golden statue represents (likely the god Bel rather than Nebuchadnezzar himself) and provides historical and dimensional details about the statue. It discusses idolatry practices among Babylonians, Persians, and other nations, and offers chronological context about when the event occurred. However, the commentary contains no explicit or implicit typological connections linking this Old Testament event or object to New Testament fulfillments. While the refusal of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego to bow to the statue might later be interpreted typologically in other contexts, this particular commentary excerpt does not develop or reference any such typological relationship.

original_text: A watcher. A vigilant angel, perhaps the guardian of Israel. (Challoner) --- Chaldean hir; (Haydock) whence Iris the messenger of the gods, is derived. (St. Jerome) --- Theodotion retains eir. See St. Jerome in Psalm 76:4. The scholiast (Rom. ed.) says: "the Septuagint render it an angel, the rest a watcher." These supernatural agents (Haydock) and saints are represented as judges, ver. 14. (Calmet)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Daniel 4:10 focuses on linguistic and definitional analysis rather than typological interpretation. The commentary discusses: (1) the term 'watcher' (a vigilant angel, possibly Israel's guardian), (2) etymological connections to Chaldean and Greek terminology, and (3) how various ancient versions (Septuagint, Theodotion) render the term. The reference to 'supernatural agents and saints...represented as judges' in verse 14 is descriptive rather than typological—it explains the role of these beings within the narrative context rather than establishing an OT type that prefigures a NT antitype. No explicit connection between an Old Testament person, event, or institution and its New Testament fulfillment is presented.

original_text: Let it, the tree, representing the king who was confined when he began to shew signs of madness: but he broke loose, and fled away. (Calmet)
notes: This commentary discusses the symbolism of the tree in Daniel 4:12 as representing King Nebuchadnezzar during his period of madness and confinement. While the tree serves as a symbol or allegory within the narrative itself, the commentary does not establish a typological relationship between an Old Testament type and a New Testament antitype. The passage is interpreted as historical narrative with symbolic elements (the tree representing the king), not as an OT prefigurement of NT fulfillment. This falls under general symbolism/allegory rather than biblical typology as traditionally defined.

original_text: Changed, etc. It does not appear, by Scripture, that Nabuchodonosor was changed from human shape, much less that he was changed into an ox, but only that he lost his reason, and became mad; and in this condition remained abroad in the company of beasts, eating grass like an ox, till his hair grew in such a manner as to resemble the feathers of eagles, and his nails to be like birds' claws. (Challoner) --- Origen represents the whole as an allegorical description of the fall of Lucifer. See St. Jerome. But his arguments have made little impression: and it is universally believed that Nabuchodonosor was thus punished for his pride, after a whole year had been allowed him to see if he would repent. The manner of this strange metamorphose has been variously explained. But it seems that he was seized with the species of madness styled Lycanthropy, (Calmet) as Virgil (Ec. 6:48.) relates of the daughters of Proetus, who "with mimick'd mooings fill'd the fields." (Haydock) --- Thus many fancy they are kings, or horses, (Calmet) and that they are continually mounting above the clouds, of which we have an instance in a woman still living at Whitby, who in other respects appears to be sufficiently sensible, (Haydock) as Tertullian and others think Nabuchodonosor was, that he might suffer more. Yet it is commonly supposed he lost his senses for a while, till God was pleased to restore them at the time appointed; when his former humiliating state might make a deep impression upon his mind, as well as upon his subjects, and caution all future generations to guard against the fatal consequences of pride. His son, Evilmerodac, probably ruled during his absence. Most of the Chaldean writings have perished; so that we need not be surprised if they take no notice of this event, which was so disgraceful to the nation. Yet Megasthenes, (in Eusebius praep. ix. ult.) seems to hint at it, when he represents the king seized with a divine fury, and crying out: (Calmet Diss.) "I, the same Nabuchodonosor, foretell unto you, Babylonians, a fatal calamity, which neither my ancestor Belus, nor even the kingdom of Bel, (Haydock, the gods) have power to avert. For a Persian mule (Cyrus; Calmet) shall come, assisted by your demons, and bring on slavery....Having uttered this oracle, he suddenly disappeared." (Haydock) --- Beast's heart. In his hypochondriac temper he imagined himself (Calmet) to be an ox, (Haydock) avoided the society of men, going naked and feeding on grass, upon his hands and feet, till (after seven years) God restored him to his senses and kingdom. (Worthington) --- The food which he used would tend to purge him, and naturally abate the disorder. (Barthol.) --- Yet none but God could tell precisely when the madness would seize or leave him. --- Times. This usually denotes years, in (Daniel 7:25.; Daniel 12:7.) and of course (Calmet) we must understand it here in this sense; (Worthington) though some have explained it of an indeterminate length of time, or of weeks, months, or seasons. Only winter and summer were admitted, so that half this period would thus suffice. See Theod. (Calmet)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Daniel 4:13 does not contain typological relationships between Old Testament and New Testament. While Origen is mentioned as having 'represented the whole as an allegorical description of the fall of Lucifer,' this is explicitly noted as an allegorical interpretation that 'has made little impression' and is not adopted by the commentators. The commentary focuses instead on: (1) historical explanation of Nebuchadnezzar's punishment (madness/lycanthropy) as a consequence of pride; (2) moral lessons about guarding against pride; and (3) textual/linguistic analysis of the terms used. The passage deals with OT history and moral instruction, but does not establish a prefigurative relationship between this OT event and any NT fulfillment or antitype. The fall of Lucifer reference, while present, is explicitly rejected as the proper interpretation and does not constitute an endorsed typological reading in this commentary.

original_text: Baltassar. He is believed to be the same as Nabonides, the last of the Chaldean kings, grandson to Nabuchodonosor. He is called his son (ver. 2, 11, etc.) according to the style of the Scriptures, because he was a descendant from him. (Challoner; St. Jerome in Isaiah xiii.; Usher, etc.) --- Some think that he was brother of Evilmerodac, ver. 11., and Baruch 1:11. But he seems rather to have been his son, Jeremias 27:7. Profane authors place Neriglissor and Laborosoarchod between them. They were not of the royal family, and might be looked upon as usurpers, or reigned in some other place; or they did not meddle with the Jews. (Calmet) --- It is wonderful that Josephus should prefer these authors; (Tirinus) yet he abandons the dates given by them. (Jewish Antiquities 10:12. et contra Apion 1.) They represent Nabonides as a simple Babylonian raised to the throne, defeated by Cyrus, and suffered to retire into Carmania; whereas, Baltassar was slain, ver. 29. (Calmet) --- The others were of a different lineage, and are mentioned by Eusebius, etc. Evilmerodac certainly preceded him on the throne, and honoured Joachin in the 37th year of his captivity. (Worthington) --- Thousand; or, "for his officers over a thousand men." (Theodotion) --- Every. Chaldean, "and drank wine before the thousand," more than any, for this was deemed a great perfection; or he drank in their presence, but apart. (Calmet) --- The Persian monarchs used to sit in a separate apartment, with a veil before the door, so that they could see the guests without being seen. A great chandelier was before them; (Athen. 4:10.) probably on the outside, otherwise it would have defeated their purpose. Light sufficient would appear for Baltassar to see the hand-writing on his chamber wall, ver. 5. (Haydock) --- According to the order of time, this chapter should be placed after the vii. and viii. (Calmet) --- But those contain visions. (Haydock)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Daniel 5:1 is primarily historical and exegetical in nature. It focuses on: (1) identifying Baltassar with Nabonides, the last Chaldean king; (2) clarifying genealogical relationships and chronological placement; (3) reconciling biblical and secular historical accounts; and (4) explaining the physical arrangement of the Persian court. While the passage describes the fall of Babylon and divine judgment (themes with eschatological dimensions), the commentary itself makes no explicit connection to New Testament fulfillment, Christ, the Church, or any other NT antitype. The commentary is concerned with historical authentication and textual clarification rather than typological interpretation.

original_text: Little horn. This is commonly understood of antichrist. It may also be applied to that great persecutor, Antiochus Epiphanes, as a figure of antichrist. (Challoner) --- He was the youngest son of Antiochus the great, and was a hostage of Rome. While he was returning, his elder brother died, and Epiphanes excluded his son Philometor, of Egypt, and the usurper Heliodorus. He also defeated three, Philometor, on the south; Artaxias, king of Armenia, on the east; and the strength, or God's people, ver 24., and Daniel 8:9. --- Man. He gained several at first, by his affability. --- Things: blasphemy, 1 Machabees 1:23, 43. (Calmet)

extractions.type_description: The Hellenistic king who persecuted God's people, depicted in Daniel 7:8 as a 'little horn' arising among the beasts; a historical figure from the Old Testament period
extractions.antitype_description: The eschatological figure of ultimate opposition to Christ and God's people, expected in the end times as described in New Testament prophecy
extractions.reasoning: The Haydock commentary explicitly states that Antiochus Epiphanes 'may also be applied to...as a figure of antichrist.' This directly establishes a typological prefigurement where the historical persecutor of God's people in the Old Testament era serves as a type foreshadowing the ultimate eschatological adversary (Antichrist) of New Testament revelation. The commentary treats Antiochus as a historical type that prefigures the NT antitype.

notes: The commentary presents a dual interpretation: the 'little horn' is 'commonly understood of antichrist' directly, but also acknowledges that Antiochus Epiphanes functions as 'a figure of antichrist.' This typological reading connects an OT historical event/person to NT eschatological expectation. The 'figure of' language is classical typological terminology.

original_text: Word, etc. That is, from the twentieth year of king Artaxerxes, when, by his commandment, Nehemias rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem, 2 Esdras 2:From which time, according to the best chronology, there were just sixty-nine weeks of years, that is 483 years, to the baptism of Christ, when he first began to preach and execute the office of Messias. (Challoner) --- The prophecy is divided into three periods: the first of forty-nine years, during which the walls were completed; (they had been raised in fifty-two days, (2 Esdras 6:15.) but many other fortifications were still requisite) the second of four hundred and thirty-four years, at the end of which Christ was baptized, in the fifteenth of Tiberius, the third of three years and a half, during which Christ preached. In the middle of this last week, the ancient sacrifices became useless, (Calmet) as the true Lamb of God had been immolated. (Theod.) --- A week of years denotes seven years, as Leviticus xxv. and thus seventy of these weeks would make four hundred and ninety years. (Ven. Bede, Rat. temp. 6 etc.; Worthington) --- Origen would understand 4900 years, and dates from the fall of Adam to the ruin of the temple. Marsham begins twenty-one years after the captivity commenced, when Darius took Susa, and ends in the second of Judas, when the temple was purified. This system would destroy the prediction of Christ's coming, and is very uncertain. Hardouin modifies it, and acknowledges that Christ was the end of the prophecy, though it was fulfilled in figure by the death of Onias 3:See 1 Machabees 1:19; Senens. Bib. viii. haer. 12; and Estius. From Daniel 7. to xii., the changes in the East, till the time of Epiphanes, are variously described. After the angel had here addressed Daniel, the latter was still perplexed; (Chap. 10:1.) and in order to remove his doubts, the angel informs him of the persecution of Epiphanes, as if he had been speaking of the same event. We may, therefore, count forty-nine years from the taking of Jerusalem (when Jeremias spoke, Daniel 5:19.) to Cyrus, the anointed, (Isaias 45:1.) who was appointed to free God's people. They should still be under the Persians, etc., for other four hundred and thirty-four years, and then Onias should be slain. Many would join the Machabees; the sacrifices should cease in the middle of the seventieth week, and the desolation shall continue to the end of it. Yet, though this system may seem plausible, it is better to stick to the common one, which naturally leads us to the death of Christ, dating from the tenth year of Artaxerxes. (Calmet) --- He had reigned ten years already with his father. (Petau.) --- All the East was persuaded that a great king should arise about the time; when our Saviour actually appeared, and fulfilled all that had been spoken of the Messias. (Calmet, Diss.) --- Ferguson says, "We have an astronomical demonstration of the truth of this ancient prophecy, seeing that the prophetic year of the Messias being cut off was the very same with the astronomical." In a dispute between a Jew and a Christian, at Venice, the Rabbi who presided....put an end to the business by saying, "Let us shut up our Bibles; for if we proceed in the examination of this prophecy, it will make us all become Christians." (Watson, let. 6.) --- Hence probably the Jews denounce a curse on those who calculate the times, (Haydock) and they have purposely curtailed their chronology. (Calmet) --- Times, etc. (angustia temporum) which may allude both to the difficulties and opposition they met with in building, and to the shortness of the time in which they finished the wall, viz. fifty-two days. (Challoner)

extractions.type_name: The sacrificial system and temple sacrifices of the Old Covenant
extractions.type_description: The ancient Jewish sacrificial system involving animal sacrifices offered in the temple, which became obsolete when Christ was crucified
extractions.antitype_name: Christ as the Lamb of God and ultimate sacrifice
extractions.antitype_description: Jesus Christ, whose crucifixion ('immolation') in the middle of the seventieth week made all previous animal sacrifices unnecessary and fulfilled their purpose
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states: 'In the middle of this last week, the ancient sacrifices became useless, (Calmet) as the true Lamb of God had been immolated.' This directly connects the OT sacrificial system as a type prefiguring Christ's sacrifice as the antitype. The language 'true Lamb of God' confirms Christological typology.

extractions.type_name: The command to rebuild Jerusalem's walls under Nehemiah/Artaxerxes
extractions.type_description: The decree and rebuilding of Jerusalem in the Persian period, marking the starting point for the seventy weeks prophecy
extractions.antitype_name: The coming of Christ the Messiah and His baptism
extractions.antitype_description: Christ's arrival and baptism, which occurred precisely at the end of sixty-nine weeks (483 years) from the rebuilding decree, fulfilling the messianic prophecy
extractions.reasoning: While this is more about prophetic fulfillment than traditional typology, the commentary presents the rebuilding of Jerusalem as prefiguring/leading to Christ's messianic ministry. The commentary states the prophecy 'naturally leads us to the death of Christ' and that Christ 'fulfilled all that had been spoken of the Messias,' suggesting a prefigurative relationship between the restoration event and Christ's coming.

notes: The primary typology is clear: OT sacrifices → Christ's sacrifice. The second extraction is somewhat less typical as it involves prophetic chronology rather than symbolic prefigurement, but the commentary does present the rebuilding of Jerusalem as a divinely appointed marker leading to Christ's fulfillment of messianic promises. The commentary also mentions Onias III as a 'figure' (prefigurement) of Christ's death, though it prioritizes the literal fulfillment in Christ over this typological interpretation.

original_text: South: Ptolemeus, the son of Lagus, king of Egypt, which lies south of Jerusalem. (Challoner) ---St. Irenaeus (IV. 43.) observes, that all prophecies are obscure till they be fulfilled. History shews that this relates to Ptolemy. The kingdoms of Egypt and of Syria are more noticed, as they had much to do with the Jews. (Worthington) --- Ptolemy took Cyprus (Calmet) and Jerusalem. (Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 12:12.) --- His princes (that is, one of Alexander's princes) shall prevail over him; that is, shall be stronger than the king of Egypt. He speaks of Seleucus Nicator, king of Asia and Syria, whose successors are here called the kings of the north, because their dominions lay to the north in respect to Jerusalem. (Challoner) --- Nicator means a "conqueror." (Haydock) ---This king was master of all from Media and Babylonia to Jerusalem. (Appian, etc.; Calmet) ---Philadelphus was more powerful than his father. (Worthington)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Daniel 11:5 is a historical-prophetic analysis rather than a typological interpretation. The commentary focuses on identifying historical fulfillment of the prophecy—specifically the kingdoms of Ptolemy (Egypt) and Seleucus Nicator (Syria)—and their geopolitical relationships to Jerusalem and the Jewish people. The commentary traces how these Old Testament prophecies were fulfilled in actual historical events (Ptolemy taking Cyprus and Jerusalem, Seleucus's dominion), but it does not connect any of these persons, events, or institutions to New Testament antitype fulfillments. There is no reference to Christ, the Church, Mary, sacraments, end times, or covenant fulfillment that would establish a typological relationship. St. Irenaeus is cited to note that 'prophecies are obscure till they be fulfilled,' but this refers to historical fulfillment, not typological prefigurement.

original_text: Vision. Many Jews, deceived by Onias, erected a temple in Egypt, falsely asserting that they fulfilled the prophecy of Isaias, 19:19. (Worthington) --- This Onias was the son of Onias III, who was slain at Antioch, Daniel 9:25. (Haydock) --- The temple of Onion was called after him. All allow that he transgressed the law, by offering sacrifice there after God had pitched upon Jerusalem. But this was done (Calmet) under Philometor, forty-seven years (Usher) or longer after those times, when Epiphanes fought against Antiochus. The rebellion of the Jews against Egypt may therefore be meant. It was decreed that they should be under Antiochus, that his son might cause them to fall, (Calmet) and punish them for their crimes. (Haydock)
notes: This Haydock commentary discusses historical events during the Hellenistic period (the temple of Onias in Egypt, conflicts between Antiochus and the Jews) as fulfillments of Daniel's prophecy, but it does not establish typological relationships between Old Testament types and New Testament antitypes. The commentary references Isaiah 19:19 as a prophecy that some Jews claimed was fulfilled by their Egyptian temple, but this is presented as a false claim by those Jews, not as a genuine typological connection endorsed by the commentator. The text focuses on historical-prophetic interpretation and moral judgment (punishment for transgression) rather than typology. No OT person, event, or institution is presented as prefiguring a NT fulfillment.

original_text: Slain. This was the perfidious policy of Epiphanes, who expected that the two brothers would destroy each other, so that he might easily seize Egypt, of which he kept the key, retaining the city of Pelusium. They were however reconciled, and reigned together. The Scripture often represents that as done which is only intended.
notes: This Haydock commentary discusses historical events from the Intertestamental period involving Epiphanes and Egyptian politics (specifically the Ptolemaic succession dispute). It is a historical-political analysis of Daniel 11:26, which relates to the Seleucid-Ptolemaic conflicts. The commentary contains no typological language or structure connecting Old Testament persons, events, or institutions to New Testament fulfillments. It is purely expository/historical in nature, explaining the political machinations and reconciliation of the two brothers mentioned in the verse. No OT type or NT antitype is identified or implied.

original_text: The god Maozim. That is, the god of forces or strong holds. (Challoner) --- Mahuzzim denotes "strong ones," (Haydock) guardians, etc. Dr. Newton (Diss.) explains, the king (ver. 36) of the Roman state; and supposes that here the guardian saints and angels are meant, whose worship he shews "began in the Roman empire, very soon after it became Christian. This exposition seems far preferable to that which interprets" Jupiter or the heavens, and understands the idol set up by Epiphanes. See Univ. Hist. X. Parkhurst. --- If these authors speak of the inferior veneration shewn to saints and angels in the Catholic Church, it had a much earlier commencement, being coeval with religion itself. But only the blindest prejudice can represent this as idolatrous, and of course this system must fall to the ground. (Haydock) --- Others suppose that Mars, Hercules, Azizus, or Jupiter, may be designated. Hebrew, "He will rise up against all, (38) and against the strong God (of Israel, ver. 31.; and Daniel 8:10.) (Calmet) he will, in his place, worship a strange god, " etc. (Junius) --- None of the ancestors of Epiphanes had ever adored Jupiter on the altar of holocausts. (Calmet) --- He and antichrist adore either the great Jupiter or their own strength. (Worthington)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Daniel 11:38 discusses the interpretation of 'the god of Maozim' (god of forces/strongholds) in the context of Antiochus Epiphanes and potentially an eschatological antichrist figure. However, the commentary does not establish typological relationships in the technical sense. Rather, it: (1) debates the historical/literal meaning of the verse (whether it refers to Jupiter, Mars, angels, saints, or the king's own strength), (2) discusses various scholarly interpretations of Epiphanes' religious practices, and (3) addresses debates about Catholic veneration of saints. While Daniel 11 is eschatological in nature and contains prophetic material that may have typological dimensions elsewhere, this particular verse and commentary focus on identifying what deity or concept is being referenced, not on establishing how an OT person or event prefigures a NT fulfillment. The possible reference to 'antichrist' (Worthington's comment) is mentioned but not developed as a typological fulfillment of an OT type.

original_text: Apadno. Some take it for the proper name of a place; others, from the Hebrew translate it, his palace. (Challoner) --- He fixed his royal tent between the Mediterranean and the Dead Sea. (Worthington) ---Porphyrius explains this of the march beyond the Euphrates, which St. Jerome does not disapprove. Apadno may denote Mesopotamia, which is styled Padan Aram. --- Glorious. Hebrew Zebi, (Calmet) or Tsebi, (Haydock) may allude to Mount Taba, where the king perished, without help, 1 Machabees 6:11., and 2 Machabees 9:9. St. Jerome and many others explain all this of antichrist, and no doubt he was prefigured. The like events will probably take place again towards the end of the world. But as the particulars cannot be ascertained, we have adhered to the history of Antiochus. (Calmet)

extractions.type_description: The historical king whose march, defeat, and death without help in the glorious land is recounted in Daniel 11. His actions and end represent a prefigurement of similar events.
extractions.antitype_description: The eschatological figure expected to arise at the end of the world, who will experience similar events and circumstances as Antiochus, including a glorious presence followed by defeat and death without assistance.
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states: 'St. Jerome and many others explain all this of antichrist, and no doubt he was prefigured.' The Haydock commentary directly affirms that Antiochus's historical events serve as a type prefiguring the antitype of the Antichrist. The commentary further notes that 'The like events will probably take place again towards the end of the world,' reinforcing the typological prefigurement of end-times events.

notes: The commentary demonstrates caution about over-specifying details of the antitype ('as the particulars cannot be ascertained'), which is typical in eschatological typology where future events are incompletely revealed. The commentary prioritizes the historical narrative of Antiochus while acknowledging the typological significance recognized by patristic sources (Jerome) and theological tradition.

original_text: Fornications. That is, a wife that hath been given to fornication. This was to represent the Lord's proceedings with his people Israel, who, by spiritual fornication, were continually offending him. (Challoner) --- The prophet reclaimed her. (St. Jerome) --- She denoted Samaria, abandoned to idolatry, Ezechiel 16:15. Several such actions were prophetical. Many have supposed that this was only a parable; but the sequel proves the contrary. (Calmet) --- Of fornications. So called from the character of their mother, if not also from their own wicked dispositions. (Challoner) --- He is ordered to marry a woman who had been of a loose character, and to have children who would resemble her; (Worthington) or he takes her children to his house; (Grotius) unless the children of the prophet were so styled because the mother had been given to fornication. So the rod of Aaron retains its name when it was become a serpent, Exodus 7:12. --- Shall, or rather, "has departed;" and therefore he denounces future chastisements.
notes: This commentary describes a symbolic or prophetic action rather than typology proper. Hosea's marriage to Gomer is presented as a representational sign-act that demonstrates Israel's spiritual unfaithfulness to God, but the commentary does not establish an Old Testament type that prefigures a New Testament antitype. The relationship described is between the prophetic action (OT) and its contemporary theological meaning (Israel's apostasy in the OT period), not between OT and NT fulfillment. The references to Samaria's idolatry and Ezekiel 16:15 are intra-testamental parallels, not typological prefigurement. While this action has typological potential in broader theological schemes, the Haydock commentary itself does not explicitly articulate an OT-to-NT typological connection.

original_text: Woman. This second woman denotes the penitent Israel, yet not quite reconciled. The people in captivity are separated both from her idols and from God, though the latter still retains an affection for them. Osee does not marry this woman, but gives his word. We must not urge the parable too far. He acts as a figure of the Lord, who has received an outrage. (Calmet) --- Grace is still offered to sinners, whose persons are never hated by God. (Worthington) --- Husks. Septuagint, etc., "cakes made with grapes," for idols. (Theodoret; St. Jerome)

extractions.type_name: Hosea's action of taking back a woman (Gomer) - the second woman
extractions.type_description: Hosea, as commanded by God, takes back a woman who represents penitent but not yet fully reconciled Israel. Hosea acts as 'a figure of the Lord, who has received an outrage,' offering grace and reconciliation despite the people's unfaithfulness and idolatry.
extractions.antitype_name: Christ's reception and reconciliation of penitent sinners/the Church
extractions.antitype_description: Jesus Christ, as Lord, receives back sinners in repentance. Grace is continually offered to those who turn from sin, and God/Christ never hates their persons despite their transgressions. This prefigures Christ's redemptive work and the reconciliation of the Church to God.
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states Hosea 'acts as a figure of the Lord, who has received an outrage,' establishing a typological connection between Hosea's redemptive action toward the penitent woman and the Lord's (Christ's) redemptive stance toward sinners. The principle that 'Grace is still offered to sinners, whose persons are never hated by God' reflects Christ's redemptive mission in the NT.

notes: The commentary itself exercises caution ('We must not urge the parable too far'), suggesting the typology is present but should not be overextended. The type is Hosea's prophetic action/role, not necessarily the woman herself, with the antitype being Christ's redemptive grace toward penitent sinners.

original_text: Altar. Hebrew, "statue;" matseba instead of mozbé, as (Haydock) others agree with St. Jerome, and there seems to have been no variation in his time. --- Theraphim. Images or representations, (Challoner) either good or bad. As the other things mentioned were good, such lawful images as were used in the temple must be meant, 3 Kings 7:36. (Worthington) --- St. Jerome explains it of cherubim. Septuagint, "altar, priesthood, and manifestations (Urim, etc.) being wanting." (Haydock) --- Yet some take it in a bad sense. The Jews adhere neither to God nor to idols. (Vatable, etc.) --- What misfortune, however, would the latter be? In exile the Jews were deprived of the exercise of their religion, and of their princes. (Calmet) --- But this was only a figure of what they endured since they rejected Christ. (Origen, Philoc. i.; St. Jerome) --- This wretched state will probably continue till they at last embrace the yoke of Christ, the true king of ages. (Calmet)

extractions.type_name: Jewish exile and deprivation of religious practice and princes
