Frivolous is the objection of certain sectarists, that Christ does not give himself to us in the blessed eucharist to be adored, but to be eaten. For Christ was not in Bethlehem, nor did he descend from heaven to be adored: He tells us in the xxth Matthew of Matthew, ver. 28, that the Son of Man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister; yet he was adored on earth, even while he was in his mortal state, by the magi, by his disciples, by the blind man that was cured of his blindness, etc. etc. "Let us imitate the magi. Thou seest him not now in the crib, but on the altar; not a woman holding him, but the priest present, and the Holy Ghost poured out abundantly upon the sacrifice." (St. Chrysostom, hom. xxiv. in 1 Cor.; Hom. vii. de Sancto Philog.)
notes: This commentary discusses the symbolic meaning of the gifts (gold, frankincense, and myrrh) presented to Jesus by the Magi, but this represents symbolism and allegory rather than typology. The gifts are interpreted symbolically as representing Jesus's kingship (gold), divinity (incense), and mortality (myrrh), but there is no Old Testament type being presented as prefiguring these gifts or their presentation. The commentary also draws a typological-adjacent connection between Christ in the manger and Christ in the Eucharist, but this is a form of correspondence or analogy within the New Testament itself, not a connection between an OT type and NT antitype. Additionally, the commentary includes a theological defense of Eucharistic adoration but does not establish an OT prefigurement of this doctrine.

original_text: Out of Egypt have I called my son.{ Ver. 15. Ex Aegypto vocai filium meum. In the Septuagint ta tekna autou, filios ejus.|} St. Jerome understands these words to be taken out of the prophet Osee, (Chap. 11:2.) and granted they might be literally spoken of the people Israel: yet as their captivity in Egypt was a figure of the slavery of sin, under which all mankind groaned, and as their delivery by Moses was a figure of man's redemption by our Saviour Christ, so these words in a mystical and spiritual sense apply to our Saviour, who in a more proper sense was the Son of God, than was the people of Israel. (Witham) --- The application of this passage of the prophet to Christ, whereas in the simple letter it might appear otherwise, teaches us how to interpret the Old Testament; and that the principal sense is of Christ and his Church. (Bristow)

extractions.type_description: The people of Israel's bondage and slavery in Egypt
extractions.antitype_description: The spiritual bondage of all humanity under sin
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states: 'their captivity in Egypt was a figure of the slavery of sin, under which all mankind groaned.' This establishes a clear OT/NT typological relationship where Egypt's bondage prefigures spiritual bondage to sin.

extractions.type_name: Israel's deliverance by Moses from Egypt
extractions.type_description: The liberation of Israel from Egyptian slavery through Moses
extractions.antitype_description: Humanity's salvation and redemption accomplished by Jesus Christ
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states: 'their delivery by Moses was a figure of man's redemption by our Saviour Christ.' This directly connects the OT type (Moses' deliverance) to the NT antitype (Christ's redemptive work).

extractions.type_description: The people of Israel referred to as God's son in the literal sense
extractions.antitype_description: Jesus Christ, who is God's Son in a more proper and ultimate sense
extractions.reasoning: The commentary states that though Hosea 11:2 'might be literally spoken of the people Israel,' 'these words in a mystical and spiritual sense apply to our Saviour, who in a more proper sense was the Son of God, than was the people of Israel.' This indicates a typological progression where the OT type (Israel as God's son) finds its fuller fulfillment in the NT antitype (Christ as God's Son).

notes: All three typological relationships are Christological in nature, demonstrating how Matthew interprets Hosea 11:2 as ultimately pointing to Christ. The commentary explicitly emphasizes that while the text may have literal reference to Israel, its 'mystical and spiritual sense' applies to Christ, which is the principle of typological interpretation.

original_text: A voice was heard in Rama.{ Ver. 18. Vox in Excelso audita est. Jeremias 31:15.|} St. Jerome takes Rama, not for the name of any city, but for a high place, as appears by his Latin translation. (Jeremias 31:15.) But in all Greek copies here in St. Matthew, and in the Septuagint in Jeremias, we find the word itself Rama, so that it must signify a particular city. Rachel, who was buried at Bethlehem, is represented weeping (as it were in the person of those desolate mothers) the murder, and loss of so many children: and Rama being a city not far from Bethlehem, in the tribe of Benjamin, built on a high place, it is said that the cries and lamentations of these children, and their mothers, reached even to Rama. Cornelius a Lapide on Jeremias xxxi. thinks that these words were not only applied by the evangelist in a figurative sense, but that the prophet in the literal sense foretold these lamentations. (Witham)
notes: This commentary describes a prophetic fulfillment rather than a typological relationship. Jeremiah 31:15 is presented as a literal prophecy that the evangelist Matthew applies to the slaughter of the innocents—a direct prophetic fulfillment, not a typological prefigurement. The commentary explicitly states that Cornelius a Lapide believes 'these words were not only applied by the evangelist in a figurative sense, but that the prophet in the literal sense foretold these lamentations.' Rachel's weeping is understood as a poetic, representative image of the mothers' lamentations, but this is figurative application of prophecy rather than type-antitype typology. Typology requires an OT person, event, or institution that prefigures (serves as a foreshadowing pattern for) a NT reality; this passage involves direct prophetic prediction and fulfillment instead.

original_text: Isaias spoke these words of the deliverance of the Jews from Babylon; but this was a figure of the freedom of mankind through Jesus Christ. The Jews expected Elias would come in person to prepare the ways of the Messias; but John the Baptist was raised up by God in the spirit and power of Elias, to precede the first coming of Jesus Christ, as Elias in person was to precede the second coming of this divine Saviour. (Bible de Vence)

extractions.type_name: The deliverance of the Jews from Babylon
extractions.type_description: The historical liberation of the Jewish people from Babylonian captivity, as prophesied by Isaiah
extractions.antitype_name: The freedom of mankind through Jesus Christ
extractions.antitype_description: Spiritual liberation and redemption of humanity accomplished through Christ's redemptive work
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that Isaiah's prophecy of deliverance from Babylon 'was a figure of the freedom of mankind through Jesus Christ,' establishing a clear OT type-to-NT antitype relationship.

extractions.type_name: Elijah (Elias) coming to prepare the way of the Messiah
extractions.type_description: The OT expectation that the prophet Elijah would personally come to prepare the way for the Messiah's coming, based on Malachi 4:5-6
extractions.antitype_name: John the Baptist in the spirit and power of Elijah
extractions.antitype_description: John the Baptist, who came in the spirit and power of Elijah to prepare the way for Jesus Christ's first coming
extractions.reasoning: The commentary states that 'John the Baptist was raised up by God in the spirit and power of Elias, to precede the first coming of Jesus Christ,' establishing a typological fulfillment where the expected role of Elijah is fulfilled through John the Baptist.

notes: The commentary also mentions an eschatological element: 'Elias in person was to precede the second coming of this divine Saviour,' suggesting a future fulfillment. However, this is presented as a distinct future event rather than a typological relationship already manifested in the NT, so it is not included as a primary extraction.

original_text: Shewed him all the kingdoms of the world, and their glory; and as St. Luke says, in a moment of time. We cannot comprehend how this could be done from any mountain, or seen with human eyes. Therefore many think it was by some kind of representation; or that the devil shewing a part, by words set forth the rest. (Witham) --- He shewed him the different climates in which each country was situated. (St. Chrysostom)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Matthew 4:8 discusses the temptation of Christ by Satan, who showed Jesus all the kingdoms of the world. The commentary addresses the interpretive challenge of how this vision could physically occur from a mountain, offering explanations such as representation or demonic description. While the passage itself (the temptation narrative) has theological significance, this particular commentary does not establish or discuss any typological relationships between Old Testament types and New Testament antitypes. The focus is on exegetical and phenomenological explanation rather than typological prefigurement.

original_text: Not to destroy the law, etc. It is true, by Christ's coming, a multitude of ceremonies and sacrifices, and circumcision, were to cease; but the moral precepts were to continue, and to be complied with, even with greater perfection. (Witham) --- To fulfil. By accomplishing all the figures and prophecies, and perfecting all that was imperfect. (Challoner) --- Our Saviour speaks in this manner, to prepare the minds of the Jews for his new instructions. For although they were not very solicitous about fulfilling the law, still they were extremely jealous of any change being made in the letter of the law; more particularly, if the proposed change exacted a more perfect morality. Our Lord fulfilled the law three several ways: 1. By his obedience to the prescribed rites; therefore he says, it behoveth us to fulfil all justice: and who shall accuse me of sin? 2. He observes the law, not only by his own observance of it, but likewise by enabling us to fulfil it. It was the wish of the law to make man just, but found itself too weak; Christ therefore came justifying man, and accomplished the will of the law. 3. He fulfilled the law, by reducing all the precepts of the old law to a more strict and powerful morality. (St. Chrysostom, hom. xvi.)

extractions.type_name: Old Testament Law (ceremonies, sacrifices, circumcision, and moral precepts)
extractions.type_description: The incomplete and imperfect system of Old Testament legal requirements, including ceremonial rites, sacrifices, circumcision, and moral precepts that were weak in their ability to justify man
extractions.antitype_name: Christ's Fulfillment of the Law and His Perfected Moral Teaching
extractions.antitype_description: Jesus Christ who accomplishes what the Old Testament law prefigured: (1) perfect obedience to prescribed rites, (2) enabling humanity to fulfill the law, and (3) perfecting and intensifying moral precepts into stricter and more powerful morality
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly uses 'fulfil' language indicating that OT legal figures and prophecies prefigure their NT fulfillment in Christ. The passage states Christ fulfills the law 'by accomplishing all the figures and prophecies, and perfecting all that was imperfect.' The three ways Christ fulfilled the law demonstrate how the imperfect OT types found their complete realization in the antitype (Christ himself and his redemptive work).

extractions.type_description: The ritualistic system of sacrifices and ceremonial observances in the Old Testament law
extractions.antitype_description: Christ's perfect obedience and self-sacrifice, which supersedes and renders obsolete the need for continued Old Testament sacrifices and ceremonies
extractions.reasoning: The commentary indicates that through Christ's coming, 'a multitude of ceremonies and sacrifices...were to cease,' suggesting that OT sacrifices were types that found their antitype in Christ's singular, perfect sacrifice and obedience.

notes: This commentary presents a fulfillment typology rather than a predictive typology—the OT law and its components are types that Christ himself fulfills through his person and work. The commentary emphasizes that the OT law was preparatory and incomplete, while Christ represents the full realization and perfection of what those types prefigured.

original_text: Amen. That is, assuredly, of a truth. This Hebrew word Amen, is here retained by the example and authority of all the four evangelists, who have retained it. It is used by our Lord as a strong asseveration, and affirmation of the truth. (Challoner) --- Not one jot (or not one jota), nor one tittle, that is not the least letter, nor stroke of a letter; that is, not the least moral precept. Besides every type and figure of the former law, now by my coming shall be fulfilled. (Witham) --- Amen, is retained in the Hebrew, Greek, Syriac, and Armenian languages, as well as in all vulgar idioms. It is a term of asseveration, and equivalent to an oath; and in many places, to make the asseveration still stronger, it is repeated. St. Luke very accurately translates it into nai. St. Paul and St. John unite them nai and amen. (Haydock)

extractions.type_description: The Old Testament law, including its types and figures that were divinely ordained to prefigure future spiritual realities
extractions.antitype_name: The Coming of Christ and Fulfillment of the Law
extractions.antitype_description: Jesus Christ's advent and his fulfillment of all the types and figures of the former law, making their spiritual reality complete
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states: 'Besides every type and figure of the former law, now by my coming shall be fulfilled.' This directly identifies the OT types and figures as prefiguring their fulfillment in Christ's coming. The commentary makes clear that the types of the former law find their antitype in Christ's incarnation and ministry.

notes: The commentary's primary focus is on the meaning of 'Amen' and the authority of Scripture (not one jot or tittle shall pass away). The typological statement appears in parenthetical form from Witham's commentary, indicating it is contextual rather than the main exegetical point. However, it represents a clear typological principle: OT types prefigure NT fulfillment in Christ.

original_text: In consequence of the faith of this Gentile, Jesus Christ takes occasion to declare that many Gentiles would be called to sit at table with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, in the kingdom of heaven, which is frequently represented under the figure of a feast. See Matthew 22:2; Luke 13:29.; Luke 14:16; Apocalypse 19:9. In ancient times, the guests were reclined on beds when they took their meals. (Bible de Vence)

extractions.type_name: The Messianic Feast with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob
extractions.type_description: The Old Testament anticipation of fellowship with the patriarchs, rooted in God's promises to Abraham and the covenant blessings that would extend to all peoples. The OT feast imagery associated with covenant fulfillment and God's provision.
extractions.antitype_name: The Kingdom of Heaven represented as a Messianic Banquet
extractions.antitype_description: The eschatological feast in the kingdom of heaven where both Jews and Gentiles (like the Gentile centurion) sit at table with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—the fulfillment of God's promise that salvation extends to all nations through faith.
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly connects the OT patriarchal covenant promises (Abraham, Isaac, Jacob) with the NT fulfillment of these promises in the eschaton. The feast is presented as the antitype that fulfills the type of OT covenant blessings. The inclusion of Gentiles 'in consequence of faith' demonstrates how the NT antitype expands and fulfills the OT type.

notes: The commentary also references the symbolic use of 'feast' language throughout Scripture (Matthew 22:2; Luke 13:29; Luke 14:16; Revelation 19:9) as reinforcement of this eschatological type-antitype relationship. While the commentary discusses ancient meal customs (reclining on beds), this is cultural context rather than typology.

original_text: Before this time the 12 were called disciples, and not apostles. But now he selects these from the disciples, and makes them, as it were, masters and interpreters of the ways of God to man. He sent afterwards 72 other disciples, (Luke 10:1,) but these 12 only to the whole world. (Haydock) --- His twelve, etc. Christ chose 12 apostles, that they might correspond to the number of the Jewish patriarchs, by whom they may be said to have been prefigured; and that as the whole Jewish people were descended according to the flesh from the 12 patriarchs, so the whole Christian people might be descended according to the spirit from the 12 apostles. (Menochius) --- Others say he chose 12, neither more nor less, to correspond with the 12 prophets of the old law, with the 12 fountains in Elim; and the 12 stones selected from the river Jordan, and preserved in the ark of the testament. Others compare the 12 apostles to the 12 months of the year, and the four evangelists to the four seasons: thus Sedulius, lib. 1:carm. Quatuor hi proceres una te voce canentes, Tempora ceu totidem latum sparguntur in orbem. Sic et apostolici semper duodenus honoris Fulget apex numero menses imitatus, et horas, Omnibus ut rebus semper tibi militet annus.

extractions.type_description: The twelve patriarchs of Israel, the ancestral heads of the twelve tribes through whom the Jewish people descended according to the flesh
extractions.antitype_description: The twelve apostles chosen by Christ to be the foundation through whom the Christian people might descend according to the spirit
extractions.reasoning: Menochius explicitly states that Christ chose 12 apostles 'that they might correspond to the number of the Jewish patriarchs, by whom they may be said to have been prefigured.' The typological correspondence is direct: as the Jewish people descended fleshly from 12 patriarchs, so Christian people descend spiritually from 12 apostles. This is a clear OT type prefiguring NT antitype.

extractions.type_name: The Twelve Prophets of the Old Law
extractions.type_description: The prophetic figures of the Old Testament, numbering twelve, who spoke God's word to Israel
extractions.antitype_description: The twelve apostles as masters and interpreters of God's ways to humanity in the New Testament
extractions.reasoning: The commentary notes that 'others say he chose 12, neither more nor less, to correspond with the 12 prophets of the old law.' While this connection is attested in the commentary, it is presented as an alternative interpretation ('Others say') rather than the primary one, suggesting somewhat less certainty than the patriarchal typology.

notes: The commentary also mentions non-typological symbolic correspondences (12 fountains in Elim, 12 stones from Jordan, 12 months/4 seasons) which are symbolic parallels rather than OT-to-NT typological prefigurations, and have therefore been excluded. The primary typological relationship in this commentary is the correspondence between the 12 patriarchs and 12 apostles, explicitly presented as fulfilling a prefigurative pattern.

original_text: That which I tell you, etc. We must not suppose that our Saviour was accustomed to deliver his instructions to his apostles in the secret of the night, or teach them in private by whispers. But here he uses a figure of speech, to convey to the minds of his apostles the insignificancy of Judea, where he was speaking in comparison of the whole world, which they were to instruct; and the low whisper of his voice, compared to the sound which they shall send forth to the ends of the earth. (St. Chrysostom, hom. xxxv.) --- Upon the house-tops. The tops of the houses in Palestine were flat, and the inhabitants were accustomed to assemble on them and discourse together in great numbers. To preach, therefore, on the top of a house, is the same as to preach where there is a great concourse of people. (Menochius)
notes: The Haydock commentary on Matthew 10:27 employs figurative language and descriptive explanation rather than typological interpretation. The commentary explains Christ's use of metaphor (whispering in secret vs. proclaiming on housetops) as a rhetorical device to convey the contrast between His limited ministry in Judea and the apostles' future universal mission. It also provides historical context about Palestinian architecture and customs. No Old Testament type is invoked or discussed as prefiguring this New Testament scene or instruction. The commentary is primarily exegetical and historical rather than typological.

original_text: All the prophets and the law prophesied until John: as if he had said, all they who prophesied before, foretold the coming of the Messias; but now John points him out present with you, so that now all the types and figures of the ancient law will be fulfilled, and are at an end. (Witham)

extractions.type_name: The Prophets and the Law of the Old Testament
extractions.type_description: All the prophets and legal ordinances of the Old Testament that prophesied and prefigured the coming of the Messiah through types and figures
extractions.antitype_name: Jesus Christ (the Messiah) revealed through John the Baptist
extractions.antitype_description: The fulfillment of all Old Testament prophecies and types; Jesus Christ present in the world, pointed out by John the Baptist
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that 'all they who prophesied before, foretold the coming of the Messias' and that 'all the types and figures of the ancient law will be fulfilled' in Christ. This is a direct typological relationship where OT prophecies and types (the type) prefigure and are fulfilled in Christ's arrival (the antitype).

notes: The commentary uses the phrase 'types and figures of the ancient law' to describe the OT prefigurations. The antitype is not a single person or event but rather the collective fulfillment represented by Christ's presence in the world, which John the Baptist identifies. John the Baptist serves as the pivotal figure marking the transition from type to antitype fulfillment.

original_text: We have piped. Christ, says, St. Jerome on this place, was represented by the children that piped, or played on pipes, and St. John by those that mourned; because Christ refused not upon occasions, to eat and converse with sinners. (Witham) --- Jesus shews the Jews by this simile, that he had endeavoured to induce them, by the common life he led, to an imitation of his virtues; and they had not complied with his desire. --- We have lamented. This part is to be understood of St. John, who led a most austere life, and notwithstanding was despised by the Jews. (St. Jerome in St. Thomas Aquinas) --- Similar to this is the complaint of the Almighty, by the mouth of the prophet Isaias: What is there that I should have done to my vineyard, and have not done? Our Redeemer and the Baptist imitated skilful huntsmen, who made use of various and opposite stratagems, that if the nimble animal escape one, he may fall into another. As men are commonly more engaged by fasting and austerities, therefore did the Baptist practise them in the highest degree, that they thus might be prevailed upon to believe his words. Christ, condescending more to their weakness, did not embrace this rigid manner of life, though at the same time he sanctified and approved it by his fast of forty days, and extreme poverty, not having where to recline his head. It was better that our Saviour's doctrine should be approved of by one who practiced austerity, than that he himself should fast and live rigidly. If the Jews admired fasting and penance, whose words should have led them to the Son of God? If fasting appeared sorrowful and forbidding, why did they not join themselves to Jesus, who came eating and drinking, and compassionating their infirmities? which way soever they chose they might have arrived at salvation? (St. Chrysostom, hom. xxxviii.)
notes: This commentary employs allegory and symbolism rather than typology. The children playing pipes and lamenting are presented as allegorical representations of Christ and John the Baptist respectively, illustrating a moral lesson about different approaches to spiritual persuasion. However, these are not Old Testament types prefiguring New Testament antitypes. The comparison is between two New Testament figures (Jesus and John the Baptist) and their contrasting lifestyles. While the commentary references Isaiah's complaint about the vineyard (an OT passage), it is used as a parallel illustration rather than as a type-antitype relationship. The commentary is primarily concerned with explaining Christ's defense of his own conduct and John the Baptist's austere lifestyle through moral and pedagogical analogy, not with establishing Old Testament prefiguration of New Testament fulfillment.

original_text: Lord ... of the sabbath. He proves that he can dispense with the observation of the feast, because he is master of the feast. In St. Mark (2:27.) it is written, the sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath; that is man's salvation is to be preferred to the observation of the sabbath. (Menochius) --- In the concurrence of two incompatible precepts, we must give the preference to that which is the end and object of the other; thus we must prefer the preservation of life to the observance of the sabbath. (Haydock) --- These loaves were twelve, corresponding to the twelve tribes of Israel. They were set six and six, one upon another, at each end of the table. Upon the uppermost loaf of each heap stood a vessel, smoking with the sweetest incense. These loaves at the week's end were, according to God's order, eaten by the priests only, when they were replaced by twelve fresh ones, made like them, with the finest flour, tempered with oil. This offering of the shew-bread before the Lord, was a continual sacrifice, as the holy Fathers observe, and a figure of a more excellent kind of shew-bread, viz. Jesus Christ himself in the holy eucharist. (Haydock)

extractions.type_description: Twelve loaves of fine flour tempered with oil, arranged six and six on the table in the holy place, replaced weekly and eaten by priests. Accompanied by incense, it served as a continual offering before the Lord in the Old Testament tabernacle/temple.
extractions.antitype_name: Jesus Christ in the Holy Eucharist
extractions.antitype_description: Jesus Christ himself as the 'more excellent kind of shew-bread,' present in the Eucharist as the ultimate and perfect offering to God, fulfilling and surpassing the Old Testament shewbread.
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that the shewbread is 'a figure of a more excellent kind of shew-bread, viz. Jesus Christ himself in the holy eucharist.' This is a clear typological connection where the OT shewbread (type) prefigures Christ present in the Eucharist (antitype). The commentary also notes it was 'a continual sacrifice,' emphasizing its sacrificial character that finds fulfillment in Christ's sacrifice made sacramentally present.

notes: The commentary also contains a secondary typological allusion: the twelve loaves correspond to the twelve tribes of Israel, which could be seen as prefiguring the twelve apostles and the Church, but this is not explicitly developed into a full type-antitype relationship in the text. The primary typology focuses on the Eucharistic dimension.

original_text: The bruised reed. The prophet here shews the mildness of our Saviour, who, though he could have broken them like a reed, and as a bruised reed, yet would not do it; and though he could have easily extinguished their rage and anger, yet he bore with it for a while, with singular clemency, till he should send forth judgment unto victory, that is till justice shall have appeared triumphant, till Christ shall have fulfilled all things, and raised his most illustrious trophy: till the Gentiles shall have placed their confidence in his most adorable name, and the Jews have no plea, notwithstanding their unparalleled obduracy, to make in reply. (St. Chrysostom, hom. xli). --- Judgment unto victory. St. Jerome and St. Hilary expound these words in conformity with their interpretation of the two foregoing verses, as follows: "The Lord will cherish and support the infirm and weak in this time of penance and probation, inviting them to greater strength, and light, and perfect charity, till the power of death be taken away, till he return to judge the world, when his judgment shall be victorious; though, in the mean while, it often may appear suppressed, and even subdued by the obstinate will of man." But the exposition, most conformable to the literal sense of the prophet, is: he will support the weak by his mildness, until it come to pass that his judgment, which he came to announce to the Gentiles, be led to victory, by his truth becoming universally triumphant over the world, and in his name all nations shall hope. (Jansenius). --- Thus will he bear with the little light and virtue of his enemies, till the bright light of his faith, and the warmth and strength of his grace, obtain in their hearts, and triumph over every opposition. (Haydock)
notes: This commentary does not establish a typological relationship between an Old Testament type and a New Testament antitype. Rather, it provides an interpretation of Isaiah 42:3 (quoted in Matthew 12:20) and explains Christ's character of mildness and clemency toward the weak and infirm. The commentary focuses on: (1) Christ's merciful disposition toward those who are 'bruised' (spiritually weak); (2) the ultimate triumph of Christ's judgment and faith among the Gentiles; and (3) Christ's patience with His enemies until His truth becomes universally triumphant. While the passage uses metaphorical language (bruised reed, smoking flax) to describe spiritual conditions, the commentary treats these as symbols of Christ's merciful character rather than as Old Testament types prefiguring Christ. The discussion is primarily Christological in its focus on Christ's attributes and His future judgment, but it does not identify a specific OT person, event, or institution as a prefigurement of a NT reality.

original_text: To them he spoke many things, from a ship, in parables; probably many more than are here recorded. By familiar and well-known objects, Jesus Christ would thus convey more pleasingly his divine instructions, and teach them to spiritualize their daily labours, and by natural things, which meet the senses, lead them to the knowledge of things divine, which we cannot naturally comprehend. (Haydock) --- Several reasons may be assigned why our Lord made use of parables: 1st. The lively imagination of the Orientals made them relish these figurative expressions, which awaken the attention, and exercise the understanding. 2d. The indisposition of his hearers made him frequently veil his instructions under similitudes or parables; but in private, he expounded the meaning to his disciples, who were better disposed, and was ever ready to give every necessary and satisfactory explanation to as many as sincerely wished for it. --- A third motive, given by St. Matthew, was the accomplishment of the prophecies; for one of the characteristics of the Messias was, that he would express himself in this parabolical manner; and Jesus Christ was pleased that the most minute circumstances should be fulfilled in his person, in order that the resemblance between him and the ancient prophets, in the mode of instructing, might induce the Jews to consider him as the great prophet, foretold by Moses. There are few Christians that do not dwell with delight and improvement on our Lord's parables. Their imagination, warmed with the singular beauty of the imagery, more easily retains them; and the greatest geniuses have ever esteemed them as very superior and striking lessons of morality and religion. --- In his sermon on the mount, Jesus Christ does not make use of parables to convey his instructions to the Jews, for then his auditors were composed of a mixed multitude, and the major part of them illiterate people; but here, on the contrary, they are the Scribes and Pharisees, the doctors of the law. (St. Chrysostom) --- Jesus Christ speaks sometimes in plain, and sometimes in obscure terms, that, by what they understand, they may be led to the search of what they do not understand. (St. Jerome)

extractions.type_name: The Ancient Prophets (OT prophets and their instructional methods)
extractions.type_description: Old Testament prophets who taught and instructed the people of Israel, establishing a pattern of prophetic communication and teaching methodology
extractions.antitype_name: Jesus Christ as the Great Prophet
extractions.antitype_description: Jesus Christ fulfilling the messianic prophecy of being 'the great prophet foretold by Moses' (Deuteronomy 18:15), particularly in his use of parables and instructional methods that parallel OT prophetic modes
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states: 'one of the characteristics of the Messias was, that he would express himself in this parabolical manner' and that 'the resemblance between him and the ancient prophets, in the mode of instructing, might induce the Jews to consider him as the great prophet, foretold by Moses.' This establishes that the prophetic teaching methods of the OT prefigure Jesus's prophetic ministry in the NT. However, this is somewhat implicit rather than a formally developed typology, making it medium confidence.

notes: The typology here is subtle and primarily focuses on functional and methodological resemblance rather than a person, event, or object explicitly prefiguring another. The commentary emphasizes continuity in prophetic teaching style between OT prophets and Jesus rather than a specific typological figure (like Joseph or Moses). The reference to 'accomplishment of the prophecies' in Matthew's gospel suggests this is typological fulfillment of the Messiah's predicted characteristics.

original_text: When any one heareth. This seed falleth upon four different kinds of soil, which represent four different sorts of persons. The 1st, such as continue obdurate in vice; the 2d, such as are unsteady and inconstant in their good resolutions; the 3d, such as are absorbed in the cares and pleasures of life; the 4th, such as have every proper disposition for receiving the word of God with fruit. --- There cometh the wicked one, o poneros, the devil, and taketh away the word that was sown in their hearts, lest believing they should be saved. (Haydock)
notes: This Haydock commentary employs allegory and moral symbolism rather than typology. The four types of soil represent four categories of spiritual receptiveness in the present time, functioning as an extended metaphor for different human responses to God's word. While the commentary uses symbolic language (soil representing persons, the devil's action representing spiritual opposition), it does not establish a prefigurative relationship between an Old Testament type and a New Testament antitype. The passage is exegetical allegory interpreting Christ's parable, not typological interpretation connecting OT and NT. No Old Testament persons, events, or institutions are cited as prefiguring these spiritual conditions.

original_text: Yet because of his oath, which could not bind him, being unjust. (Witham) --- See the preposterous religion of this wicked prince. He feels no remorse for his impious conduct to his brother and his own wife; murder, adultery, and incest do not appal him; and yet he is terrified with the thought of violating a vain and wicked oath on no occasion and in no circumstances obligatory. Herod did wrong in taking such a rash oath, but he did worse in fulfilling it. (Jansenius) --- David swore to kill Nabal. He swore rashly; but with greater piety, he refused to keep his oath. Perhaps it is because Catholics inculcate this principle, that they have been accused by their adversaries of teaching that faith is not to be kept, and also the doctrine of expediency. (Haydock)
notes: This commentary discusses Herod's moral failure regarding a rash oath (Matthew 14:9) and compares it to David's contrasting piety when he refused to fulfill a rash oath against Nabal (1 Samuel 25). While both examples are from Scripture, this is a moral/ethical comparison between two Old Testament figures and their conduct, not a typological relationship. Typology requires an OT type that prefigures a NT antitype (fulfillment in Christ or the Church). Here, the commentary uses David as a positive counterexample to Herod's negative behavior to illustrate a principle about the binding nature of oaths and moral conscience. This is ethical instruction and contrast, not typology.

original_text: And they did all eat, and were filled. This miraculous multiplication of the loaves was effected on a Thursday evening --- an excellent figure of the blessed Eucharist. On the next morning, Friday, he cured the sick at Genesareth, and arrived at Capharnaum for the first vespers of the sabbath; where, in the Synagogue, he made his promise of the holy Eucharist, which he instituted on a Thursday evening, the eve of his death. See Evangile medite. Tom. iii, p. 425.
notes: While the Haydock commentary describes the miraculous multiplication of loaves as 'an excellent figure of the blessed Eucharist,' this represents typological prefigurement within the New Testament itself (Matthew 14 prefiguring the Eucharist institution in Matthew 26), not an Old Testament type prefiguring a New Testament antitype. The commentary explicitly compares a Gospel narrative to a Gospel sacrament, both occurring in the same Testament. True typology in the biblical sense requires an Old Testament type to prefigure a New Testament antitype. The reference to the Eucharist as a sacrament and the parallel timing of events (Thursday evening multiplication → Friday teaching → Thursday evening institution) suggests symbolic/thematic connection rather than typological fulfillment as classically defined in biblical typology studies.

original_text: Kago. And I say to thee, and tell thee why I before declared, (John 1:42.) that thou shouldst be called Peter, for thou art constituted the rock upon which, as a foundation, I will build my Church, and that so firmly, as not to suffer the gates (that is, the powers) of hell to prevail against its foundation; because if they overturn its foundation, (that is, thee and thy successors) they will overturn also the Church that rests upon it. Christ therefore here promises to Peter, that he and his successors should be to the end, as long as the Church should last, its supreme pastors and princes. (Tirinus) --- In the Syriac tongue, which is that which Jesus Christ spoke, there is no difference of genders, as there is in Latin, between petra, a rock, and Petrus, Peter; hence, in the original language, the allusion was both more natural and more simple. (Bible de Vence) --- Thou art Peter;{ Ver. 18. St. Augustine, serm. 13, de Verbis Domini, in the new edit. serm. 76. t. v. p. 415, expounds these words super hanc Petram, that is super hanc Petram, quam confessus es, super meipsum. See also tract. 24. in Joan, t. iii. p. 822. But he elsewhere gave the common interpretation, as he says, lib. i. Retrac. and in Psal. lxix. Petrus, qui paulo ante Christum confessus erat filium Dei, et in illa Confessione appellatus erat Petra, super quam fabrificatur Ecclesia, etc. See St. Jerome on this place, lib. iii. p. 97. aedificabo (inquit Christus) super te Ecclesiam meam. (St. Chrysostom, hom. lv. in Matt. etc.)|} and upon this (that is, upon thee, according to the literal and general exposition of the ancient Fathers) I will build my church. It is true St. Augustine, in one or two places, thus expounds these words, and upon this rock, (that is, upon myself:) or upon this rock, which Peter hath confessed: yet he owns that he had also given the other interpretation, by which Peter himself was the rock. Some Fathers have also expounded it, upon the faith, which Peter confessed; but then they take not faith, as separated from the person of Peter, but on Peter, as holding the true faith. No one questions but that Christ himself is the great foundation-stone, the chief corner-stone, as St. Paul tells the Ephesians; (Ephesians 2:20.) but it is also certain, that all the apostles may be called foundation-stones of the Church, as represented Apocalypse 21:14. In the mean time, St. Peter (called therefore Cephas, a rock) was the first and chief foundation-stone among the apostles, on whom Christ promised to build his Church. (Witham) --- Thou art Peter, etc. As St. Peter, by divine revelation, here made a solemn profession of his faith of the divinity of Christ, so in recompense of this faith and profession, our Lord here declares to him the dignity to which he is pleased to raise him: viz. that he, to whom he had already given the name of Peter, signifying a rock, (John 1:42.) should be a rock indeed, of invincible strength, for the support of the building of the church; in which building he should be next to Christ himself, the chief foundation-stone, in quality of chief pastor, ruler, and governor; and should have accordingly all fulness of ecclesiastical power, signified by the keys of the kingdom of heaven. --- Upon this rock, etc. The words of Christ to Peter, spoken in the vulgar language of the Jews, which our Lord made use of, were the same as if he had said in English, Thou art a rock, and upon this rock I will build my church. So that, by the plain course of the words, Peter is here declared to be the rock, upon which the church was to be built; Christ himself being both the principal foundation and founder of the same. Where also note, that Christ by building his house, that is, his Church, upon a rock, has thereby secured it against all storms and floods, like the wise builder. (Matthew 7:24, 25.) --- The gates of hell, etc. That is, the powers of darkness, and whatever Satan can do, either by himself or his agents. For as the Church is here likened to a house, or fortress, built on a rock; so the adverse powers are likened to a contrary house or fortress, the gates of which, that is the whole strength, and all the efforts it can make, will never be able to prevail over the city or Church of Christ. By this promise we are fully assured, that neither idolatry, heresy, nor any pernicious error whatsoever shall at any time prevail over the Church of Christ. (Challoner) --- The gates, in the Oriental style, signify the powers; thus, to this day, we designate the Ottoman or Turkish empire by the Ottoman port. The princes were wont to hold their courts at the gates of the city. (Bible de Vence)

extractions.type_description: In OT imagery, the rock serves as a symbol of strength, stability, and foundation (e.g., Psalm 18:2, Isaiah 26:4). The commentary references Christ as 'the great foundation-stone, the chief corner-stone' per Ephesians 2:20, and notes that 'all the apostles may be called foundation-stones' per Revelation 21:14.
extractions.antitype_name: Peter as Foundation Stone of the Church
extractions.antitype_description: Peter, renamed Cephas (rock), becomes the first and chief foundation-stone among the apostles upon which Christ builds His Church. He receives the keys of the kingdom of heaven and serves as chief pastor and governor with full ecclesiastical power.
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly traces the OT concept of the rock as a foundation of strength to its NT fulfillment in Peter's role as the foundational leader of the Church. The name change from Simon to Peter/Cephas (rock) directly parallels OT naming practices where name changes signified typological fulfillment of a new role. The commentary notes this prefigurement was declared in John 1:42.

extractions.type_name: The Wise Builder's House Built Upon the Rock
extractions.type_description: Matthew 7:24-25 describes a house built upon rock that withstands storms and floods, symbolizing stability and security against adversity.
extractions.antitype_description: Christ builds His Church upon Peter as a rock foundation, securing it against 'the gates of hell' (powers of darkness, Satan's efforts) so that neither idolatry, heresy, nor error shall prevail against it.
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly cites Matthew 7:24-25 as a parallel, stating 'Christ by building his house, that is, his Church, upon a rock, has thereby secured it against all storms and floods, like the wise builder.' This directly connects the OT parable about foundational security to the NT promise of the Church's indefectibility.

notes: This commentary is primarily concerned with ecclesiology rather than extensive typology. The typological connections present are relatively restrained, focusing on rock/foundation imagery. The commentary emphasizes that while Christ is the principal foundation-stone, Peter holds a subordinate but crucial foundational role. Augustine's alternative interpretation (that Christ himself is 'the rock') is noted but the commentary adopts the more common patristic view that Peter is the rock foundation.

original_text: Till they see the Son of man coming in his kingdom. Some expound this, as fulfilled at his transfiguration, which follows in the next chapter. Others understand it of the glory of Christ, and of his Church, after his resurrection and ascension, when he should be owned for Redeemer of the world: and this state of the Christian Church might be called the kingdom of Christ. (Witham) --- This promise of a transitory view of his glory he makes, to prove that he should one day come in all the glory of his Father, to judge each man according to his works: not according to his mercy, or their faith, but according to their works. (St. Augustine, de verb. apos. serm. 35.) --- Again, asks St. Augustine, how could our Saviour reward every one according to his works, if there were no free will? (lib. 2:chap. 4. 5. 8, de act. cum Foelic. Manich.) (Bristow)
notes: This Haydock commentary discusses Matthew 16:28 and offers various interpretations of Christ's promise that some disciples would see 'the Son of man coming in his kingdom' before tasting death. The commentary presents three main interpretations: (1) fulfillment at the Transfiguration, (2) Christ's glory after resurrection/ascension, and (3) the state of the Christian Church as Christ's kingdom. However, none of these interpretations establish a typological relationship between an Old Testament person, event, or institution and a New Testament fulfillment. Rather, the commentary addresses: eschatological promises about Christ's future coming and judgment, the nature of Christ's kingdom in its present and future states, and theological questions about free will and divine justice. These are hermeneutical and theological discussions, not typological connections linking OT prefigurement to NT fulfillment.

original_text: And after six days. St. Matthew reckons neither the day of the promise, nor the day of the transfiguration; St. Luke, including both, calls the interval about eight days, osei emerai okto. (St. Chrysostom) --- He took Peter, as head of the apostolic college; James, as first to shed his blood for the faith; and John, as he was to survive all the rest, and to transmit to posterity the circumstances of this glorious mystery; or, according to St. Chrysostom on account of their more excellent love, zeal, courage, sufferings and predilection. The mountain is generally believed to be Thabor, and as such is considered by Christians as holy, and was much frequented by pilgrims, as St. Jerome testifies. Ven. Bede tells us that three churches were built upon it; and Mr. Maundrell, in his Journey from Aleppo to Jerusalem, p. 112, says there are still three grottoes, made to represent the three tabernacles proposed by St. Peter. According to Le Brun, Thabor is situated about 12 miles from the sea of Galilee, and eight from Nazareth. Others, however, do not think the transfiguration took place on Mount Thabor, which was in the middle of Lower Galilee, because St. Mark 9:29, says, that Christ and his apostles, departing thence, passed through Galilee, and not out of Galilee, and suppose it might be Libanus, because it was near Caesarea Philippi; in the borders of which Christ appears at this time to have been, at least the promise of the transfiguration was made there, and this place is distant about 60 miles from Mount Thabor. (Matthew 16:13.) --- Mount Libanus is the highest in Palestine, according to St. Jerome; and of it Isaias prophesied: "the glory of Libanus is given to it, the beauty of Carmel and Saron; they shall see the glory of our God," 35:2. (Tirinus) --- But, as we said above, Thabor is very generally supposed to have been the mountain.
notes: This Haydock commentary on Matthew 17:1 (the Transfiguration) focuses on historical, geographical, and exegetical matters rather than typological interpretation. The commentary addresses: (1) the chronological discrepancy between Matthew and Luke's accounts of 'six days' vs. 'eight days'; (2) the symbolic significance of Christ choosing Peter, James, and John based on their roles and virtues; (3) the geographical location of the mountain (likely Mount Thabor vs. Mount Libanus); and (4) historical details about churches and grottoes built on the site. While the commentary mentions Isaiah 35:2 in relation to Mount Libanus, this is cited as a prophetic description of the mountain's glory rather than as a typological prefigurement of the Transfiguration event itself. The selection of the three apostles is explained through their spiritual qualities and future roles, not as types of OT persons or institutions. No explicit Old Testament type is presented as prefiguring the New Testament antitype of the Transfiguration.

original_text: Moses and Elias. Jesus Christ had been taken by the people for Elias, Jeremias, or one of the prophets. He therefore chose the chief of all the prophets to be present, that he might shew his great superiority over them, and verify the illustrious confession of Peter. The Jews had accused Christ of blasphemy, and of breaking the sabbath; the presence of Moses and Elias refuted the calumny; for the founder of the Jewish laws would never have sanctioned him who was a transgressor of those laws; and Elias, so full of zeal for the glory of God, would never have paid homage to one who made himself equal to God, had he not really been the Son of the Most High. (St. Chrysostom, hom. lvii.) --- St. Hilary thinks that Moses and Elias (who represent the law and the prophets, and who here bear witness to the divinity of Jesus Christ,) will be the precursors of his second coming, alluded to in (Apocalypse 11.), though the general opinion of the Fathers is, that the two witnesses there mentioned are Enoch and Elias. (Jansenius) --- It is hence evident, that the saints departed can and do, with the permission of God, take an interest in the affairs of the living. (St. Augustine, de cura pro mort. Matthew 15:16.) --- For as angels elsewhere, so here the saints also, served our Saviour; and as angels, both in the Old and New Testament, were frequently present at the affairs of men, so may saints. (Bristow) --- All interpreters agree, that Elias appeared in his own body, but various are their opinions with regard to the apparition of Moses. (Haydock)

extractions.type_name: The Law and the Prophets (represented by Moses and Elijah)

original_text: And were very much afraid. There were two causes that might produce this fear in the apostles, the cloud that overshadowed them, or the voice of God the Father, which they heard. Their human weakness could not bear such refulgent beams of glory, and trembling in every limb, they fall prostrate on the ground. (St. Jerome) --- The Almighty, it seems, was pleased to fulfil the wish of Peter, thereby to shew that Himself is the tent or pavilion, under the shade of which the blessed shall live for ever, and to sanction the public and explicit confession of Peter relative to the divinity of Jesus Christ, by his own no less public and explicit confession, joined with an express command to hear and obey him. St. Chrysostom very justly remarks, that this voice was not heard till after the departure of Moses and Elias, that no possible doubt might exist to whom it was referred, and that it was to Christ only and to no other. --- Hear ye Him: that is as the law and the prophets are fulfilled and verified in Jesus Christ, your new legislator and prophet, you are to hear and obey Him in preference to either Moses or Elias, or any other teacher. original_text: If you have faith as a grain of mustard-seed. Christ insinuates to his apostles, as if they had not yet faith enough to work great miracles, which require a firm faith joined with a lively confidence in God. The mustard-seed is brought in with an allusion to its hot and active qualities. (Witham) --- That is, a perfect faith; which, in its properties and its fruits, resembles the grain of mustard-seed in the parable. (chap. 13:31.) (Challoner) --- By faith is here understood, not that virtue by which we assent to all things that are to be believed of Christ, the first, of the theological virtues, in which the apostles were not deficient, but that confidence in the power and goodness of God, that he will on such an occasion exert these, his attributes, in favour of the supplicant. To have a true faith of this kind, and free from all presumption, is a great and high privilege, which the Holy Ghost breathes into such only as he pleases. (Jansenius) --- Examples of this efficacious faith are given by St. Paul. (Hebrews 11.) St. Gregory of Neo-Caesarea is also related, by Eusebius and Ven. Bede, to have removed by the efficacy of his faith a rock, which obstructed the building of a church; thus literally fulfilling the promise of Jesus Christ. (Tirinus) --- The faith of the apostles, especially of those that had not been present at the transfiguration, was not perfect and complete in all its parts, till after the resurrection and ascension of Jesus Christ, and the descent of the Holy Ghost. (Haydock) --- St. Jerome understands by mountains, things the most difficult to be effected.
notes: This commentary discusses faith, miracles, and spiritual virtue in the context of Matthew 17:19, but contains no typological relationships between Old Testament types and New Testament antitypes. The reference to the mustard-seed parable (Matthew 13:31) is an intra-New Testament cross-reference, not an OT/NT typological connection. The mention of Hebrews 11 (examples of efficacious faith) and the anecdote about St. Gregory of Neo-Caesarea illustrate the principle of faith but do not establish typological prefigurement. The commentary focuses on spiritual interpretation and moral lessons rather than typological correspondence between testaments.

original_text: But that we may not. Jesus Christ pays the tribute, not as one subject to the law, but as consulting the infirmity of the people; but he first shews himself exempt from the above example, lest his disciples might take occasion of scandal therefrom. (St. Chrysostom, hom. lix.) --- For me and thee. A great mystery this: Jesus Christ paid not only for himself, but for the future representative of Him and his Church, in whom, as chief, the rest were comprised. (St. Augustine, q. ex Nov. Tes. q. lxxv. tom. 4.) Jesus Christ here, as well as on many other occasions, pointedly marks the precedence of Peter, which might give rise to the strife and contention of the disciples, in the commencement of the ensuing chapter, on the subject of superiority. Thus St. Jerome, St. Chrysostom, Tirinus, etc.

However, this is ecclesial typology rather than strict OT-to-NT typology, as Peter himself is a NT figure. The commentary treats his singular mention in this incident as typologically significant for understanding Church hierarchy.

Rather, it describes a typological-like relationship where a NT figure (Peter) is interpreted typologically within the NT narrative itself. St. Augustine's statement about Peter representing 'his Church' uses typological language but applies it to an intra-NT relationship. original_text: Moses, because of the hardness of your hearts, permitted you, etc. Whether this was permitted in the old law, so that the man who was divorced from his wife could marry another woman, is disputed. Some think this second marriage was still unlawful, though tolerated, and not punished. At least in the new law, a divorce upon just causes may be sometimes permitted; but this does not make it lawful for the man or woman so separated to marry another. (Witham) --- The latter part of this verse, of St. Paul, (Romans 7:3,) and the constant tradition of the Church, shew that the exception only refers to separation, but not to the marrying another during the life of the parties. In this place Christ restores the original condition of the marriage state, and henceforth will have it to be a perfect figure of the hypostatic union of his divine person with our human nature, as also of his nuptial union with his Church, and consequently that it should be indissoluble. (Tirinus)

extractions.type_name: The marriage covenant of the Old Testament
extractions.type_description: The Old Testament marriage institution as permitted under Mosaic law, which allowed for divorce due to human hardness of heart, representing an imperfect and dissoluble state
extractions.antitype_name: Christian marriage as restored by Christ
extractions.antitype_description: The New Testament marriage restored to its original indissoluble condition by Christ, perfected and made a figure of Christ's hypostatic union with human nature and His nuptial union with the Church
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that Christ 'restores the original condition of the marriage state' and that 'henceforth will have it to be a perfect figure of the hypostatic union of his divine person with our human nature, as also of his nuptial union with his Church.' This directly establishes the OT marriage covenant as a type prefiguring its NT fulfillment in Christ's redemptive union with the Church. The progression from imperfect (tolerated divorce) to perfect (indissoluble union) is characteristic of typological fulfillment.

notes: While the primary typology focuses on marriage as an Ecclesial type, it also contains Christological elements (the hypostatic union). The commentary emphasizes that Christ's teaching on marriage represents a restoration and perfection of the original institution, moving from accommodated practice (Mosaic permission) to eschatological reality (the Church as Christ's bride). The connection is explicitly theological rather than merely symbolic.

original_text: All receive not this word.{ Ver. 11. Non omnes capiunt, ou pantes chorousi. Maldonat will needs have chorein, to signify intelligere, as it does sometimes. But St. Jerome on this place, unusquisque consideret vires suas, etc. And St. Chrysostom (hom. lxiii.) ut singulare esse certamen perdiscas. St. Jerome adds, Sed his datum est, qui petierunt; qui voluerunt; qui ut acciperent, laboraverunt. And St. Chrysostom, His enim datum est, qui spontè id eligunt. dedotai gar ekeinois tois boulomenois. Ed. Sav. p. 397.|} To translate all cannot take, or cannot receive this word, is neither conformable to the Latin nor Greek text. To be able to live singly, and chastely, is given to every one that asketh, and prayeth for the grace of God to enable him to live so. (Witham) --- Jesus Christ takes occasion from the remark of the Pharisees to praise holy virginity, which he represents as a great and good gift of heaven; and such it has ever been considered in the eye of true and genuine religion. Hence it appears that besides commandments, there are evangelical counsels, to the observance of which it is both lawful and meritorious for a Christian to devote himself, especially for the purpose of employing himself with greater liberty and less encumbrance in the service of his God. --- Our Lord does not approve of the conclusion his disciples drew from his doctrine on the indissolubility of marriage, lest he should seem to condemn matrimony both good and necessary; neither does he reprove them for it, lest he should seem to prefer it before the state of continency. His answer therefore prudently avoids both difficulties, by seeming to grant, on the one hand, that it was more expedient not to marry, because chastity is a great gift of God; (1 Corinthians vii.) and plainly shewing on the other, that only few can have this privilege, because all do not receive this word, that is all are not called to this state. (Jansenius) --- All cannot receive it, because all do not wish it. The reward is held out to all. Let him who seeks for glory, not think of the labour. None would overcome, if all were afraid of engaging in the conflict. If some fail, are we to be less careful in our pursuit of virtue? Is the soldier terrified, because his comrade fights and falls by his side? (St. Chrysostom) --- He that can receive it, let him receive it. He that can fight, let him fight, overcome and triumph. It is the voice of the Lord animating his soldiers to victory. (St. Jerome)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Matthew 19:11 discusses Jesus's teaching on celibacy and virginity as an evangelical counsel. While the commentary employs spiritual and moral language (references to 'soldiers,' 'conflict,' 'victory'), these are metaphorical exhortations rather than typological connections. The commentary emphasizes that continency is a gift from God available to those who seek it through prayer and grace, and encourages Christians to pursue virtue. However, no explicit Old Testament type is presented as prefiguring this New Testament teaching on virginity or the celibate state. The passage focuses on practical moral theology and spiritual encouragement rather than typological interpretation connecting OT persons, events, or institutions to NT fulfillment.

original_text: I will also give. Some are called to the service of their God, and to a life of virtue, from their infancy, whilst others, by a powerful call from above, are converted late in life, that the former may have no occasion to glory in themselves, or to despise those who, even in the 11th hour, enter upon the path of rectitude; and that all might learn that there is time sufficient, however short, left them to repair by their diligence and fervour their past losses. (St. Chrysostom, hom. lxv.) --- Jesus Christ does not count so much the number of years, as the fervour and diligence we employ in his service. Calvin is rather unhappy in his choice of this parable to prove his favourite tenet, that salvation is not the reward of good works, but of faith alone, or predestination, since Jesus Christ represents heaven as given wholly as a just reward of meritorious labour in the vineyard, though some labour a shorter, and others a longer time, and God of his great goodness may give more to some than to others, while to all He gives at least their due. And a truly humble Christian will be ever satisfied with his lot, without envying that of others. (Haydock) --- As star differeth from star in glory in the firmament, (1 Corinthians 15:41,) so will there be different degrees of glory in heaven. (St. Augustine, de virgin. ch. XXVI.)
notes: This commentary on Matthew 20:14 discusses the parable of the laborers in the vineyard but does not establish typological relationships between Old Testament persons, events, or institutions and New Testament fulfillments. The commentary focuses on: (1) moral lessons about conversion and spiritual diligence, (2) theological arguments about reward and merit in Christian life, (3) degrees of heavenly glory illustrated by 1 Corinthians 15:41 (a NT passage, not an OT type). While the parable itself uses vineyard imagery that could evoke OT vineyard symbolism (e.g., Isaiah 5), the Haydock commentary does not explicitly connect OT vineyard types to NT antitypes. Instead, it treats the parable allegorically as a moral teaching about spiritual labor and reward, which is allegory/symbolism rather than typology as formally defined in biblical scholarship.

original_text: In the morning, returning into the city, he was hungry. This hunger, though real and pressing, was mysterious, and affords an opportunity of giving instruction both to the Jews and to all his disciples. By the fig-tree, was represented the Jewish synagogue; the hunger of Christ was a figure of his extreme desire of finding it productive of good works, (and there is no time nor season when the servants of God can be excused from bringing forth good works) answerable to the pains of cultivation he had taken for more than three years. The leaves were their pompous shew of exterior service, the barren foliage of legal rites, void of the internal spirit and good works, the only valuable produce of the tree. By the withering of the tree subsequent to Christ's imprecation, the reprobation and utter barrenness of the synagogue are represented. St. Mark 11:13 observes that it was not the season for figs; nor are we to suppose that our Saviour went up to the tree expecting to find fruit; but if some of the evangelists mention this circumstance, they only relate the surmises of the disciples. Though he had before shewn his power by innumerable miracles, Christ still thought this necessary to excite the hearts of his disciples to greater confidence. He had often exercised his power to do good, but now for the first time shews himself able to punish. Thus he testifies to the apostles and to the Jews themselves, that he could with a word have made his crucifiers wither away, and therefore that he willingly bore the extremity of the sufferings he should in a few days have to undergo. (St. Chrysostom, hom. lxviii.)

extractions.type_description: A fig tree representing the Jewish synagogue, with leaves symbolizing pompous exterior religious service and legal rites lacking internal spirit and good works
extractions.antitype_description: The contemporary Jewish religious institution that Christ expected to bear fruit in good works but found barren; its withering represents the reprobation and utter barrenness that would follow
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly establishes a typological correspondence: 'By the fig-tree, was represented the Jewish synagogue.' The type (fig tree) from the OT narrative event prefigures the antitype (the synagogue's spiritual state and ultimate rejection). This follows the classic typological pattern where an OT object/event foreshadows an NT reality.

extractions.type_name: Christ's Hunger and Search for Fruit

extractions.antitype_name: Christ's Redemptive Desire and Coming Judgment
extractions.antitype_description: Christ's extreme desire for Israel to bear spiritual fruit and his willingness to exercise punitive power, demonstrating he could have destroyed his crucifiers but chose to bear suffering instead
extractions.reasoning: While less explicitly typological than the fig tree itself, the commentary presents Christ's actions as demonstrating his power and character—his willingness to bear suffering voluntarily. This approaches typological interpretation in showing how this event prefigures Christ's redemptive work and future judgment power, though the connection is more typological of Christ's character than a strict OT/NT type-antitype relationship.

notes: The primary typology is clear: the fig tree represents the Jewish synagogue. However, this is somewhat ambiguous as to whether it represents a strict OT type (since the fig tree itself is from the Gospel narrative), or whether the commentary is using symbolic interpretation of the current event to represent Israel's spiritual condition. The strongest typological reading is that the fig tree event itself, as a symbolic action by Christ, prefigures the judgment and rejection of unfaithful Israel. The commentary cites St. Chrysostom as support for this interpretive approach.

original_text: Not having a wedding garment. By this one person, are represented all sinner void of the grace of God. He is said to be silent, because having nothing to advance in his own defence, he remains self-condemned, and is hurried away to torments; the horrors of which words can never express. notes: This commentary employs allegorical and symbolic interpretation rather than typology. The 'wedding garment' functions as a symbol of sanctifying grace and moral purity, and the man without it represents sinners in general. However, no explicit connection is drawn between an Old Testament type (person, event, or institution) and a New Testament antitype. The passage is focused on moral application and eschatological warning rather than typological prefigurement. While wedding imagery appears in OT contexts, this commentary does not establish a typological relationship between an OT wedding or garment and the NT antitype represented here.

original_text: On these two, etc. Whereby it is evident that all dependeth not upon faith only, though faith be the first, but much more upon charity, which is the love of God and of our neighbour, and which is the sum of all the law and the prophets; because he that hath this double charity, expressed here by these two principal commandments, fulfilleth all that is commanded in the law and the prophets. (Bristow)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Matthew 22:40 focuses on moral and ethical instruction rather than typological interpretation. The passage discusses the relationship between faith and charity, and how the two greatest commandments (love of God and love of neighbor) summarize the entire law and prophets. While the commentary mentions 'the law and the prophets' (which are OT texts), it does not establish a typological relationship where an OT person, event, or institution prefigures a NT fulfillment. Instead, it presents a hermeneutical principle: that the OT law and prophets find their summation in the NT ethic of double charity. This is theological synthesis and moral teaching, not typology in the technical sense of OT types foreshadowing NT antitypes.

original_text: Woe to you. Jesus Christ here condemns, in forcible language, the principal vices of the Pharisees, viz. their hypocrisy, false devotion, boundless ambition, insatiable avarice, false zeal, and ignorance in deciding upon cases of conscience. St. Luke represents our Saviour as saying this to the Pharisees at dinner; (Luke 11.) so that Christ must either have repeated these things at different times; or, St. Matthew according to custom, must have added them to other words of our Saviour, which, though spoken on another occasion, had some connection with the same subject. In vain do you, Pharisees, boast of your external sanctity. Do not imagine, that fornication, adultery, and other actions, are the only sins to be attended to; and that pride, avarice, anger, and other spiritual sins, are of no moment. He who made the body, made also the soul; and it is of equal consequence that both be kept clean and free from sin. (Nicholas of Lyra.) --- By the similitude of the cup, and of whited sepulchres, as also that of building the sepulchres of the prophets, he shews that they did all their actions purposely to be seen by men, and that this was their only motive in all they did. (Idem. [Nicholas of Lyra.]) --- Like Ezekiel's bitter roll, we have here a dreadful list of woes, like as many thunderbolts, levelled against hypocrisy, avarice, ambition, and all bitter zeal. We should be careful not to suffer such rank weeds to grow up in our soil, to the ruin of all good.

extractions.type_description: The bitter roll that Ezekiel was commanded to eat (Ezekiel 2:8-3:3), symbolizing God's judgment and bitter messages of condemnation

Both represent divine condemnation delivered through prophetic utterance. However, this is somewhat atypical typology as it emphasizes formal and thematic similarity rather than a clear historical prefigurement of Christ's judgment role.

notes: The commentary's primary focus is on identifying the vices condemned (hypocrisy, avarice, ambition, false zeal) rather than developing explicit typological doctrine. The Ezekiel comparison appears more as a literary/thematic parallel than a formal typological relationship in the classical sense. The other elements discussed (whited sepulchres, building sepulchres of prophets) are presented as metaphors or symbols rather than typological types.

original_text: And Jesus answering. Various are the interpretations given here. Some will have it refer to the destruction of Jerusalem, which took place, A.D. 70; and others, to the end of the world. That of St. Chrysostom seems to be very conformable to the context, and is followed by many. He explains all, to the 23d verse exclusively, of what shall precede the destruction of Jerusalem; nor is there any circumstance which cannot easily be referred to that event, as will appear from a careful and attentive observation of the history of the Jews, and of the Church at that time, in the writings of Josephus and Eusebius. Even the preaching of the gospel to the whole world, which seems to favour the contrary explanation, is by the same father said to have taken place before the destruction of Jerusalem. St. Paul tells the Colossians, that even in his time the faith was spread all over the world. The abomination of desolation may be explained of the Roman soldiery, or, of the seditious zealots, who, by their murders and other atrocities, polluted the temple. See Josephus, b. 4. and 5. of the Jewish war. As deicide was a crime peculiar to the Jews and exceeded every other crime, their punishment was severe above measure. Had the Almighty punished them to the full of what they had deserved, not one of the Jews would have escaped. But as he formerly would have spared Sodom and Gomorrha, had there been found therein ten just men to avert the impending ruin; so shall these days of affliction be shortened for the sake of some who believe. The verses subsequent to the 22d, are explained by St. Chrysostom of the second coming of Christ, previous to the general judgment. (Jansenius) --- Such as wish for a more particular explanation of every thing preceding the 23d verse, how it applies to the Jews, may consult the concordance of Jansenius, who thus concludes his observations: "Hitherto we have explained all things of the destruction of Jerusalem, which prophecies, though they principally regarded the times of the apostles, may be of use to us in two ways. 1. It will confirm our faith, when we see clearly fulfilled whatever was distinctly foretold of this people; and may serve to increase our fears, when we reflect, that what is immediately added concerning the day of judgment, shall be fulfilled with the same rigorous exactitude and certainty. It is another effect of divine Providence for the increase of our faith, that this prophecy, which was to take place with regard to Jerusalem, is not mentioned by St. John, who lived long enough to see it accomplished, but by the other evangelists, who died long before the event. 2. It should animate us in the practice of virtue, and gratitude to reflect, that whatever tribulations happen to the Church, or throughout the earth, all co-operate to the advantage of the elect. Such as will be good, have nothing to fear." (Jansenius)

extractions.type_description: The OT cities that would have been spared if ten righteous men had been found within them (Genesis 18:32), thus establishing the principle that God's judgment can be averted through the presence of the righteous

extractions.antitype_description: The NT fulfillment where the impending destruction of Jerusalem is shortened/mitigated for the sake of the elect who believe, paralleling God's willingness to spare Sodom and Gomorrah for the sake of the righteous
