This establishes a typological relationship where the OT principle of divine mercy toward the righteous prefigures the NT application of that same principle to the destruction of Jerusalem.

notes: This typology is somewhat implicit rather than explicitly labeled as such by the Haydock commentary. The commentary uses comparative language ('as...so') rather than technical typological terminology. The connection relies on the principle of divine mercy being consistent across testaments rather than on a specific person or institution prefiguring another. The confidence is marked 'medium' because while the parallelism is clear, the commentary does not explicitly frame this as typology in the technical sense.

original_text: Then shall they deliver you up, etc. The fourth sign, common to both these events, shall be the persecution raised against the Church, which will be two-fold; it will regard both body and soul. See Luke 21:12; Mark 13:9. All this happened to the apostles previously to the siege of Jerusalem, as well as to the martyrs in subsequent times. A similar persecution, attended probably with additional severity, will most probably be the lot of the faithful during the reign of Antichrist. The calamities, bloodshed, and utter ruin which took place at the destruction of the city and temple of Jerusalem, are a figure of the still more dreadful calamities, bloodshed, and ruin to be expected towards the end of the world; and which should be frequently present to our minds. The late learned and venerable prelate Walmesly admonishes all parents to stand prepared for the bloody trial themselves, and to teach their children to be ever ready to meet, with Christian resignation, the awful and approaching event; for the rest of the world, as we learn from revelation, will be taken by surprise, as the people at the deluge. Yes, this last may literally be styled a bloody trial; for the Church, which was purified with blood, began in blood, increased in blood, and will end in blood. Sanguine mundata est ecclesia, sanguine coepit, Sanguine succrevit, sanguine finis erit. The last chapter of the Apocalypse, which is the last communication of the divine will to man, is deserving our frequent and very attentive perusal. In it Jesus Christ, by his repeated warnings, wishes to awaken us to a sense of that day of general retribution, saying: surely I come quickly: behold I come quickly: and my reward is with me, to render to every man according to his works. (Behold the merit of good works proceeding from faith and charity.) With what earnestness have the servants of God, in every age, prayed with St. John: (Apocalypse 22:20.) Come, Lord Jesus; come, put a final end to the reign of sin and Satan; come, admit thy elect, who have been purified in the waters of the great persecution, and in the blood of the Lamb, to thy heavenly bosom; to that happy sanctuary and asylum, where no hunger or thirst, no scorching heat of the sun, no fiery temptation will any more reach or molest them; where the sigh and the groan will not be heard; where all tears will be wiped away from every eye, and where they will be inebriated at the torrent of immortal delights, and will see and enjoy the Lord Jesus, without any apprehension of offending him, for ever and ever. (Haydock)
notes: While this Haydock commentary contains rich theological and eschatological content, it does not establish explicit typological relationships between Old Testament types and New Testament antitypes. The commentary discusses: (1) persecution of the Church as a sign common to both the destruction of Jerusalem and the end times, (2) the destruction of Jerusalem as a 'figure' (figura) of future eschatological calamities, and (3) the Church's history marked by blood from its beginning to its end. However, these are typological patterns or symbolic parallels within the New Testament era itself, not typological connections from OT to NT. The 'figure' mentioned (Jerusalem's destruction prefiguring end-times calamities) represents an intra-NT typological pattern, not an OT-to-NT typological relationship. The commentary is primarily eschatological and hortatory in nature rather than typological in the strict sense of OT prefiguring NT fulfillment.

original_text: The abomination of desolation was first partly fulfilled by divers profanations of the temple, as when the image of Caesar was set up in the temple by Pilate, and Adrian's statue in the holy of holies, and when the sacrifices were taken away; but will be more completely fulfilled by Antichrist and his precursors, when they shall attempt to abolish the holy sacrifice of the mass. St. Hyppolitus, in his treatise de Anti-Christo, mentioned by Eusebius, St. Jerome, and Photius, thus writeth: "The churches shall lament with great lamentations, because there shall neither be made oblations, nor incense, nor worship grateful to God. ... In those days the liturgy (or mass) shall be neglected, the psalmody shall cease, the reciting of Scripture shall not be heard." --- The prophet Daniel 12:11. calculates the reign of Antichrist, from the time that the daily sacrifice shall be taken away; which, by able commentators, is understood of the sacrifice of the mass, which Antichrist will endeavour to suppress. --- The abomination of desolation,{ Ver. 15. Abominationem desolationis. Bdelugma tes eremoseos. The same words are in the Septuagint, Daniel ix. See St. Jerome on this place, and St. Chrysostom, hom. lxxvi. and lxxvii. in Matt.|} or the abominable desolation. Instead of these words, we read in St. Luke, (xxi. 20.) When you shall see Jerusalem surrounded by an army. Christ said both the one and the other. But the words in St. Luke, seem rather to give us a sign of the ruin of Jerusalem, than of the end of the world. --- Spoken of by Daniel, the prophet. The sense is, when you shall see that very prophecy of Daniel literally fulfilled hereafter. What follows in the prophecy of Daniel, confirms this exposition; when the prophet adds, that the desolation shall continue to the end; that the Jews from that time, shall be no more the people of God, for denying their Messias; and that they shall put the Christ to death. But what then was this desolation, which by the following verse, was to be a sign to the Christians to fly out of Judea? Some expound it of the heathen Roman army, approaching and investing Jerusalem, called the holy city. Others understand the profanation of the temple, made by the Jews themselves, a little before the siege under Vespasian; when the civil dissensions, those called the Zealots, had possessed themselves of the temple, and placed their warlike engines upon the pinnacles; and a part, at least, of the temple was defiled with the dead bodies of those killed there. It was at that time that the Christians, according to Christ's admonition, left Jerusalem and Judea, and fled to Pella, beyond the river Jordan. See Eusebius, lib. 3:Hist. ch. V. (Witham)

The Sacramental typology of the daily sacrifice to the Mass is the most explicitly articulated typological relationship in the text.

original_text: This generation; that is the nation of the Jews shall not cease to exist, until all these things shall be accomplished: thus we see the nation of the Jews still continue, and will certainly continue to the end of the world. (Tirinus) --- Then the cross, which has been a scandal to the Jew, and a stumbling-block to the Gentile, shall appear in the heavens, for the consolation of the good Christian. Hoc signum crucis erit in coelo, cum Dominus ad judicandum venerit. --- If it be to be understood of the destruction of Jerusalem, the sense may be, this race of men now living; if of the last day of judgment, this generation of the faithful, saith Theophylactus,{ Ver. 34. Generatio haec. Theophylact, e genea ton christianon.|} shall be continued: that is the Church of Christ, to the end of the world. (Witham) --- This race, I tell you in very truth, shall not pass away till all this be finally accomplished in the ruin of Jerusalem, the most express figure of the destruction and end of the world. (Bible de Vence) --- By generation, our Saviour does not mean the people that were in existence at that time, but the faithful of his Church; thus says the psalmist: this is the generation of them that seek the Lord. (Psalm xxiii, ver. 6.) (St. Chrysostom, hom. lxxvii.)

The commentary cites Psalm 24:6 ('this is the generation of them that seek the Lord') to support this spiritual reinterpretation.

A secondary ecclesial typology appears in St. Chrysostom's interpretation, where the concept of 'generation' shifts from ethnic/national to spiritual/ecclesial. The commentary reflects patristic and medieval interpretive traditions attempting to harmonize different fulfillment theories (literal/historical vs. eschatological).

original_text: In the parable of the talents, the master is God, talents, graces, etc. (Witham) --- From this, it appears, we can do no good of ourselves, but only by means of God's grace, though he requires our co-operation; since the servants could only make use of the talents given them to gain others. (A talent is £187 10s.) It is also worthy of remark, that both he who received five and he who received only two talents, received an equal reward of entering into the joy of our Lord; which shews, that only an account will be taken according to what we have received, and that however mean and despicable our abilities may be, we still have an equal facility with the most learned of entering heaven. (Jansenius) --- The servant to whom this treasure was delivered, is allegorically explained of the faithful adorers of God, in the Jewish law, who departing from it, became followers of Christ, and therefore deserving of a double recompense. ... The servant to whom the two talents were delivered, is understood of the Gentiles, who were justified in the faith and confession of the Father and the Son, and confessed our Lord Jesus Christ, God and man, composed of body and soul; and as the people of the Jews doubled the five talents they received, so the Gentiles, by the duplication of their two talents, merited a double recompense also. ... But the servant who received only one talent, and hid it in the ground, represented such of the Jews as persisted in the observation of the old law, and thus kept their talent buried in the ground, for fear the Gentiles should be converted. (St. Hilary)
notes: This commentary presents an allegorical interpretation of the Parable of the Talents (Matthew 25:14-30) rather than a typological one. The commentary uses allegory to interpret the parable's elements (master = God, talents = graces, servants = faithful Jews, Gentiles, and apostate Jews) as spiritual lessons about stewardship and judgment. However, no Old Testament type is identified that prefigures these New Testament realities. The parable itself is a New Testament teaching that uses symbolic language, but the commentary does not establish any connection between an OT person, event, or institution and these NT fulfillments. The discussion of Jewish law observers becoming Christians and Gentiles receiving equal reward is theological allegory applied to a parable, not typology in the strict sense (which requires an explicit OT/NT prefigurement relationship).

original_text: He that had received the one. The man who hid this one talent, represents all those who, having received any good quality, whether mental or corporal, employ it only on earthly things. (St. Gregory) --- Origen is also of the same sentiment: if you see any one, says he, who has received from God the gift of teaching and instructing others to salvation, yet will not exercise himself in this function, he buries his talent in the ground, like this unworthy servant, and must expect to receive the like reward.
notes: This commentary presents an allegorical and moral interpretation rather than a typological one. The servant who buries his talent is interpreted as a symbol of those who misuse God's gifts (whether mental, corporal, or spiritual like the gift of teaching). While the passage uses symbolic language (the talent = God's gifts; burying = failing to use them), this is allegory applied within the New Testament narrative itself, not a connection between an Old Testament type and a New Testament antitype. The Haydock commentary offers moral and spiritual application rather than typological prefigurement. No Old Testament person, event, or institution is presented as prefiguring this servant or his actions.

original_text: After a long time. This represents the time that is to intervene between our Saviour's ascension and his last coming. For, as he is the Master, who went into a far country, that is to heaven, after he had inculcated the relative duties of each man in his respective state of life; so shall he come at the last day, and reckon with all men, commending those who have employed their talents well, and punishing such as have made a bad use of them. (St. Jerome)
notes: This commentary presents an allegorical interpretation of the Parable of the Talents (Matthew 25:14-30) rather than a typological relationship. While it does connect an Old Testament narrative pattern (a master departing and returning to reckon with servants) to a New Testament fulfillment (Christ's ascension and final judgment), this is not typology in the technical sense. Typology requires an OT type that prefigures an NT antitype. Here, the commentary is interpreting a parable within the New Testament itself—explaining what Christ's departure to heaven and future return symbolize regarding judgment and accountability. The 'master in the parable' is a narrative device used by Jesus to teach about eschatological accountability, not an OT historical type prefiguring Christ. This is better classified as parabolic allegory or New Testament typological imagery rather than classic OT-to-NT typology.

original_text: I know that thou art a hard man. This is an insignificant part, that is, an ornament of the parable only; as also when it is said: I should have received mine with usury. ver. 27. (Witham) --- This seems to have been an adage levelled at avaricious men, who are never pleased but with what increases their hoards. Under this symbol is also depicted the excuse of many, who accuse God of being the cause of their idleness, both here and in the judgment to come; as that God is too severe and unbending, whose service is extremely hard, and who adopts, rejects, and reprobates whom he pleases; who deals out heavier burdens than the weak nature of man is made to support; who denies the grace of obedience, and thus wishes to reap where he has not sown. (Jansenius)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Matthew 25:24 employs allegory and moral symbolism rather than typology. The commentary describes: (1) the wicked servant's excuse as symbolic of human excuses to God about His severity, and (2) a general adage about avaricious men. While the passage uses figurative language ('under this symbol is also depicted'), it does not establish an Old Testament type that prefigures a New Testament antitype. The commentary interprets the parable's meaning for moral instruction regarding human responsibility before God's judgment, but makes no explicit connection between an OT person, event, or institution and its NT fulfillment. This is allegory/moral exegesis without typological structure.

original_text: Not on the festival day. Such a day seemed to them at first improper, at least to some of them; but this was overruled, when Judas informed them how he could and would put him into their hands on Thursday night. St. Jerome takes notice, that when they said, Not on the festival, it was not through a motive of religion that they made this objection, but only lest a tumult should happen in his favour among the people; (Witham) for they looked upon him as a great prophet. --- Behold how fearful these people are, not of offending God, nor of increasing the enormity of their most atrocious crime, by committing it on the solemnity of the Passover, but of offending men by raising a tumult. Still boiling over with rage, they no sooner found the Traitor, than yielding to the impulse of their blind fury, they gladly seized the opportunity offered, and immolating their victim in the middle of their solemnity. Though this their wickedness was the instrument of the divine dispensation, to bring about the greatest good, still they will not go without receiving condign punishment; which the perversity of their wills so richly deserved, for murdering innocence itself; and at a time when guilt was accustomed to meet with mercy and forgiveness. (St. Chrysostom, hom. lxxx.) --- We know that by a decree of divine Providence, what had been so long and so earnestly sought for by the Jewish princes, viz. an opportunity of murdering the innocent Lamb of God, was not granted to them, except on the very feast of the Pasch. For it was only fitting, that what had been for such a length of time figuratively promised, should be manifestly fulfilled; that the true Lamb should supersede the figurative one; and that by one grand sacrifice, the vast variety of offerings and holocausts should be done away. (St. Leo the great)

extractions.type_description: The lamb sacrificed during the Jewish Passover festival, which was offered annually as a figurative sacrifice and was prescribed by Old Testament law (Exodus 12)
extractions.antitype_name: Jesus Christ as the Lamb of God
extractions.antitype_description: Jesus Christ, who was crucified on the day of Passover and whose sacrificial death supersedes and fulfills the Old Testament Passover lamb offering. He is the 'true Lamb' whose 'one grand sacrifice' replaces all previous offerings and holocausts
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states this typological relationship through St. Leo the Great: 'it was only fitting, that what had been for such a length of time figuratively promised, should be manifestly fulfilled; that the true Lamb should supersede the figurative one; and that by one grand sacrifice, the vast variety of offerings and holocausts should be done away.' The commentary identifies the Passover lamb as a long-standing prefiguration ('figuratively promised') that is fulfilled in Jesus's crucifixion on Passover.

notes: The commentary emphasizes the providential timing of Christ's death coinciding with the Passover feast, making the typological fulfillment manifest and complete. The phrase 'innocent Lamb of God' directly connects Christ to the Passover lamb type. St. Leo the Great's statement is the primary source establishing this typological relationship within the commentary.

original_text: I will not drink from henceforth of this fruit of the vine. In St. Luke, (xxii. 15, 16,) Christ said to his disciples; I earnestly desired to eat this Pasch with you before I suffer; (or this paschal sacrifice) for I say to you, that, from this time I will not eat thereof, till it be fulfilled in the kingdom of God. These expressions seem to import no more, than that it was the last time he would eat and drink with them in a mortal body. And if, as some expound it, Christ, by the generation of the vine, understood the consecrated cup of his blood, he might call it wine, or the fruit of the vine; because he gave them his blood under the appearance of wine; as St. Paul calls the body of Christ bread, because given under the appearance of bread. (1 Corinthians 11:26.) (Witham) --- Fruit of the vine. These words, by the account of St. Luke, (xxii. 18,) were not spoken of the sacramental cup, but of the wine that was drunk with the paschal lamb. Though the Sacramental cup might also be called the fruit of the vine, because it was consecrated from wine, and retains the likeness, and all the accidents, or qualities, of wine. (Challoner) --- As St. Paul calleth the body of Christ bread, so the blood of Christ may still be called wine, for three reasons: 1. Because it was so before; as in Genesis xi.[ii.?] 23, Eve is called Adam's bone; in Exodus vii, Aaron's rod devoured their rods, whereas they were not now rods but serpents; and in John ii, He tasted the water made wine, whereas it was now wine not water. 2. Because the blessed Eucharist retaineth the forms of bread and wine, and things in Scripture are frequently called from their appearance; as Tobias v, the archangel Raphael, is called a young man; and Genesis xviii, three men appeared to Abraham; whereas they were three angels. 3. Because Jesus Christ in the blessed Sacrament is the true bread of life, refreshing us in soul and body to everlasting life. (Bristow) --- Drink it new, after a different manner most wonderful and hitherto unheard of, not having a passible body, but one clothed with immortality; and henceforth no longer in need of nourishment. Thus he brings to their minds the idea of his resurrection, to strengthen them under the ignominies of his passion, and eats and drinks with them, to give them a more certain proof of this grand mystery. (S. Chrysostom, hom lxxxiii.)

extractions.type_description: The lamb sacrificed and eaten during the Passover feast in the Old Testament, commemorating Israel's deliverance from Egypt
extractions.antitype_description: Jesus Christ as the ultimate paschal sacrifice whose body and blood are consumed in the Eucharist, fulfilling and superseding the Old Testament Passover meal
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly references Luke 22:15-16 where Christ says 'I earnestly desired to eat this Pasch with you before I suffer' and notes that the Passover sacrifice prefigures Christ's own sacrificial offering. The Eucharist (the sacramental cup of his blood) fulfills the typology of the paschal lamb meal, with Christ himself being the antitype of the Old Testament sacrifice.

notes: The commentary emphasizes that just as the paschal lamb was called by its original name even after its fulfillment in Christ, the Eucharist is called 'wine' and 'bread' because of its former material identity and retained accidents (appearances), drawing parallels to how Scripture names things by their previous or apparent form (e.g., Aaron's rod called a rod even when it became a serpent, water called wine after transformation). This reinforces the typological fulfillment: the OT Passover meal type finds its complete antitype in the NT Eucharistic sacrament.

original_text: He began to grow sorrowful.{ Ver. 37. Lupeisthai kai ademonein. In St. Mark, ekthambeisthai.|} The Greek signifies to be dispirited. St. Mark, to be in a consternation with fear: to wit, when all he was to undergo was represented to him, as well as the ingratitude of sinners. (Witham)
notes: This commentary describes Jesus's emotional and psychological response to his impending passion (sorrow, consternation, fear) at Gethsemane (Matthew 26:37). While the passage itself is deeply significant to Christology, the Haydock commentary provided focuses on the phenomenological meaning of the Greek words (lupeisthai, ademonein, ekthambeisthai) and the circumstances of Jesus's distress—the weight of his suffering and human sinfulness—rather than identifying an Old Testament type that prefigures this moment. The commentary is exegetical and linguistic in nature, not typological. To find typology here, one would need commentary explicitly connecting this event to an OT person, event, or institution, which is not present in this excerpt.

original_text: In that same hour, etc. The reason why the Jewish princes did not seize our Lord in the temple, was, because they feared the multitude; on which account Jesus retired, that he might give them an opportunity, both from the circumstances of place and time, to apprehend him: thus shewing us, that without his permission they could not so much as lay a finger upon him. The evangelist informs us in the following verse of the reason of this conduct; that the writings of the prophets might be fulfilled. (St. Chrysostom) See Luke 22:53.
notes: This commentary discusses Jesus's arrest at Gethsemane (MAT 26:55) and explains the historical and theological circumstances surrounding it. While the passage mentions 'the writings of the prophets might be fulfilled,' the commentary does not identify or elaborate on specific Old Testament types that prefigure this New Testament event. The reference to prophetic fulfillment appears to be about messianic prophecies generally rather than typological prefigurement (where an OT person, event, or institution specifically prefigures a later NT reality). The commentary focuses on: (1) Jesus's permissive will in allowing his arrest, (2) the fear of the Jewish leaders regarding the multitude, and (3) the general fulfillment of prophetic writings. None of these constitute explicit typological relationships as defined by the distinction between types and antitypes.

original_text: Then was fulfilled that which was spoken by Jeremias. Jeremias is now in all Latin copies, and the general reading of the Greek; whereas the passage is found in Zacharias 11:12. Some judge it to have been in some writing of Jeremias, now lost; as St. Jerome says he found it in a writing of Jeremias, which was not canonical. Others conjecture, that Zacharias had also the name of Jeremias. Others, that St. Matthew neither put Jeremias nor Zacharias, but only of the prophet: and that the name of Jeremias had crept into the text. Jeremias is not in the Syrica[Syriac?]; and St. Augustine says it was not in divers copies. --- And they took the thirty pieces of silver; each of which was called an argenteus. The evangelist cites not the words, but the sense of the prophet, who was ordered to cast the pieces into the house of the Lord, and to cast them to the potter:{ Ver. 9. Zacharias 11:13. projice illud ad staturium, decorum pretium. ... Et projeci illos in domum Domini ad statuarium; where the Hebrew word signifies, ad figulum.|} which became true by the fact of Judas, who cast them into the temple: and with them was purchased the potter's field. The price of him that was prized. In the prophet we read, the handsome price, spoken ironically, as the Lord did appoint me; that is as he had decreed. (Witham)

extractions.type_name: Zechariah's symbolic action with thirty pieces of silver cast into the temple
extractions.type_description: In Zechariah 11:12-13, the prophet receives thirty pieces of silver as a 'handsome price' (spoken ironically by God) and is commanded to cast them into the house of the Lord, specifically to the potter. This symbolic action represents God's ironic judgment on the undervaluing of His covenant.
extractions.antitype_name: Judas's betrayal of Jesus for thirty pieces of silver, cast into the temple, used to purchase the potter's field
extractions.antitype_description: In Matthew 27:9-10, Judas receives thirty pieces of silver for betraying Jesus, then casts them into the temple. The money is subsequently used to purchase the potter's field (Hakeldama). This fulfills the prophetic pattern established in Zechariah.
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly presents this as a fulfillment formula ('Then was fulfilled that which was spoken by Jeremias'). The OT symbolic action in Zechariah prefigures the specific historical event of Judas's betrayal, including the identical sum (thirty pieces), the casting into the temple, and the potter connection. The type-antitype relationship involves the price paid for covenant betrayal, ultimately pointing to Christ's betrayal and the redemptive value placed upon Him.

notes: This is primarily a typological relationship involving historical event and monetary value rather than a person or institution. The commentary notes textual transmission issues (whether 'Jeremias' or 'Zacharias' appears in various manuscripts), but this does not affect the underlying typological relationship. The irony emphasized in Zechariah ('handsome price') carries through to the NT fulfillment, suggesting the type carries semantic as well as literal correspondence.

original_text: Cyrene was the capital of a province in Africa, near Lybia. See Acts 2:10. Some are of opinion that this Simon was a Jew; his name favours that sentiment, and there were many Jews in that province. (Bible de Vence) --- St. John says that Christ went out carrying his own cross, while the other three evangelists state that they forced Simon of Cyrene to carry it for him. Both are true: for seeing Christ unequal to the weight, they compelled the other to take it up for him; not a part only, as some painters represent, but the whole, to Mount Calvary, as Jesus Christ had carried the whole before. (St. Augustine) --- The evangelists would not have been so particular in this part, had they not wished to inculcate, that all who desire to follow Christ, must also take up their cross and follow him. (St. Jerome and Jansenius) --- The latter says, in his Commentaries on the Gospels; as no one liked to carry the ignominious cross, the insolence of the soldiery compelled a stranger to carry it. By this we learn, that the cross is not taken up by many except with compulsion; but, when once taken up, they carry it with willingness. (Jansenius)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Matthew 27:32 (Simon of Cyrene carrying the cross) does not present typological relationships between Old Testament types and New Testament antitypes. Instead, the commentary focuses on: (1) harmonizing the Gospel accounts of who carried the cross, (2) establishing the historical-geographical context (Cyrene in Africa), (3) drawing moral and spiritual lessons about discipleship (the call to 'take up your cross and follow him'), and (4) offering allegorical or exegetical interpretation about how the cross represents difficulty willingly embraced. While the passage contains rich theological symbolism and spiritual instruction, these are not typological in the technical sense—they do not trace how an OT person, event, or institution prefigures its NT fulfillment. The commentary is primarily hortatory (moral exhortation) and harmonistic rather than typological.

original_text: Golgotha, that is the place of Calvary,{ Ver. 33. Calvariae locus. kraniou topos.|} of heads and skulls: perhaps, says St. Jerome, from the skulls of persons executed, and buried there. Several ancient writers would have it so called, from Adam's skull, whom they guess to have been buried there. Some also say that a part of this mountain was called Moria, the place where Abraham was ready to have sacrificed his son Isaac. (Witham) --- Isaac, carrying the wood on his shoulders for the sacrifice, was a figure of Jesus Christ carrying his cross. The mountain was situated to the north-west of Jerusalem.

extractions.type_description: Isaac, obedient to his father Abraham, carried the wood/timber on his shoulders for the sacrifice on Mount Moriah, prefiguring a substitutionary offering
extractions.antitype_description: Jesus Christ carrying his cross to Golgotha for crucifixion as the ultimate sacrificial offering
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states 'Isaac, carrying the wood on his shoulders for the sacrifice, was a figure of Jesus Christ carrying his cross.' This is a direct typological statement connecting the OT event to its NT fulfillment, with both involving: (1) a willing victim, (2) carrying an instrument of sacrifice, (3) movement toward a place of sacrifice, and (4) sacrificial purpose.

notes: The commentary also mentions the possibility that Golgotha/Calvary was located on or near Mount Moriah (where Abraham nearly sacrificed Isaac), which would create additional geographical and contextual resonance between the type and antitype, though this is presented as speculation ('Some also say') rather than established fact. The typological connection between Isaac and Christ is well-established in Christian theology as a prefigurement of substitutionary atonement.

original_text: From the sixth hour. St. Mark says, it was the third hour, and they crucified him. St. John says, it was about the sixth hour, when Jesus was condemned. To reconcile these expressions, we may take notice, that the third greater hour lasted till the sixth hour; and so St. Mark calls it the third hour, because the third great hour (which contained three lesser hours) did not end till mid-day, when the sixth hour was beginning; so that the end of the third, and the beginning of the sixth, happened together. --- Darkness,{ Ver. 45. Tenebrae, a darkness. What is brought out of Phlegon, on the 4th year of 202d Olympiad, is no convincing proof that this was by an eclipse, but may be understood of a great and extraordinary darkness.|} at mid-day, and at full moon. Some call it an eclipse of the sun. It was rather by an interposition of clouds, or by the substraction of the rays of the sun. --- Over all the earth, until the ninth hour. It could be no miracle to be night in the opposite hemisphere; but whether it was in all those parts of the world where, of course, it should have been light, is doubted. Origen thinks this darkness was only in Palestine, and the neighbouring countries: for as to the words, over the whole earth, or over the whole land, we find one kingdom or empire, by a common way of speaking, called the whole earth, or the whole world. Here, in the history of Christ's passion, we should take notice of his seven last words, or sentences on the cross. 1. He prayed for his enemies, and those that put him to death, (Luke 23:34.) Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do. 2. His mercy called the good thief, This day thou shalt be with me in Paradise, Luke 23:43. 3. He recommended his beloved disciple to his mother, saying: woman, behold thy son; and his mother to the same disciple, with, Behold thy mother. (John 19:26-27.) 4. Here (ver. 46) he cried out with a loud voice, Eli, Eli, lamma sabacthani, that is my God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? These words, out of Psalm 21:1[2?], were to express his violent sufferings. The Arians objected them against the divinity of Christ; to whom the Fathers answer, that he spoke these words in the person of sinners, for whose sake he suffered, as they shew by the following words of the same Psalm: far from my salvation are the words of my sins: which cannot be applied to Christ, he being incapable of sinning. Besides, these words may be expounded as a prayer, by which he desires of his Father, not to be abandoned any longer, but that his sufferings may now have an end. In fine, that these words were uttered with an entire confidence, and an assurance in the presence and assistance of God, appears by what he presently added, recommending his spirit into the hands of his Father. The fifth sentence was, I thirst, to let us know the violent thirst of his exhausted body. St. John (xix. 28,) says it was that the Scripture might be fulfilled. (Psalm 68:22.) And in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink. The sixth sentence was, It is consummated; (John 19:30) that is the work of man's redemption, and all the prophecies, and decrees of heaven, concerning me, the Saviour of the world, are now accomplished. The seventh and last sentence was, Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit; and with these words, says St. Luke, (xxiii. 46.) pronounced with a loud voice, he expired. (Witham) --- The learned are divided on this passage: 1st, As to the cause of the obscuration of the sun; and, 2ndly, as to the extent of its darkness. Origen is inclined to think that the darkness was partial, and confined to Judea and the neighbouring countries, as the darkness of Egypt was only perceived in that country, and not in Gessen, where the children of Israel were. St. Jerome imagines that the obscurity was caused by the rays of the sun being suddenly withdrawn by divine power, as was the case in Egypt. These they give as conjectures only. But St. Dionysius, the Areopagite, speaks from his own observations, being, as he informs us in a letter to St. Polycarp, then at Heliopolis, a city of Egypt, for the purpose of astronomical observations. He noticed this miraculous eclipse. He saw the moon rise from the east, and placing itself directly under the sun, cause the above mentioned darkness. This made him cry out to his companion, in the greatest admiration. He observes in this eclipse, four things contrary to the ordinary course of nature: 1. The time, full moon, when there cannot be an eclipse of the sun; 2. the moon being under the sun at the sixth hour, returned to its place in the east for the evening; 3. the order in which the sun was obscured. In ordinary eclipses, the western limb of the sun is first obscured, on account of the motion of the moon in its orbit, being from west to east; whereas, in the present case, the moon having already passed the sun, and being removed from the sun the distance of a semicircle, returned from the east to the sun, and of course first eclipsed it on the eastern limb: 4. contrary to the manner of common eclipses, in which that part is first visible which was first obscured, that part of the sun first appeared which was last eclipsed, because the moon returned again to the east after the eclipse was full. To this may be added the observation of St. Chrysostom and St. Jerome: that the duration of natural eclipses is very short, whilst this lasted the space of three whole hours. But this interposition of the moon, which suffers the greatest parallax, could not cause an universal eclipse; if, therefore, the text is to be understood literally of the whole earth, another cause must be supposed for this universal darkness. But it may be understood in a more limited sense, of the land of Judea. (Denis the Carthusian)

extractions.type_name: The Darkness of Egypt (Plague of Darkness)
extractions.type_description: The supernatural darkness that afflicted Egypt during the ninth plague (Exodus 10:21-23), which did not extend to the land of Goshen where the Israelites dwelt
extractions.antitype_description: The miraculous darkness that covered the land during Jesus's crucifixion from the sixth to the ninth hour (Matthew 27:45), understood as a sign of divine judgment and the cosmic significance of Christ's redemptive work
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly compares the two darkness events: 'Origen is inclined to think that the darkness was partial, and confined to Judea and the neighbouring countries, as the darkness of Egypt was only perceived in that country, and not in Gessen, where the children of Israel were.' Additionally, St. Jerome notes that both involved 'the rays of the sun being suddenly withdrawn by divine power.' This establishes a typological parallel where the Egyptian darkness prefigures the eschatological darkness accompanying Christ's passion—both are supernatural divine acts with salvific significance for God's people.

notes: This is an implicit rather than explicit typology. The commentary uses the Egyptian darkness as a historical and hermeneutical parallel to help explain the extent and nature of the crucifixion darkness, but does not explicitly state it as a prefigurement. The typological connection is strengthened by the parallel structure: both involve supernatural darkness, both are divine judgments, and both are associated with redemptive history (liberation from Egypt; redemption through Christ's sacrifice).

original_text: And he called James, etc. The words, he called, are no addition, as they only express the literal sense: they are included in what is said, ver. 13, that he called to him whom he would. --- Boanerges, the sons of thunder, or thunderers, is only to express their great zeal. (Witham) --- He gave also the two sons of Zebedee the name of Boanerges, (Boanerges) from the Syriac, Benairegesch; or the Hebrew, Beni, sons, regesch, thunder, noise or tumult. In conformity to their name, we find these two apostles asking Jesus, (Luke 9:54.) wilt thou that we command fire to come down from heaven, to consume them? They spread the fame of the gospel through the whole world. So great was the zeal of St. James, that he incurred the resentment of king Agrippa, and was the first of the apostles to seal the doctrines of Jesus Christ with his blood. St. John also fulfilled the import of his name, as appears from his gospel, epistles, apocalypse, and the sufferings he underwent at Rome for the faith. Sts. Peter, James, and John, were the only apostles to whom our Saviour gave particular names, a mark, perhaps, of his special affection for them. (Tirinus)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Mark 3:17 does not describe typological relationships between Old Testament types and New Testament antitypes. Instead, it discusses: (1) the etymological meaning of 'Boanerges' (sons of thunder) from Syriac and Hebrew; (2) the symbolic significance of the name in relation to the apostles' temperament and zeal; (3) biographical and historical facts about James and John's martyrdom and writings; and (4) Jesus' special affection for Peter, James, and John. While the commentary uses symbolic language (e.g., their name expressing 'great zeal'), this constitutes general symbolism and moral characterization rather than typological prefiguration of an OT type by an NT antitype. No connection to Old Testament persons, events, or institutions is established.

original_text: Ven. Bede gives a beautiful explanation of this miracle. He says that it represents the Gentiles, who were converted to the faith by the apostles. The legion represents the innumerable vices to which they were subject, neither restrained by the laws of God nor man, but breaking through every restraint, and wallowing in all kinds of uncleanness. (Ven. Bede) --- The three evangelists agree in the expulsion of the legion of devils, except that St. Matthew makes mention of two demoniacs, and Sts. Mark and Luke only of one. The difficulty is thus solved by St. Augustine. St. Mark and St. Luke only mention one, as being more generally known, and particularly frightful in the neighbourhood. (St. Augustine)
notes: This commentary employs allegorical and symbolic interpretation rather than typological analysis. Venerable Bede interprets the demon-possessed man as representing Gentiles and the legion of demons as representing vices, but this is allegory/moral symbolism applied to a New Testament narrative event, not a typological relationship where an Old Testament type prefigures a New Testament antitype. Typology specifically requires an OT prefigurement of an NT fulfillment; this commentary stays entirely within the NT (the Gospels) and uses symbolic language to extract spiritual lessons. The discussion of the textual variants among the evangelists regarding one versus two demoniacs is exegetical rather than typological.

original_text: Touch his garment. Almighty God is pleased to give occasionally to the relics and clothes of his pious and faithful servants, a degree of virtue. See Acts v, and xix, where the very shadow of St. Peter, and the handkerchiefs and aprons that had touched the body of St. Paul, and were brought to the sick, cured their diseases, and banished the wicked spirits. See St. Chrysostom, T. 5. contra Gent. in vit. Babyloe. St. Basil saith: "he that toucheth the bone of a martyr, receiveth in some degree holiness of the grace or virtue that is therein. (St. Basil in Psalm cxv.)
notes: The Haydock commentary on MRK 5:28 does not describe typological relationships between Old Testament types and New Testament antitypes. Instead, the commentary discusses: (1) the miraculous power God grants to relics and clothing of saints (a doctrine of divine grace working through sacred objects), and (2) supporting examples from Acts 5 and 19 regarding Peter's shadow and Paul's handkerchiefs/aprons healing the sick. While the commentary cites Church Fathers (Chrysostom and Basil) on the transmission of holiness through contact with martyrs' relics, this is a discussion of sacramental theology and the veneration of relics—not typology. No Old Testament type is presented that prefigures the New Testament healing power described. The commentary is concerned with demonstrating how God's power operates through material objects associated with holy persons, not with showing how an OT person, event, or institution prefigures an NT fulfillment.

original_text: Only three resurrections from the dead are mentioned as performed by our Saviour: one just dead; one carried out to be buried; and Lazarus, already in his tomb. These represent the different states of sinners dead in sin, some more desperate than others. To such as have been for years in sin, and have none to intercede for them, we must apply the words of Christ, suffer the dead to bury the dead. (Ven. Bede, and St. Augustine, de verb. Dom. serm. 44.)
notes: This commentary employs allegorical and spiritual symbolism rather than typology. It interprets Christ's three resurrections (the ruler's daughter, the widow's son, Lazarus) as symbolic representations of different spiritual conditions of sinners—not as New Testament antitypes fulfilling Old Testament types. The commentary discusses the symbolic meaning of these resurrections within the New Testament narrative itself (comparing three NT events to each other) and applies them to spiritual states and moral lessons. There is no explicit connection to Old Testament persons, events, or institutions that would prefigure these New Testament miracles. This is allegorical interpretation and moral application, which falls outside the definition of typology as the OT-to-NT prefigurative relationship.

original_text: It was usual for the Jews to prescribe oil as a proper thing to anoint the sick; but its virtue in the present instance, when used by the apostles, was not natural but supernatural, and was derived from him who sent them; because this unction always produced a certain and constant cure in those who were anointed. This miraculous gift of healing the sick with oil, which Christ conferred on his apostles, was a prelude or gradual preparation to the dignity to which he raised this unction, when he established it a perpetual rite in his holy Church. (Rutter) --- With oil, etc. This anointing the sick, was at least a figure of the sacrament, which Christ was pleased to institute for the spiritual relief of persons in danger of death: and which is fully expressed by St. James, in his Catholic Epistle. (James vi.[v.?]) The Council of Trent says this sacrament was insinuated in St. Mark, and published in the Epistle of St. James. (Council of Trent, session xiv., Mark 1.) (Witham)
notes: This commentary describes a prefigurative or preparatory relationship between apostolic healing practices and the sacrament of Extreme Unction (Anointing of the Sick), but this is NOT typology in the technical sense. Typology requires an Old Testament type prefiguring a New Testament antitype. Here we have: (1) an apostolic practice in the New Testament (healing with oil), and (2) a later ecclesiastical sacrament (also in the New Testament/Church tradition). The commentary uses language like 'prelude,' 'preparation,' and 'figure,' but these describe a developmental or institutional progression within the New Testament era, not an OT-to-NT typological relationship. The Haydock commentary conflates prefiguration language with typology, but no Old Testament type is identified or discussed.

original_text: Although Christ clearly establishes here the strict obligation of paying to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, to the confusion of his very enemies, we shall still find them bringing forward against him the charge of disloyalty, as if he forbade tribute to be paid to Caesar. (Luke 23:2.) After the example of her divine Model, the Catholic Church has uniformly taught with St. Paul, the necessity of obeying the powers in being; and this not for fear of their wrath, but for conscience sake. Render to Caesar the money on which his image is stamped, but render yourselves cheerfully to God; for the light of thy countenance, O Lord, is stamped upon us, (Psalm iv.) and not the image of Caesar. (St. Jerome) --- With reason were they astonished at the wisdom of this answer, which eluded all their artifices, and taught them at the same time what they owed to their prince, and what they owed to God: and whoever hopes for the favour of heaven, must conscientiously observe this double duty to God and to the magistrate.
notes: The Haydock commentary on MRK 12:17 does not establish typological relationships between Old Testament and New Testament persons, events, or institutions. Instead, the commentary focuses on: (1) Christ's ethical teaching regarding civil and religious obligations, (2) the moral principle of rendering to Caesar and to God their respective dues, and (3) the Church's application of this principle through apostolic tradition (St. Paul, St. Jerome). While the commentary includes a Psalm reference (Psalm IV) to support the metaphorical idea that God's image is stamped upon us, this functions as an allegorical or symbolic support for moral teaching rather than as a typological prefigurement. The passage teaches doctrine and ethics, not typology.

original_text: When shall these things be? The miseries that took place previously to the destruction of the temple and city of Jerusalem, were a figure of the extreme calamity that will happen before the last day, in the reign of Antichrist: hence Jesus Christ speaketh indifferently of both. (Bristow)

extractions.type_name: The destruction of the temple and city of Jerusalem
extractions.type_description: The miseries and calamities that preceded the destruction of Jerusalem in 70 AD, including siege, famine, persecution, and social upheaval
extractions.antitype_name: The tribulations before the last day in the reign of Antichrist
extractions.antitype_description: The extreme calamities and miseries that will occur before the final judgment and end times, during the reign of Antichrist
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that the Jerusalem destruction events 'were a figure of the extreme calamity that will happen before the last day.' This is a clear prefigurement relationship where a historical OT/early NT event (Jerusalem's fall) serves as a type for a future eschatological event (end-times tribulation). The commentary notes that Christ speaks 'indifferently of both,' indicating deliberate typological connection between the proximate historical event and the ultimate eschatological fulfillment.

notes: This represents typology in the broader sense where a historical event prefigures a future eschatological reality, rather than strict OT-to-NT typology. The 'type' here is from the apostolic period (70 AD) rather than the Old Testament proper, but it functions typologically as a pattern or figure of the greater end-times fulfillment. Haydock's commentary reflects the hermeneutical principle of multiple fulfillment (near and far) common in eschatological interpretation.

original_text: This vine represents the Synagogue, according to Isaias. The vine, or vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel. Of this vine Christ drank for some time; and though many of the branches were become useless, there were yet many that still brought forth fruit. But Christ now going to his passion, declares that it would be no longer acceptable to him, since the figures were not to pass into reality. (Ven. Bede)

extractions.type_description: The vineyard of the Lord of hosts representing the house of Israel, as described in Isaiah. A vine that produced both fruitful branches and useless branches.
extractions.antitype_description: Christ's declaration that the old vine (Synagogue/Israel under the old covenant) would no longer be acceptable to Him after His passion, as the figurative/typical system gives way to the reality of the New Covenant.
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly identifies the OT vine/vineyard (from Isaiah) as a type that prefigured a reality to be fulfilled in the NT. Bede states that Christ 'declares that it would be no longer acceptable to him, since the figures were not to pass into reality.' This is a clear typological transition where the OT figure (type) is superseded by NT fulfillment (antitype), specifically relating to covenant transition from Old to New.

notes: The commentary emphasizes the principle of typological fulfillment: 'the figures were not to pass into reality,' indicating that once the antitype (the reality of the New Covenant) arrived, the OT type (the Synagogue/old covenant system) would cease to function as acceptable to Christ. This is a covenantal typology marking the transition from shadow to substance.

original_text: Our Lord received the kiss of the traitor, that he might not appear to avoid being delivered up; and at the same time he fulfilled that of the Psalmist, with those who hated peace, I was peaceful. (Psalm 119:7.)

extractions.type_name: The Psalmist's peaceable conduct amid enemies (Psalm 119:7)
extractions.type_description: The OT psalmist maintained peace and did not resist those who hated peace, demonstrating patient endurance in the face of hostility
extractions.antitype_name: Christ's acceptance of betrayal and arrest
extractions.antitype_description: Jesus received Judas's kiss of betrayal without resistance or avoidance, fulfilling the pattern of patient acceptance demonstrated in the Psalms
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that Jesus 'fulfilled that of the Psalmist, with those who hated peace, I was peaceful' (Psalm 119:7). This presents a direct OT/NT connection where the psalmist's attitude and behavior prefigures Christ's response to his betrayal. However, the connection is more typological-prophetic (direct fulfillment of a scriptural pattern) rather than a traditional type/antitype relationship, since the psalmist himself is not presented as a deliberate prefigurement of Christ, but rather his words are shown to apply to Christ's actions.

notes: This is a borderline case. The commentary cites an OT text (Psalm 119:7) that is fulfilled in Jesus's behavior at Mark 14:45, but it functions more as prophetic fulfillment or scriptural correspondence than as traditional typology. In strict typological terms, a type is typically an OT person, event, or institution that God designed to prefigure the antitype. Here, the psalmist's general statement about maintaining peace amid hatred is shown to find its ultimate fulfillment in Christ, which is typological in the broader sense but not in the narrower sense of deliberate OT prefigurement.

original_text: Caiphas, in order to excite their hatred against what was said, rent his garments, and thus deprived himself of the priestly dignity, by transgressing the precept; which, speaking of the high priest says: He shall not uncover his head, and his garments he shall not rend. (Leviticus 21:10.) (St. Leo the Great) --- By the high priest rending his garments he shews, that the Jewish priesthood, on account of their crimes, was now dissolved; whereas the tunic of Christ, by which the one true Catholic Church is prefigured, was seamless, and not to be divided. (Ven. Bede)

extractions.type_name: The High Priest's Garments (specifically the rended garments of Caiaphas)
extractions.type_description: Caiaphas rent his garments in violation of Leviticus 21:10, which prohibited the high priest from rending his garments. This act signified the dissolution of the Jewish priesthood due to their crimes.
extractions.antitype_name: Christ's Seamless Tunic and the Catholic Church
extractions.antitype_description: Christ's seamless tunic, which prefigures the one true Catholic Church. Unlike the rended garments of the Jewish priesthood, Christ's tunic remains undivided, representing the unity and indivisibility of the Church.
extractions.reasoning: Venerable Bede explicitly establishes a typological contrast: the rending of the high priest's garments prefigures the dissolution of the Jewish priesthood, while Christ's seamless tunic prefigures the undivided Church. This is a clear OT/NT typological relationship where the type (rended priestly garments) and antitype (Christ's seamless tunic representing the Church) are directly connected to show fulfillment and supersession.

notes: This typology functions as a 'negative type' or 'antitype contrast' - the rending demonstrates what is abandoned (the old Jewish priesthood) in favor of what is established (the unified Church in Christ). The commentary attributes this interpretation to Venerable Bede. The seamless tunic is mentioned in John 19:23-24 as a historical detail that carries typological significance here.

original_text: St. Matthew says mixed with gall; for gall is here used for bitterness, and wine that has myrrh in it is a very strong bitter; although, perhaps, both gall and myrrh might have been ingredients to increase the bitterness. (St. Augustine) --- Or, in the confusion that was occasioned, some might have offered him one thing, some another; one person giving vinegar and gall, another wine mixed with myrrh. (Theophylactus) --- Wine mingled with myrrh may perhaps be used for vinegar. (St. Jerome) --- This was given to criminals, to lessen their torments. Our Lord was pleased to taste the bitterness, but he would not permit the relief which the admittance of the same into his stomach might have afforded. Thus also were the scriptures fulfilled: they gave me gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink. (Psalm lxviii.) (Ven. Bede)

extractions.type_name: The bitter drink offered to the Psalmist (Psalm 68:21)
extractions.type_description: In Psalm 68, the righteous sufferer is given gall for food and vinegar to drink in his affliction - a prophecy of bitter suffering and humiliation
extractions.antitype_description: Jesus is offered wine mixed with myrrh (a bitter drink) at his crucifixion, fulfilling the Psalmist's prophecy of the righteous sufferer's bitter trial
extractions.reasoning: The Haydock commentary explicitly cites Psalm 68:21 as scriptural fulfillment of the crucifixion narrative ('Thus also were the scriptures fulfilled: they gave me gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink'), making this a direct typological connection where the OT prophecy prefigures Christ's specific sufferings

notes: The commentary attributes this typological insight to Venerable Bede. This is fulfillment typology rather than institutional typology - the OT passage describes a type of suffering that Christ (the antitype) experienced literally at the crucifixion. The commentary also notes the theological significance that Christ tasted the bitterness but refused full relief, emphasizing the completeness of his suffering.

original_text: This appearance of our Saviour is more fully related by St. John. Our Lord arose early from the monument in which he had been placed late in the evening, thus fulfilling the words of the psalmist: In the evening weeping shall have place, and in the morning gladness. (Psalm xxix.) (Ven. Bede) --- Rising early. It appears from this that our Saviour arose early, about sunrise, as was the sentiment of St. Augustine; though St. Gregory seems to think that he arose at midnight, in the same manner as Samson, who was a figure of Christ, arose in the middle of the night and carried away the gates of Gaza. If we follow this opinion, we must understand the word early as referring to the verb appeared, not to the participle rising, and then the sentence will be: he rising, (having arisen) appeared early the first day of the week. The first interpretation, however, of St. Augustine seems more agreeable to the text: he rising early the first day of the week, appeared, etc.

extractions.type_description: Samson, who arose in the middle of the night and carried away the gates of Gaza, serving as a figure prefiguring Christ's resurrection
extractions.antitype_description: Christ rising from the dead, potentially at midnight, breaking through the bonds of death as Samson broke through the gates
extractions.reasoning: St. Gregory explicitly identifies Samson as 'a figure of Christ' in relation to his nocturnal rising and his breaking through barriers (gates of Gaza), which prefigures Christ's resurrection and triumph over death. However, this is presented as one interpretive opinion among others, and the commentary debates whether it applies to this specific instance.

notes: The commentary presents St. Gregory's Samson typology as an alternative interpretation rather than the primary one. St. Augustine's interpretation (early morning rising) is noted as 'more agreeable to the text.' The Samson typology, while explicitly called a 'figure of Christ,' is offered tentatively as supporting evidence for a midnight resurrection rather than an early morning one. The Psalm xxix reference regarding evening weeping and morning gladness is thematic/prophetic fulfillment rather than typological in the strict sense.

original_text: By these words it is not to be understood that Jesus is to be confined to that particular posture of body, or that the Father has any hands, or any human shape; for God is a pure, incorporeal, and all-perfect Spirit. The image of God, as he is in himself, comes not within the reach of our mortal senses. When the Scripture, therefore, speaks of God, it uses such imagery of language as is adapted to our senses, that it may thereby convey to us some imperfect knowledge of those sublime mysteries, which are ineffable in themselves, and incomprehensible to our understanding. Thus we are informed that Jesus Christ sits at the right hand of God, the Father Almighty, to signify that, as man, our Lord is raised to the height of glory, and to that supreme beatitude, than which there is nothing higher, and nothing greater in the whole bliss of heaven; and that he moreover holds the same sovereign dominion with the Father over all creatures; because, as God, he is equal to the Father in power, in wisdom, and in all perfection. See Pouget, p. 256. ed. in fol. --- On the right hand of God. Jesus Christ, our Redeemer, was not man only, but truly God, the same God with his eternal Father: and hereby is signified that the person, who took upon him human nature, and became man, is equal in dignity with the Father: he, who, as man, ascended into heaven. { Ver. 19. St. Hieron.[St. Jerome,] Ep. ad Hebidiam, q. 3, tom. 4, part 1, p. 172: omnibus Graecis Libris penè hoc capitulum non habentibus.|} When St. Jerome says that most Greek copies wanted this chapter, he speaks not of chapters according to our present division, but only of the last 12 verses, which formerly made what was called a little chapter: yet these twelve verses must have been omitted in those manuscripts by some negligent transcribers. Now they are found in all, both Latin and Greek copies. They are found in the Canons of Eusebius on the Gospels; in St. Jerome in several places; in St. Ambrose, lib. iii, in Luc. tom. iii, p. 292. Ed. Paris, an. 1582; in St. Augustine, lib. iii, de consensu Evang. ch. XXV, tom. 3, part 2, p. 142, etc. (Witham) --- St. Gregory of Nyssa, (orat. 2. de Resurr.) says, that the best copies of St. Mark's gospel finished with the 8th verse, a trembling and fear had seized them: En tois akribesterois to Kata Markon Euaggelion mekri tou ephobounto gar, echei to telos. It is the very generally received sentiment of the learned, that the last 12 verses were given by St. Mark; and the most probable reason yet offered for the omission of them in various copies is, that the transcribers followed a mutilated copy, where the last page was wanting. (Bible de Vence)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Mark 16:19 (the Ascension of Jesus) focuses on exegetical clarification rather than typology. The commentary addresses: (1) the metaphorical nature of anthropomorphic language about God ('right hand of God'); (2) Christological doctrine (Christ's equality with the Father); and (3) textual criticism (the manuscript tradition of Mark 16:9-20). While the passage itself contains theological significance regarding Christ's exaltation, the commentary does not establish any Old Testament prefiguration or typological relationship. No OT type is identified as prefiguring the NT reality of Christ's ascension or heavenly session.

original_text: The Almighty appointed to Moses that there should be but one high priest at a time, to whom, at his decease, a successor should be chosen. This rule obtained till the time of David, by whom, by the inspiration of God, many were appointed at once. (1 Paralipomenon 24.) According to this regulation, Zachary (Zacharias) is said to perform the office of priest, according to the order of his course. (Ven. Bede) --- Zacharias seems here to be described as high priest, who once a year entered alone in the inward sanctuary with the blood of the victims, which he offered for himself and the sins of the people. (St. Ambrose) --- He was not chosen by a fresh lot to offer up incense, but by a previous lot, according to which the family of Abia succeeded to the office of high priest. The people waited without, according to Leviticus 16:12.; whilst the high priest carried the incense into the holy of holies, on the 10th day of the 7th month. (Ven. Bede) --- Of the course of Abia.{ Ver. 5. De vice Abia, ex ephemerias.|} What we read in the Greek for course, is commonly put for the employment of one day, but here for the functions of a whole week. For by appointment of David, (1 Paralipomenon xxiv,) the descendants from Aaron were divided into 24 families; of which the eighth was Abia, from whom descended this Zacharias, who at this time was in the week of his priestly functions. (Witham) --- It is worthy of remark, that there were three Herods. The first was the one here spoken of, (surnamed Ascalonite, from his palace in the city of Ascalon, in Palestine) the same who murdered the Innocents. The second was the son of the first, (surnamed Antipas) who derided Christ at the time of his passion, the same who beheaded the Baptist. The third was Herod Agrippa, who beheaded St. James, imprisoned St. Peter, and who was afterwards, for his great pride, stricken by an angel, and devoured by worms. Our Saviour was born in the reign of the first Herod, by whom the prophecy of Jacob, related in the book of Genesis (Genesis 49.) was fulfilled: The sceptre shall not be taken, etc. Herod was an Idumaean, and made king of the Jews by the Romans. The Jews, after they entered the land of promise, were first governed by judges, until Saul: then by kings, until the Babylonian captivity; after that by high priests, until the time of Hyrcanus, whom Herod having killed, succeeded. From that period to the present day, they have been governed by strangers. (Ven. Bede, and Denis the Carthusian) --- Elizabeth was of the race of Aaron, by her father; but her mother was probably of the race of David, from whom the blessed Virgin, cousin of Elizabeth, descended. See below, ver. 36.
notes: This Haydock commentary on Luke 1:5 focuses on historical, institutional, and genealogical information rather than typological relationships. While the commentary discusses: (1) the high priesthood of Zacharias and the priestly order of Abia, (2) the fulfillment of Jacob's prophecy regarding the scepter through Herod's reign, and (3) Elizabeth's lineage from Aaron and David - none of these are presented as OT types prefiguring NT antitypes. The commentary is primarily concerned with explaining the historical context of John the Baptist's father, the structure of Jewish priesthood, and the genealogical connections of the holy family. The reference to Jacob's prophecy (Genesis 49) being 'fulfilled' in Herod's time is about historical fulfillment of a messianic prophecy rather than typological prefigurement of a person or event. No explicit type-antitype relationships are identified or articulated in this passage.

original_text: This was fulfilled not only at his birth, but ever after by the Catholic Church, celebrating his nativity. (Haydock)
notes: This commentary describes the fulfillment and ongoing celebration of John the Baptist's birth by the Catholic Church, but it does not establish a typological relationship between an Old Testament type and a New Testament antitype. The passage references the historical event of John's nativity and its commemoration in Church tradition, which is historical fulfillment and liturgical practice rather than typology. Typology requires an OT person, event, or institution that prefigures a corresponding NT reality; this commentary lacks any OT type component.

original_text: The evangelist here mentions the city of David, to remind us how exactly that was fulfilled, which God promised to David, that an everlasting king should be born of him: and the reason why the inspired writer was content to mention the relationship between Joseph and David, omitting that of the Blessed Virgin and the royal prophet, was, because in the law it was commanded that persons of the same family should intermarry; hence it is added in the subsequent verse, with Mary, his espoused wife. (St. Irenaeus, haer. lib. 3:chap. 11.)

extractions.type_description: God's promise to David (2 Samuel 7) that an everlasting king would be born from his lineage
extractions.antitype_name: Jesus Christ born in Bethlehem (the City of David)
extractions.antitype_description: Jesus as the fulfillment of the promise that an everlasting king would descend from David
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that Luke mentions 'the city of David' to demonstrate 'how exactly that was fulfilled, which God promised to David, that an everlasting king should be born of him.' This directly connects the OT promise (type) to Jesus's birth (antitype), fulfilling the Davidic covenant.

notes: The commentary also references the genealogical connection between Joseph and David, noting the legal requirement for same-family intermarriage under Jewish law. While the focus is on covenant fulfillment rather than typological prefigurement in the strict sense, the relationship between the OT promise and its NT fulfillment in Jesus's Davidic lineage constitutes a typological connection. The Virgin Mary's royal lineage is mentioned but deliberately de-emphasized by the evangelist in favor of Joseph's legal connection to David for purposes of establishing Jesus's legitimate claim to the Davidic throne.

original_text: Because the light of life is risen to us, dwelling in the region of the shadow of death. (Ven. Bede)

extractions.type_name: Light arising in the region of the shadow of death
extractions.type_description: A reference to Isaiah 9:2 (and related OT prophecies of light dispelling darkness), where the coming of divine light is prophesied to pierce the darkness and shadow of death experienced by those in spiritual bondage
extractions.antitype_name: Jesus Christ as the Light of Life
extractions.antitype_description: Christ's incarnation and redemptive work as the fulfillment of OT prophecies, bringing spiritual light and salvation to humanity dwelling in spiritual darkness and death
extractions.reasoning: Bede's commentary explicitly identifies Christ as 'the light of life' rising to illuminate those in 'the region of the shadow of death.' This directly fulfills Isaiah 9:2 and reflects standard Christological typology where OT prophecies of divine light prefigure Christ's coming. The language mirrors messianic prophecy and its NT fulfillment in Luke 2:11 (announcing Christ's birth).

notes: This commentary employs typological language characteristic of patristic interpretation (Bede). The 'shadow of death' echoes Psalm 23:4 and Isaiah 9:2, both understood in the early Christian tradition as types fulfilled by Christ's incarnation. While the language is typological and prophetic in nature, it should be noted that Bede is applying OT imagery rather than identifying a distinct historical OT 'type' with a structured prefiguration relationship.

original_text: See Matthew 3:11. That baptism cannot be valid, in which the name of the Holy Ghost only is invoked. For, the tradition concerning life-giving grace, must be preserved entire. To add or to omit any thing, may exclude from life everlasting. For, as we believe, so also are we baptized, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. (St. Basil, lib. de Spirit. Sanc. ch. XXII.) --- Fire. This is a metaphor, to signify the Holy Ghost and his gifts, particularly the fire of divine love to the expiation of sins, and is very common in Scripture. Sometimes also he is represented by water, as in St. John 4:10, et dein. and 7:38.-39; Isaias xliv. etc. etc. Hence, in the hymn to the Holy Ghost, the Church uses both figures. Thou who art call'd the Paraclete, Best gift of God above, The living Spring, the living Fire, Sweet unction and love.
notes: This Haydock commentary on Luke 3:16 discusses symbolism and metaphor rather than typology. The references to water and fire representing the Holy Ghost are symbolic/metaphorical uses of natural elements to convey spiritual realities, not Old Testament types prefiguring New Testament antitypes. The commentary emphasizes the proper form of Christian baptism (invoking the Trinity) and uses poetic imagery (including a hymn) to describe the Holy Ghost's attributes. While the commentary references Old Testament passages (Isaiah 44) and New Testament passages (John 4, 7), it does not establish a typological relationship between an OT type and NT antitype. The water and fire language is presented as common scriptural figures/symbols, not as deliberate prefigurative types.

original_text: By the barn-floor is here prefigured the Church of Christ, in which many are called, but few are chosen. This perfect cleansing of the floor, as it is in the Greek, is performed both here when the wicked, on account of their open crimes, are excluded from the communion of the faithful by the Church; or, on account of their hidden sins, are after death by infinite justice chastised; but most especially at the end of the world, when the Son of man shall send his angels to gather from his kingdom all scandals. (Ven. Bede)

extractions.type_description: The threshing floor from OT agricultural practice where grain is separated from chaff through winnowing
extractions.antitype_description: The Church as the place of separation where the faithful are distinguished from the wicked, both in the present age and at the final judgment
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states 'By the barn-floor is here prefigured the Church of Christ' - a direct statement of typological prefigurement. The OT image of the threshing floor (a place of separation and purification) is connected to the NT reality of the Church's function of distinguishing the elect from the reprobate.

extractions.type_name: The Winnowing/Cleansing of the Threshing Floor
extractions.type_description: The agricultural process of separating wheat from chaff at harvest
extractions.antitype_name: The Final Judgment by the Son of Man
extractions.antitype_description: Christ's sending of angels to gather scandals (the wicked) from His kingdom at the end of the world
extractions.reasoning: The commentary describes how the 'perfect cleansing of the floor' is performed both in the present (Church discipline) and 'most especially at the end of the world, when the Son of man shall send his angels.' The OT agricultural image of winnowing prefigures the final eschatological separation of the righteous from the wicked.

notes: This passage (Luke 3:17) presents John the Baptist's words about Jesus coming with winnowing fork. The Haydock commentary finds dual fulfillment: present (the Church's ongoing separation of the faithful from the wicked) and future (the final judgment). Both dimensions are typological, with the OT threshing floor image prefiguring NT ecclesial and eschatological realities.

original_text: The reason why the Holy Ghost shewed himself in the shape of a dove, was because he could not be seen in the substance of his divinity. But why a dove? To express that simplicity acquired in the sacrament of baptism. Be ye simple as doves; to signify that peace bestowed by baptism, and prefigured by the olive branch which the dove carried back to the ark, a true figure of the Church, and which was the only security from the destructive deluge. (St. Ambrose) --- You will object: Christ, though he was God, would not be baptized till the age of 30, and do you order baptism to be received sooner? When you say, though he was God, you solve the difficulty. For, he stood not in need of being purified at all; of course, there could be no danger in deferring his baptism. But you will have much to answer for, if, being born in corruption, you pass out of this world without the garment of incorruption. (St. Gregory of Nazianzus, orat. 40.)

extractions.type_name: The Dove with the Olive Branch (Genesis 8:11)
extractions.type_description: In the Noah narrative, the dove returns to the ark carrying an olive branch, signifying peace and deliverance from the destructive flood
extractions.antitype_description: Baptism confers peace and represents the Church (figured as the ark), which is the means of security and salvation from spiritual destruction
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states the olive branch 'prefigured by the dove carried back to the ark, a true figure of the Church.' This directly connects the OT narrative (dove/olive branch/ark) to NT realities (baptism/Church/salvation). The connection is stated with typological language ('prefigured,' 'true figure').

notes: The commentary also employs the dove as a symbol of simplicity and peace, but this is moral/symbolic application rather than typology proper. The typological relationship is specifically between the Genesis account of Noah's dove and the eschatological/ecclesial reality of the Church receiving baptismal grace. St. Ambrose is the attributed source for this typological reading.

original_text: What could be more beautiful, than that this holy race should begin from the Son of God, and be continued up to the Son of God; that the creature might go before in figure, and the Son of God might follow after in reality; that he who was made after the image of God, might first appear, that the true image of his eternal Father may descend from his glory. Thus did St. Luke mean to refer the origin of Christ to God, of whom he was the true and eternal Son. To shew this still more evidently, the evangelist had before introduced the Almighty speaking from heaven: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. (St. Ambrose)

extractions.type_description: The first human creature made in the image of God (Genesis 1:27), representing humanity in its created state and bearing God's image
extractions.antitype_description: The true and eternal Son of God, the perfect image of God the Father, who descends from divine glory in reality rather than mere figure
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly contrasts 'he who was made after the image of God' (Adam in Genesis) with 'the true image of his eternal Father' (Christ). The passage describes Adam as appearing 'in figure' while Christ follows 'in reality,' establishing a typological progression from the OT type to the NT antitype. The phrase 'creature might go before in figure' directly references Adam, while 'Son of God might follow after in reality' refers to Christ's incarnation.

notes: The commentary emphasizes the genealogical structure of Luke 3 (tracing lineage from Jesus back to Adam) as a typological framework.
