(Witham) --- Compare the words here spoken with those he delivered at his last supper, and you will see that what he promises here was then fulfilled: "this is my body given for you." Hence, the holy Fathers have always explained this chapter of St. John, as spoken of the blessed sacrament. See the concluding reflexions, below.
notes: This Haydock commentary on John 6:52 focuses on Christological doctrine (Christ's real presence in the Eucharist) and apologetics against both Jewish incredulity and Protestant denial of transubstantiation. While the passage discusses the Eucharist as fulfilling Christ's promise, and references Isaiah 55:9 regarding God's transcendence, the commentary does not establish an explicit typological relationship where an Old Testament type prefigures the New Testament antitype. The commentary emphasizes the literal fulfillment of Christ's words at the Last Supper rather than typological prefigurement from OT persons, events, or institutions. The Isaiah reference is used rhetorically to support an argument about God's incomprehensibility, not as a typological type-antitype relationship.

original_text: The fountain of Siloe was at the foot of the walls of Jerusalem, to the east, where its waters were collected in a reservoir for the benefit of the city. Thither our Saviour sent the blind man. The word Siloe signifies sent, and was a figure of Christ, who was sent by his eternal Father into the world to enlighten all men, of whom this blind man was the emblem. The pool of Siloe represents the sacrament of baptism, by which we are sanctified and made Christians. It is still to this day held in great veneration by the Turks, who think its waters very beneficial in diseases of the eyes. (Calmet) --- Its waters signify those of divine grace and light, communicated to the faithful soul through Jesus Christ, who was sent of God. (Bible de Vence) --- Thus Sedulius: ---------------------------Cognoscite cuncti, Mystica quid doceant animos miracula nostros. Coeca sumus proles miserae de foetibus Hevae, Portantes longo natas errore tenebras. Sed dignante Deo mortalem sumere formam Tegminis humani, facta est de Virgine nobis Terra salutaris, quae fontibus oblita sacris Clara renascentis referat spiracula lucis.

extractions.type_description: A fountain at the foot of Jerusalem's walls whose waters were collected in a reservoir for the city's benefit
extractions.antitype_description: The Christian sacrament through which believers are sanctified and made Christians
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states 'The pool of Siloe represents the sacrament of baptism, by which we are sanctified and made Christians.' The waters of the pool are interpreted as signifying divine grace and light communicated to faithful souls through Christ.

extractions.type_description: The name itself signifies 'sent' and was associated with the Jerusalem fountain
extractions.antitype_description: Christ, who was sent by his eternal Father into the world to enlighten all men
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states 'The word Siloe signifies sent, and was a figure of Christ, who was sent by his eternal Father into the world to enlighten all men.' This directly connects the OT name/concept to Christ as the sent one of the Father.

extractions.type_description: The blind man in the narrative who is sent to wash in the pool of Siloam
extractions.antitype_description: All people whom Christ came to enlighten; the emblem of sinful humanity in need of spiritual illumination
extractions.reasoning: The commentary states 'this blind man was the emblem' of those whom Christ came to enlighten. While this is symbolic representation rather than explicit typology, it serves as a prefiguration of humanity's spiritual blindness and need for Christ's light.

notes: The commentary employs multiple layers of typological interpretation. The primary typology is Sacramental (pool → baptism), with secondary Christological typology (the name 'Siloe' → Christ the Sent One). The poetic excerpt from Sedulius reinforces these connections, describing humanity as blind children of Eve who are enlightened through God's redemptive work in Christ.

original_text: This is addressed to princes established to govern the people of God. They are the image of God on earth by the authority they exercise, and which they have received from Him. --- Is it not written in your law, (under which were also comprehended the Psalms) I have said: you are Gods? etc. Christ here stops the mouths of the Jews, by an argument which they could not answer, that sometimes they were called Gods, who acted by God's authority. I have said: you are Gods. (Psalm 81:6.) But then he immediately declares, that it is not in this sense only that he is God. 1st, Because he has been sanctified by the Father, which St. Augustine and others understand of that infinite sanctification, which he has necessarily by always proceeding from the Father. Others expound it of a greater sanctity and fulness of grace above all other saints, given to him, even as he was man. But 2ndly, he adds at the same time, and confirms what he had often told them, that he was the Son of God, sent into the world: that his works shew that he was in the Father, and the Father in him. by this they saw that he was far from recalling or contradicting what he had said before. And therefore (ver. 30.[39.?]) they sought to apprehend him, and put him to death for blasphemy. (Witham) --- Eloim, which name of God was so called from judging, and may be interpreted judges. (Menochius)

extractions.type_description: Old Testament judges and princes who were called 'Elohim' (Gods) because they exercised God's authority to govern His people and act in His name
extractions.antitype_description: Christ as the ultimate judge and Son of God, who possesses divine authority and sanctification in a way infinitely superior to earthly judges, confirmed by His works and His unity with the Father
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly presents OT judges bearing the title 'Gods' as a prefigurement of Christ's claim to be God. Christ uses the lesser case (earthly judges called 'Gods') to argue for the greater case (His own divinity). The commentary notes that Christ 'immediately declares that it is not in this sense only that he is God,' indicating He transcends and fulfills what the type merely suggested. This is a classic a fortiori typological argument where the OT type demonstrates the principle that leads to the NT antitype's superior fulfillment.

notes: The commentary presents this as an argumentative typology rather than a prophetic one—Christ uses existing OT language about judges to make a logical case for His superiority. The type demonstrates the principle (God's representatives are called 'Gods'), while the antitype (Christ) embodies this principle absolutely and infinitely. Augustine and others understand Christ's 'sanctification by the Father' as an infinite sanctification by eternal procession, making His case categorically different from temporal judges.

original_text: Shall lift up his heel against me. It is the sense of those words, (Psalm 40:10.) hath supplanted me; and they were spoken of Judas's sin in betraying Christ. (Witham) --- Jesus Christ applies in this place to the perfidy of Judas, that which David appears to have said on occasion of the perfidy of Achitophel, who was thus a figure of the perfidious Judas. (Bible de Vence)

extractions.type_description: Ahithophel was David's trusted counselor who betrayed him, described in Psalm 40:10 as one who 'lifted up his heel' against David
extractions.antitype_description: Judas, one of Christ's apostles and trusted disciples, betrayed Jesus, fulfilling the pattern of intimate betrayal prefigured by Ahithophel
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly identifies Ahithophel as 'a figure of the perfidious Judas' and demonstrates how Jesus applies the language of Psalm 40:10 (originally concerning Ahithophel's betrayal of David) to Judas's betrayal of himself. This is a clear typological correspondence where the OT betrayal pattern prefigures the NT betrayal event.

notes: The typology here is relatively straightforward: both involve trusted intimates ('lifting up the heel') who betray their masters. The commentary sources (Witham and Bible de Vence) both recognize this as typological fulfillment, with the OT event/figure serving as a prefigurement of the NT antitype.

original_text: The Paraclete, the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in my name, as proceeding also from me: and therefore Christ saith, in the next chapter, (ver. 26) that he himself will send him from the Father. He will teach you all things, etc. He will give you a more perfect knowledge of all those truths, which I have taught you. (Witham) --- Teach you all things. Here the Holy Ghost is promised to the apostles, and their successors, particularly, in order to teach them all truth, and to preserve them from error. (Challoner) --- The Scripture, in different places, remarks, that the apostles did not understand the accomplishment of prophecies, as soon as they were fulfilled. (Luke 24:27.) They could not draw the comparison between the actions of our Saviour, and the figures of the old law: but no sooner had the Holy Ghost descended upon them, than they explained the Scriptures, their hearts and eyes being opened and enlightened by the light of the Holy Spirit. (Calmet) --- See John 16:12-13.

extractions.type_name: Old Testament figures and laws (OT types generally)
extractions.type_description: The figures, actions, and legal institutions of the Old Testament that prefigured Christ and Christian truth
extractions.antitype_name: Jesus Christ and His fulfilled actions
extractions.antitype_description: The accomplishment and fulfillment of Old Testament prophecies and types in the person and work of Christ
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that apostles 'could not draw the comparison between the actions of our Saviour, and the figures of the old law' until the Holy Ghost enabled them. This directly describes typological interpretation—how OT figures (types) prefigure NT fulfillment in Christ (antitype). Calmet notes that the apostles explained the Scriptures by connecting OT figures to Christ's actions after Pentecost.

notes: This commentary discusses typology as a hermeneutical principle rather than identifying a specific individual type-antitype pair. The passage emphasizes that the Holy Spirit enabled the apostles to understand typological relationships that were previously obscure to them. The focus is on the interpretive role of the Spirit in discerning how OT prefigurations were fulfilled in Christ's ministry, making this a discussion about typological methodology rather than a particular type.

original_text: On account of our being in this world, we sometimes ask for that, which is not expedient for us. But these things will not be granted us, if we remain in Christ, who never grants us any thing, unless it be profitable to us. (St. Augustine, tract. 81. in Joan.) --- If we abide in Christ, by a lively faith, and his words abide in us by a lively, ardent charity, which can make us produce the fruits of good works, all that we ask, will be granted us. (Bible de Vence) --- These conditional expressions, if you remain in the vine, if you keep my commandments, etc. give us to understand, that our perseverance and salvation are upon conditions, to be fulfilled by us. --- (St. Augustine, de cor. et gra. John 13.)

extractions.type_description: The vineyard as a symbol of God's people Israel, cultivated and pruned by God, expected to bear fruit (Isaiah 5:1-7; Psalm 80:8-16)
extractions.antitype_name: Christ as the True Vine; believers as branches
extractions.antitype_description: In John 15:1-7, Jesus identifies himself as 'the true vine' and his disciples as branches. The relationship of abiding in Christ and bearing fruit fulfills and transforms the OT vineyard typology, with Christ replacing Israel as the true vine
extractions.reasoning: Jesus explicitly states 'I am the true vine' in John 15:1, which directly references and fulfills OT vineyard typology. The commentary's reference to 'remaining in the vine' and 'abiding in Christ' reinforces this typological transformation where the OT type (Israel as God's vineyard) finds its antitype in Christ as the true vine

notes: While the commentary itself does not explicitly mention OT typology, the verse being commented upon (John 15:7) is embedded in Jesus's vine discourse (John 15:1-8), which contains clear typological fulfillment of OT vineyard imagery. The Haydock commentary emphasizes the condition of 'abiding in Christ' and bearing fruit, which parallels the OT expectation that God's vineyard would produce good fruit. The typology is implicit rather than explicit in this particular commentary passage.

original_text: While I was with them, I kept them in thy name.{ Ver. 12. Cum essem, cum eis, etc. He speaks, says St. Chrysostom, as man, os anthropos dialegetai. (hom. pa. p. 480.) --- In the same place, nisi filius perditionis, ei me, etc. nisi, it is not, alla, sed. --- Non perdom, that is, says St. Chrysostom in the same place, quantum in me erit, non perdam ... non me impellente, vel relinguente: quod si spontè resiliant, non ex necessitate traham. ei de aph eauton apodedosi, pros anagken ouch elko. St. Augustine, Quomodo diabolus intravit in cor Judae, non intraret, nisi ille locum daret.|} He still speaks, says St. Chrysostom, as man, and after a human manner, by mentioning the advantage they seemed to enjoy, as long as he conversed visibly with them on earth, not that his invisible presence should be less beneficial to them. --- And none of them hath perished, except the son of perdition, the wretched Judas, whose fall was foretold in the Scriptures. (Psalm cviii.) He hath perished, that is, now is about being lost, by his own fault, says St. Chrysostom on this place. And St. Augustine on Psalm cxxxviii. How did the devil enter into the heart of Judas? he could not have entered, had not he given him place. (Witham) --- That the Scripture may be fulfilled: this does not any ways shew, that it was the will of God that Judas should be lost; but only that what happened to Judas was conformable to the prophecies, and not occasioned by them. Who will doubt, says St. Augustine, (lib. de Unit. Eccl. ch. IX.) but that Judas might, if he pleased, have abstained from betraying Christ. But God foretold it, because he foresaw clearly the future perversity of his disposition. (Calmet) --- See above, (chap. 13:18.) one of the principal passages of Scripture relative to the treachery of Judas, in which the traitor's crime had been predicted.

extractions.type_description: The Old Testament prophecy in Psalm 108 that foretold the betrayal and fall of one who would be lost, specifically the traitor among the chosen
extractions.antitype_description: The apostle of Jesus who betrayed Christ and fulfilled the OT prophecy by his own freely chosen perversity and spiritual loss
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that Judas's fall 'was foretold in the Scriptures (Psalm cviii)' and that 'what happened to Judas was conformable to the prophecies.' This represents a clear OT prefigurement (type) of an NT fulfillment (antitype), though notably one involving judgment rather than salvation. The prophecy anticipated the specific betrayer among Christ's chosen apostles.

notes: This is a typology of judgment rather than redemption. The commentary emphasizes that while God foreknew and foretold Judas's perversity, this foreknowledge did not cause his fall—Judas freely chose his own perdition. The typological connection is between the prophetic prediction in Psalm 108 and its historical fulfillment in Judas's betrayal of Christ. The reference to John 13:18 (noted in the commentary) provides the explicit connection between the OT prophecy and its NT fulfillment.

original_text: They made four parts. Christ's upper garment had seams, which the four executioners could easily divide; but his under garment, or vest, was without seam, so that being cut, it would have been of no use. (Witham) --- This coat without seam is a figure of the unity of the Church. (St. Cyprian, de unit. Eccles.) --- The Rev. Fred. Nolan, of Woodford, in Essex, in his late work, entitled, Objections of a Churchman to uniting with the Bible Society, after quoting 2 Peter 3:15, 16, says: "That the Bible may, therefore, prove the remote, but innocent cause of harm, is not, I apprehend, to be disputed, if we are to admit of its own authority:" p. 23, and again, p. 24, "that the present mode of circulating the Scriptures must prove a most effectual specific for multiplying sects and schisms; and consequently, for increasing, to an infinite degree, the greatest evil, under which Christianity has suffered, from the time of its promulgation, down to the memorable epoch of this happy invention, for the establishment of Christian faith, and the extension of Christian unanimity." P. 62., in the same work, "That the Bible is the foundation of our religion, is new doctrine, unless in the divinity of the conventicle. We are built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone. (Ephesians 2:20.) On this foundation others still build, who are labourers together with God; (1 Corinthians 11:9. 10.) of which divine co-operation the successors of the apostles have an express promise, to the end of the world. (Matthew 28:20.) And by persons thus authorized (John 20:21.) apostolical tradition has been delivered down to the present day, p. 63. The one body, of which our Lord was resolved his Church should consist, was to have one faith, (Ephesians 4:4, 5.) it was to contain no schism, (1 Corinthians 12:25.) but the present confederacy is formed on the principle of combining every sect and party, and this, while we have received an express prohibition against associating with those, who reject apostolical traditions, committed to the Church." (2 Thessalonians 3:6. 14.) In a foot-note on the above, the learned divine very appositely cites St. Ignatius, in which quotation we find these emphatic words: Me planasthe adelphoi mou, ei tis schizonti akolouthei, Basileian theou ou Kleronomei. Be not deceived, my brethren, not only acknowledged schismatics, but whoever shall join with a schismatic, shall not inherit the kingdom of God. The same apostolic Father, in another part, adds: he who corrupts the faith of God, for which Christ suffered, shall go into unquenchable fire: eis to pur to asbeston choresei. St. Alexander, in the fourth century, says of the Arians: that seamless garment, which the murderers of Jesus Christ would not divide, these men have dared to rip asunder. Tou arrekton chitona schisai eiolmesan.
notes: While the commentary does describe Christ's seamless garment as 'a figure of the unity of the Church' (attributed to St. Cyprian), this represents typological symbolism or allegory rather than classical biblical typology. The seamless garment is a New Testament object (Jesus's garment at the crucifixion in John 19:23) being interpreted symbolically to represent an ecclesial truth (Church unity). True typology requires an Old Testament type that prefigures a New Testament antitype. There is no Old Testament type presented here that prefigures the seamless garment or Church unity. The commentary uses the garment as a symbol or figure with spiritual significance, but does not establish an OT/NT typological relationship. The bulk of the commentary consists of a lengthy digression quoting Rev. Nolan on Bible societies and ecclesiastical authority, which contains no typological analysis whatsoever.

original_text: You shall not break a bone of him. This, which was literally spoken of the paschal lamb, (Exodus 12:46.) the evangelist applies to Christ, of whom the lamb was a figure. (Witham) --- This had been said of the paschal lamb, which was a figure of Jesus Christ. (Exodus 12:46.; Numbers 9:12.)

extractions.type_description: The lamb sacrificed during Passover in Exodus 12, whose bones were not to be broken according to the law (Exodus 12:46; Numbers 9:12)
extractions.antitype_description: Christ as the fulfillment of the Passover lamb, whose bones were not broken at his crucifixion (John 19:36)
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that the paschal lamb 'was a figure of Jesus Christ' and that the evangelist applies the literal Old Testament law about not breaking the lamb's bones to Christ. This is a direct type-antitype correspondence where the OT prefigurement is fulfilled in the NT antitype.

notes: This is one of the most explicit typological connections in the Gospel accounts. The Passover lamb was understood throughout Jewish tradition as prefiguring Christ, and John's Gospel deliberately uses this connection to interpret the crucifixion events. The detail about unbroken bones appears in all four gospels but is most emphasized by John with the explicit typological reference.

original_text: Simon Peter went up, and drew the net to land, full of great fishes, one hundred and fifty-three; a figure of the great number to be converted by the labours of the apostles. (Witham)
notes: This commentary describes a symbolic or allegorical interpretation rather than a typological relationship. The 153 fishes are presented as a figure or symbol of the great number to be converted by apostolic labor. However, this is not typology in the strict sense because: (1) there is no Old Testament type being referenced as a prefigurement, (2) the symbolic meaning is drawn directly from the narrative event itself (the miraculous catch) rather than from an OT person, event, or institution that prefigures an NT fulfillment, and (3) this represents allegorical or symbolic interpretation of a NT event, not an OT/NT typological connection. The commentary treats the fishing miracle as carrying spiritual significance about missionary success, but does not establish an OT type-antitype relationship.

original_text: The world{ Ver. 25. Nec ipsum arbitror mundum, etc. St. Cyril on this expression, p. 1123, uperbolikos. See St. Augustine at the end of his 124. tract. where he says, such hyperboles are found elsewhere in the holy Scripture.|} itself, I think, etc. It is an hyperbolical way of speaking, says St. Cyril, common enough, even in the holy Scriptures; and only signifies, that a very great number of things, which Christ did and said, have not been recorded. (Witham) --- This is a figure of speech, called hyperbole, and only means, that it would require many, many books, to contain all the various actions and sayings of our divine Lord.
notes: This Haydock commentary on John 21:25 discusses a literary device (hyperbole) rather than typology. The passage addresses the figurative nature of Christ's statement that the world itself could not contain all the books that would need to be written about His works. St. Cyril and St. Augustine are cited as explaining this as hyperbolic language common in Scripture. There is no reference to any Old Testament type prefiguring a New Testament antitype. The commentary is concerned with rhetorical analysis and the abundance of Christ's deeds, not with typological fulfillment.

original_text: A sound, etc. Perhaps this was a kind of thunder, accompanied with a great wind, which filled with terror and awe the whole company, and disposed them to receive the gift of heaven with humility and fervour. This noise appears to have been heard over a great part of the city, and to have gathered together a great crowd, who came to learn the cause. This noise and wind were symbols of the divinity. It was thus also that formerly on Mount Sinai, thunder and lightning, the dark cloud, the smoking mountain, etc. marked the majesty of God. (Calmet) --- Jesus Christ, our Pasch, to answer perfectly the figure, was offered on the day of the great Jewish passover; so fifty days after, for accomplishing the like figure of the law given on Mount Sinai, He sent down the Holy Ghost on the day of their Pentecost, which meaneth fifty. But our feasts, as St. Augustine remarks, besides the remembrance of benefits past, contain great mysteries also of the life to come. (Ep. cxix. Acts 16.)

extractions.type_name: The giving of the Law on Mount Sinai
extractions.type_description: The OT event where God gave the Law to Moses on Mount Sinai, marked by thunder, lightning, dark clouds, and a smoking mountain as symbols of God's majesty and divinity (Exodus 19-20)
extractions.antitype_name: The outpouring of the Holy Ghost at Pentecost
extractions.antitype_description: The NT event recorded in Acts 2:2 where the Holy Spirit is given to the disciples on the day of Pentecost (50 days after Passover), accompanied by a sound like a mighty rushing wind and other signs of divine presence
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly establishes this as a typological fulfillment: 'Jesus Christ, our Pasch...was offered on the day of the great Jewish passover; so fifty days after, for accomplishing the like figure of the law given on Mount Sinai, He sent down the Holy Ghost on the day of their Pentecost.' The parallel is structural (both at 50-day intervals from their respective starting events) and symbolic (both feature auditory/meteorological manifestations of God's presence and power).

extractions.type_description: The OT Jewish festival commemorating God's deliverance of Israel from Egypt, which prefigured Christ's redemptive work
extractions.antitype_name: Jesus Christ as the Pasch (Paschal Lamb)
extractions.antitype_description: Jesus Christ fulfilling the Passover type through His crucifixion and resurrection, which occurred on the day of the Jewish Passover
extractions.reasoning: The commentary states: 'Jesus Christ, our Pasch, to answer perfectly the figure, was offered on the day of the great Jewish passover.' This explicitly identifies Christ as the fulfillment of the Passover type, connecting His sacrificial death to the OT institution.

notes: The commentary presents a sophisticated typological framework where Pentecost mirrors Sinai (50 days after their respective foundational events), and both Christ's Passover sacrifice and the giving of the Spirit at Pentecost represent fulfillments of OT types. The commentary also notes that Christian feasts contain both commemorative and eschatological/future dimensions, suggesting typology extends beyond simple past-to-present prefigurement.

original_text: I will shew wonders, etc. These prodigies are commonly expounded of those that shall forerun the last day; or of the prognostics of the destruction of Jerusalem, which was a figure of the destruction of the world. (Witham) --- Blood, fire, etc. These prodigies were accomplished at our Saviour's death, or before the destruction of Jerusalem. We must not expect in these prophecies, where the descriptions are so grand, pathetic, and hyperbolical, to find that the accomplishment of them is literal, and precisely according to terms. The sun shall suffer an eclipse, the moon turn red, like blood, etc. (Calmet)

extractions.type_description: The historical destruction of Jerusalem as described in OT prophecy, involving signs, wonders, and cosmic disturbances
extractions.antitype_name: Destruction of the World / Last Day
extractions.antitype_description: The final eschatological destruction and judgment of the world at the end times, prefigured by Jerusalem's destruction
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that the destruction of Jerusalem 'was a figure of the destruction of the world.' This directly identifies Jerusalem's destruction as a typological prefigurement of the final eschatalogical judgment. The commentary notes that the prodigies (blood, fire, cosmic signs) described in Acts 2:19 are 'commonly expounded of those that shall forerun the last day' or of 'the prognostics of the destruction of Jerusalem.'

notes: The commentary emphasizes that in prophetic literature with 'grand, pathetic, and hyperbolical' descriptions, the accomplishment should not be expected to be 'literal, and precisely according to terms.' This suggests the typological relationship operates on a symbolic/thematic level rather than requiring precise literal correspondence. The passage also acknowledges fulfillment in Christ's death and the destruction of Jerusalem (70 AD), creating a multi-level eschatological typology.

original_text: But what I have, I give thee. Though St. Luke told us, (chap. 2:43.) that the apostles did many miracles and prodigies, yet this is the first specified. In the name of Jesus of Nazareth, (known by that name, though of Bethlehem) arise, and walk. In the name of Jesus, lately nailed to a cross. (Witham) --- This is not the shadow of a great name, magni nominis umbra, but the truth of what it signifies, a Saviour. Not without reason is this name in the Canticles compared to oil, in its three-fold properties, of affording light, food, and medicine. When preached, it enlightens; thought on, it feeds us; and called on, it assuages our grief. Whence has such a sudden light of faith spread over the world, but in preaching the name of Jesus? How did this light shine, and attract the eyes of all, when proceeding like lightning from the mouth of Peter, it strengthened the weakness of the lame man's feet, and enlightened the minds of many spiritually blind? Did he not then scatter fire, when he exclaimed, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, arise and walk? This name is food too. Are you not refreshed, as often as you recall it to your mind? What is as powerful in consoling the mind? What so soon repairs our wearied senses, and gives new vigour to our strength; encourages virtues, cherishes chaste affections? All food is dry to me, if not seasoned with this oil; insipid, unless sprinkled with this salt. If you write, I relish it not, unless I read the name of Jesus. If your read, or speak, I take no pleasure in it, unless I hear the name of Jesus. Jesus is honey in the mouth, music to the ear, but ecstasy to the heart. This is also my medicine. Are you sad? let Jesus enter your heart, and thence ascend upon your tongue. And behold, at the rising of this star, every cloud will retire, and serenity return. Do you fall into a crime, or run on the brink of despair: call on this name of life, and you shall be restored to life, etc. (St. Bernard, Serm. xv. super Cant. propè medium.)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Acts 3:6 focuses primarily on symbolic and allegorical interpretation of the NAME OF JESUS rather than typological connections. The commentary extensively develops the metaphorical properties of Jesus's name (light, food, medicine) drawn from the Song of Canticles (Songs of Solomon), but this represents symbolic exegesis and spiritual allegory, not typology. Typology requires an explicit Old Testament type that prefigures a New Testament antitype; this passage instead applies poetic symbolism from an OT wisdom book to enhance understanding of a NT reality (the power of Jesus's name). The reference to the Song of Canticles is used for its metaphorical language, not as a type-antitype relationship. The miracle itself (healing the lame beggar) is not presented as typologically fulfilling any OT type.

original_text: Which will not hear that prophet. St. Peter's argument is this. If disobedience to the ordinances of God by the voice of Moses, was punishable with death, how much more severe will be the punishment of those, who refuse obedience to the doctrines of Jesus, to whom all the prophets bore testimony, and whom the apostles then preached. How different is this system of submission to the teaching of the prophets, and apostles, from that libertinism, which undermines the whole fabric of religion, by taking away from the Church the power of commanding, and from the disciple the necessity of obeying. By what wonderful and progressive shades of light was the prediction of this great prophet made to man! From the fall of Adam, it was predicted, that the seed of the woman would crush the serpent's head. Many ages after, God manifested that from Abraham's loins the Redeemer should spring, "in whom all nations should be blessed." The promise is renewed to Isaac, and that he is to spring from his son, but not from Esau, but from Jacob; and of the twelve sons of Jacob, the posterity of Juda is to have the privilege of bestowing a Messias to the world, and the token of its accomplishment is, "the failure of the sceptre in the posterity of Juda." After a long series of events, and of ages, an humble shepherd is chosen in the tribe of Juda: he is led to the throne; and to this man, David, it is repeated, that from him the Messias shall spring, and that his kingdom shall have no end. The oracle is so explicit in the psalms of that king, and in the writings of successive prophets, that it not only expresses the race, the tribe, the family, but also the character of the mother, the place of his birth, the precise period of the event, the ministry, the power, the dignity, the circumstances of his death, the change of the covenant, and conversion of the world. The particular prophecies, in their accomplishment, were a visible earnest to the Jews of the accomplishment of the prophecies relative to the Messias. Hence Pascal very justly remarks: "The prophets mingle particular prophecies with those of the Messias; that the prophecies regarding the Messias may not be without proof, and that the particular prophecies may not be without effect." (Pensées. xv.) --- These oracles, which during a period of four thousand years, have been delivered to the world, and which have been completely and visibly fulfilled, still exist in books, scrupulously preserved by the greatest enemies of Christ, and of his holy religion, and satisfactorily demonstrate Jesus Christ to be the great prophet, and the Christian religion to be the new covenant, which had been announced so many ages before, in so many different manners.

extractions.type_description: The Old Testament prophets, particularly Moses, who delivered God's ordinances and commands to Israel, with disobedience punishable by death
extractions.antitype_name: Jesus Christ as the Great Prophet
extractions.antitype_description: Jesus as the ultimate prophet whose doctrines demand obedience, with greater severity of punishment for those who reject His teachings
extractions.reasoning: St. Peter explicitly argues a progressive fulfillment: obedience to Moses prefigured and foreshadowed the greater obedience required to Jesus. The commentary establishes Jesus as the culmination of the prophetic office, with heightened authority and consequent penalty for disobedience.

extractions.type_name: The Seed of the Woman and Patriarchal Promises (Adam, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Judah, David)
extractions.type_description: A series of Old Testament prophecies and promises progressively narrowing from humanity to Abraham's seed, to Jacob's descendants, to the tribe of Judah, to David's line, detailing the Messiah's race, tribe, family, birthplace, time, ministry, death, and covenant change
extractions.antitype_name: Jesus Christ and the New Covenant
extractions.antitype_description: Jesus as the complete fulfillment of all messianic prophecies; His incarnation, ministry, death, resurrection, and establishment of the new covenant that converts the world
extractions.reasoning: The commentary presents an explicit typological progression spanning 4,000 years, where particular OT prophecies and promises find their complete antitype in Jesus Christ and the Christian dispensation. The detailed catalog of fulfilled messianic predictions demonstrates classical typological fulfillment.

extractions.type_name: The Old Covenant (Mosaic Law and Prophetic System)
extractions.type_description: The system of God's revelation through Moses and the prophets, involving submission to divine ordinances and teaching
extractions.antitype_name: The New Covenant (Christian Religion and Apostolic Teaching)
extractions.antitype_description: The new system of revelation and redemption through Jesus Christ and the apostles, requiring obedience to Christ's doctrines and inaugurating a transformed relationship between God and humanity
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that the change of covenant was predicted in the OT prophecies and fulfilled in the NT. The old prophetic system prefigured the new apostolic proclamation of Christ, representing a covenantal transition from Moses to Jesus.

notes: This commentary is rich with typological content. St. Peter's argument itself is fundamentally typological: he uses the pattern of obedience to Moses as a type prefiguring the greater obligation to obey Jesus. The broader historical narrative traces how particular OT predictions served as 'earnests' (proof) that messianic prophecies would also be fulfilled, making typology central to the apologetic argument.

original_text: On ... couches, meaner beds for the poorer sort. --- That Peter's shadow, etc. Thus was partly fulfilled what Christ had foretold, (John 14:12.) that his disciples should do even greater miracles than he had done. (Witham) --- St. Ambrose compares with these miracles wrought by St. Peter's shadow, those which the linen cloths, that had touched the relics of the holy martyrs, also wrought. (Epis. liv.) Si inanis quaedam species vacuae imaginis habere potuit in se vim salutis, quanto plus de corpore meruerunt attrahere salubritatis sacris impressa membris vincula passionis? If the empty appearance of an unsubstantial shadow possessed the power of giving health, how much more efficacy must the chains of the martyrs have drawn from the holy members, which they bound? --- In appendice operum. (St. Augustine, serm. cciii.) --- St Augustine, speaking of the miracle performed by the saints now reigning in heaven, says: "If the shadow of Peter's body could afford help, how much more now the fulness of his power? And if then a certain little wind of him, passing by, did profit them that humbly asked, how much more the grace of him, now being permanent and remaining?" (Serm. xxxix. de sanctis.)
notes: This commentary discusses miracles performed through St. Peter's shadow and relics of martyrs in the apostolic period, but does not establish any Old Testament type prefiguring these New Testament antitypes. The commentary makes three main points: (1) fulfillment of Jesus's promise in John 14:12 that disciples would perform great miracles, (2) comparison between Peter's shadow and relics of martyrs as channels of healing power, and (3) reflection on the increasing efficacy of the saints' intercession. While the text contains figurative language ('shadow,' 'chains,' 'grace'), these are not typological connections. The commentary is concerned with apostolic signs and wonders, sacramental efficacy of relics, and the power of saints' intercession—none of which involve Old Testament types prefiguring New Testament antitypes.

original_text: Moses, whom they refused. Literally, denied. So have you rejected, and denied Jesus, of whom Moses prophesied, when he said that God would raise up to them a prophet like to himself, and commanded them to hear him. (Witham) --- Redeemer. In the Greek Lutroten; Protestant version, Deliverer; though the learned Polus, in his Synopsis Criticorum, on this place, says, "that no greater injury is done to God, by calling Moses a Redeemer, in this place, than by calling him a Mediator, in Galatians 3:19. He is called a Redeemer, says this learned Protestant commentator, in as much as he led forth, and preserved the people of God safe by the blood of a lamb, and thus exhibited a figure of the true redemption, through the blood of Christ." We all own that Jesus Christ, as having paid the ransom of our delivery with his own blood, is, strictly speaking, our only true Redeemer, and Advocate with his Father, who asks and obtains all things immediately by his own merit; but this does not exclude the prayers of the saints, both alive and dead. Did not the apostles pray for the people, and desire the people to pray for them? "Our Lord Jesus Christ still intercedes for us, and all the martyrs that are with him, pray for us: nor will their intercession cease, till we cease our groanings," says St. Augustine, in Ps. lxxxv. in fine.

extractions.type_description: Moses, who led the people of God out of Egypt, preserved them safe, and was associated with the blood of the Passover lamb that secured their deliverance
extractions.antitype_name: Jesus Christ as the True Redeemer
extractions.antitype_description: Jesus Christ, who paid the ransom of humanity's delivery with his own blood, serving as the true and ultimate Redeemer and Mediator between God and humanity
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that Moses 'exhibited a figure of the true redemption, through the blood of Christ.' It directly connects Moses's redemptive role (delivering Israel through the blood of the lamb) to Christ's redemptive work (paying the ransom through his own blood). This is a clear type-antitype relationship where the OT figure prefigures the NT fulfillment.

extractions.type_description: Moses, whom God promised to raise up as a prophet that the people should hear, prefiguring a future prophet to come
extractions.antitype_description: Jesus Christ, the ultimate Prophet whom God raised up, to whom people are commanded to listen and obey
extractions.reasoning: The commentary references Deuteronomy 18:15, where Moses prophesied that God would raise up a prophet like himself whom the people must hear. This is applied directly to Jesus Christ as the fulfillment of that prophecy. The commentary emphasizes that by rejecting Moses, the audience rejected Jesus, of whom Moses prophesied.

notes: The commentary also discusses intercessory prayer and the role of saints, but this is not typological in nature—it is doctrinal rather than a prefigurement of OT to NT realities. The primary typological content concerns Moses as a type of Christ in his dual roles as Redeemer (through the blood of the Passover lamb) and as Prophet.

original_text: Why dost thou persecute me? My disciples, my brothers, and my friends. The head speaks for the members, and by a figure of speech, calls them itself. (St. Augustine, in Ps. xxx.) --- Here Jesus Christ identifies himself with his Church, as on a former occasion, when he said: he that heareth you, heareth me; and he that despiseth you, despiseth me. (Luke 10:16.)
notes: This commentary describes a theological principle of identification and solidarity between Christ and his Church (the 'head and members' doctrine), but does not establish a typological relationship between an Old Testament type and New Testament antitype. The commentary explains how Jesus Christ mystically identifies with his disciples through a figure of speech, drawing on Pauline theology (the body of Christ metaphor). While this reflects biblical typological thinking in a broader sense, it does not present an OT person, event, or institution prefiguring this NT reality. The reference to St. Augustine's interpretation of Psalm 30 is exegetical/theological rather than typological in the strict sense. To be typological, the commentary would need to identify a specific OT type (e.g., 'the head of a household represents its members') that prefigures Christ's identification with the Church as its antitype.

original_text: Washed. This custom of washing the dead was observed among the Greeks, Romans, Hebrews, and most other nations. It is still practised in monasteries, and formerly was observed with much ceremony. St. Chrysostom observes, that our Saviour's body was washed and embalmed. The same custom is mentioned in Homer and Virgil: Corpusque lavant frigentis, et ungunt. --- And again, Date, vulnera lymphis abluam. --- Aeneid. 4:--- Tertullian, in his Apology, testifies, that the Christians performed that office to the dead. It was a proof of their respect for the image of God impressed upon his creature, and for the character of Christian, which these persons have borne during their lives. It was likewise a sign of the confidence they had in a future resurrection.
notes: This Haydock commentary discusses the historical and cultural practice of washing the dead body of Tabitha (Dorcas) in Acts 9:37. While the commentary mentions that Christ's body was washed and embalmed, this reference is presented as a historical parallel or analogy rather than as a typological prefigurement. The commentary focuses on: (1) the widespread ancient custom of washing corpses among various cultures, (2) the symbolic significance of the practice as a sign of respect for God's image and Christian character, and (3) its expression of belief in resurrection. No Old Testament type is presented as prefiguring this New Testament event or practice. The mention of Christ's body being washed is illustrative of the custom's importance rather than establishing an OT/NT typological relationship.

original_text: Stated hours for prayer were appointed both in the old and new law. Of this St. Cyprian writes: "In celebrating their prayers, we find that the three children of Daniel observed the third, sixth, and ninth hour. Thus afterwards, at the third hour, the Holy Ghost descended upon the apostles, fulfilling the grace of our Lord's promise: at the sixth hour, Peter going up to the higher room of the house, was both by voice and sign from God instructed, that all nations should be admitted to the grace of salvation, of which he before doubted; and our Lord being crucified at the sixth hour, at the ninth washed away our sins by his blood. But to us, besides the seasons observed of old, the set times of praying are increased; for we must pray in the morning early, that the resurrection of our Lord may be celebrated by morning prayer; in the morning early will I stand before Thee, early in the morning wilt thou hear my voice. (Psalm v.) Towards the evening also, when the sun departeth, we must of necessity pray again." (De Orat. Dom. No. 15) St. Jerome, writing to Eustochia, a virgin, and a religious, (ep. 22.) says, "though the apostle bid us to pray always, and, to holy persons, their very sleep is prayer; yet we must have distinct hours for prayer, that if perhaps we be otherwise occupied, the very time may admonish us of our duty. The third, sixth, ninth hour, morning early, and evening, no man can be ignorant of."

extractions.type_name: The Three Children of Daniel praying at the third, sixth, and ninth hours
extractions.type_description: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego observing fixed hours of prayer (third, sixth, and ninth hours) as established practice in the Old Testament
extractions.antitype_name: The Apostles and Peter praying at appointed hours in the New Testament
extractions.antitype_description: The fulfillment of prayer at these same hours: Holy Ghost descending at the third hour (Acts 2:15), Peter receiving the vision at the sixth hour (Acts 10:9), and Christ's crucifixion and redemptive work at the sixth and ninth hours
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that the OT practice of prayer at specific hours by Daniel's three children 'fulfilled' or prefigured the NT fulfillment of grace at those same hours. St. Cyprian directly connects the OT observance to subsequent NT events as fulfillment of an earlier pattern.

extractions.type_name: Christ's crucifixion at the sixth hour and death at the ninth hour
extractions.type_description: The timing of Christ's passion and the shedding of His blood for redemption at the ninth hour
extractions.antitype_name: The washing away of sins through Christ's blood
extractions.antitype_description: The redemptive fulfillment whereby Christ's sacrifice at the ninth hour accomplished the atonement for all sins
extractions.reasoning: While this is more directly about Christ's redemptive work than a type-antitype relationship in the classical sense, the commentary frames the crucifixion timing as fulfilling the grace promised through the earlier pattern of prayer hours, making it part of the typological schema being presented.

notes: The primary typology here is the pattern-fulfillment relationship between OT prayer practice (Daniel's three children) and NT fulfillment events occurring at those same appointed hours. This is somewhat unconventional typology as it involves the recurrence of a temporal pattern rather than a person or object prefiguring a future reality. The commentary is attributed to St. Cyprian and emphasizes how established prayer disciplines of the old law found their completion and deepened meaning in the new law through specific historical events in the apostolic age.

original_text: There was a dissension,{ Ver. 39. Dissentio, paroxusmos, acris disceptatio. See. St. Chrysostom.|} or dispute, with reasoning, and arguing upon the matter. St. Paul represented to St. Barnabas, that he was not for having John Mark to be their companion, because he had before left them, but St. Barnabas was for having with them his kinsman Mark; and the dispute was such, that upon it St. Paul and Barnabas separated; which gave occasion to the preaching of the gospel in more places. See St. Chrysostom, hom. xxxiii. --- The fault in this contention lay with St. Barnabas; o Paulos to dikaion, o Barnabas to philanthropon: Paul sought what was just; Barnabas what was pleasing to nature. The Greeks, moreover, remark, that this severity of Paul was of service in strengthening the too pliant character of Mark, and as such he is saluted by Paul. (Colossians 4:10.) They separated, as formerly Abraham and Lot, without prejudice to their friendship. (Genesis 13:9.) (Mat. Polus, synop. criticorum, fol. 4. p. 1528.)

extractions.type_description: Abraham and Lot separated their ways in Genesis 13:9 due to strife between their herdsmen, yet maintained their familial relationship and friendship despite the division
extractions.antitype_description: Paul and Barnabas separated their missionary partnership in Acts 15:39 due to their dispute over John Mark, yet maintained their Christian fellowship without prejudice to their friendship
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly draws a parallel comparison between the two separations: 'They separated, as formerly Abraham and Lot, without prejudice to their friendship.' Both involve division of labor/mission while preserving the underlying relationship. This illustrates how God can use even contentious separations to advance His purposes (Abraham and Lot's separation led to both being blessed; Paul and Barnabas's separation led to gospel preaching in more places). The typology is ecclesial in nature as it demonstrates principles of Church community and missionary endeavor.

notes: The typological reference here is relatively modest and illustrative rather than deeply theological. The commentary uses the Abraham-Lot precedent primarily to show that such separations can occur 'without prejudice to friendship' and that God uses them for His purposes. This is an implicit typology where the OT pattern illustrates and validates the NT event, rather than an explicit prophecy-fulfillment typology.

original_text: To the Areopagus. In this place sat the Athenian judges: but some think that by this word may be here signified, some large hall or court, joining to the Areopagus, where all sorts of people met. (Witham) --- The Areopagus was the supreme and most famous tribunal of all Greece, before which all great causes were tried. The persons who composed it were much renowned for their wisdom. Cicero, and many other Romans, were ambitious of the honour of being an Areopagite; but the power of Athens being now much diminished, this court had sunk in importance, and was now not much more than the shadow of a great name. (Calmet)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Acts 17:19 provides historical and geographical information about the Areopagus as a physical location and judicial institution in Athens. It discusses the nature of the tribunal, its composition, its prestige in Greek and Roman society, and its diminished status at the time of Paul's visit. While the passage describes an important setting for Paul's evangelistic address, the commentary contains no explicit or implicit typological connections between Old Testament persons, events, or institutions and New Testament fulfillments. This is descriptive/historical commentary rather than typological analysis.

original_text: Cherubim, with extended wings, were ordered by God to be made, and placed over the propitiatory; (Exodus 37:7.) the brazen serpent is declared by Jesus Christ himself to have been a figure of him; therefore to blame the universally received practice of the Catholic Church, with regard to pictures and images, betrays either great prevention, or great ignorance. St. Gregory says: "What writing does for readers, that a picture does for the ignorant; for in it they see what they ought to follow, and in it they read, who know no letters." And he sharply rebukes Serenus's indiscreet zeal for removing pictures, instead of teaching the people what use may be made of them. (lib. ix. ep. 9.)

extractions.type_description: The bronze serpent made by Moses and lifted up in the wilderness (Numbers 21:8-9) as a means of healing for the Israelites bitten by serpents
extractions.antitype_description: Christ lifted up on the cross as the means of salvation and spiritual healing for all people
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that Jesus Christ himself declared the brazen serpent to be 'a figure of him.' This is a direct typological connection affirmed by Christ in John 3:14-15, where Jesus explicitly compares his crucifixion to the lifting up of the serpent in the wilderness.

notes: The commentary also mentions the Cherubim with extended wings over the propitiatory (mercy seat), but this reference does not establish a clear OT-to-NT typological relationship in the text provided—it is cited to support the legitimacy of Christian art and images, not as a prefigurement of something in the New Testament. The primary focus of the passage is the brazen serpent typology, which is explicitly affirmed by Christ himself.

original_text: Aprons. It is likely such as he used in working, cured diseases, and cast out devils. What wonder, then, if God work miracles by the relics of martyrs and saints, to testify the sanctity of his servants, and to encourage others both to give them a reasonable honour, and to imitate their lives? (Witham) --- Thus was fulfilled the promise which Christ had made his disciples, viz. that they should perform greater miracles than he himself had done. St. Chrysostom repeats more than once, that these clothes raised the dead, and that the apostles' shadow chased away all maladies, and triumphed over death. Perhaps the unprejudiced reader may observe in this verse some reason for paying due regard to the relics, or whatever has belonged to the saints.
notes: This commentary discusses the miraculous power of apostolic relics and objects (aprons, shadows) in Acts 19:12, but does not establish any typological connection between Old Testament types and New Testament antitypes. The passage references Christ's promise to his disciples about performing greater miracles, which is a direct NT promise rather than an OT/NT typological prefigurement. The commentary's discussion of honoring saints' relics and the general principle that God works miracles through holy objects involves symbolism and theological principle, but not typology as technically defined (OT person/event/institution prefiguring NT fulfillment). The mention of relics of martyrs and saints is devotional rather than typological in nature.

original_text: Who made silver temples for Diana.{ Ver. 24. Aedes argenteas, naous argurous.|} Perhaps figures of Diana's temple in silver; or boxes and shrines, in which was the statue or figure of Diana. (Witham)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Acts 19:24 discusses the material practice of Demetrius the silversmith making silver shrines of Diana (Artemis) in Ephesus. The commentary focuses on the literal, historical meaning of these objects—whether they were figurines, boxes, or shrines containing statues—rather than exploring any typological prefigurement from the Old Testament. This is a historical-descriptive commentary without typological analysis. No Old Testament type is identified that would prefigure these New Testament-era pagan religious artifacts.

original_text: Great is Diana of the Ephesians. This they shouted out without intermission for about two hours, though the greatest part knew not why they had met together. A true representation of an unthinking rash mob. (Witham)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Acts 19:28 focuses on a sociological observation about mob behavior and religious fervor without rational understanding. The commentary criticizes the Ephesians for shouting about Diana 'without intermission for about two hours, though the greatest part knew not why they had met together,' and characterizes them as 'an unthinking rash mob.' This is a moral/ethical commentary on human nature and crowd psychology, not a typological analysis connecting Old Testament persons, events, or institutions to New Testament fulfillments. No OT type/NT antitype relationship is presented or implied in the text.

original_text: The town-clerk, etc. Literally, the scribe, or the recorder of the city. --- Jupiter's offspring.{ Ver. 35. Jovisque prolis, kai tou diopetous. Simulachri a caelo dilapsi. See Suidas.|} His daughter, according to the poets. The Greek text seems to signify a statue, or figure of Diana, which was pretended to have fallen from heaven, and from Jupiter. (Witham) --- Is a worshipper. Neokoron ousan; the word Neokoros is found in this sense in the Arundelian marbles, and more frequently on ancient coins and inscriptions. Its derivation is from neos, a temple, and kore, a virgin, or rather korein, to cleanse and decorate; as if this city were especially destined to ornament the Diana of Ephesus, which the people supposed came to them not by the work of man, but a present from heaven.
notes: This Haydock commentary on Acts 19:35 discusses the town-clerk of Ephesus and provides historical/linguistic analysis of pagan religious practices in Ephesus, specifically regarding the cult of Diana and a purported statue that fell from heaven. The commentary focuses on: (1) the definition and role of the town-clerk (neokoros); (2) the etymology of Greek terms; and (3) the cultural/religious context of Diana worship in Ephesus. No typological relationships connecting Old Testament persons, events, or institutions to their New Testament fulfillments are present or discussed. This is purely historical and linguistic commentary on a New Testament narrative passage without reference to prefigurative OT types.

original_text: I knew not, etc. Some think St. Paul here speaks ironically, or to signify that now he could be no longer high priest, since the Mosaic law, with its rites and ceremonies, was abolished. But St. Chrysostom rather judges that St. Paul, having been long absent from Jerusalem, might not know the person of the high priest, who was not now in the sanhedrim but in the place whither the tribune had called the council, and who did not appear with that habit, and those marks which distinguished him from others. (Witham) --- It seems rather surprising that St. Paul did not know that he was the high priest. The place which he held in the council, one would suppose, would have been sufficient to have pointed him out. The apostle's absence from Jerusalem is perhaps a sufficient reason to account for his not knowing this circumstance; especially, as the order of succession to the priesthood was at that time much confused and irregular, determined by favour of the Roman emperor, or by purchase. (Calmet) --- At all events, any difficulties we may now find in assigning a probable or true reason, are merely negative arguments; and therefore too futile to be an impeachment of the apostle's veracity. (Haydock) --- St. Cyprian supposes that St. Paul, considering the mere shadow of the name of priest, which Ananias then held, said: I knew not, brethren, that he is high priest. (Ep. 65:69. nu. 2.) St. Chrysostom says, that the apostle here shews the wisdom of the serpent; but that in his preaching, teaching, and patience, he used the simplicity of the dove.

extractions.type_name: The Mosaic Priesthood and its Temple Rites
extractions.type_description: The Old Testament system of priesthood with its ceremonies, rituals, and distinguishing marks (habits, signs of office) that identified the high priest under the Mosaic law
extractions.antitype_name: The Abolition of the Levitical Priesthood in Christ
extractions.antitype_description: The New Testament fulfillment in which Christ's sacrifice renders the Mosaic law, its rites, ceremonies, and priesthood obsolete. The high priest no longer holds the essential typological significance he once did.
extractions.reasoning: St. Cyprian's comment (cited in the commentary) explicitly states that Ananias held 'the mere shadow of the name of priest,' indicating the Mosaic priesthood is now reduced to a shadow—a classic typological vocabulary indicating that the OT type has been fulfilled and superseded in the NT. The commentary notes 'the Mosaic law, with its rites and ceremonies, was abolished,' which is the direct fulfillment formula of typology.

notes: This is a typology of fulfillment and supersession rather than prefigurement. The OT Mosaic priesthood is the type; its NT antitype is its own abolition through Christ's priesthood and sacrifice (see Hebrews 7-10). St. Cyprian's reference to the high priest as a 'shadow' is particularly significant—the word 'shadow' (σκιά) is key typological language indicating an OT type that has been fulfilled and made obsolete in the NT.

original_text: That Christ should suffer, etc. Literally, if Christ be passible. If, here is expounded not as implying a condition, but as an affirmation; so that the sense is, that Christ, according to the predictions of the prophets, was to suffer, was to be the first that should rise from the dead, etc. (Witham) --- First, etc. Many had been raised from the dead before Jesus; the child of the widow of Sarepta, Lazarus, and others. How, then, is Jesus first? He is the first who rises not to die again; and as such the Messias is always represented by the prophets. Others were raised from the dead, but returned again to their graves. Jesus dies no more. He is the first too who raises himself. (Calmet)

extractions.type_name: The raising of the dead in the Old Testament (e.g., the widow's son at Zarephath, Lazarus)
extractions.type_description: Various Old Testament and pre-resurrection instances of people being raised from the dead, who subsequently returned to their graves and died again
extractions.antitype_description: Christ's resurrection as the first and unique resurrection to eternal life, never to die again; He alone raises Himself and represents the Messiah's perpetual victory over death
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly contrasts OT resurrections (Zarephath widow's son, Lazarus, etc.) with Christ's resurrection as the fulfillment of messianic prophecy. The distinction is that earlier raisings were temporary (recipients died again), whereas Christ's resurrection is permanent and self-initiated, making it the antitype that fulfills what the prophets predicted about the Messiah. This represents Christ as the ultimate and archetypal resurrection.

notes: The commentary uses the principle of progressive revelation: earlier resurrections in Scripture prefigure but do not fully embody the reality of Christ's resurrection. The typological relationship hinges on the qualitative difference—Christ's resurrection is not merely a return to mortal life (like Lazarus) but an entry into eternal, glorified existence, making it the true fulfillment of what earlier raisings foreshadowed. Calmet's point about Jesus being 'first who raises himself' adds a Christological dimension emphasizing Christ's divine agency.

original_text: Do we then destroy the law through faith? No: but we establish the law. See the words of Christ: (Matthew 5:17.) 1. Because the figures and types of the law of Moses, and the predictions of the prophets, are fulfilled. 2. Because Christians are now taught to fulfil the moral precepts, and the chief part of the law, with greater perfection, in the spirit of faith, charity, etc. (Witham)

extractions.type_name: The Figures and Types of the Law of Moses
extractions.type_description: The Old Testament ceremonial, sacrificial, and institutional practices of the Mosaic Law that functioned as prefigurative symbols
extractions.antitype_description: Jesus Christ as the fulfillment of the ceremonial types, and Christians practicing the moral law with spiritual perfection through faith and charity
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that 'figures and types of the law of Moses...are fulfilled' in connection with Christ's words (Matthew 5:17), establishing a direct OT type to NT antitype relationship. The ceremonial law's types prefigure Christ's redemptive work.

extractions.type_description: Old Testament prophetic utterances and messianic expectations
extractions.antitype_name: The Fulfillment in Christ and the Christian Era
extractions.antitype_description: The realization of prophetic promises through Christ's coming and the establishment of the Christian faith
extractions.reasoning: The commentary identifies prophetic predictions as types that are 'fulfilled,' indicating they prefigured their NT fulfillment in Christ and the Christian dispensation, consistent with typological interpretation.

notes: The commentary emphasizes two aspects of how faith 'establishes' rather than destroys the law: (1) through typological fulfillment of OT types and predictions, and (2) through the spiritual fulfillment of moral precepts. The reference to Matthew 5:17 confirms the typological framework being employed.

original_text: etc. I lived some time without the law; that is without the knowledge of the law. This some understand of St. Paul in the time of his childhood, before he came to the knowledge of what was forbidden by any law. But the exposition, which agrees with the rest of this chapter, is this; that St. Paul, though he seems to speak of himself, yet represents the condition of any person that lived before the written law was given: but when the commandment came, after that the written law was given, and its precepts came to my knowledge, then sin revived, by giving me a perfect knowledge: and by transgressing those precepts, I became more guilty and without excuse. --- I died: that is became guilty by transgression of the known law, and guilty of eternal death: and the commandments or precepts, which were unto life, which were good in themselves, and designed to direct me what I was to do, and what I was to avoid in order to obtain eternal life, were found to be unto death to me, but by my own fault; and occasionally only, from the commandments of the law and the knowledge of them, when with full knowledge I transgressed them. Thus I was seduced by sin, which with it brought death, though the law and the commandment (ver. 12) were in themselves holy, and just, and good. They could not but be good, as St. Chrysostom says, their author being the true God, and not any evil principle or cause, that was the author of evils, as the impious Manicheans pretended. We might as well, says St. Chrysostom, find fault with the tree of life [the tree of knowledge of good and evil?] and the forbidden fruit in Paradise, which was not the cause, but only the occasion of our misery, when Adam eat of it. It cannot then be said, that that which was good, (to wit, the law ) was made death to me, or the cause of my death; but sin, and my unresisted sinful inclinations, that it might appear sin, or that it might evidently appear how great an evil sin is, by that which is good, (that is, by the transgression of the law which is good) wrought and brought death to me, that by the occasion of the precepts given and known, sin might become sinful above measure. He speaks of sin as it were of a certain person; and the sense is, that sin, which was in my corrupt nature, might become sinful above measure, when it led me into all manner of disorders and excess, which I yielded to. (Witham)

extractions.type_name: Adam's transgression in Paradise / The tree of knowledge of good and evil
extractions.type_description: Adam's eating of the forbidden fruit in Genesis 3, which brought knowledge of good and evil and resulted in death and guilt through transgression of God's commandment
extractions.antitype_name: Paul's (and humanity's) experience under the written law
extractions.antitype_description: The condition of those who receive the written law and through knowledge of its precepts become aware of sin, guilt, and spiritual death when they transgress
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly compares Adam's experience with the forbidden fruit to Paul's experience with the law: both involve a commandment given by God, both result in death through transgression, and both show how a good thing (the tree/the law) becomes the occasion for death through human sin. The parallel suggests Adam's fall under the original commandment prefigures humanity's condemnation under the written law at Sinai.

notes: This is a somewhat implicit typology drawn by St. Chrysostom (cited in the commentary) rather than being the primary focus of the Haydock commentary itself. The commentary is primarily exegetical, explaining Romans 7:9 as describing either Paul's personal experience or the human condition generally before and after the written law. The typological connection appears as an illustrative analogy rather than as explicit typological doctrine. The confidence is marked 'medium' because while the parallel is drawn, it functions more as explanatory analogy than formal typological interpretation.

original_text: I am carnal, sold under sin, a slave subject to sinful inclinations, which are only properly sins when they are consented to by our free-will. There has been a great dispute both among the ancient and later interpreters, whether St. Paul from this verse to the end of the chapter speaks of a person remaining in sin, either under the law of nature or of the written law, (which was once the opinion of St. Augustine) or whether he speaks of a person regenerated by baptism, and in the state of grace in the new law, and even of himself when he was a faithful servant of God. This is the opinion of St. Augustine in many of his later writings against the Pelagians, for which he also cites St. Hilary, St. Gregory of Nazianzus, and St. Ambrose. It is also the opinion of St. Jerome, (Ep. ad Eustochium de custod. Virg.) of St. Gregory the great, of Ven. Bede, and the more approved opinion, according to which the apostle here by sin does not understand that which is properly speaking a sin, or sinful, but only speaks of sin improperly such, that is of a corrupt inclination, of a rebellious nature corrupted by original sin, of a strife betwixt the spirit and the flesh, which remains for a trial in the most virtuous persons: of which see again St. Paul, Galatians 5:17. We may take notice that the apostle before spoke of what he was and what he had been, but now speaks in the present time of what he is, and what he doth. (Witham) --- The law is styled spiritual: 1st, because it prescribes what appertains to the spirit, and to the spiritual man: that is to follow virtue and shun vice: 2nd, because it directs man to the worship of God, which is spirit and truth: 3rd, because it cannot be fulfilled by spiritual men, unless by spirit and grace: 4th, because it directs the spirit of man and disposes him properly towards God, towards his neighbour, and towards himself: and lastly, because the law spiritually received and understood, leads and prepares men for the evangelical law, which is the law of grace and spirit. (Menochius)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Romans 7:14 focuses on exegetical debate regarding Paul's spiritual condition (whether he speaks as an unregenerate or regenerate person) and the nature of the Law as spiritual. The commentary discusses the internal conflict between flesh and spirit, the fulfillment of the Law through grace, and the transition from the written law to the evangelical law of grace. While the commentary mentions the relationship between the old written law and the new evangelical law, this represents covenantal progression or fulfillment rather than typological prefiguration. No explicit typological connections between OT persons, events, or institutions and their NT fulfillments are presented in this passage.

original_text: That the justification of the law. That is, that was aimed at, but never attained to, by the written law, might now be fulfilled in us; that is, that we, by the grace of Christ, may be enabled to fulfil and comply with the law, and its moral precepts, by walking according to the spirit of Christ. (Witham)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Romans 8:4 discusses the fulfillment of the law through Christ's grace, but it does not establish a typological relationship between an Old Testament type and New Testament antitype. Rather, it presents a theological contrast: the written law of the Old Testament aimed at justification but could not achieve it, whereas Christ's grace in the New Testament enables believers to fulfill the law's moral precepts through the Holy Spirit. This is a matter of supersession and enablement through grace, not typological prefigurement. The commentary focuses on the functional relationship between law and grace rather than on how an OT person, event, or institution prefigures a specific NT reality.

original_text: etc. They are the sons of God, by this new grace of adoption, by which also they call God, Abba; that is to say, Father, whereas under the former law of Moses, God rather governed his people by fear; they were his servants, we are his sons; and if sons, also the heirs of God, with the promise of an eternal inheritance in his kingdom, provided we suffer for Christ's sake, as he suffered for us. And surely the short sufferings in this world have no proportion, nor can be put in balance with the future endless glory, which is promised and prepared for us in heaven. (Witham) --- Abba is a Syriac word, which signifies my father. This is properly the word of free and noble children; for amongst the Hebrews, the children of slaves were not allowed to call their fathers Abba, nor their mothers Imma. This kind of expression was very rarely used under the old law. The Hebrews called the Almighty their Lord, their God, their Salvation, their King, their Protector, their Glory, etc. but seldom their father, scarcely ever, except in the case of Solomon, who was a particular figure of the Messias, the true Son of God. On this account God said to him: "He shall call me Father and God; and I will be to him a Father, and will treat as my first-born." But it is the property of the Christian to call the Almighty his Father with confidence indeed, yet tempered with a filial awe; remembering at the same time that he is his judge. (Calmet) --- Mat. Polus says that not any one of the just dared to call God, my Father, before the coming of Christ, as this favour was reserved for the time of the gospel. (In this location.) (Haydock) --- St. Chrysostom{ Ver. 15. Abba (Pater) St. Chrysostom, hom. XIV. p. 115. oude euchomenous outos, etc.|} takes notice, that God was also called the Father of the Israelites, and they his children, in the Old Testament, when God rather governed his people by fear of punishments, and promises of temporal blessings, but not in that particular manner as in the new law. (Witham) --- The Spirit himself, etc. By the inward motions of divine love, and the peace of conscience, which the children of God experience, they have a kind of testimony of God's favour; by which they are much strengthened in the hope of their justification and salvation; but yet not so as to pretend to an absolute assurance, which is not usually granted in this mortal life: during which we are taught to work out our salvation with fear and trembling. (Philippians 2:12.) And that he who thinketh himself to stand, must take heed lest he fall. (1 Corinthians 10:12.) See also Romans 11:20, 21, 22. (Challoner) --- He hath given to us, says St. John, (chap. 1:12.) the power, or dignity, of being the sons of God. Christ taught us to pray, and to begin our prayers with our Father, etc. (Matthew 6:9.) (Witham)

extractions.type_description: Solomon in the Old Testament, who was permitted to call God 'Father' and to whom God said 'He shall call me Father and God; and I will be to him a Father, and will treat as my first-born.' Solomon is presented as a particular figure prefiguring the Messiah.
extractions.antitype_description: In the New Testament, Christ is the true Son of God who calls God 'Father,' and Christians inherit this privilege through adoption in Christ. This intimate father-child relationship becomes the distinguishing mark of the Christian under the new law, replacing the servant-master relationship of the Old Testament.
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly identifies Solomon as 'a particular figure of the Messias, the true Son of God' and quotes God's promise to Solomon as a type of the relationship Christ has with God the Father. The commentary further indicates this privilege of calling God 'Father' was reserved for Christ's coming and is now extended to Christians through Him.

notes: The commentary contrasts the Old Testament mode of relating to God (as servants governed by fear under the Mosaic law) with the New Testament mode (as sons through adoption in Christ). While this presents a structural typology of relationship rather than a specific person/event/object type, the explicit identification of Solomon as a 'figure of the Messias' constitutes a clear typological connection. The commentary emphasizes that this intimate father-child relationship is the property of Christians and was scarcely used in the Old Testament except in Solomon's case.

original_text: The expectation{ Ver. 19. Expectatio creaturae, e gar apokaradokia. St. Chrysostom, hom. XIV. p. 119. apokaradokia gar e sphodra prosdokia estin, intenta et sollicita expectatio. See Mr. Legh, Crit. Sac.|} of the creature. He speaks of the corporal creation, made for the use and service of man; and, by occasion of his sin made subject to vanity, that is, to a perpetual instability, tending to corruption and other defects; so that by a figure of speech, it is here said to groan and be in labour, and to long for its deliverance, which is then to come, when sin shall reign no more; and God shall raise the bodies, and united them to their souls, never more to separate, and to be in everlasting happiness in heaven. (Challoner) --- Waiteth for the revelation of the sons of God. That is, for the time after this life, when it shall be made manifest that they are the sons of God, and heirs of the kingdom of his glory.
