Several interpreters understand all creatures whatsoever, even irrational and inanimate creatures of this world, which are represented as if they had a knowledge and sense of a more happy condition, of a new unchangeable state of perfection, which they are to receive at the end of the world. See 2 Peter 1:13; Apocalypse 21:1. Now every insensible creature is figuratively brought in groaning like a woman in labour, waiting, and wishing for that new and happy state; but in the mean time unwillingly made subject to vanity, that is to these changeable imperfections of generations and corruptions, which then they shall be delivered from. (Witham) --- The creature, etc. The creatures expect with impatience, and hope with confidence, to see a happy change in their condition; they flatter themselves that they will be delivered from the captivity of sin, to which man has reduced them, and enter into the liberty of the glory of the sons of God. Not that the inanimate creation will really participate the happiness and glory of the elect; although in some sense they may be said to have part in it, since they will enter into a pure, incorruptible and perfect state to the end of ages. They will no longer be subject to those changes and vicissitudes which sin has brought upon them; nor will sinful man any longer abuse their beauty and goodness in offending the Creator of all. St. Ambrose and St. Jerome teach that the sun, moon, and stars will be then much more brilliant and beautiful than at present, no longer subject to those changes they at present suffer. Philo and Tertullian teach that the beasts of prey will then lay aside their ferocity, and venomous serpents their poisonous qualities. (Calmet) --- Other, by the creature or creatures, understand men only, and Christians, who groan under miseries and temptations in this mortal life, amidst the vanities of this world, under the slavery of corruption; who having already (ver. 23.) received the first-fruits of the Spirit,{ Ver. 23. Redemptionem corporis, that is complete happiness, says St. Chrysostom, p. 119. toutesti ten apertismenen doxan.|} the grace of God in baptism, have been made the children of God, and now, with expectation and great earnestness, wait and long for a more perfect adoption of the sons of God: for the redemption of their bodies, when the bodies, as well as the souls of the elect, shall rise to an immortal life, and complete happiness in heaven. (Witham)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Romans 8:19 discusses the eschatological expectation of creation for redemption and transformation at the end times, but it does not establish typological relationships between Old Testament types and New Testament antitypes. The commentary uses figurative language (creation 'groaning like a woman in labour') and includes references to 2 Peter 1:13 and Apocalypse 21:1, but these are supporting NT passages rather than OT types prefiguring NT fulfillment. The commentary focuses on exegesis of the Pauline text regarding creature expectation, the redemption of bodies, and the glorification of the elect, but does not connect these to specific OT persons, events, or institutions as prefigurative types. The labor metaphor is employed allegorically to describe creation's condition, but this is not typology in the technical sense.

original_text: For whom he foreknew, he also predestinated to be made conformable to the image of his Son, in suffering with Christ, in following his doctrine, in imitating his life. This foreknowledge of God, according to St. Augustine,{ Ver. 29 St. Augustine, de dono persev. Romans 18. praedestinatione Deus ea praescivit, quae fuerat ipse facturus. And again, Romans 14. Praedestinatio est praescientia et praeparatio beneficiorum, quibus certissimè liberantur quicunque liberantur. See Bellarmine and Petau, as to St. Augustine's opinion. But I never in these short notes touch upon any thing that regards the opinions in Catholic schools; my design being no more than a literal exposition of the text.|} is not merely a foreseeing of what men will do by the assistance and graces of God's ordinary providence, much less a foreseeing of what they will do by their own natural strength, as the Pelagian heretics pretended: but is a foreknowledge including an act of the divine will, and of his love towards his elect servants; (as to know in the Scriptures, when applied to God, is many times the same as to approve and love) God therefore hath foreseen or predestinated, or decreed that these elect, by the help of his special graces, and by the co-operation of their free-will, should be conformable to the image of his Son, that so his Son, even as man, might be the first-born, the chief, and the head of all that shall be saved. (Witham) --- God hath preordained that all his elect shall be conformable to the image of his Son. We must not here offer to dive into the secrets of God's eternal election: only firmly believe that all our good, in time and eternity, flows originally from God's free goodness; and all our evil from man's free will. (Challoner)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Romans 8:29 focuses on theological doctrines of predestination, foreknowledge, divine will, and Christian conformity to Christ's image. While it discusses Christ as the 'first-born' and 'head of all that shall be saved,' these references are used in a doctrinal rather than typological framework. The commentary does not establish any Old Testament type that prefigures a New Testament antitype. The passage emphasizes moral and spiritual conformity ('in suffering with Christ, in following his doctrine, in imitating his life') rather than typological correspondence between OT persons/events and NT fulfillments. No OT-to-NT prefigurative relationships are explicitly identified or discussed.

original_text: etc. And not only she (Sara) brought forth Isaac, who was the only child of Abraham, to whom the promises descended, though he was the father of Ismael, by Agar, and of all the Ismaelites. And lest the Jews should say that the Ismaelites, though descending from Abraham, according to the flesh, were not to be reputed as his children for another reason, because they came of Agar, who was only the handmaid of Sara; he brings them another example to which they could make no such reply; to wit, that Rebecca also at once had two sons of Isaac, Esau and Jacob; where, though Esau was the first-born, these promises were not reputed as made to him, and his descendants, the Idumeans, who were equally the descendants of Isaac, yet not the favourite people, nor the children of God, as the Jews saw very well. (Witham) --- Not yet born. By this example of these twins, and the preference of the younger to the elder, the drift of the apostle is, to shew that God, in his election, mercy, and grace, is not tied to any particular nation, as the Jews imagined, nor to any prerogative of birth, or any foregoing merits. For as, antecedently, to his grace, he sees no merit in any, but finds all involved in sin, in the common mass of condemnation; and all children of wrath; there is no one whom he might not justly leave in that mass; so that whomsoever he delivers from it, he delivers in his mercy: and whomsoever he leaves in it, he leaves in his justice. As when, of two equally criminal, the king is pleased out of pure mercy to pardon one, whilst he suffers justice to take place in the execution of the other. (Challoner) --- Nor had done any good or evil. God was pleased to prefer, and promise his blessings to the younger of them, Jacob, declaring that the elder shall serve the younger; that is, that the seed of the elder should be subject to that of the younger, as it happened afterwards to the Idumeans. And the prophet, Malachias, said of them, I have loved Jacob, but hated Esau, and turned his mountains into a desert, etc. --- That the purpose of God, his will, and his decree, (see Romans 8:28.) might stand according to election, might be, not according to any works they had done, or that he foresaw they would do, but merely according to his mercy. And though the preference which God gave to Jacob was literally true, as to temporal benefits; yet St. Augustine observes in divers places, that Jacob was a figure of the elect or predestinate, and Esau of the reprobate; and that as Jacob and his posterity was more favoured, purely by the mercy of God, without any merits on their side; so are God's elect, whom he has called, and to whom, according to his eternal purpose, he decreed to give eternal glory, and special graces to bring them thither. (Witham)

extractions.type_name: Jacob (the younger twin preferred over Esau)
extractions.type_description: Jacob, the younger son of Isaac and Rebecca, whom God chose and favored over his elder brother Esau, receiving the promises and blessings despite being born second, with no merit of his own works.
extractions.antitype_description: Those whom God has chosen and called according to His eternal purpose to receive eternal glory and special graces, selected purely by God's mercy without regard to their works or merits.
extractions.reasoning: St. Augustine is explicitly cited as observing that 'Jacob was a figure of the elect or predestinate,' establishing a direct typological connection between Jacob's election and status as the chosen one, and the Church's election by God's grace alone. The commentary draws a parallel between Jacob's preferential treatment based solely on God's mercy and the election of God's chosen people.

extractions.type_name: Esau (the elder twin rejected in favor of the younger)
extractions.type_description: Esau, the firstborn son of Isaac and Rebecca, whom God did not favor despite his priority of birth, whose descendants (the Idumeans) were not the chosen people, representing those not elected.
extractions.antitype_description: Those whom God has not elected or chosen for salvation, left in their condemnation through divine justice rather than mercy.
extractions.reasoning: St. Augustine is explicitly cited as observing that 'Esau [was a figure] of the reprobate,' establishing a direct typological parallel. The commentary notes that as Esau's descendants were not favored despite their Abrahamic/Isaaic descent, so the reprobate are not among God's chosen elect, illustrating God's sovereign selection based on mercy rather than natural descent or merits.

notes: This commentary is explicitly typological, with St. Augustine cited as the theological authority establishing these connections. The typology illustrates the doctrine of election and predestination: God's choice of the elect (Jacob/antitype) versus the reprobate (Esau/antitype) is grounded in divine mercy and sovereign will, not in birth order, nationality, or works. The passage emphasizes that God's election transcends natural privilege and is based entirely on His grace.

original_text: etc. Whom also he hath called, etc. That is, he hath called some of the Jews, and many of the Gentiles, to be vessels of election, as he foretold by his prophet Osee 2:24. I will call them my people, that were not my people,...and I will make them the children of the living God. And as it was also foretold by the prophet Isaias, of all the numerous nation of the Jews, only a remnant shall be saved, by their obstinacy in not receiving, and refusing to believe in, their Messias. For finishing his word, and reducing it by his justice to a little, because the Lord will bring to pass his word reducing it to a small compass upon the earth. The sense and construction of this verse is equally obscure in the Greek and in the Latin text: the true sense seems to be, that finishing his word, or fulfilling his promises to Israel, those that are to be saved, will be reduced by his justice for their sins, to a few; because, though he bring to pass his word, and his promises, the saved among the Israelites will be reduced to a small compass, in comparison of the great number of the Gentiles. This exposition agrees with the rest of the text, and with what follows, and was foretold by Isaias, (chap. 1:9.) that unless the God of Sabaoth (of hosts) had, through his mercy, left them a seed, a small number, they would all in a manner have deserved to be utterly destroyed, like Sodom and Gomorrha. (Witham) --- What I say, shall come to pass, that in those places, viz. Greece, Italy, etc. where those who are strangers to the worship of the true God dwell, and have been called, on account of their profane worship, not my people. In those very places, they shall receive the true worship of God, and by this means shall become and be called the children of the living God. He is so particular as to place, lest the Jews should imagine that the Gentiles would be converted like their former proselytes, and either dwell in Judea, or repair to it at certain stated times. Thus the apostle repeats what Jesus Christ had before said to the Samaritan woman. The hour will come when neither in this mountain, nor in Jerusalem, shall you adore the Father. (Estius) (John iv.) --- A remnant. That is, a small number only of the children of Israel shall be converted and saved. How perversely is this text quoted for the salvation of men of all religions, when it speaks only of the converts of the children of Israel. (Challoner) --- St. Paul is here speaking of the reprobation of the Jews, and of the vocation of the Gentiles, and foretells that a remnant, or small number of the children of Israel shall be converted, and saved. In the sense of St. Paul, we sincerely hope, and confidently trust, that a remnant of all will be saved through a timely conversion. But we no where read, in the Old, or New Scriptures, that a remnant of all will be saved, as if it were a matter of indifference to what society or connexion a Christian was joined. (Haydock)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Romans 9:24 discusses the fulfillment of Old Testament prophecies (Hosea 2:24 and Isaiah 1:9, 10:22-23) in the New Testament calling of both Jews and Gentiles. However, the commentary does not establish typological relationships in the technical sense. Instead, it presents: (1) prophetic fulfillment - where OT prophecies are directly fulfilled in NT events (the calling of Gentiles and salvation of a Jewish remnant), and (2) historical continuity - the extension of God's covenant promises from Israel to include the Gentiles. While prophecy fulfillment shares structural similarities with typology, it is distinct in that it involves direct prediction and fulfillment rather than the prefigurative pattern of type-antitype. The commentary emphasizes the literal fulfillment of what the prophets foretold, not a typological correspondence where OT persons, events, or institutions prefigure their NT counterparts through symbolic resemblance.

original_text: God hath given them, etc. Not by his working, or acting in them; but by his permission, and by withdrawing his grace in punishment of their obstinacy. (Challoner) --- Permitted them (says St. Chrysostom) to fall into the spirit of insensibility. Literally, the spirit of { Ver. 8. Spiritum compunctionis; pneuma katanuxeos. In the Latin Vulgate, Isaias xxix. 10, the same Greek words are translated, spiritum soporis; the spirit of slumber. See Mr. Legh, Crit. Sacr. on the word katanusso. St. Chrysostom, om. ith. p. 163. katanuxin, entautha ten peri to cheiron exin tes psuches, etc. See Cornelius a Lapide. St. Chrysostom in the same place; katanugenai gar ouden eteron esti to empagenai, kai proselosthai.|} compunction. Compunction is not here taken, as in some spiritual writers, for a great sorrow for sins. In the Latin Vulgate (Isaias 6:9.) it is called the spirit of slumber, as in the Protestant translation. We cannot have a better judge of the sense of the word than St. Chrysostom, who tells us, that it signifies a habit of the soul, firmly fixed in evil, and an insensible disposition: as, saith he, persons under a pious compunction are not to be removed from their good resolutions; so the wicked, under a hardened compunction, are nailed, as it were, to vice. And that here this is the true sense, appears by the following words out of Isaias: he hath given them eyes that they should not see, etc. And also out of David, (Psalm 68:23.) let their table be made a snare, etc. We may understand the spiritual food of the word of God, and of the Scriptures; which by the blindness of this people, have served to their great condemnation. --- And a recompense, that is, for a just punishment of their obstinacy. --- And bow down their back always, a metaphor to represent the condition of such, as are under heavy oppressions. (Witham) --- Although by bending their back is literally understood the yoke of servitude and captivity, with which the Jews were oppressed at the destruction of Jerusalem; yet it seems more conformable to the apostle's meaning, when considered in a spiritual sense, and then it will signify the insensibility of the Jews, as to heavenly things, and their anxious solicitude for the things of the earth. This their avaricious and carnal disposition was so manifest, that the poet said of them--- O curvae in terram animae et coelestium inanes.--- (Estius)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Romans 11:8 discusses the hardening of the Jewish people and their spiritual blindness as a consequence of divine permission and withdrawal of grace. While the passage quotes from Isaiah 29:10 and Psalm 68:23, the commentary treats these as illustrative proof texts supporting Paul's theological point about obstinacy and spiritual insensibility, rather than as typological prefigurements. The exegesis focuses on: (1) the meaning of 'spirit of compunction/slumber' as a hardened state of soul, (2) the metaphorical sense of 'bowing down their back' as spiritual blindness and carnal preoccupation, and (3) the historical fulfillment in Jerusalem's destruction. No OT person, event, or institution is presented as prefiguring an NT antitype. This is theological interpretation and application of Old Testament language to a New Testament situation, not typological correspondence.

original_text: These things, brethren, I have in a figure transferred to myself, and to Apollo. Literally, these things have I transfigured in me and Apollo, that is, I have represented the divisions and disputes among you, as if it were by your contending, whether I, or Apollo, or Cephas were the best preachers, without naming those, as I might do, who are the true causes of these divisions, by striving who should be thought men of the greatest and brightest parts. --- That in us, and by our example, who have no such proud disputes, you might learn that one be not puffed up against the other, and above that which is written, against the admonitions given in the holy Scriptures of being humble: or against what I have now written to you, that we must strive for nothing, but to be the faithful ministers of God, and not seek the esteem of men. (Witham) --- It is the opinion of St. Thomas Aquinas and likewise of Estius, that St. Paul, Apollo, and Cephas were not the real causes of the divisions that existed amongst the new converts at Corinth, but that in making use of these names, he wished to teach them, that if it was unlawful to keep up these divisions even for the sake of the apostles, how far should they be from doing any thing of this kind for those whose authority was much less in the Church. But Calmet is of opinion, that the divisions amongst the Corinthians were certainly on account of Paul, Apollo, Cephas, and perhaps some others, whose names are not mentioned.
notes: This Haydock commentary on 1 Corinthians 4:6 does not contain typological analysis. The passage addresses Paul's rhetorical use of himself and Apollos as examples to correct divisions among the Corinthian church. The commentary discusses: (1) Paul's pedagogical method of using named figures as illustrations without naming the actual troublemakers, and (2) debates among scholars about whether these divisions were genuinely caused by the apostles or were merely attributed to them. The focus is entirely on first-century ecclesial discipline and moral instruction, not on Old Testament types prefiguring New Testament antitypes. No connection is drawn to OT persons, events, or institutions.

original_text: Now you are satiated, etc. You great, vain preachers, you are rich in every kind, blessed with all gifts, etc. You reign over the minds of the people, without us, you stand not in need of our assistance. And I would to God you did reign, that we also might reign with you. I wish your reigning and governing the people were well grounded on virtue and truth, that we might be sharers of the like happiness. St. Chrysostom takes notice, that St. Paul speaks thus, meaning the contrary, by the figure called irony: and so also St. Chrysostom understands the two following verses, as if St. Paul only represented what those vain preachers said with contempt of him, as if he were only an apostle of an inferior rank, not one of the chief, nor of the twelve. And when he says, we are fools for Christ's sake, but you are wise: it is certain the apostles were not fools, nor these preachers whom he blames, wise, especially in Christ. But though the apostle partly use this figure of irony, intermixing it in his discourse, yet he also represents the condition of all true apostles, and preachers of Christ crucified, whose persons and doctrine were slighted, ridiculed, and laughed at by men that were wise only with worldly wisdom, especially by profane libertines, and atheistical men, that make a jest of all revealed religion. To go about preaching in hunger, in thirst, in nakedness, in want, under afflictions and persecutions, is what they think is to be miserable: they despise such men as the out-cast, the dross,{ Ver. 8. Tanquam purgamenta, omnium peripsema, os perikatharmata, Sordes, quisquiliae, panton peripsema, Scobes, ramentum. See Mr. Legh, Crit. Sacra.|} and the dregs of mankind. (See the Greek text.) (Witham) --- He speaks to the Corinthians, who forgetting their first fervour, and the Christian modesty which St. Paul had taught them, both by word and example, were endeavouring to distinguish themselves by the reputation and honour of the apostle, who had converted them, by their antiquity of faith, and by other things more frivolous. (Calmet)
notes: This Haydock commentary on 1 Corinthians 4:8 does not contain typological analysis. The commentary focuses on: (1) Paul's use of irony to critique the Corinthian church's spiritual pride and worldly wisdom, (2) the contrast between false apostles who seek honor and true apostles who suffer persecution, and (3) moral and ethical lessons about Christian humility and authentic apostolic ministry. While the passage discusses apostolic suffering and its spiritual significance, the commentary does not establish any Old Testament type that prefigures the New Testament antitype of apostolic persecution or Christian suffering. The commentary is exegetical and homiletical in nature rather than typological.

original_text: An idol is nothing. The apostle seems to allude in this place to the Greek signification of this word, eidolon, signifying a false representation; as for instance in ghosts, which are said to appear sometimes at night. Umbroe tenues, simulacra luce carentium. (Calmet)
notes: This Haydock commentary on 1 Corinthians 8:4 discusses the etymological and philosophical meaning of the Greek word 'eidolon' (false representation, shadow, ghost-like image) as it relates to Paul's argument about idols being 'nothing.' The commentary provides linguistic analysis and classical references (Virgil's 'Umbrae tenues, simulacra luce carentium') but does not establish any typological connection between an Old Testament type and New Testament antitype. This is linguistic and conceptual exegesis rather than typological analysis.

original_text: In a figure of us. That is, this was done and written to teach us, what we may expect, if we imitate the murmurs, infidelities, ingratitude, and disobedience of the Hebrew people. Unless we renounce our irregular desires, unless we mortify our passions, baptism and communion will prove our greater condemnation. The greatest graces are but subjects of alarm, unless our life correspond with them.

extractions.type_name: The Hebrew people's murmurs, infidelities, ingratitude, and disobedience in the wilderness
extractions.type_description: The Old Testament Israelites' repeated failures of faith, complaints, and disobedience during their wilderness journey after the exodus
extractions.antitype_name: Christian believers who fail to mortify passions and renounce irregular desires
extractions.antitype_description: New Testament Christians who receive the sacraments (baptism and communion) but do not align their lives with the graces received, risking greater condemnation
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states this was 'done and written to teach us' (1 Corinthians 10:6 context), establishing a prefigurative relationship. The OT negative example (Hebrew disobedience) prefigures the NT warning (Christian condemnation if sacramental graces are not matched by moral transformation). The connection is didactic and typological: past events instruct present believers about consequences of unfaithfulness.

notes: This is an inverse or warning typology—the type illustrates what NOT to do. The commentary applies the OT narrative as a cautionary type for NT sacramental practice, warning that baptism and communion without corresponding moral transformation become instruments of judgment rather than grace.

original_text: In all this discourse, a comparison is instituted between the Christian host and oblation, its effects, conditions and properties, with the altars, hosts, sacrifices and immolations of the Jews and Gentiles; which the apostle could not have done, had there not been a proper sacrifice in the Christian worship. The holy Fathers teach the same with the ancient Councils. This in the council of Nice: The lamb of God laid upon the altar. Conc. Ephes., The unbloody service of the sacrifice. In St. Cyril of Alexandria, in Conc. Ephes., Anath. 11, The quickening holy sacrifice; the unbloody host and victim. Tertullian, de coron. milit., The propitiatory sacrifice both for the living and the dead. This Melchisedech did most singularly prefigure in his mystical oblation of bread and wine; this also according to the prophecy of Malachias, shall continue from the rising to the setting sun, a perpetual substitute for all the Jewish sacrifices; and this, in plain terms, is called the Mass, by St. Augustine, Serm. CCLI. 91.; Conc. Cartha. II. C. 3. 4. C. 84. Milevit. 12.; St. Leo, ep. 81. 88. 1 Corinthians 2.; St. Gregory, lib. 2:ep. 9. 92. etc. etc. See next chapter ver. 24.

extractions.type_name: Melchizedek's oblation of bread and wine
extractions.type_description: The priestly offering of bread and wine by Melchizedek, the priest-king of Salem, as recorded in Genesis 14:18
extractions.antitype_description: The unbloody sacrifice of Christ in the form of bread and wine offered in Christian worship, perpetually continuing from the rising to the setting of the sun
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states 'This Melchisedech did most singularly prefigure in his mystical oblation of bread and wine' and connects it directly to the Christian Eucharistic sacrifice. This is a classic typological relationship where the OT priestly act prefigures the NT sacramental reality.

extractions.type_description: The entire system of Jewish sacrificial offerings, altars, hosts, and immolations prescribed in the Mosaic law
extractions.antitype_name: The Christian Eucharist and the sacrifice of Christ
extractions.antitype_description: The unbloody sacrifice of the Eucharist, which serves as the perpetual substitute fulfilling all the Jewish sacrificial system
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly compares Jewish sacrifices with the Christian host and oblation, stating that the Eucharistic sacrifice is 'a perpetual substitute for all the Jewish sacrifices.' This represents typological fulfillment where the shadows of the old covenant give way to the reality in the new covenant.

notes: The commentary cites Malachi's prophecy regarding the perpetual nature of this sacrifice 'from the rising to the setting sun,' suggesting an additional prophetic-typological dimension. Both extracted types are explicitly identified as prefiguring the Eucharistic sacrifice in Christian practice.

original_text: The head of the woman is the man, etc. To have the head covered at public meetings, is, according to St. Paul, a mark of subjection: The man was created to be head over the woman, who was made subject to the man, being made of him, of his rib, and the woman made for him, not he for the woman. The man in a special manner, is the image of God, not only by his immortal soul, in which sense also the woman was made to God's image, and likeness, but inasmuch as God gave him a power over all creatures, and so he is called, the glory of God. For these reasons, as well as from a received custom, St. Paul tells every woman, that in prayer or prophesying in public meetings, she must have her head veiled, and covered in testimony of her subjection to man, her head, otherwise she dishonours herself, and her head. This is what he tells her, (ver. 10.) that she ought to have a power over her head,{ Ver. 3. Debet mulier potestatem habere super caput suum, exousian, but some Greek copies have peribolaion, cinctorium, velum.|} that is, to have a veil or covering, as a mark of man's power over her: and because of the angels, that is, out of a respect to the angels there present. Some understand the priests and ministers of God, called angels, particularly in the Apocalypse. St. Paul adds, that nature{ Ver. 3. Nec ipsa natura docet vos. I do not find an interrogation in the Latin copies, as it is marked in the Greek, oude didaskei umas. The rest of the text seems to be better connected, if we read it with an interrogation.|} having given to women long hair, designed it to be as a natural veil. In fine, he appeals to them, to be judges, whether it be not unbecoming in women to pray without a veil. But he will have men to be uncovered, and not to bear such a mark of subjection, as a veil is, by which a man would dishonour his head, that is, himself, and Christ, who is his head, and who appointed him, when he created him, to be head over the woman. He looks upon it as a dishonour and a disgrace for men to nourish their hair, as women should do. He also calls God the head of Christ, that is, of Christ, as man. Lest he should seem to lessen the condition of women more than necessary, he adds, that the propagation of mankind now depends on the woman, as well as on the man, seeing every man is by the woman. (Witham)
notes: This Haydock commentary on 1 Corinthians 11:3 discusses the hierarchical relationship between man and woman, grounded in creation theology (woman made from man's rib, for man's benefit) and the chain of headship (God → Christ → man → woman). While the commentary references the created order and God's design, it does not establish an Old Testament type that prefigures a New Testament antitype. The commentary is primarily exegetical and ethical in nature, explaining Paul's instruction about head coverings in public worship as a sign of subjection. It appeals to nature, custom, and the order of creation, but does not connect an OT person, event, or institution to its NT fulfillment in the typological sense. The reference to 'angels' present and appeals to 'nature' are explanatory, not typological. This is doctrinal and moral instruction rather than typology.

original_text: St. Timothy, it appears, had been sent to Corinth to confirm the faithful in the doctrine which they had received from St. Paul. After he had fulfilled this commission, he returned to St. Paul, and gave him an account how they had behaved, and what good effects his first letter had produced. He styles him brother, to conciliate to him the esteem and respect of the Corinthians. This epistle is not merely addressed to the Corinthians, but to all Achaia, of which Corinth was the capital. (Estius) --- Others think that Timothy had left Corinth before St. Paul's first epistle had arrived thither; and that this determined St. Paul to send Titus with another disciple thither. See 2 Corinthians 12:18. From him St. Paul had the consolation to learn the happy effects produced by his first letter. See 2 Corinthians 6:7. 11.
notes: This Haydock commentary on 2 Corinthians 1:1 discusses the historical and contextual details of Paul's epistle—specifically Timothy's mission to Corinth, the effects of Paul's first letter, and the addressees of the second letter. It contains no references to Old Testament persons, events, or institutions that prefigure New Testament realities. The commentary is purely historical and exegetical in nature, explaining the circumstances of the epistle's composition rather than identifying typological relationships.

original_text: The doctrine which the apostle delivered to them was not ambiguous, doubtful, or contradictory, first one thing, then another; on the contrary, it was such, that the apostle could say, (ver. 14.) we are your glory. --- Amen. All the promises made by God, with regard to Christ, are fulfilled in him; therefore we may say Amen, and give glory to God, through Jesus Christ, who hath fulfilled all his promises. (Calmet) --- One of the distinctive marks, as the holy fathers affirm, between separatists and Catholics is; the former are fond of innovation, changes, and reform, the latter are scrupulously tenacious of what has been delivered from the beginning. See St. Irenaeus, lib. 1:chap. 18.; Tertullian, de praescript.; St. Basil, ep. 12. Vine: Lyr. See also Les Variations, by Bossuet.

extractions.type_description: The various promises made by God throughout the Old Testament concerning the coming of Christ and His redemptive work
extractions.antitype_name: Jesus Christ and His Fulfillment of All Promises
extractions.antitype_description: Christ as the ultimate fulfillment and realization of all Old Testament promises; the Amen in whom all divine promises find their yes and completion
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states 'All the promises made by God, with regard to Christ, are fulfilled in him.' This directly identifies OT promises as types that find their fulfillment (antitype) in the person and work of Jesus Christ. The reference to 'Amen' emphasizes Christ as the confirmed reality of what was promised in the OT.

notes: The commentary also includes discussion of doctrinal consistency and ecclesiastical tradition regarding the preservation of apostolic doctrine, but these elements do not constitute typological relationships. The typological content is clearly centered on the fulfillment of messianic promises in Christ.

original_text: The apostle here informs the Corinthians that the apostles speak with confidence, without any veil, discovering to men mysteries hidden from the foundation of the world; not like Moses, who put a veil on his face that the Israelites might not look steadfastly, or might not discover the weakness and short duration of the law, which was represented by the light that surrounded his face, and which quickly passed away. St. Paul here gives the allegorical explanation of the light and veil on the face of Moses. (Estius)

extractions.type_description: The veil that Moses placed on his face after receiving the law, which prevented the Israelites from seeing the fading glory/light on his face and thus from perceiving the weakness and temporary nature of the Mosaic law
extractions.antitype_name: The Unveiled Ministry of the Apostles / The New Covenant in Christ
extractions.antitype_description: The apostolic proclamation that speaks with confidence without a veil, openly revealing mysteries previously hidden and disclosing the surpassing glory and permanence of the New Covenant in Christ, in contrast to the temporary law
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly contrasts Moses' veiled ministry under the Old Covenant with the apostles' unveiled ministry under the New Covenant. The veil serves as a type representing the obscuring and temporary nature of the Mosaic law, while its removal in the NT antitype represents the clarity and permanence of Christ's covenant. This is a direct OT/NT prefigurement relationship.

extractions.type_name: The Fading Light on Moses' Face
extractions.type_description: The transient glory/light that surrounded Moses' face, which represented the temporary and weakening nature of the Mosaic law
extractions.antitype_name: The Permanent Glory of Christ / The New Covenant
extractions.antitype_description: The enduring and surpassing glory of the New Covenant in Christ, which does not fade but remains and increases in splendor
extractions.reasoning: The commentary presents the fading light as an allegorical representation of the law's temporary nature. While less explicit as a formal type, this symbolic connection between the transient Mosaic glory and the permanent glory of the New Covenant reflects typological thinking about covenant fulfillment.

notes: This passage (2 Corinthians 3:12-18) is Paul's own allegorical and typological interpretation of Exodus 34:29-35. The Haydock commentary appropriately identifies this as allegory with typological import, distinguishing between the temporary Mosaic dispensation and the permanent New Covenant reality. The veil particularly functions as a type of spiritual blindness under the old covenant versus spiritual clarity under the new.

original_text: Not imputing, that is truly taking away our sins, blotting out the handwriting of the decree which was against us,...fastening it to the cross, as it is said, Colossians 2:14. And to us, who are his apostles and the ministers of his gospel, he hath imparted and committed this word of reconciliation, by the preaching of his doctrine, and the administration of his sacraments, etc. In these functions we act and we speak to you as the ambassadors of Christ; we speak to you in his name, we represent his person, when we exhort you to be reconciled to God. "He that heareth you, heareth me." (Luke 10:16.) (Witham)
notes: This Haydock commentary on 2 Corinthians 5:19 discusses the reconciliation of sins through Christ and the apostolic ministry, but does not establish explicit typological relationships between Old Testament types and New Testament antitypes. The reference to Colossians 2:14 (the 'handwriting of the decree') and the 'fastening it to the cross' are metaphorical rather than typological in nature. The commentary emphasizes the functional roles of apostles as ambassadors and ministers of reconciliation, which is theological application rather than typology. While one might argue that Old Testament priests or prophets could be considered types of the apostolic ministry, the commentary itself does not make this connection explicit or develop it as a typological relationship.

original_text: The apostles maintained the character, and fulfilled the duties of the ministers of Christ, equally in prosperity and adversity; they continued to speak the truth, though regarded by the Jews as seducers; exposed to all kinds of dangers, they relied on God, who preserved them, though in the midst of dangers, and of death itself. Though they possessed nothing in this world, yet God never permitted them to remain in want: his providence procured for them all things necessary. Though they had nothing in their possession, yet they procured relief for others, by the alms, of which they were made the disposers, though this latter part is generally understood of the spiritual riches, which they bestowed upon their auditors. (Estius)
notes: This Haydock commentary on 2 Corinthians 6:8 focuses on the apostolic character and conduct of New Testament ministers—specifically their faithfulness in both prosperity and adversity, their reliance on God's providence, and their spiritual generosity. While the passage discusses Christian virtues and divine providence, the commentary does not explicitly establish connections between Old Testament persons, events, or institutions and their New Testament fulfillments. The commentary is primarily exhortative and descriptive of apostolic conduct rather than typological in nature. No OT type is referenced or implied as prefiguring the apostolic ministry described here.

original_text: Having in readiness. God gave power, not only to persuade, and to convince the incredulous, but also to punish them, as we see in the examples of Simon Magus and Elymas. What then should hinder him from using the same against these false apostles? But he says, your obedience must first be fulfilled. God forbid that I should first use the sword, before I have tried the ways of sweetness and conciliation. But if any remain obstinate, then I will employ the arms that God has given me. (Grotius) --- This sweet and forcible example of the apostle is worthy the imitation of all superiors, temporal and ecclesiastical, how ever high their dignity or command. (Haydock)
notes: This Haydock commentary on 2 Corinthians 10:6 does not describe typological relationships between Old Testament persons/events and New Testament fulfillments. Rather, it discusses Paul's apostolic authority and his pastoral approach—attempting persuasion before employing corrective measures against false apostles. While the commentary mentions examples from Acts (Simon Magus and Elymas) as illustrations of God's power to punish, these are presented as precedents or historical examples of divine judgment, not as OT types prefiguring NT antitypes. The commentary concludes with a moral exhortation for superiors to imitate Paul's approach, which is ethical instruction rather than typological interpretation. No OT type is invoked to prefigure any NT antitype.

original_text: This was customary with both Jews and Persians, as we learn from Xenophon and Herodotus, and with other oriental nations. And in process of time, from the custom of common life, it was introduced into ecclesiastial assemblies. The ancients were in the habit before they began their meal to embrace each other, to manifest by that sign their mutual cordiality and friendship; then they contributed their alms, that they might give a substantial proof of what was represented by their kiss of charity. (Pastorini)
notes: This Haydock commentary discusses the historical and cultural practice of the 'holy kiss' (osculum sanctum) in early Christian assemblies, tracing its origins to Jewish and Persian customs. While the passage describes the evolution of a religious practice and its symbolic meaning (representing mutual charity and cordiality), it does not establish a typological relationship between an Old Testament type and a New Testament antitype. The commentary explains the origin and significance of a Christian practice but does not connect it to OT prefigurement. This is a discussion of custom, practice, and symbolism rather than typology.

original_text: It is written in the law, that is, in Genesis, (Genesis 16.; Genesis 21.) that Abraham had two sons, etc. that his two sons, Ismael, born of his servant, Agar, and Isaac of his wife, Sara, in an allegorical sense, represent the two testaments or covenants, which God made with his people: that by Ismael was represented that covenant of the former law delivered to Moses on Mount Sina, by which the Jews were made his elect people, yet as it were his servants, to be kept to their duty by fear of punishments; but by Isaac is represented the new covenant or testament of Christ, given at Jerusalem, where he suffered, where the new law was first published; by which law, they who believe in Christ were made the spiritual children of Abraham, the sons of God, and heirs of the blessings promised to Abraham: that Sina, the mountain in Arabia, hath{ Ver. 25. Qui conjunctus est ei, quae nunc est Jerusalem, sustoichei te nun Ierousalem. See Budaeus, Estius, Mr. Legh, etc.|} an affinity with Jerusalem, and with her children, who remain under the servitude of the law of Moses: we cannot understand a conjunction, or an affinity, as to place and situation, Sina and Jerusalem being near twenty days' journey distant from each other; therefore it can only be an affinity in a mystical signification, inasmuch as Jerusalem was the capital of the Jews, where the children of those who received the law on Mount Sina lived still under the servitude of the same law: but Christians, who believe in Christ, must look upon themselves as belonging to Jerusalem, and not to the city of Jerusalem upon earth, but to the celestial Jerusalem in heaven, which is our mother, now no longer servants and slaves to the former law, but free, being made the sons of God by the grace of Christ, and heirs of heaven. And these blessings were promised to all nations, not only to the Jews, of which the much greater part remained obstinate, and refused to believe in Christ, but also particularly to the Gentiles, according to the prophecy of Isaias, (Isaias 54.) rejoice thou that hast been barren, like Sara, for a long time; that is rejoice, you Gentiles, hitherto left in idolatry, without the knowledge or worship of the true God, now you shall have more children among you than among the Jews, who were his chosen people. (Witham)

extractions.type_description: Born of the servant Hagar; represents the covenant of the former law delivered to Moses on Mount Sinai, by which the Jews were made God's elect people yet as servants kept to duty by fear of punishments
extractions.antitype_description: The covenant of Moses characterized by servitude, fear-based obedience, and legal bondage
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that Ishmael 'in an allegorical sense' represents the former law and covenant. This is a clear typological correspondence where the OT person prefigures the NT covenant reality.

extractions.type_description: Born of Sarah, Abraham's wife; represents the new covenant or testament of Christ given at Jerusalem through which believers in Christ are made spiritual children of Abraham and heirs of God's promises
extractions.antitype_description: The covenant of Christ through which believers are made spiritual children of Abraham, sons of God, and heirs of the blessings promised to Abraham; characterized by freedom and grace rather than servitude
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly identifies Isaac as representing 'the new covenant or testament of Christ.' This demonstrates a typological relationship where the OT person prefigures the NT covenantal fulfillment.

extractions.type_description: The mountain in Arabia where the law was delivered to Moses; represents the former covenant and the servitude of the law
extractions.antitype_description: The celestial Jerusalem in heaven, mother of Christians who are no longer servants to the former law but free sons of God through Christ's grace
extractions.reasoning: The commentary describes a mystical affinity between Sinai and earthly Jerusalem (representing the old covenant) versus the heavenly Jerusalem (representing the new covenant and ultimate fulfillment). While not strictly typological in the classical sense, it presents a prefigurative relationship between the earthly law-covenant and the eschatological heavenly reality.

notes: The commentary frames these relationships explicitly as 'allegorical' representations of covenants rather than strict typology. However, the pattern of OT persons/events prefiguring NT covenant realities fits typological analysis. The commentary is interpreting Galatians 4:22-31, where Paul himself employs this allegorical/typological reading of the Genesis account.

original_text: St. Paul makes another observation upon this example of Ismael and Isaac: that as Ismael was troublesome to Isaac, for which he and his mother were turned out of the family, so also now the Jews insulted and persecuted the Christians, who had been Gentiles; but God will protect them as heirs of the blessings promised: they shall be accounted the spiritual children of Abraham, while the Jews, with their carnal ceremonies, shall be cast off. (Witham) --- This, says St. Augustine, is a figure of heretics, (who are the children of the bond-woman) unjustly persecuting the Catholic Church. (Ep. 48.)

extractions.type_description: In Genesis, Ishmael (child of the bond-woman Hagar) was cast out of Abraham's household because he persecuted Isaac (the child of promise). Ishmael represents those born according to the flesh rather than promise.
extractions.antitype_name: Jews and Jewish opponents of Christianity
extractions.antitype_description: In the New Testament era, the Jews who persecuted Christians (particularly Gentile converts) represent the spiritual descendants of Ishmael - those relying on carnal ceremonies and the works of the law rather than faith in Christ.
extractions.reasoning: Paul explicitly makes this typological connection in Galatians 4:21-31, comparing the bond-woman and free-woman, their children, and their respective fates. The commentary directly states that Ishmael's expulsion prefigures how 'Jews...shall be cast off.' This is a type-antitype relationship spanning OT to NT with covenantal significance regarding inheritance of Abraham's promises.

extractions.type_description: Isaac represents the child born according to God's promise, the heir of Abraham's spiritual blessings, born of the free-woman Sarah.
extractions.antitype_name: Christians (particularly Gentile converts to the Church)
extractions.antitype_description: Gentile Christians are the true spiritual heirs of Abraham's promises, accounted as the spiritual children of Abraham through faith rather than carnal descent or observance of the law.
extractions.reasoning: The commentary states that Christians 'shall be accounted the spiritual children of Abraham' just as Isaac was Abraham's true heir. This prefigurement shows the Church as the antitype of Isaac - inheriting the blessings promised to Abraham's offspring through faith.

extractions.type_name: Hagar and Ishmael (bond-woman and her child)
extractions.type_description: Representatives of bondage, the flesh, carnal ceremonies, and those not truly inheriting the promise.
extractions.antitype_name: Heretics and those practicing external religion without faith
extractions.antitype_description: According to St. Augustine (cited in the commentary), heretics represent spiritual descendants of the bond-woman - those persecuting the Catholic Church through false doctrine and reliance on external observances rather than true faith.
extractions.reasoning: St. Augustine interprets the Hagar/Ishmael type as representing heretics who unjustly persecute the Church. While this extends the typology beyond Paul's primary application, it maintains the OT-NT connection, applying the type to internal Church opponents rather than external Jewish persecution.

notes: The primary typology is explicitly Pauline (from Galatians 4:21-31). The Augustine interpretation adds a secondary layer, applying the same type to heretics. All three extractions stem from the Genesis account of Abraham, Sarah, Hagar, Isaac, and Ishmael as the OT types with various NT antitypes.

original_text: All the law, as far as it regards our duty to our neighbour, is contained in this text of the apostle; he says the same in his epistle to the Romans (Romans 13.) He that loves his neighbour has fulfilled the law.
notes: This Haydock commentary on Galatians 5:14 discusses the fulfillment and summarization of Old Testament law through the New Testament principle of loving one's neighbor. However, it does not establish a typological relationship in the technical sense. Rather, it presents a thematic continuity and ethical fulfillment: the OT law is 'contained in' or 'fulfilled by' the NT commandment of love. This is a matter of doctrinal fulfillment and moral principle rather than typology proper. Typology requires that a specific OT person, event, or institution prefigure a corresponding NT antitype, whereas this commentary discusses how an OT legal corpus is summarized or completed by an NT ethical principle. The commentary references Romans 13 as parallel teaching but makes no claim that an OT type prefigures this NT antitype.

original_text: He that soweth in his flesh, etc. The apostle represents the flesh and the spirit like two fields, on which men sow good or bad seed, according to which they shall reap. (Witham)
notes: The Haydock commentary on Galatians 6:8 employs metaphorical and allegorical language (flesh and spirit as 'fields' where one 'sows' good or bad 'seed' to 'reap' consequences), but this represents general moral symbolism rather than typology. No explicit connection is made between an Old Testament type and a New Testament antitype. The commentary is teaching a principle about spiritual consequences through figurative language, not establishing a typological prefigurement relationship between OT and NT persons, events, or institutions.

original_text: That he might make known to us, and to all men, the mystery of his will and pleasure in establishing his new law, of calling all Gentiles, as well as Jews, to believe in his Son, made man for us, in the dispensation of the fulness of times, (that is, at the time decreed from eternity) to establish, to accomplish, and, as it is in the Greek, to recapitulate all things in heaven and on earth, in Christ, and through him, and his merits; on earth, by fulfilling all the types, figures, and prophecies concerning the Messias; and in heaven, by filling up the number of his elect. (Witham) --- The mystery of his will. The word mystery signifies a secret, an unknown design. It was the will of God, to reveal to us the great design he had in the incarnation of his Son, viz. the formation of one great body of true adorers; composed, without distinction, of Jew and Gentile: till (ver. 10) when the time appointed shall come, he will reunite and perfect in or under Christ this one body, composed of the Church triumphant, Angels and saints in heaven, and the Church militant upon earth. (St. Chrysostom, Estius, etc.) [For additional comments on verses 9 and 10, see the Notes section, below.]

extractions.type_name: Old Testament Types, Figures, and Prophecies concerning the Messiah
extractions.type_description: The collective system of OT types, figures, and prophecies that prefigured the coming Messiah and his redemptive work
extractions.antitype_description: Christ's incarnation, life, death, and resurrection, which fulfills all the types, figures, and prophecies of the Old Testament
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states that Christ accomplishes 'all things in heaven and on earth...on earth, by fulfilling all the types, figures, and prophecies concerning the Messias.' This is a direct statement of typological fulfillment where OT types find their antitype in Christ.

extractions.type_name: Old Testament prefigurations of a unified people of God
extractions.type_description: The OT types and patterns that pointed to a people composed of both Jews and Gentiles united in worship
extractions.antitype_name: The Church (composed of Jews and Gentiles)
extractions.antitype_description: The New Testament Church formed as 'one great body of true adorers; composed, without distinction, of Jew and Gentile,' uniting the Church triumphant and Church militant under Christ
extractions.reasoning: While the commentary does not explicitly use the word 'type' for this relationship, it describes how God's design to unite Jews and Gentiles was progressively revealed and fulfilled in the formation of the Church. This represents a typological pattern where OT separation and anticipation gives way to NT fulfillment in unified ecclesial reality.

notes: The commentary emphasizes the concept of 'recapitulation' (anakephalaiosis) - the gathering up or summing up of all things in Christ. The primary typology is clearly Christological, with all OT types being fulfilled in Christ. The ecclesial typology is more implicit but present in the discussion of God's mystery being 'the formation of one great body of true adorers' without ethnic distinction.

original_text: In the dispensation of the fulness of times. It may perhaps be translated, at the appointed fulness of time, which is generally expounded to signify at the time decreed from eternity. --- To establish (or restore) all things in Christ.{ Ver. 10. Instaurare, anakephalaiosasthai, recapitulare. See St. Jerome, p. 330.|} The Greek is to recapitulate, or, as the Protestant translation, to gather together all things in Christ; which St. Jerome expounds, by a fulfilling at once in Christ all the ancient figures and prophecies of the former law. (Witham)

extractions.type_name: The ancient figures and prophecies of the former law
extractions.type_description: The Old Testament types, figures, and prophetic prefigurations that were established under the Mosaic law
extractions.antitype_name: Christ and all things established/recapitulated in Christ
extractions.antitype_description: Jesus Christ as the fulfillment in whom all Old Testament types, figures, and prophecies are simultaneously fulfilled and gathered together
extractions.reasoning: St. Jerome's explicit statement that Christ 'fulfills at once in Christ all the ancient figures and prophecies of the former law' directly describes a typological relationship where OT types find their ultimate fulfillment in the person of Christ. The term 'recapitulate' (anakephalaiosasthai) means to gather up or sum up, indicating that Christ is the apex toward which all OT types pointed.

notes: The commentary presents typology in broad, general terms rather than identifying specific individual types (e.g., not stating 'the brazen serpent prefigures Christ'). Instead, it affirms the principle that the entire system of OT 'figures and prophecies' functions typologically, with Christ as the comprehensive antitype. This reflects a holistic view of OT typology rather than discrete type-antitype pairs.

original_text: This....sacrament, (or mystery)....in Christ, and in the Church. This sacrament, in construction, must be referred to what immediately went before, that is to the conjunction of marriage betwixt man and wife; and this is called a great sacrament, or mystery, as representing the union or spiritual nuptials of Christ with his spouse, the Church. (Witham)
notes: While this commentary discusses a spiritual relationship between marriage and Christ's union with the Church, it does not present a typological relationship in the strict sense. The passage describes marriage as representing or symbolizing the union of Christ and the Church, but this is allegory or spiritual symbolism rather than typology. Typology requires an OT type that prefigures an NT antitype. Here, there is no OT marriage type explicitly identified as prefiguring the NT antitype of Christ and the Church. The commentary treats the conjugal bond as a sacramental sign or mystery with spiritual significance, but does not establish an OT/NT prefigurative relationship. This is sacramental theology and spiritual symbolism, not typology proper.

original_text: God....hath given him a name, etc. The name or word Jesus represents the dignity of him who is signified by the name, and who is exalted even as man, above all creatures in heaven, earth, and hell; all which creatures either piously reverence him, or are made subject to him against their will, that every tongue may confess our Lord Jesus to be now, and to have been always, in the glory of his Father, equal to him in substance and in all perfections. (Witham)
notes: The Haydock commentary on Philippians 2:9 focuses on christological exaltation and the universal acknowledgment of Christ's divine glory and equality with God the Father. While the passage deals with Christ (a central figure in typological interpretation), this particular commentary does not establish or reference any explicit Old Testament type that prefigures Jesus. Instead, it provides a doctrinal exposition of Christ's exalted status, His universal lordship, and the confession of His divinity. No OT person, event, or institution is mentioned as prefiguring or being fulfilled in Christ in this commentary. To constitute typology, there would need to be a specific reference to an OT type (e.g., 'as Joshua prefigures Jesus' or 'like the High Priest entering the Holy of Holies'), which is absent here.

original_text: Let no man, therefore, judge you in meat or in drink. That is, for not abstaining from meats, called unclean, for drinking out of a cup without a cover, (see Numbers xix.) or for not keeping the Jewish festivals. For these were but shadows, types and figures of future things to be fulfilled in the new law of Christ: but the body is of Christ, (ver. 17.) that is was the body, the truth, the substance signified by these shadows and types. (Witham) --- He means with regard to the Jewish observations of the distinction of clean and unclean meats; and of their festivals, new moons, and sabbaths; as being no longer obligatory. (Challoner) --- Modern dogmatizers wilfully or ignorantly misapply this text of the apostle, to disprove the fasts and festivals observed in the Catholic Church; but it is evident, as St. Augustine observes, that the apostle is here condemning the legal distinction of clean and unclean meats, and the feasts of the new moon, to which false brethren wanted to subject the Colossians. (St. Augustine, ep. 59. ad Paulin. in solut. quaes. 7.)

extractions.type_name: Jewish dietary laws (clean and unclean meats)
extractions.type_description: The Old Testament legal distinction between clean and unclean meats prescribed in the Mosaic Law
extractions.antitype_name: The body of Christ and the new law of Christ
extractions.antitype_description: The New Testament fulfillment in Christ's body (the Church) and the new covenant law that supersedes the old legal distinctions
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states these were 'shadows, types and figures of future things to be fulfilled in the new law of Christ' and identifies 'the body is of Christ' as 'the truth, the substance signified by these shadows and types.' This is a clear type-antitype relationship showing how OT ceremonial law prefigured NT covenant fulfillment.

extractions.type_description: The Old Testament Jewish festivals, new moons, and sabbaths prescribed in the Mosaic Law
extractions.antitype_name: The body of Christ and new covenant observances
extractions.antitype_description: The New Testament fulfillment in Christ that makes these ceremonial observances no longer obligatory
extractions.reasoning: The commentary groups festivals with dietary laws as 'shadows, types and figures of future things to be fulfilled in the new law of Christ,' indicating these OT observances prefigured their NT fulfillment and are now superseded in the new covenant.

notes: The commentary emphasizes that these typological relationships validate discontinuity between OT ceremonial law and NT practice, while defending against misapplication to Catholic Church fasting and festivals (which operate under different authority). The type-antitype relationship here centers on covenantal supersession rather than Christological or sacramental prefigurement.

original_text: According to the image of him who created him. We are created to the image of God, inasmuch as our souls are spiritual and immortal, but here we are put in mind to imitate God by sanctity and justice, as God is holy and the fountain of justice. (Witham) --- The image or resemblance of our Creator was effaced by sin, but is retraced by Jesus Christ, who forms in us this new man. (Bible de Vence)
notes: This commentary discusses the restoration of the divine image in humans through Christ's work, but it does not establish a typological relationship between an Old Testament type and a New Testament antitype. Rather, it presents: (1) a theological principle about humanity being created in God's image (Genesis 1:27), (2) how sin effaced this image, and (3) how Christ restores it. While Christ is mentioned as the agent of restoration, there is no OT person, event, or institution presented as prefiguring Christ's redemptive work here. The commentary is primarily concerned with moral exhortation (to imitate God's holiness and justice) and soteriological doctrine (restoration through Christ), not typological correspondence.

original_text: We live. That is, we live in joy and comfort, if you stand firm in the faith of Christ, as you ought. (Witham) --- The news that you stand steadfast in the Lord, reanimates me under all my sufferings, and as it were raises me to life again from the shadow of death, under which I am placed. O that I could see you, to complete the work of instructing you in the faith, which I have begun.
notes: This Haydock commentary on 1 Thessalonians 3:8 contains no typological relationships. The passage discusses Paul's pastoral concern for the Thessalonian believers and his spiritual encouragement upon hearing of their steadfastness in faith. While the commentary uses figurative language ('raises me to life again from the shadow of death'), this is metaphorical expression of emotional/spiritual revival rather than a typological connection between an Old Testament type and New Testament antitype. The commentary focuses on Paul's apostolic work and the practical matter of completing his instruction in the faith, without reference to any Old Testament persons, events, or institutions that would prefigure New Testament realities.

original_text: That thou keep the commandment. Some understand that of fighting manfully; others of loving God; others rather comprehend all that St. Paul had commanded him, and all the instructions given. --- Unto the coming of our Lord;{ Ver. 14. Usque ad Adventum Domini, quem, etc. mechri tes epiphaneias...en, not on, and so must agree with adventum.|} which coming, he in due time will shew. This is the construction by the Greek. (Witham) --- This coming will be desirable for Christians who have preserved or recovered their baptismal innocence, and for pastors who have faithfully fulfilled their ministry; but terrible, in the extreme, for all who have lived in the constant neglect and omission of their duties.
notes: This commentary discusses eschatological themes (Christ's Second Coming, the final judgment, Christian perseverance) but does not establish typological relationships between Old Testament types and New Testament antitypes. The passage emphasizes the practical spiritual meaning of Christ's coming for Timothy and other believers, and contrasts the desirable coming for the faithful with its terrifying nature for the negligent. However, no OT person, event, or institution is presented as prefiguring this NT reality. The reference to 'baptismal innocence' could tangentially suggest typological thinking about baptism, but the commentary does not explicitly connect OT baptismal types (such as the flood or Red Sea crossing) to Christian baptism. The focus is exhortatory and eschatological rather than typological.

original_text: The Lord stood, etc. All agree that Nero is here meant by the lion. St. Chrysostom thinks that St. Paul was set at liberty after this first justification of his conduct, but that having afterwards converted the cupbearer of Nero, he was by him beheaded. (St. Chrysostom, hom. X. p. 611.) --- But the Lord assisted and fortified me on this occasion by a vision, in which he assured me that he would prolong my life for the more perfect preaching of the gospel. (Bible de Vence) --- The times predicted by the apostle in this epistle, (ver. 3. and 4.) are now arrived; and the warnings he gives to Timothy and to all preachers of the word, should be sedulously attended to: preach the word: be instant in season and out of season; reprove, entreat, rebuke with all patience and doctrine. There will arrive a time when men will not bear sound doctrine; eager in the extreme to hear what flatters, they will have recourse to a variety of teachers not lawfully sent or ordained, calculated to tickle their ears: Assentatores populi, multitudinis levitatem voluptate quasi titillantes. (Cicero) In the same sense Plutarch says: ta ota apoknaiousin. It is yours, adds St. Paul, os kalos stratiotes Christou Iesou, [2 Timothy 2:3.] as a valiant soldier of Jesus Christ, to oppose yourself as a wall to all these evils, to attend to every branch of your ministerial duty, not to yield to either opponents or dangers, and to see that the gospel is both preached and practised in all its purity. Thus may the Church find in you, and in her other ministers, what she is soon to lose in me, knowing as I do that my course is nearly run. --- That by me the preaching may be accomplished, (or fulfilled) and that all the Gentiles may hear it. This is an argument that he wrote this letter in his first imprisonment. --- And I was delivered from the mouth of the lion; that is, according to the common exposition, from Nero. (Witham)
notes: This Haydock commentary on 2 Timothy 4:17 does not describe typological relationships between Old Testament types and New Testament antitypes. Instead, it contains: (1) Historical interpretation identifying 'the lion' as Nero, (2) Symbolic/metaphorical language (lion representing an enemy/persecutor), (3) Moral and pastoral instruction to Timothy about preaching and maintaining doctrinal purity, and (4) General exegetical observations about the context of Paul's imprisonment. While the commentary uses figurative language ('lion'), this represents allegory or symbolism rather than typology proper, as there is no Old Testament type being prefigured by or connected to the New Testament antitype.

original_text: All presumption of human merits, which have not the grace of Jesus Christ for their principle, is here completely confounded; and the whole glory of our salvation is justly attributed to the mercy of God, through Jesus Christ. A new birth, new creature, new spirit. The effusion of the water upon the body in baptism, is a figure of the salutary effusion of the holy Spirit in the soul to renew it, and to make it a child of God.

extractions.type_description: The physical application of water to the body in the baptismal ceremony, as practiced in Old Testament purification rituals and Jewish ablutions
extractions.antitype_name: The effusion of the Holy Spirit in the soul
extractions.antitype_description: The spiritual renewal and sanctification of the soul through the indwelling and action of the Holy Spirit in the New Testament sacrament of Baptism, making one a child of God
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states 'The effusion of the water upon the body in baptism, is a figure of the salutary effusion of the holy Spirit in the soul.' This directly connects the OT practice of water purification (the type) to its NT fulfillment in Christian baptism as a means of spiritual renewal through the Holy Spirit (the antitype). The language of 'figure' confirms a typological relationship.

notes: The commentary operates within a sacramental typology framework, where the material sign (water) prefigures the spiritual grace (Holy Spirit). This reflects traditional Catholic understanding of sacraments as visible signs of invisible grace, with roots in OT purification practices.

original_text: Who being the spendour,{ Ver. 3. Splendor gloriae, apaugasma, refulgentia, effulgentia, etc.|} or brightness of his glory, not as beams or rays are derived from a lightsome body, but by a necessary and eternal communication of the same substance, and of the whole light; in which sense the council of Nice[Nicaea] understood the eternal Son of God to be light of light. This partly helps us to conceive the eternal generation of the Son from the Father, because the brightness is at the same time with the sun, though all comparisons fall short of this mystery. (Witham) --- We may here observe the two natures of Christ. As God, he is the Creator of all things; as man, he is constituted heir of the goods of God. Not content to possess the inheritance of his Father in his own person, he will have us as coheirs to share it also with him. May we so live as to hear one day that happy sentence: Come, ye blessed of my Father, etc. --- And the figure of his substance.{ Ver. 3. Figura substantiae, charakter tes upostaseos. Hypostasis signifies persona, subsistentia, and also substantia.|} In the Greek is the character of his substance; which might be translated, the express image. There are different ways by which a thing may be said to be a figure or image of another: here it is taken for such a representation of the substance of the Father, that though the Father and the Son be distinct persons, and the Son proceed from the Father, yet he is such a figure and image, as to have the same nature and substance with the Father, as the Catholic Church always believed and declared against the ancient heretics, and particularly against the Arians. Their words may be partly seen in Petavius, lib. 2:de Trin. Hebrews 11.; lib. 4:chap. 6.; lib. vi. Hebrews 6., being too prolix for these short notes. And this may be understood by the following words concerning the Son: and upholding or preserving all things by the word of his power. As he had said before, that all things were made by him, so all things are preserved by him, equally with the Father. See Colossians 1:16, 17. See also ver. 10. of this chapter, and the annotations on John 1:3. (Witham) --- Figure. This does not exclude the reality. So Christ's body in the eucharist, and his mystical death in the mass, though called a figure, image, or representation of Christ's visible body and sacrifice upon the cross, yet may be and is the self-same substance. (Bristow) ---Sitteth on the right hand of the majesty on high. This also may be taken to express the equality of the Son with the Father, if considered as God; but this sitting on the right hand of God, both here, in St. Mark 16. and in the apostles' creed, express what agrees with Christ, as our Redeemer, God made man by his incarnation, and who as man is made the head of his Church, the judge of the living and of the dead; and so St. Stephen said, (Acts vii.) I see the heavens open, and the Son of man standing at the right hand of God. (Witham)
notes: This Haydock commentary on Hebrews 1:3 focuses on Christological theology rather than typology. The passage discusses Christ's nature as the 'brightness of God's glory' and the 'figure of his substance,' but these are presented as direct theological descriptions of Christ's divine attributes and relationship to the Father, not as typological fulfillments of Old Testament types. The commentary defends orthodox Trinitarian doctrine against Arian heresy and discusses Christ's incarnation, redemptive work, and exaltation. While the commentary mentions that 'figure' does not exclude reality (using the Eucharist as an example of how a figure can be the same substance), this is sacramental symbolism rather than typology. There is no explicit identification of Old Testament persons, events, or institutions that prefigure Christ as their antitype in this particular commentary text.

original_text: Let us not flatter ourselves with having quitted Egypt by our baptism, unless we also quit that opposition, and that disobedience of our heart to the laws and maxims of the gospel. The Israelites, under the guidance of Moses, left Egypt for the promised land, and after travelling in the desert for the space of two years, found themselves on the confines of the so much desired country; but the possession of it was denied them, and they were left to perish in the desert, because they distrusted God's promises, and were incredulous to his word. All that happened to this chosen people, says St. Paul, was a figure of what was to happen to us. Here then we may read our destiny, if, like them, we prove ungrateful to God.

extractions.type_name: The Israelites' Exodus from Egypt and Desert Wandering
extractions.type_description: The OT event where the Israelites, guided by Moses, left Egypt for the promised land but were denied entry and perished in the desert due to disbelief and disobedience to God's word
extractions.antitype_name: Christian Baptism and the Christian Journey to Salvation
extractions.antitype_description: NT believers who are baptized (symbolically leaving 'Egypt') must also abandon spiritual opposition and disobedience to the gospel to reach their promised destination (salvation/heaven), lest they perish like the Israelites
extractions.reasoning: The commentary explicitly states 'All that happened to this chosen people...was a figure of what was to happen to us' (direct typological claim by St. Paul). The type-antitype correspondence is clear: baptism parallels the Exodus; disobedience/disbelief in the desert prefigures potential Christian failure; the promised land prefigures Christian salvation. The connection is sacramental because baptism is the explicit antitype mentioned.

extractions.type_description: The geographical destination promised by God to the Israelites, representing the fulfillment of God's covenant promise
extractions.antitype_description: The spiritual destination for Christians who remain faithful and obedient to the gospel
extractions.reasoning: While not explicitly developed, the commentary implies a typological connection between the promised land (OT type of future blessing) and Christian salvation (NT antitype). The passage warns that just as Israelites were denied entry, Christians can miss their ultimate destination through disobedience.

notes: The commentary explicitly cites St. Paul's typological interpretation, indicating this represents traditional patristic typology. The primary focus is sacramental (baptism as antitype of Exodus), with an implicit eschatological dimension regarding the promised land.

original_text: Some may perhaps wonder why St. Paul does not dwell more in this epistle on the eucharistic sacrifice; but until the Hebrews understood the bloody sacrifice on the cross, they could not be supposed to understand the unbloody sacrifice of the altar. The holy Fathers observe, that the sacrifice of Melchisedech, (Genesis 14:18.) offered in bread and wine, prefigured the unbloody sacrifice offered by Jesus Christ at his last supper. See Clement of Alexandria, lib. 4. Strom. ch. VIII.; St. Cyprian, lib. 2. ep. 3. ad Caeul.; Eusebius of Caesarea, lib. 5. Dem. Evang. ch. III.; St. Jerome, ad Marcel.; St. Augustine, ep. 95. ad Inn. Pap.; St. Ambrose; St. Epiphanius; St. Chrysostom; etc. apud Bellarmine, lib. 1. de missa. ch. VI. Hence it follows, that the holy Eucharist is truly and properly a sacrifice as well as a sacrament, as the paschal lamb or passover of the old law was both a sacrament and sacrifice. For either our Saviour offered sacrifice at his last supper under the forms of bread and wine, or he cannot be called a priest forever according to the order of Melchisedech. For the different orders of priests are chiefly distinguished by their sacrifice; (see ver. 1.) and if it be supposed that our Saviour only offered a bloody sacrifice, he would with more propiety have been called a priest according to the order of Aaron, and not of Melchisedech.
